laws.name: Bernoulli
laws.convention: X takes the value 1 (success) with probability p and the value 0 (failure) with probability 1 − p.
limits: p = 0 and p = 1 give point masses at 0 and at 1.
Bernoulli(p) is Binomial(1, p).
A categorical law with 2 labels is 1 + X with X ~ Bernoulli(p_2).

moments.existence: All moments exist: E[X^r] = p for every r ≥ 1. The MGF exists for all real t.

links.relation: special case: Binomial(1, p)
relabelled case: a categorical law with 2 labels

laws.name: Binomial
laws.convention: X counts the successes in n independent trials. Each trial has the same success probability p.
limits: n = 1 gives the Bernoulli law.
If n → ∞ and np → λ, the law converges to Poisson(λ): the law of small numbers.
If n → ∞ with p fixed in (0, 1), (X − np)/√(np(1 − p)) converges in law to the standard normal law (de Moivre–Laplace).
Hypergeometric(N, K, n) converges to Binomial(n, p) as N → ∞ with K/N → p.
Each component of a multinomial count vector has a binomial law.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for all real t.

links.relation: special case n = 1
limit: n → ∞ with np → λ
limit of the hypergeometric law as N → ∞ with K/N → p
each multinomial component, and the case k = 2
the standardised count converges to N(0, 1) (de Moivre–Laplace)
the beta law is the conjugate prior of p

laws.name: Categorical
laws.convention: X takes the label j ∈ {1, …, k} with probability p_j. The labels are names. Their order and their values as numbers are a convention, so the CDF and the mean depend on the labels.
limits: k = 1 gives a point mass.
k = 2 gives a relabelled Bernoulli law.
Equal weights p_j = 1/k give the discrete uniform law on 1, …, k.
The indicator vector of one categorical draw is Multinomial(1, p).

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the support is finite. They depend on the labels.

links.relation: the case k = 2, relabelled
Multinomial(1, p) is the indicator vector of one draw
equal weights
an empirical law of the labels 1 … k

laws.name: Multinomial
laws.convention: X = (X_1, …, X_k) counts the draws in each of k categories after n categorical trials that are independent, with probabilities p.
laws.pmf: \mathbb{P}(X = x) = \frac{n!}{x_1! \cdots x_k!} \prod_{j=1}^{k} p_j^{x_j}, \quad x_j \ge 0, \ \textstyle\sum_j x_j = n
limits: Each component has the law X_j ~ Binomial(n, p_j).
k = 2 gives (X_1, n − X_1) with X_1 ~ Binomial(n, p_1).
n = 1 gives the indicator vector of one categorical draw.
As n → ∞, (X − np)/√n converges in law to a multivariate normal law with covariance diag(p) − pp^T.

moments.variance: \operatorname{Var}(X_j) = n p_j (1 - p_j), \quad \operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = -n p_i p_j \ (i \ne j)
moments.existence: All moments exist. The components have a negative covariance, because they share the fixed total n.

links.relation: each component, and the case k = 2
the case n = 1
the standardised count vector converges to a normal law with the singular covariance diag(p) − ppᵀ. Any k − 1 components converge to a multivariate normal law of this page (all p_j > 0)
the Dirichlet law is the conjugate prior of the category probabilities

laws.name: Discrete uniform
laws.convention: X takes each integer from a to b with the same probability 1/m, with m = b − a + 1.
laws.pmf: \mathbb{P}(X = k) = \frac{1}{b - a + 1}, \quad k = a, a + 1, \dots, b
limits: a = b gives a point mass.
The Zipf law with s = 0 on 1, …, N is the discrete uniform law on 1, …, N.
(X − a)/m converges in law to the continuous uniform law U(0, 1) as m → ∞.
The sum of 2 discrete uniform values that are independent has a triangular PMF, not a uniform one.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the support is finite.

links.relation: a categorical law with equal weights, relabelled
the Zipf law with s = 0
the limit of (X − a)/m, and ⌊a + (b − a + 1)U⌋ of a continuous uniform value

laws.name: Geometric
laws.convention: X counts the failures before the first success in independent trials with success probability p. The other convention counts the trials, Y = X + 1 on {1, 2, …}.
limits: p = 1 gives a point mass at 0.
The geometric law is the negative binomial law with r = 1.
pX converges in law to Exponential(1) as p → 0.
It is the only law on {0, 1, 2, …} without memory: P(X ≥ s + t | X ≥ s) = P(X ≥ t).

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for t < −log(1 − p).

links.relation: special case r = 1
⌊E⌋ of an exponential value E, and pX converges to Exponential(1) as p → 0
geometric terms give the Pólya–Aeppli law
truncated below, it is a shifted geometric law

laws.name: Negative binomial
laws.convention: X counts the failures before success number r in independent trials with success probability p. A real r > 0 gives the gamma–Poisson mixture: Λ has a gamma law with shape r and scale (1 − p)/p, and X | Λ ~ Poisson(Λ).
limits: r = 1 gives the geometric law.
For an integer r, X is the sum of r geometric values that are independent.
If r → ∞ with the mean μ = r(1 − p)/p fixed, the law converges to Poisson(μ).
With the mean μ, the variance is μ + μ²/r. Thus the law shows overdispersion: its variance is larger than its mean.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for t < −log(1 − p).

links.relation: special case r = 1
limit: r → ∞ with the mean fixed
a Poisson count with a gamma rate is negative binomial
the negative binomial law is a gamma mixture of Poisson laws, and a finite mixture is the discrete form of it

laws.name: Poisson
laws.convention: X counts events. The parameter λ is the mean count.
limits: λ = 0 gives a point mass at 0.
Binomial(n, λ/n) converges to Poisson(λ) as n → ∞.
The negative binomial law with mean λ converges to Poisson(λ) as r → ∞.
The sum of independent Poisson(λ_1) and Poisson(λ_2) values has the law Poisson(λ_1 + λ_2).
(X − λ)/√λ converges in law to the standard normal law as λ → ∞.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for all real t.

links.relation: limit of Binomial(n, λ/n)
limit of the negative binomial law as r → ∞
the standardised count converges to N(0, 1) as λ → ∞
the times between the events of a Poisson process are exponential
P(N(t) < k) = P(Erlang(k, λ) > t)
a finite mixture of Poisson laws, with a variance above its mean
the number of terms of a compound Poisson sum
the zero-truncated Poisson law

laws.name: Hypergeometric
laws.convention: X counts the success items in n draws without replacement from N items, of which K are success items.
laws.pmf: \mathbb{P}(X = k) = \frac{\binom{K}{k} \binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}, \quad \max(0, n + K - N) \le k \le \min(n, K)
limits: n = N gives a point mass at K.
As N → ∞ with K/N → p, the law converges to Binomial(n, p).
The variance is the binomial variance times the finite population correction (N − n)/(N − 1).

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the support is finite.

transforms.pgf: G(z) = \textstyle\sum_k \mathbb{P}(X = k)\, z^k, \ \text{a polynomial of degree} \min(n, K)

links.relation: limit: N → ∞ with K/N → p

laws.name: Zipf and zeta
laws.convention: X is a rank from 1 to N with a probability proportional to k^(−s). N = ∞ gives the zeta law, which needs s > 1.
limits: s = 0 gives the discrete uniform law on 1, …, N.
N → ∞ with s > 1 gives the zeta law.
The zeta law has a regularly varying tail: P(X > k) ~ k^(1 − s)/((s − 1)ζ(s)) as k → ∞.

moments.existence: For a finite N, all moments exist. For the zeta law, E[X^r] is finite if and only if r < s − 1. Thus the mean is infinite for s ≤ 2 and the variance is infinite for s ≤ 3. The MGF of the zeta law is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: the case s = 0
the zeta sampler rejects from ⌊X⌋ with X ~ Pareto I(1, s − 1)

laws.name: Continuous uniform
laws.convention: X takes a value in [a, b], and intervals of equal length inside [a, b] have equal probability.
limits: a = 0 and b = 1 give the standard uniform law U(0, 1), the input of every sampler of this page.
If U ~ U(0, 1), then −log(U)/λ has the exponential law with rate λ, and log(U/(1 − U)) has the standard logistic law.
For integers a ≤ b, ⌊a + (b − a + 1)U⌋ has the discrete uniform law on {a, …, b}.
The sum of n independent U(0, 1) values has the Irwin–Hall law. For a large n it is near the normal law with mean n/2 and variance n/12.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the support is bounded. The MGF exists for all real t.

links.relation: U(0, 1) is Beta(1, 1)
−log(U)/λ is exponential: the inverse transform
log(U/(1 − U)) is standard logistic
the discrete version: ⌊a + (b − a + 1)U⌋
the GPD with ξ = −1 is uniform on [μ, μ + σ]

laws.name: Normal
laws.convention: X has the mean μ and the standard deviation σ. The density is symmetric about μ.
limits: σ → 0 gives the point mass at μ.
The central limit theorem: a normalised sum of i.i.d. values with a finite, positive variance converges in law to N(0, 1).
Binomial(n, p) is near N(np, np(1 − p)) for a large n (de Moivre–Laplace), and Poisson(λ) is near N(λ, λ) for a large λ.
Student's t law with ν degrees of freedom converges to N(0, 1) as ν → ∞.
If Z ~ N(0, 1), then Z² has the chi-square law with 1 degree of freedom.
Each component of a multivariate normal vector is normal.
A normal law whose variance is exponential gives the Laplace law.

moments.existence: All moments exist. P(|X − μ| > kσ) is about 0.317, 0.0455 and 0.0027 for k = 1, 2 and 3. The MGF exists for all real t.

links.relation: each component of a multivariate normal vector
the limit of Student's t law as ν → ∞
Z² is χ²(1), and a sum of ν squared independent N(0, 1) values is χ²(ν)
the limit of the standardised binomial law (de Moivre–Laplace)
the limit of the standardised Poisson law as λ → ∞
a normal law with an exponential variance is Laplace
exp(X) is lognormal
the ratio of two independent standard normal values is Cauchy
μ + c/Z² is Lévy for a standard normal Z
the stable law with α = 2 is N(δ, 2γ²)
a finite mixture of normal laws
the kernel of the kernel density model

laws.name: Multivariate normal
laws.convention: X = (X₁, …, X_k) has the mean vector μ and the covariance matrix Σ, which is symmetric and positive definite. The model text writes Σ as k² entries, row by row.
limits: k = 1 gives the normal law N(μ, Σ₁₁).
Each component X_j is N(μ_j, Σ_jj). Each linear form a + bᵀX is normal, with the mean a + bᵀμ and the variance bᵀΣb.
Components with covariance 0 are independent, because the vector is jointly normal. For other laws, covariance 0 does not imply independence in general.
X = μ + LZ, with L the Cholesky factor of Σ and Z a vector of independent N(0, 1) values.
For |ρ| < 1 the joint tails are asymptotically independent: the normal law has no tail dependence. Group 5 adds copulas with tail dependence.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The page reads the vector through its components X[j], their sums and their linear forms.

links.relation: each component and each linear form is normal
the limit of the standardised multinomial count vector, a degenerate normal law with the singular covariance diag(p) − ppᵀ. Any k − 1 components have a positive definite limit

laws.name: Exponential
laws.convention: X is a waiting time with a constant rate λ: P(X > t) = e^(−λt). The mean is 1/λ.
limits: Memorylessness: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). It is the only continuous law with this property.
Exponential(λ) is Gamma(1, 1/λ) and Erlang(1, λ).
The times between the events of a Poisson process with rate λ are i.i.d. Exponential(λ). Thus the count of events in [0, t] is Poisson(λt).
⌊X⌋ has the geometric law with the success probability 1 − e^(−λ).
The minimum of independent exponential values with rates λ_i is exponential with the rate Σλ_i.
The difference of two i.i.d. exponential values has the Laplace law.
χ²(2) is the exponential law with rate 1/2.

moments.existence: All moments exist: E[X^r] = r!/λ^r. The MGF exists for t < λ.

links.relation: the special case k = 1, θ = 1/λ
the special case k = 1
⌊X⌋ is geometric with p = 1 − e^(−λ)
the waiting times of a Poisson process
the difference of two i.i.d. exponential values is Laplace
−log(U)/λ for U ~ U(0, 1)
χ²(2) is exponential with rate 1/2
the Weibull law with k = 1
the limit of the Gompertz law as b → 0 with ηb fixed
log(X/x_m) of a Pareto I value
the law of the waiting time given its rate, in the gamma mixture that gives the Pareto II law
the GPD with ξ = 0
the maximum of n exponential values minus log n tends to the Gumbel law
a common law of censoring times

laws.name: Gamma
laws.convention: X has the shape k and the scale θ, so its mean is kθ. For an integer k it is the sum of k independent exponential values with mean θ.
limits: k = 1 gives the exponential law with rate 1/θ.
An integer k gives the Erlang law: Erlang(k, λ) = Gamma(k, 1/λ).
Gamma(ν/2, 2) is the chi-square law with ν degrees of freedom.
For independent values with the same scale, Gamma(k₁, θ) + Gamma(k₂, θ) = Gamma(k₁ + k₂, θ).
As k → ∞, (X − kθ)/(θ√k) converges in law to N(0, 1).
If G₁ ~ Gamma(a, 1) and G₂ ~ Gamma(b, 1) are independent, then G₁/(G₁ + G₂) ~ Beta(a, b). Normalised gamma values give the Dirichlet law.
A Poisson count whose rate has a gamma law has the negative binomial law.

moments.existence: All moments exist: E[X^r] = θ^r Γ(k + r)/Γ(k). The density is unbounded at 0 for k < 1. The MGF exists for t < 1/θ.

links.relation: the special case k = 1
an integer shape: Erlang(k, λ) = Gamma(k, 1/λ)
χ²(ν) = Gamma(ν/2, 2)
G₁/(G₁ + G₂) is beta
normalised gamma values are Dirichlet
a gamma mixture of Poisson laws is negative binomial
the law of the rate in an exponential–gamma mixture, which gives the Pareto II law

laws.name: Erlang
laws.convention: X is the sum of k independent exponential phases, each with rate λ: the time of the k-th event of a Poisson process with rate λ.
limits: k = 1 gives the exponential law.
Erlang(k, λ) = Gamma(k, 1/λ).
P(X > t) = P(N(t) < k) = Σ_{j<k} e^(−λt)(λt)^j/j!, with N(t) ~ Poisson(λt).
As k → ∞ with the mean k/λ fixed, X converges to the constant k/λ: the coefficient of variation is 1/√k.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for t < λ.

links.relation: the special case k = 1, and the law of each phase
Erlang(k, λ) = Gamma(k, 1/λ)
P(X > t) = P(N(t) < k) for a Poisson process

laws.name: Beta
laws.convention: X is a proportion in [0, 1] with the shapes a and b. The mean is a/(a + b).
limits: a < 1 and b < 1 give a U shape. a = b gives a law that is symmetric about 1/2.
G₁/(G₁ + G₂) with independent G₁ ~ Gamma(a, 1) and G₂ ~ Gamma(b, 1).
Each component of a Dirichlet vector is beta, and the Dirichlet law with 2 parts is the beta law.
Beta(a, b) is the conjugate prior of a binomial success probability. After k successes in n trials, the posterior is Beta(a + k, b + n − k).
If Y ~ Beta(d₁/2, d₂/2), then d₂Y/(d₁(1 − Y)) has the F(d₁, d₂) law.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the support is bounded. The density is unbounded at 0 for a < 1 and at 1 for b < 1.

links.relation: Beta(1, 1) is U(0, 1)
G₁/(G₁ + G₂) of independent gamma values
the case k = 2, and each component
the conjugate prior of the success probability
d₂Y/(d₁(1 − Y)) is F(d₁, d₂)

laws.name: Dirichlet
laws.convention: X = (X₁, …, X_k) is a vector of proportions with X_j ≥ 0 and Σ X_j = 1. The concentrations α_j set the means α_j/α₀, with α₀ = Σ α_j. At fixed means, a larger α₀ gives a smaller spread: Var X_j = m_j(1 − m_j)/(α₀ + 1), with m_j = α_j/α₀.
limits: k = 2 gives the beta law: X₁ ~ Beta(α₁, α₂).
Each component X_j ~ Beta(α_j, α₀ − α_j).
X_j = G_j/Σ G_i, with independent G_j ~ Gamma(α_j, 1).
It is the conjugate prior of multinomial probabilities: after the counts n_j, the posterior is Dirichlet(α_j + n_j).
α_j = 1 for every j gives the uniform law on the simplex.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because each component is in [0, 1].

transforms.mgf: M(t) = \mathbb{E}\,e^{t^{\top}X} \ \text{is finite for every} \ t \in \mathbb{R}^k \ \text{(no closed form)}

links.relation: each component, and the case k = 2
normalised independent gamma values
the conjugate prior of the category probabilities

laws.name: Chi-square
laws.convention: X is the sum of ν squared independent standard normal values. A real ν > 0 gives Gamma(ν/2, 2).
limits: χ²(ν) = Gamma(ν/2, 2).
χ²(2) is the exponential law with rate 1/2.
(X − ν)/√(2ν) converges in law to N(0, 1) as ν → ∞. The right tail converges slowly.
For n i.i.d. normal values with variance σ², (n − 1)S²/σ² ~ χ²(n − 1).
Z/√(V/ν), with Z ~ N(0, 1) and V ~ χ²(ν) independent, has Student's t law.
(V₁/d₁)/(V₂/d₂), with independent chi-square values, has the F law.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for t < 1/2.

links.relation: the sum of ν squared standard normal values
χ²(ν) = Gamma(ν/2, 2)
ν = 2 gives the exponential law with rate 1/2
V in T = Z/√(V/ν)
the ratio of two scaled chi-square values is F

laws.name: Student's t
laws.convention: T = Z/√(V/ν), with Z ~ N(0, 1) and V ~ χ²(ν) independent. The page uses the standard t law: write μ + sT for a location μ and a scale s.
limits: ν = 1 gives the Cauchy law, which has no mean.
ν → ∞ gives N(0, 1).
T² ~ F(1, ν).
The tail is regularly varying: P(T > t) ~ c t^(−ν) as t → ∞.
T is a scale mixture of normal laws: T = Z/√W with νW ~ χ²(ν).

moments.existence: E|T|^r is finite if and only if r < ν. Thus the mean exists only for ν > 1, and the variance only for ν > 2. The MGF is infinite for every t ≠ 0.

links.relation: the limit as ν → ∞, and Z in Z/√(V/ν)
V in Z/√(V/ν)
T² ~ F(1, ν)
the case ν = 1

laws.name: F (Fisher–Snedecor)
laws.convention: X = (V₁/d₁)/(V₂/d₂), with independent V₁ ~ χ²(d₁) and V₂ ~ χ²(d₂): the ratio of two variance estimates.
limits: T² ~ F(1, ν) for Student's T with ν degrees of freedom.
d₁X converges in law to χ²(d₁) as d₂ → ∞.
1/X ~ F(d₂, d₁).
d₁X/(d₁X + d₂) ~ Beta(d₁/2, d₂/2).
The right tail is regularly varying with index d₂/2.

moments.existence: E[X^r] is finite if and only if r < d₂/2. Thus the mean needs d₂ > 2, and the variance needs d₂ > 4. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: the ratio of two scaled chi-square values
T² ~ F(1, ν)
d₁X/(d₁X + d₂) is Beta(d₁/2, d₂/2)

laws.name: Logistic
laws.convention: X has the location μ and the scale s. Its CDF is the logistic (sigmoid) function of (x − μ)/s.
limits: The CDF is the inverse of the logit function log(p/(1 − p)).
log(U/(1 − U)) for U ~ U(0, 1) is standard logistic.
The difference of two i.i.d. standard Gumbel values is standard logistic.
The variance is s²π²/3. At the same variance its tails are heavier than normal tails: P(X > μ + 3σ) is about 0.0043, against 0.00135 for the normal law.
A logistic latent variable gives the logit model of a binary response, and the Elo model of a game.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for |t| < 1/s.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = e^{\mu t}\,\frac{\pi s t}{\sin(\pi s t)}, \quad |t| < 1/s
transforms.cf: \varphi(t) = e^{i\mu t}\,\frac{\pi s t}{\sinh(\pi s t)}

links.relation: log(U/(1 − U)) of a uniform value
each is the rejection proposal of the other, with M = 2
exp(X) is log-logistic

laws.name: Laplace
laws.convention: X has the location μ and the scale b: a symmetric law with a sharp peak at μ and exponential tails, P(|X − μ| > t) = e^(−t/b).
limits: The difference of two i.i.d. exponential values with mean b is Laplace(0, b).
|X − μ| is exponential with mean b.
A normal law whose variance is exponential gives the Laplace law: a scale mixture.
The median of a sample is the maximum likelihood estimate of μ, as the mean is for the normal law.
The Laplace mechanism of differential privacy adds Laplace(0, Δ/ε) noise to a statistic with sensitivity Δ.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for |t| < 1/b.

links.relation: the difference of two i.i.d. exponential values, and |X − μ| is exponential
a scale mixture of normal laws with an exponential variance
each is the rejection proposal of the other, with M = 2

laws.name: Lognormal
laws.convention: X = exp(μ + σZ), with Z ~ N(0, 1). Thus log X ~ N(μ, σ²). The median is e^μ, and σ is the standard deviation of log X.
limits: σ → 0 gives the point mass at e^μ.
The product of independent lognormal values is lognormal: the values of μ add, and the values of σ² add.
X^a is lognormal with the parameters aμ and |a|σ for a ≠ 0. Thus 1/X is lognormal with −μ and σ.
The tail is subexponential but not regularly varying. P(X > x) decreases faster than every power of x and more slowly than every exponential function.
The moments do not identify the law: other laws have the same moments E[X^r] for all integers r (Heyde 1963).

moments.existence: All moments exist: E[X^r] = exp(rμ + r²σ²/2) for every real r. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0. The Laplace transform E[e^(−sX)] is finite for s ≥ 0 but has no closed form.

links.relation: log X ~ N(μ, σ²)
another subexponential lifetime law when k < 1. All moments are finite in both laws
a competing positive law: the experiment of the inverse Gaussian law compares two laws with the same mean and variance
lognormal lifetimes under censoring

laws.name: Weibull
laws.convention: X has the shape k and the scale λ: P(X > x) = exp(−(x/λ)^k). The hazard k x^(k−1)/λ^k decreases for k < 1, is constant for k = 1 and increases for k > 1.
limits: k = 1 gives the exponential law with the rate 1/λ.
k = 2 gives the Rayleigh law with the scale λ/√2.
(X/λ)^k is standard exponential.
The minimum of n independent Weibull(k, λ) values is Weibull(k, λn^(−1/k)): the weakest-link property.
k → ∞ gives the point mass at λ.
For k < 1 the tail is subexponential, but all moments are finite.

moments.existence: All moments exist: E[X^r] = λ^r Γ(1 + r/k) for r > −k. The MGF is finite for every t when k > 1, and for t < 1/λ when k = 1. It is infinite for every t > 0 when k < 1.

links.relation: the case k = 1, with the rate 1/λ
−X is reverse Weibull with the same shape
1/X is Fréchet with the shape k and the scale 1/λ
another positive lifetime law. The lognormal tail is heavier than every Weibull tail
Burr XII(c, k, λk^(1/c)) tends to Weibull(c, λ) as k → ∞
another parametric hazard: a power of x against an exponential function of x
−k·log(X/λ) is standard Gumbel
Weibull lifetimes under censoring

laws.name: Inverse Gaussian
laws.convention: X has the mean μ and the shape λ. Let a Brownian motion have the drift ν > 0 and the variance σ² per unit time. The time at which it first reaches the level a > 0 is IG(μ, λ), with μ = a/ν and λ = a²/σ².
limits: The sum of n independent IG(μ, λ) values is IG(nμ, n²λ). Thus the sample mean is IG(μ, nλ).
μ → ∞ gives the Lévy law with the location 0 and the scale λ: the first-passage time of a Brownian motion with no drift.
λ → ∞ gives the point mass at μ, and (X − μ)/√(μ³/λ) tends to N(0, 1).
cX is IG(cμ, cλ) for c > 0.
λ(X − μ)²/(μ²X) has the χ²(1) law.
The tail decreases as x^(−3/2) e^(−λx/(2μ²)): an exponential tail.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF is finite for t ≤ λ/(2μ²) and infinite for t > λ/(2μ²).

links.relation: a competing positive law: with the same mean and variance, the lognormal law has the heavier tail
IG(μ, λ) tends to Lévy(0, λ) as μ → ∞: the first-passage time of a Brownian motion with no drift

laws.name: Gompertz
laws.convention: X has the hazard ηb·e^(bx): it starts at ηb and grows by the factor e^b in each unit of time. P(X > x) = exp(−η(e^(bx) − 1)). The hazard doubles every log(2)/b units of time.
limits: b → 0 with ηb fixed gives the exponential law with the rate ηb.
η(e^(bX) − 1) is standard exponential, so X = log(1 + E/η)/b with E ~ Exp(1).
The Gompertz law is the minimum-Gumbel law with the scale 1/b and the location log(1/η)/b, conditioned to be positive.
The mode is log(1/η)/b for η < 1, and 0 for η ≥ 1.
A constant added to the hazard gives the Gompertz–Makeham law.

moments.variance: \frac{\eta e^{\eta}}{b^2}\int_1^\infty (\log u)^2 e^{-\eta u}\,du - \left(\frac{e^{\eta} E_1(\eta)}{b}\right)^2 \ \text{(no elementary closed form)}
moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF is finite for every real t, because the tail decreases faster than every exponential function.

links.relation: the Gompertz law is the minimum-Gumbel law with the scale 1/b, conditioned to be positive
another parametric hazard: an exponential function of x against a power of x
b → 0 with ηb fixed gives the exponential law with the rate ηb

laws.name: Log-logistic (Fisk)
laws.convention: X has the scale α, which is the median, and the shape β. log X is logistic with the location log α and the scale 1/β. Economists call it the Fisk law.
limits: k = 1 in Burr XII(c, k, λ) gives the log-logistic law with α = λ and β = c.
β = 1 gives X/α ~ F(2, 2), which is also Pareto II with μ = 0, σ = α and the tail index 1.
β → ∞ gives the point mass at α.
The hazard β x^(β − 1)/(α^β + x^β) decreases for β ≤ 1. For β > 1 it rises to a maximum at x = α(β − 1)^(1/β) and then falls.
The tail is regularly varying: P(X > x) ~ (x/α)^(−β) as x → ∞.
For an income model, the Gini coefficient is 1/β (β > 1).

moments.existence: E[X^r] is finite if and only if −β < r < β. Thus the mean is infinite for β ≤ 1, and the variance is infinite for β ≤ 2. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: log X is logistic with location log α and scale 1/β
the case k = 1 of Burr XII, with λ = α and c = β

laws.name: Pareto I
laws.convention: X has the least value x_m and the tail index α: P(X > x) = (x/x_m)^(−α) for x ≥ x_m.
limits: log(X/x_m) is exponential with rate α.
Scale invariance: for t ≥ x_m, the law of X given X > t is Pareto I(t, α). Thus P(X > 2t)/P(X > t) = 2^(−α) for every t ≥ x_m.
The minimum of n independent Pareto I(x_m, α) values is Pareto I(x_m, nα).
For n independent values, max/(x_m n^(1/α)) converges in law to the Fréchet law with the shape α.
α → ∞ gives the point mass at x_m.
Pareto I(x_m, α) is Pareto II with μ = σ = x_m, and GPD with ξ = 1/α, σ = x_m/α and μ = x_m.

moments.existence: E[X^r] is finite if and only if r < α: E[X^r] = α x_m^r/(α − r). Thus the mean is infinite for α ≤ 1, and the variance is infinite for α ≤ 2. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: Pareto I(x_m, α) is Pareto II with μ = σ = x_m
GPD with ξ = 1/α, σ = x_m/α, μ = x_m
the normalised maximum of Pareto I draws tends to the Fréchet law
log(X/x_m) is exponential with rate α
rejection from ⌊X⌋ with X ~ Pareto I(1, s − 1) draws the zeta law: the page's zeta sampler

laws.name: Pareto II (Lomax)
laws.convention: X has the least value μ, the scale σ and the tail index α: P(X > x) = (1 + (x − μ)/σ)^(−α) for x ≥ μ. μ = 0 gives the Lomax law.
limits: Gamma mixture: if Λ ~ Gamma(α, 1/σ) and X − μ, given Λ, is exponential with rate Λ, then X ~ Pareto II(μ, σ, α).
α → ∞ with σ/α = θ fixed gives μ plus an exponential value with mean θ.
Excess over a threshold: for u ≥ μ, X − u given X > u is Pareto II(0, σ + u − μ, α). Thus the mean excess σ + u − μ over α − 1 increases linearly in u (α > 1).
μ = σ = x_m gives Pareto I(x_m, α).
The tail is regularly varying with index α. Thus the law is subexponential: P(X₁ + … + X_n > x) ~ n P(X > x) as x → ∞.

moments.existence: E|X − μ|^r is finite if and only if r < α. Thus the mean is infinite for α ≤ 1, and the variance is infinite for α ≤ 2. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: the case μ = σ = x_m is Pareto I(x_m, α)
Pareto II(μ, σ, α) is GPD with ξ = 1/α, σ_GPD = σ/α
the case c = 1 of Burr XII
an exponential value with a gamma-distributed rate
the conditional law given the rate

laws.name: Burr XII (Singh–Maddala)
laws.convention: X has the shapes c and k and the scale λ: P(X > x) = (1 + (x/λ)^c)^(−k). c sets the body near 0. The product ck is the tail index. Economists call it the Singh–Maddala law.
limits: k = 1 gives the log-logistic law with α = λ and β = c.
c = 1 gives Pareto II with μ = 0, σ = λ and the tail index k.
k → ∞ with λ = θk^(1/c) gives the Weibull law with the shape c and the scale θ.
(X/λ)^c is Pareto II(0, 1, k).
The tail is regularly varying: P(X > x) ~ (x/λ)^(−ck) as x → ∞.
For c < 1 the density has no bound near 0. For c > 1 the mode is λ((c − 1)/(ck + 1))^(1/c).

moments.existence: E[X^r] = λ^r k B(k − r/c, 1 + r/c) is finite if and only if −c < r < ck. Thus the mean is infinite for ck ≤ 1, and the variance is infinite for ck ≤ 2. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: the case k = 1, with α = λ and β = c
the case c = 1, with μ = 0, σ = λ and α = k
the limit k → ∞ with the scale λk^(1/c)

laws.name: Fréchet
laws.convention: X = m + sY, with P(Y ≤ y) = exp(−y^(−α)) for y > 0. α is the tail index, s the scale and m the least value. The Fréchet law is the GEV law with ξ = 1/α > 0.
limits: Max-stability: the maximum of n independent Fréchet(α, s, m) values has the law Fréchet(α, n^(1/α)s, m).
Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko: let P(X > x) be regularly varying with the tail index α. Then the maximum of n draws, divided by the 1 − 1/n quantile, tends in law to Fréchet(α, 1, 0).
α·log((X − m)/s) has the Gumbel law with location 0 and scale 1, for every α.
1/(X − m) has the Weibull law with shape α and scale 1/s.
The tail is regularly varying: P(X > x) ~ ((x − m)/s)^(−α) as x → ∞.

moments.existence: For r > 0, E|X|^r is finite if and only if r < α, and E[((X − m)/s)^r] = Γ(1 − r/α) for r < α. Thus the mean is infinite for α ≤ 1, and the variance is infinite for α ≤ 2. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: GEV with ξ = 1/α > 0: Fréchet(α, s, m) = GEV(μ = m + s, σ = s/α, ξ = 1/α)
1/X with X ~ Weibull(α, 1/s) is Fréchet(α, s, 0)
the limit law of the normalised maximum: the maximum of n Pareto I(x_m, α) draws over n^(1/α)x_m tends to Fréchet(α, 1, 0)

laws.name: Cauchy
laws.convention: X = x_0 + γ tan(π(U − 1/2)), with U uniform on (0, 1). x_0 is the median and the mode. γ is the half-width at half-maximum and half the interquartile range.
limits: x_0 = 0 and γ = 1 give Student's t law with ν = 1.
Z_1/Z_2, with Z_1 and Z_2 independent standard normal values, has the law Cauchy(0, 1).
The mean of n independent Cauchy(x_0, γ) values has the law Cauchy(x_0, γ) for every n. The law of large numbers does not apply.
If X ~ Cauchy(0, γ), then 1/X ~ Cauchy(0, 1/γ).
The tail is regularly varying with index 1: P(X > x) ~ γ/(πx) as x → ∞.
Cauchy(x_0, γ) is the stable law S(1, 0, γ, x_0; 0).

moments.existence: For r > 0, E|X|^r is finite if and only if r < 1. The mean does not exist, because E[max(X, 0)] and E[max(−X, 0)] are both infinite. The median x_0 and the interquartile range 2γ always exist. The MGF is infinite for every t ≠ 0.

links.relation: Cauchy(x₀, γ) is S(1, 0, γ, x₀; 0)
Student's t with ν = 1 is Cauchy(0, 1)
the ratio of two independent standard normal values is Cauchy(0, 1)

laws.name: Lévy
laws.convention: X = μ + c/Z², with Z standard normal. μ is the least value and c the scale. X − μ has the law of the first-passage time of a standard Brownian motion to the level √c. The CDF is F(x) = erfc(√(c/(2(x − μ)))).
limits: The first-passage time of a standard Brownian motion with no drift to the level a ≠ 0 has the law Lévy(0, a²).
IG(μ, λ) tends to Lévy(0, λ) as μ → ∞: a drift towards the level gives the inverse Gaussian law, and no drift gives the Lévy law.
The sum of n independent Lévy(μ, c) values has the law Lévy(nμ, n²c). Thus their mean has the law Lévy(μ, nc).
X − μ has the inverse gamma law with shape 1/2 and scale c/2.
The tail is regularly varying with index 1/2: P(X > x) ~ √(2c/(π(x − μ))) as x → ∞.
Lévy(μ, c) is the stable law S(1/2, 1, c, μ + c; 0). The mode is μ + c/3.

moments.existence: E[(X − μ)^r] is finite if and only if r < 1/2. Thus the mean and the variance are infinite. The median μ + c/(2 (erfc⁻¹(1/2))²) ≈ μ + 2.198c exists. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: Lévy(μ, c) is S(1/2, 1, c, μ + c; 0)
Lévy(0, c) is the limit μ → ∞ of IG(μ, λ) with λ = c
μ + c/Z² with Z standard normal

laws.name: Stable (S0)
laws.convention: Nolan's S0 parameterisation S(α, β, γ, δ; 0): α is the index of stability, β the skewness, γ the scale and δ the location. The S0 form is continuous in all parameters. The S1 form has the location δ₁ = δ − βγ tan(πα/2) for α ≠ 1, and δ₁ = δ − (2/π)βγ log γ for α = 1. The page computes the density and the CDF by numerical integrals (Nolan 1997), so their reference values have the tag "numerical". The inverse transform uses an interpolated table of 401 quantiles of this CDF, so it is approximate. The Chambers–Mallows–Stuck method samples exactly.
laws.pdf: f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-itx}\,\varphi(t)\,dt \ \text{(no closed form in general)}
limits: α = 2 gives N(δ, 2γ²) for every β.
α = 1 and β = 0 give Cauchy(δ, γ).
α = 1/2 and β = 1 give Lévy(δ − γ, γ).
The sum of n independent S(α, β, γ, δ; 0) values is S(α, β, n^(1/α)γ, δ_n; 0).
In the sum law, δ_n = nδ + βγ tan(πα/2)(n^(1/α) − n) for α ≠ 1, and δ_n = nδ + (2/π)βγ n log n for α = 1.

Generalised central limit theorem: let the two tails of a law be regularly varying with the tail index α, with 0 < α < 2, with a limit of their ratio. Then centred and scaled sums of i.i.d. draws tend in law to a stable law with this α.
For α < 2, P(X > x) ~ γ^α c_α (1 + β) x^(−α) as x → ∞, with c_α = Γ(α) sin(πα/2)/π.

moments.existence: For α < 2 and r > 0, E|X|^r is finite if and only if r < α. Thus the variance is infinite for α < 2, and the mean exists only for α > 1. For α = 2 all moments exist. For α < 2 and |β| < 1 the MGF is infinite for every t ≠ 0. For α < 2 and β = 1 it is finite only for t ≤ 0, and for β = −1 only for t ≥ 0.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = \infty \ \text{for every} \ t \ne 0 \ (\alpha < 2, |\beta| < 1); \quad M(t) = e^{\delta t + \gamma^2 t^2} \ (\alpha = 2)

links.relation: α = 1 and β = 0 give Cauchy(δ, γ)
α = 1/2 and β = 1 give Lévy(δ − γ, γ)
α = 2 gives N(δ, 2γ²)

laws.name: Generalised extreme value (GEV)
laws.convention: The GEV law with shape ξ, location μ and scale σ is the law of a normalised maximum. ξ > 0 gives the Fréchet type, with a power tail. ξ = 0 gives the Gumbel type. ξ < 0 gives the reverse Weibull type, with a finite upper end point μ − σ/ξ.
laws.pdf: f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma}\, t(x)^{\xi+1} e^{-t(x)}, \quad t(x) = \left(1 + \xi\,\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi} \ (\xi \ne 0), \quad t(x) = e^{-(x-\mu)/\sigma} \ (\xi = 0)
limits: ξ = 0 gives the Gumbel law with location μ and scale σ.
ξ = 1/α > 0 gives a Fréchet law: X = μ + σ(Y − 1)/ξ with Y ~ Fréchet(α, 1, 0).
ξ = −1/α < 0 gives a reverse Weibull law with the upper end point μ − σ/ξ.
Max-stability: the maximum of n independent GEV(ξ, μ, σ) values is GEV(ξ, μ + σ(n^ξ − 1)/ξ, σ n^ξ).
Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko: every non-degenerate limit law of a normalised maximum of i.i.d. values is a GEV law.

moments.existence: For ξ > 0 and r > 0, E|X|^r is finite if and only if r < 1/ξ: the mean needs ξ < 1 and the variance needs ξ < 1/2. For ξ ≤ 0 all moments exist. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0 when ξ > 0.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = e^{\mu t}\,\Gamma(1 - \sigma t) \ (\xi = 0, \ t < 1/\sigma); \ \text{infinite for every} \ t > 0 \ (\xi > 0)
transforms.cf: \text{no closed form for} \ \xi \ne 0; \ \varphi(t) = e^{i\mu t}\,\Gamma(1 - i\sigma t) \ (\xi = 0)

links.relation: the case ξ = 1/α > 0, after a change of location and scale
the case ξ = 0
the case ξ = −1/α < 0, after a change of location and scale
the excesses over a high threshold of a law in the domain of attraction of GEV_ξ tend to GPD_ξ

laws.name: Generalised Pareto (GPD)
laws.convention: X is the threshold μ plus an excess Y with P(Y > y) = (1 + ξy/σ)^(−1/ξ), for y ≥ 0 and 1 + ξy/σ > 0. For ξ = 0 this is the limit e^(−y/σ). ξ is the shape and σ > 0 is the scale. ξ > 0 gives a power tail with the index 1/ξ. ξ < 0 gives the end point μ + σ/|ξ|.
limits: ξ = 0 gives the exponential law with the mean σ, moved by μ.
ξ = −1 gives the uniform law on [μ, μ + σ].
ξ > 0 gives the Pareto II (Lomax) law with α = 1/ξ and the scale σ/ξ.
Threshold stability: for a threshold u ≥ μ below the end point, the excess X − u given X > u is GPD(ξ, σ + ξ(u − μ)).
The mean excess E[X − u | X > u] = (σ + ξ(u − μ))/(1 − ξ) is linear in u, for ξ < 1.
Pickands–Balkema–de Haan: take a law in the domain of attraction of GEV_ξ. Its excess over a threshold u, scaled suitably, tends to GPD_ξ as u tends to the upper end point.

moments.existence: For ξ > 0 and r > 0, E|X|^r is finite if and only if r < 1/ξ. Thus the mean exists only for ξ < 1, and the variance only for ξ < 1/2. For ξ ≤ 0, all moments exist. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0 when ξ > 0. It exists for t < 1/σ when ξ = 0, and for every t when ξ < 0.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = \frac{e^{\mu t}}{1 - \sigma t} \ (\xi = 0, \ t < 1/\sigma); \quad M(t) = \infty \ \text{for every} \ t > 0 \ (\xi > 0); \quad \text{no closed form for } \xi < 0 \text{ in general}
transforms.cf: \varphi(t) = \frac{e^{i\mu t}}{1 - i\sigma t} \ (\xi = 0); \quad \text{no closed form in elementary functions for } \xi \ne 0

links.relation: the excesses over a high threshold of a law in the domain of attraction of GEV_ξ tend to GPD_ξ (Pickands–Balkema–de Haan)
for ξ > 0, GPD(ξ, σ, μ) is Pareto II with α = 1/ξ, the scale σ/ξ and the location μ
Pareto I(x_m, α) is the GPD with ξ = 1/α, σ = x_m/α and μ = x_m
ξ = 0 gives μ plus an exponential value with the mean σ
ξ = −1 gives the uniform law on [μ, μ + σ]

laws.name: Gumbel
laws.convention: X has the Gumbel law for maxima: P(X ≤ x) = exp(−e^(−(x − μ)/β)). μ is the mode and β > 0 is the scale. This is the GEV law with ξ = 0. The Gumbel law for minima is the law of −X.
limits: Max-stability: the maximum of n i.i.d. Gumbel(μ, β) values is Gumbel(μ + β log n, β).
If E is a standard exponential value, μ − β log E is Gumbel(μ, β).
The maximum of n standard exponential values minus log n tends to the standard Gumbel law.
The maxima of normal, lognormal, gamma and Weibull values have the Gumbel law as their limit after a suitable scaling.
The difference of two i.i.d. Gumbel(μ, β) values has the logistic law with the location 0 and the scale β.
The Gumbel-max rule: if G_i are i.i.d. standard Gumbel values, the index of the largest log p_i + G_i has the categorical law with the probabilities p_i.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for t < 1/β and is infinite for t ≥ 1/β, because the right tail is exponential.

links.relation: the GEV law with ξ = 0
if G ~ Gumbel(μ, β), then −G given −G > 0 is Gompertz with b = 1/β and η = e^(μ/β). This is the minimum-Gumbel law, conditioned to be positive
−k log(X/λ) of a Weibull(k, λ) value X is standard Gumbel
the maximum of n standard exponential values minus log n tends to the standard Gumbel law

laws.name: Reverse Weibull
laws.convention: X has the upper end point μ: P(X ≤ x) = exp(−((μ − x)/σ)^α) for x < μ, and 1 for x ≥ μ. α > 0 is the shape and σ > 0 is the scale. μ − X has the Weibull law with the shape α and the scale σ. This is the GEV law with ξ = −1/α < 0, written with its end point.
limits: α = 1: μ − X is exponential with the mean σ.
α = 2: μ − X has the Rayleigh law with the scale σ/√2.
The maxima of i.i.d. values with an end point x* and P(X > x* − y) ~ c y^α as y → 0 have this law as their limit. The uniform law gives α = 1, and the GPD with ξ < 0 gives α = −1/ξ.
As α → ∞, α(X − μ + σ)/σ tends to the standard Gumbel law.
Max-stability: the maximum of n i.i.d. values has the same law with the scale σ n^(−1/α).

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for every t ≥ 0, because X ≤ μ. For t < 0 it exists for every t when α > 1, for t > −1/σ when α = 1, and for no t < 0 when α < 1.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = e^{\mu t}\,\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-t\sigma W}\right], \ W \sim \text{Weibull}(\alpha, 1): \ \text{no closed form in general}; \quad M(t) = \frac{e^{\mu t}}{1 + \sigma t} \ (\alpha = 1, \ t > -1/\sigma)
transforms.cf: \varphi(t) = e^{i\mu t}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-i\sigma t)^n}{n!}\,\Gamma\left(1 + \frac{n}{\alpha}\right) \ (\alpha > 1); \quad \varphi(t) = \frac{e^{i\mu t}}{1 + i\sigma t} \ (\alpha = 1)

links.relation: the GEV law with ξ = −1/α < 0, the location μ − σ and the scale σ/α
μ − X is Weibull(α, σ)

laws.name: Censored observations
laws.convention: T is the lifetime and C is the censoring time. T and C are independent. Right censoring observes Y = min(T, C) and δ = 1{T ≤ C}. Left censoring observes Y = max(T, C) and δ = 1{T ≥ C}. C can be a random variable, a parameter or a number. The model line "censoring: right T by C" (or "left") defines the names T_obs = Y and T_event = δ. For a variable X the names are X_obs and X_event.
laws.pdf: \text{right: } f_{Y,\delta}(y, 1) = f_T(y)\,S_C(y), \quad f_{Y,\delta}(y, 0) = g_C(y)\,S_T(y); \qquad \text{left: } f_{Y,\delta}(y, 1) = f_T(y)\,F_C(y), \quad f_{Y,\delta}(y, 0) = g_C(y)\,F_T(y)

params.name: T
params.domain: \text{a lifetime law with the density } f_T, \text{ the CDF } F_T \text{ and the survival function } S_T

params.name: C
params.domain: \text{a censoring time independent of } T, \text{ with the density } g_C, \text{ the CDF } F_C \text{ and } S_C; \ \text{or a constant } c

limits: C = ∞: complete data. Y = T and δ = 1.
C = c, a constant: Type I censoring. Y = min(T, c) has an atom of mass S_T(c) at c.
Exponential T with the rate λ and exponential C with the rate κ: Y is exponential with the rate λ + κ, and P(δ = 1) = λ/(λ + κ).
Under right censoring P(Y > t) = S_T(t) S_C(t). Thus the fraction of observed times above t estimates S_T(t) S_C(t), not S_T(t).
The Kaplan–Meier estimator is the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimate of S_T under independent right censoring. It identifies S_T only up to the largest time with S_C > 0.
If C depends on T (informative censoring), S_T is not identifiable from (Y, δ) alone.

moments.existence: Under right censoring Y ≤ T and Y ≤ C, so E[Y^r] ≤ min(E[T^r], E[C^r]) for nonnegative T and C. A fixed censoring time c bounds Y by c, so all moments of Y exist even when T has none. The MGF of Y then exists for every t. Under left censoring Y ≥ T and Y ≥ C, and E[Y^r] ≤ E[T^r] + E[C^r]. P(δ = 1) = ∫ f_T(y) S_C(y) dy under right censoring.

transforms.mgf: M_Y(t) = 1 + t\int_0^\infty e^{ty}\,S_T(y)\,S_C(y)\,dy \ (\text{right censoring, nonnegative } T, C, \text{ where the integral is finite})

links.relation: a common law of lifetimes T in censored reliability tests
a standard law of times to an event in trials, and of concentrations left-censored by a detection limit
with exponential T, the maximum likelihood estimate of the rate from censored data is the number of events divided by the total time observed
truncation removes the values outside the limit, and censoring keeps a bound for them

laws.name: Finite mixture
laws.convention: With probability w_j, X comes from the law F with the parameters θ_j, for j = 1, …, k. The model text names the family: mixture_poisson(w = [0.7, 0.3], lambda = [2, 9]). Each parameter of F is a vector with one entry for each component, or one number that all components share. The weights add to 1. The page does not show the component of a draw. Θ_F is the parameter domain of F.
laws.pmf: \mathbb{P}(X \in A) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} w_j\, \mathbb{P}_{\theta_j}(X \in A), \quad p(x) = \sum_j w_j\, p_{\theta_j}(x) \ \text{or} \ f(x) = \sum_j w_j\, f_{\theta_j}(x)
limits: k = 1, or one weight equal to 1, gives the law F itself.
Components with the same parameters merge: their weights add.
A Poisson component with λ = 0 is a point mass at 0, so mixture_poisson(w = [w0, 1 − w0], lambda = [0, λ]) is the zero-inflated Poisson law.
A mixture over a continuous law of the parameter is not a finite mixture. An example is the gamma mixture of Poisson laws, the negative binomial law.
Different weights and parameters can give the same mixture law. The labels of the components can change places, so the data identify the components only up to a permutation.

moments.existence: E|X|^r is finite if and only if E|X|^r is finite for every component with a positive weight. The variance is the mean of the component variances plus the variance of the component means (the law of total variance). Thus a mixture of Poisson laws has a variance at least its mean, and above it when the component means differ.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = \sum_j w_j M_j(t), \ \text{finite where every } M_j(t) \text{ with } w_j > 0 \text{ is finite}

links.relation: a mixture of Poisson laws with different means has a variance above its mean
the gamma mixture of Poisson laws, a mixture over infinitely many components
a mixture of normal laws can give several modes and heavier shoulders
a kernel density model is the equal-weight mixture of normal laws centred at the data

laws.name: Compound Poisson
laws.convention: S = Y_1 + … + Y_N, with N ~ Poisson(freq) and Y_1, Y_2, … i.i.d. from the law F of a term, independent of N. S = 0 when N = 0. The model text names the law of the terms, and λ is freq. Thus compound_geometric(freq = 12, p = 0.4) has geometric terms. compound_poisson(freq = 3, lambda = 2) has Poisson terms: the Neyman type A law. The terms take values in [0, ∞). Integer terms give a law on {0, 1, 2, …}. Continuous terms give a law on [0, ∞) with an atom at 0.
laws.pmf: \mathbb{P}(S = 0) = e^{-\lambda(1 - f_0)}, \quad \mathbb{P}(S = s) = \frac{\lambda}{s} \sum_{j=1}^{s} j\, f_j\, \mathbb{P}(S = s - j) \ \ (\text{Panjer, terms on } \{0, 1, 2, \dots\})
limits: Terms equal to 1 give S = N, the Poisson law itself.
freq = 0 gives the point mass at 0.
Poisson terms give the Neyman type A law, and geometric terms give the Pólya–Aeppli law.
As λ = freq → ∞, (S − λE[Y])/√(λE[Y²]) converges in law to N(0, 1) when E[Y²] < ∞.
With a subexponential term law, P(S > x) ~ λ P(Y > x) as x → ∞: one large term makes a large total.

moments.existence: For λ > 0, E[S^r] is finite if and only if E[Y^r] is finite. Thus a term law with a heavy tail gives S the same tail order. The MGF of S is finite exactly where the MGF of Y is finite.

links.relation: the number of terms is Poisson, and terms equal to 1 give the Poisson law
geometric terms give the Pólya–Aeppli law of clustered counts

laws.name: Empirical discrete law
laws.convention: The law that puts the mass w_i / Σw on each observed value x_i. Equal weights (w = 1) give each of n observations the mass 1/n. Counts as weights give the same law for grouped data. Equal values add their masses. A draw from it is a draw with replacement from the data, which is the resampling step of the ordinary bootstrap. The parameter w is a weight for each value, or one number for equal weights.
limits: One distinct value gives a point mass.
With n i.i.d. observations of a law F, the empirical CDF converges to F uniformly, almost surely (Glivenko–Cantelli).
The law gives no value outside [min x_i, max x_i], so it says nothing about the tail beyond the data.
On the integers 1 … k, the empirical law is a categorical law with p_j = w_j / Σw.

moments.existence: All moments exist: the law has finitely many values. The variance divides by Σw, not Σw − 1. It is the variance of this law, not an unbiased estimate for the law that made the data. A finite variance here does not show that the law of the data has one.

links.relation: the empirical law on the labels 1 … k is a categorical law
the kernel density model spreads each value of the empirical law with a normal kernel

laws.name: Kernel density model
laws.convention: X = x_J + hZ: J picks an observation with probability w_J / Σw, and Z ~ N(0, 1) is independent of J. The bandwidth h is the standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel. The density is the kernel density estimate of the data, which the model uses as a law. The parameter w is a weight for each value, or one number for equal weights.
limits: h → 0 gives the empirical law of the data.
One observation gives N(x_1, h²).
As h → ∞, the law spreads without bound, and its standardised law tends to N(0, 1).
Let the data be i.i.d. from a density f, with h → 0 and nh → ∞. Then the estimate converges to f at each point of continuity. The mean squared error is smallest for h of the order n^(−1/5).
Silverman's rule of thumb gives h = 0.9 min(s, IQR/1.34) n^(−1/5).

moments.variance: s_w^2 + h^2, \quad s_w^2 = \frac{\sum_i w_i (x_i - \bar x_w)^2}{\sum_i w_i}
moments.existence: All moments exist, and the MGF is finite for all real t: the law is a finite mixture of normal laws. The kernel adds h² to the variance, so a large bandwidth spreads the law. Values outside the range of the data, and negative values for positive data, have a positive probability.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = e^{h^2 t^2 / 2} \sum_i \frac{w_i}{\sum w}\, e^{t x_i}
transforms.cf: \varphi(t) = e^{-h^2 t^2 / 2} \sum_i \frac{w_i}{\sum w}\, e^{i t x_i}

links.relation: the limit h → 0 of the kernel density model
each kernel is N(x_i, h²)
an equal-weight finite mixture of normal laws

laws.name: Truncated law
laws.convention: X has the law F conditioned on lower ≤ X ≤ upper. The model text names F: truncated_poisson(lambda = 2, lower = 1, upper = inf). Values outside [lower, upper] do not occur at all: no record of them exists. The kept mass Z = P_F(lower ≤ X ≤ upper) must be positive.
laws.pmf: f_t(x) = \frac{f(x)}{Z}\, \mathbf{1}\{\ell \le x \le u\}, \quad F_t(x) = \frac{F(x) - F(\ell^-)}{Z}, \quad Z = F(u) - F(\ell^-)
limits: lower = −∞ and upper = ∞ give F itself.
The zero-truncated Poisson law has the mean λ/(1 − e^(−λ)).
A geometric law truncated below at b is b plus a geometric law: the geometric law has no memory.
Truncation differs from censoring. Censoring keeps a bound for each value outside the limit. Truncation keeps no record of it.

moments.existence: A bounded interval [lower, upper] keeps all moments. An unbounded side keeps the tail order of F on that side, so a heavy right tail stays heavy after truncation from below.

transforms.mgf: M_t(t) = \frac{1}{Z}\, \mathbb{E}_F\left[e^{tX} \mathbf{1}\{\ell \le X \le u\}\right], \ \text{finite for all } t \ \text{on a bounded interval}

links.relation: the zero-truncated Poisson law of counts that are at least 1
truncation from below gives a shifted geometric law, because the law has no memory
censoring keeps a bound for each value outside the limit, and truncation keeps no record

laws.name: Conditional model
laws.convention: A conditional model draws a parent variable first, then a child variable whose law has parameters that read the parent. The model text writes this as K ~ categorical(p = w) and then N ~ poisson(lambda = rates[K]). The joint law is the product of the parent law and the conditional law of the child. The parent can be a regime, a state or an uncertain parameter.
laws.formula: p(x, y) = p_X(x)\, p_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), \qquad Y \mid X = x \sim F_{\theta(x)}
limits: If θ(x) does not depend on x, Y is independent of X and has the law F_θ.
A parent with a finite set of values gives a finite mixture as the law of Y.
A gamma parent for the Poisson rate gives a negative binomial law for the count.
A beta parent for the binomial probability gives the beta-binomial law.
A chain of conditional models in which each step reads only the previous one is a Markov chain.

moments.existence: E|Y| is finite if and only if E[E[|Y| | X]] is finite. The variance formula is the law of total variance. It holds when E Y² is finite. The second term is the variance that the uncertain parent adds.

methods: Ancestral sampling: draw the parent, then draw the child from its conditional law with the parent value. Each replicate is an exact draw of the pair.
Enumeration: when the parent and the child are discrete, the page adds p_X(x) p(y | x) over the support. It gives exact references, with the neglected mass of a truncated tail stated.
Inverse transform: the sampler draws each variable by the inverse of its conditional CDF. The pair is exact, and stratification can act on the parent uniform.

links.relation: a copula gives dependence with fixed margins, but a conditional model changes the law of the child
a chain of conditional draws in which each draw reads the previous state
the event rate is conditional on the past events

laws.name: Gaussian copula
laws.convention: The Gaussian copula is the dependence structure of a multivariate normal vector with the correlation matrix R. A component U_i = Φ(Z_i) is uniform on (0, 1). The parameter rho is one correlation for all pairs, or the d(d − 1)/2 entries above the diagonal of R, row by row. Sklar's theorem joins it with any margins through u = U[j].

params.name: rho
params.domain: \rho \in (-1, 1), \; R \text{ positive definite } (\rho > -1/(d-1) \text{ for one common } \rho)

limits: ρ = 0 gives the independence copula.
ρ → 1 gives the comonotone copula: U_1 = U_2.
ρ → −1 in two dimensions gives the countermonotone copula: U_2 = 1 − U_1.
The t copula with the same R converges to the Gaussian copula as ν → ∞.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because each U_i lies in [0, 1]. Each margin is uniform. Spearman's rho is 12 E[U_1 U_2] − 3. For a pair, Spearman's rho is (6/π) arcsin(ρ/2).

transforms.cf: No closed form is used. The page describes the copula by its CDF: Φ_R at the normal quantiles, by Genz's bivariate normal method for d = 2.

dependence.tau: Kendall's tau of the pair (i, j) is τ = (2/π) arcsin(ρ_ij).
dependence.tails: λ_L = λ_U = 0 for every |ρ| < 1. The joint exceedance P(U_1 > q, U_2 > q)/(1 − q) tends to 0 as q → 1, but slowly when ρ is large.
dependence.domain: Every dimension d from 2 to 16. R must be a positive definite correlation matrix. The page checks it with a Cholesky factorisation.

methods: Independent (exact): Z = L N with the Cholesky factor L of R and independent standard normals N (Box–Muller), then U_i = Φ(Z_i).
Inverse (exact): the conditional distribution method. Each normal comes from the inverse transform Φ⁻¹(V) (AS 241), and L gives each conditional normal law.
Rejection: the page refuses it. The copula density has no finite bound near the corners of the unit cube, so in general no bounded envelope exists.
Euler: a copula has no time, so under this method the page uses the exact sampler.

links.relation: the limit of the t copula as ν → ∞
another symmetric copula with no tail dependence
a conditional model with normal latent variables gives the same dependence

laws.name: Student t copula
laws.convention: The t copula is the dependence structure of a multivariate Student t vector with ν degrees of freedom and the correlation matrix R. A common random scale √(W/ν) gives joint extremes in both tails. The parameter rho has the same convention as for the Gaussian copula.
limits: ν → ∞ gives the Gaussian copula with the same R.
ρ = 0 does not give independence when ν is finite: the common scale still makes the components dependent, with λ = 2 t_{ν+1}(−√(ν + 1)) > 0.
ρ → 1 gives the comonotone copula.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because each U_i lies in [0, 1]. Each margin is uniform. Spearman's rho is 12 E[U_1 U_2] − 3. The margins of the copula are uniform for every ν, so the copula has all moments even when the t law has none.

transforms.cf: No closed form is used. The page describes the copula by its CDF: the bivariate t CDF by quadrature of the conditional t law, error about 1e−9.

dependence.tau: Kendall's tau of the pair (i, j) is τ = (2/π) arcsin(ρ_ij), the same as for the Gaussian copula.
dependence.domain: Every dimension d from 2 to 16, 0.5 ≤ ν ≤ 10^6, and a positive definite correlation matrix R.

methods: Independent (exact): Z = L N as for the Gaussian copula, W ~ χ²(ν) by the gamma sampler, T = Z/√(W/ν), then U_i = F_ν(T_i).
Inverse (exact): the normals come from the inverse transform Φ⁻¹(V). W comes from the gamma sampler, as above.
Rejection: the page refuses it. The copula density has no finite bound near the corners of the unit cube, so in general no bounded envelope exists.
Euler: a copula has no time, so under this method the page uses the exact sampler.

links.relation: the limit as ν → ∞
another copula with upper tail dependence, but with no lower tail dependence

laws.name: Clayton copula
laws.convention: The Clayton copula is an Archimedean copula with the generator ψ(t) = (1 + θt)^(−1/θ). For θ > 0, small values come together: it has lower tail dependence and no upper tail dependence. The parameter θ is the same for all pairs, so the copula is exchangeable.
limits: θ = 0 (the limit θ → 0) gives the independence copula.
θ → ∞ gives the comonotone copula.
θ → −1 in two dimensions gives the countermonotone copula, which this page does not sample.
For θ < 0 in d = 2 the CDF is max(u_1^{−θ} + u_2^{−θ} − 1, 0)^{−1/θ}.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because each U_i lies in [0, 1]. Each margin is uniform. Spearman's rho is 12 E[U_1 U_2] − 3.

transforms.cf: The generator is the Laplace transform of the frailty V ~ Gamma(shape 1/θ, scale θ): ψ(t) = E[e^{−tV}] = (1 + θt)^{−1/θ}.

dependence.tau: τ = θ/(θ + 2). It is negative for −1 < θ < 0.
dependence.domain: In two dimensions θ > −1. For d ≥ 3 this page needs θ ≥ 0. The generator is d-monotone down to θ = −1/(d − 1), but the page does not sample θ < 0 for d ≥ 3. θ ≤ 200.

methods: Independent (exact): the Marshall–Olkin frailty algorithm. V is gamma, E_i are standard exponential, and U_i = ψ(E_i/V). For θ < 0 in two dimensions, the page uses conditional inversion in closed form.
Inverse (exact, d = 2 only): U_1 = V_1 and U_2 = C⁻¹(V_2 | U_1) in closed form. For d ≥ 3 the page refuses the method, because it needs derivatives of order d − 1 of ψ.
Rejection: the page refuses it. The copula density has no finite bound near the corners of the unit cube, so in general no bounded envelope exists.
Euler: a copula has no time, so under this method the page uses the exact sampler.

links.relation: another Archimedean copula, with no tail dependence
the Archimedean copula with dependence in the upper tail instead of the lower tail

laws.name: Gumbel copula
laws.convention: The Gumbel copula is an Archimedean copula with the generator ψ(t) = exp(−t^(1/θ)). It links large values: it has upper tail dependence and no lower tail dependence. It is the only Archimedean copula that is also an extreme-value copula, so it suits the joint law of annual maxima.
limits: θ = 1 gives the independence copula.
θ → ∞ gives the comonotone copula.
The copula is max-stable: C(u_1^t, …, u_d^t) = C(u_1, …, u_d)^t for t > 0.
It has no negative dependence: τ ≥ 0 for every θ.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because each U_i lies in [0, 1]. Each margin is uniform. Spearman's rho is 12 E[U_1 U_2] − 3.

transforms.cf: The generator is the Laplace transform of a positive stable frailty V with index 1/θ: ψ(t) = E[e^{−tV}] = exp(−t^{1/θ}).

dependence.domain: θ ≥ 1 in every dimension from 2 to 16, and θ ≤ 100. Negative dependence is not possible.

methods: Independent (exact): the Marshall–Olkin frailty algorithm. V is positive stable (Kanter's method), E_i are standard exponential, and U_i = ψ(E_i/V).
Inverse (d = 2 only): U_1 = V_1 and U_2 = C⁻¹(V_2 | U_1) by bisection to 2^−60, so it is exact up to that tolerance. For d ≥ 3 the page refuses the method.
Rejection: the page refuses it. The copula density has no finite bound near the corners of the unit cube, so in general no bounded envelope exists.
Euler: a copula has no time, so under this method the page uses the exact sampler.

links.relation: the Archimedean copula with dependence in the lower tail instead of the upper tail
a copula with tail dependence in both tails

laws.name: Frank copula
laws.convention: The Frank copula is an Archimedean copula with the generator ψ(t) = −log(1 − (1 − e^(−θ)) e^(−t))/θ. It is radially symmetric and has no tail dependence. In two dimensions θ can be negative, which gives negative dependence.
limits: θ → 0 gives the independence copula. The page also accepts θ = 0 as independence.
θ → ∞ gives the comonotone copula.
θ → −∞ in two dimensions gives the countermonotone copula.
The copula is radially symmetric: (U_1, U_2) and (1 − U_1, 1 − U_2) have the same law.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because each U_i lies in [0, 1]. Each margin is uniform. Spearman's rho is 12 E[U_1 U_2] − 3.

transforms.cf: For θ > 0 the generator is the Laplace transform of a logarithmic series frailty V with p = 1 − e^{−θ}: ψ(t) = −log(1 − p e^{−t})/θ.

dependence.tau: τ = 1 − (4/θ)(1 − D_1(θ)), with the Debye function D_1(θ) = (1/θ) ∫_0^θ t/(e^t − 1) dt. For θ = −5, τ = −0.4567.
dependence.tails: λ_L = λ_U = 0 for every θ. Joint extremes are rarer than under a t, Clayton or Gumbel copula with the same τ.
dependence.domain: In two dimensions any θ ≠ 0 with |θ| ≤ 700. For d ≥ 3 the generator is completely monotone only for θ > 0, so negative θ is valid in two dimensions only.

methods: Independent (exact): for θ > 0, the Marshall–Olkin frailty algorithm with a logarithmic series V (Kemp's algorithm). For θ < 0 in two dimensions, conditional inversion in closed form.
Inverse (exact, d = 2 only): U_1 = V_1 and U_2 = C⁻¹(V_2 | U_1) in closed form. For d ≥ 3 the page refuses the method.
Rejection: the page refuses it. The copula density has no finite bound near the corners of the unit cube, so in general no bounded envelope exists.
Euler: a copula has no time, so under this method the page uses the exact sampler.

links.relation: another Archimedean copula, with lower tail dependence
another symmetric copula with no tail dependence

laws.name: Brownian motion
laws.convention: X is a Brownian motion with drift: X_t = X_0 + μt + σW_t, with W a standard Brownian motion. A draw is the path at the grid times t_k = kT/n, so X[1] = X_0 and X[n + 1] = X_T. The drift μ and the volatility σ are for each unit of time.
limits: σ = 0 gives the straight line X_t = X_0 + μt.
Donsker's theorem: a random walk with steps of variance σ²h converges in law to σW as h → 0.
The variance-gamma process converges to a Brownian motion as its variance rate ν → 0.
The OU process with κ = 0 is a Brownian motion.
log S_t of a GBM is a Brownian motion with drift μ − σ²/2.

moments.existence: X_t is normal, so all its moments exist. The maximum M_T has all moments too. For μ = 0, P(M_T ≥ b) = 2 P(X_T ≥ b) for b ≥ X_0 (the reflection principle).

conditions.stationarity: Not stationary: Var X_t = σ²t grows without bound. The increments are stationary and independent, so X is a Lévy process.
conditions.stability: No mean reversion: the law spreads as √t, and no stable level exists. With μ ≠ 0 the path moves to +∞ or −∞ almost surely.
conditions.explosion: No explosion: X_t is finite for every t, almost surely. The paths are continuous but nowhere differentiable.
conditions.boundary: No boundary: the state space is the real line. A first-passage level belongs to the quantity, not to the process.
conditions.discretisation: The grid values are exact for every h. The sampler does not draw the path between grid times. Thus a first-passage probability on the grid is lower than in continuous time, by a monitoring bias of order √h.

methods: Independent: exact Gaussian increments μh + σ√h Z, with Box–Muller normals. The grid values have the exact law.
Inverse: each normal is Φ⁻¹(V) of a uniform V, so stratification and antithetic pairs act on the increments. The grid values are exact.
Euler: X_{k+1} = X_k + μh + σΔW_k. With constant coefficients this is the exact scheme, so the grid values have no time discretisation bias.
Rejection: refused, because an increment is a direct normal draw.
With coarsen = c, the coarse path adds the fine increments in groups of c. The pair (n, 1) and (n/2, 2) shares one Brownian path: the coupled pair of MLMC.

links.relation: log S of a GBM is a Brownian motion with drift
the OU process with κ = 0
a Brownian motion run on a gamma clock

laws.name: Geometric Brownian motion
laws.convention: S is a geometric Brownian motion (GBM): S_t = S_0 exp((μ − σ²/2)t + σW_t). The drift μ is the growth rate of the mean, E S_t = S_0 e^{μt}. The typical path grows at the lower rate μ − σ²/2. A draw is the path at the grid times t_k = kT/n.
limits: σ = 0 gives the exponential curve S_t = S_0 e^{μt}.
log S_t is a Brownian motion with drift μ − σ²/2, so S_t is lognormal with the parameters log S_0 + (μ − σ²/2)t and σ√t.
If μ < σ²/2, S_t → 0 almost surely, while E S_t → ∞ when μ > 0: the time average and the ensemble average differ.
With μ = r, the risk-free rate, E[max(S_T − K, 0)] e^{−rT} is the Black–Scholes price of a call.

moments.existence: Every positive and negative moment exists: E S_t^p = S_0^p exp(pμt + p(p − 1)σ²t/2). The MGF of S_t is infinite for t > 0 and σ > 0, because the lognormal law has a heavy right tail in this sense. The median is S_0 e^{(μ − σ²/2)t}.

transforms.cf: \text{no closed form for } S_t; \ \varphi_{\log S_t}(u) = \exp\!\big(iu(\log S_0 + (\mu - \tfrac12\sigma^2)t) - \tfrac12\sigma^2u^2t\big)

conditions.stationarity: Not stationary: log S_t is a Brownian motion with drift μ − σ²/2, so its variance σ²t grows without bound.
conditions.stability: The typical path grows at the rate μ − σ²/2: S_t → 0 almost surely if μ < σ²/2 and S_t → ∞ if μ > σ²/2. The mean E S_t = S_0 e^{μt} follows μ, not this rate.
conditions.explosion: No explosion: S_t is finite for every t, almost surely. The moments grow exponentially in t.
conditions.boundary: The exact process stays in (0, ∞): 0 is not attainable from S_0 > 0. One Euler step can cross 0, with the probability Φ(−(1 + μh)/(σ√h)).
conditions.discretisation: The exact log-step has no time discretisation error at the grid times. The Euler scheme has a weak bias of order h and a strong error of order √h. A first-passage probability on the grid has a monitoring bias of order √h.

methods: Independent: the exact log-step S_{k+1} = S_k exp((μ − σ²/2)h + σ√h Z), with Box–Muller normals. The grid values have the exact law.
Inverse: the same exact step with each normal Φ⁻¹(V), so stratification and antithetic pairs act on the increments.
Euler: S_{k+1} = S_k(1 + μh + σΔW_k). It is not exact: the weak bias is of order h and the strong error of order √h, and a path can become negative.
Rejection: refused, because a lognormal step is a transformed normal draw.
With coarsen = c, the coarse path adds the fine increments in groups of c. Thus the coupled pair of MLMC uses one Brownian path for the fine and the coarse Euler path.

links.relation: log S is a Brownian motion with drift μ − σ²/2

laws.name: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process
laws.convention: X is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process: it reverts to the long-run mean θ at the rate κ, with Gaussian noise of volatility σ. With κ > 0 its law approaches the stationary law N(θ, σ²/(2κ)). A draw is the path at the grid times t_k = kT/n. In interest-rate models this is the Vasicek model.
laws.formula: dX_t = \kappa(\theta - X_t)\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t, \qquad X_{t_{k+1}} = \theta + (X_{t_k} - \theta)e^{-\kappa h} + \sigma\sqrt{\tfrac{1 - e^{-2\kappa h}}{2\kappa}}\,Z_k
limits: κ = 0 gives a Brownian motion with volatility σ and no drift.
σ = 0 gives the deterministic relaxation X_t = θ + (X_0 − θ)e^{−κt}.
As t → ∞ with κ > 0, X_t converges in law to N(θ, σ²/(2κ)), for every X_0.
If X_0 has the law N(θ, σ²/(2κ)), the process is stationary, with Cov(X_s, X_t) = σ²/(2κ) e^{−κ|t − s|}.
The time average (1/T)∫X_t dt converges to θ almost surely as T → ∞ when κ > 0 (ergodicity).

moments.existence: X_t is normal, so all moments exist for every κ. The stationary variance σ²/(2κ) exists only for κ > 0. For κ < 0 the variance grows as e^{2|κ|t}.

conditions.stationarity: For κ > 0 the stationary law is N(θ, σ²/(2κ)), and the law of X_t approaches it at the rate e^{−κt}. For κ ≤ 0 no stationary law exists.
conditions.stability: The exact process is stable for κ > 0. The Euler scheme multiplies the distance to θ by 1 − κh in each step, so it is stable only for 0 < κh < 2. With κh ≥ 2 its paths oscillate and grow.
conditions.explosion: No explosion: X_t is finite for every t, almost surely, for every real κ.
conditions.boundary: No boundary: the state space is the real line. Thus X_t can be negative, for example a negative interest rate.
conditions.discretisation: The exact transition has no time discretisation error for any h. The Euler scheme has the stationary variance σ²/(κ(2 − κh)) instead of σ²/(2κ), a bias of order h.

methods: Independent: the exact Gaussian transition with the factor e^{−κh} and the variance σ²(1 − e^{−2κh})/(2κ). It is exact for every step size.
Inverse: the same exact transition with each normal Φ⁻¹(V).
Euler: X_{k+1} = X_k + κ(θ − X_k)h + σΔW_k. It has a bias of order h, and it is unstable for κh ≥ 2.
Rejection: refused, because a Gaussian transition needs no rejection.
With coarsen = c, the sampler draws each step as c exact sub-steps (or c fine Brownian increments for Euler). This gives the coupled pair of MLMC.

links.relation: the OU process with κ = 0 is a Brownian motion
a mean-reverting Markov process in continuous state, with a finite chain as the discrete analogue

laws.name: Poisson process
laws.convention: N(t) counts the events in [0, t]. The rate λ(t) = λ(1 + a sin(2πt/P)) is the mean number of events for each unit of time. With a = 0, the process is homogeneous. The page records N at the grid times t_k = kT/n, with N(0) = 0.
laws.formula: \mathbb{P}\big(N(t+h) - N(t) = 1 \mid \mathcal{F}_t\big) = \lambda(t)\,h + o(h), \quad \lambda(t) = \lambda\big(1 + a \sin(2\pi t / P)\big), \quad N(t) - N(s) \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\big(\Lambda(t) - \Lambda(s)\big), \quad \Lambda(t) = \int_0^t \lambda(u)\,du
limits: a = 0 gives the homogeneous process: N(t) ~ Poisson(λt), and the times between events are i.i.d. exponential with rate λ.
For a time T that is a whole number of periods, Λ(T) = λT for every a.
The superposition of independent Poisson processes with rates λ_1 and λ_2 is a Poisson process with rate λ_1 + λ_2.
(N(t) − Λ(t))/√Λ(t) converges in law to N(0, 1) as Λ(t) → ∞.
N(t)/t → λ almost surely as t → ∞ (the strong law of large numbers for the homogeneous process).

moments.existence: All moments of N(t) exist for every finite t. The count has the Poisson law with mean Λ(t), so P(N(t) = 0) = e^{−Λ(t)}.

conditions.stationarity: With a = 0 the increments are stationary and independent. With a > 0 the increments are independent but not stationary. The count N(t) itself is never stationary: it grows.
conditions.stability: The count grows at the mean rate λ. N(t)/t → λ almost surely, also with a periodic rate, because the average of λ(t) over a period is λ.
conditions.explosion: No explosion: the rate is at most λ(1 + a), so there are finitely many events in a finite time almost surely.
conditions.boundary: N(t) is an integer, 0 at t = 0, and it never decreases. Each event adds exactly 1.
conditions.discretisation: The exact methods count every event. The time discretisation allows at most one event in each step of length h, so it loses about (λh)²/2 events in each step.

methods: Exact on the grid (independent sampling): the sampler draws the increment in each step from Poisson(Λ(t_{k+1}) − Λ(t_k)). The values at the grid times have the exact law.
Inverse transform: the sampler maps the unit-rate event times Γ_i = Γ_{i−1} − log V_i to t_i = Λ⁻¹(Γ_i). It computes Λ⁻¹ by bisection. The method is exact up to the bisection tolerance.

Thinning (Lewis and Shedler, 1979): candidates come at the constant rate λ̄ = λ(1 + a) = max λ(t), and the sampler keeps each candidate with probability λ(t)/λ̄. The method is exact when λ̄ ≥ λ(t) for all t.
With failure = envelope, thinning uses λ̄ = λ(1 + a)/2. Then λ(t)/λ̄ can be above 1, the method keeps too few events, and the page counts these violations.
Euler time discretisation: one event in a step with probability λ(t_k)h, none otherwise. The bias is of order λh.

links.relation: the jump times of a compound Poisson process
the Hawkes process with α = 0

laws.name: Compound Poisson process
laws.convention: X_t = x_0 + c t + S_t, where S_t is the sum of the jumps up to time t. The jumps come at the times of a Poisson process with rate λ. Each jump is exponential with mean |m|. It goes up when m > 0 and down when m < 0. With m < 0 and c > 0, X is the Cramér–Lundberg surplus of an insurer.
laws.formula: X_t = x_0 + c\,t + \operatorname{sign}(m) \sum_{i=1}^{N(t)} Y_i, \quad N \sim \text{Poisson process}(\lambda), \quad Y_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{Exp}(\text{mean } |m|)
laws.support: X_t \in \mathbb{R}; \ \text{piecewise linear paths with slope } c \text{ and jumps of sign } \operatorname{sign}(m)
limits: λ → 0 with c fixed gives the deterministic line x_0 + c t.
With the exponential jumps of this page, (X_t − E X_t)/√(2λm²t) → N(0, 1) as λt → ∞.
Let m < 0, c > 0 and the safety loading θ = c/(λ|m|) − 1 > 0. Then ruin in infinite time has the probability ψ(u) = e^{−θu/((1 + θ)|m|)}/(1 + θ) (Cramér–Lundberg, exponential claims).
With θ ≤ 0, ruin in infinite time is certain for every initial capital u.

moments.existence: All moments of X_t exist, because the exponential jumps have all moments. The MGF E e^{s sign(m) X_t} is finite for s < 1/|m|, and infinite for s ≥ 1/|m|.

transforms.cf: \mathbb{E}\,e^{i s X_t} = \exp\Big(i s (x_0 + c t) + \lambda t \Big(\frac{1}{1 - i s m} - 1\Big)\Big)

conditions.stationarity: X is a Lévy process: its increments are stationary and independent. The level X_t is not stationary, because Var X_t = 2λm²t grows with t.
conditions.stability: X_t/t → c + λm almost surely. For a surplus, ruin in infinite time has a probability below 1 only if the safety loading θ = c/(λ|m|) − 1 is positive.
conditions.explosion: No explosion: there are finitely many jumps in a finite time almost surely, and each jump is finite.
conditions.boundary: The process has no boundary. A ruin level, such as min(X) < 0, is part of the quantity, not of the process.
conditions.discretisation: The exact methods add every jump at its step. A quantity of the grid values, such as min(X), does not see the path inside a step. With downward jumps and c > 0, the path is lowest just after a jump, so the grid can miss a short drop below a level.

methods: Exact on the grid (independent sampling): the number of jumps in a step is Poisson(λh). The sampler draws their sum from Gamma(N_k, |m|) by the Marsaglia–Tsang method. The values at the grid times have the exact law.
Inverse transform: exponential gaps −log(V)/λ give the jump times, and −|m| log(V) gives the jump sizes. The method is exact.
The page has no thinning sampler for this process: exponential gaps and exponential jumps need no rejection.
Euler time discretisation: one jump in a step with probability λh, none otherwise. The bias is of order λh.

links.relation: the jump times are a Poisson process
a Lévy process with finitely many jumps (VG has infinitely many small jumps)

laws.name: Finite-state Markov chain
laws.convention: A Markov chain X_0, X_1, X_2, … takes values in the states 1, …, k, and the next state depends only on the present state. The parameter P is the transition matrix, with k² entries row by row. Row i is the law of X_{n+1} when X_n = i. The chain starts in state x0 and makes steps transitions, one for each unit of time.
laws.formula: \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i, X_{n-1}, \dots, X_0) = P_{ij}, \qquad \mathbb{P}(X_n = j \mid X_0 = x_0) = (e_{x_0} P^{n})_j
limits: If all rows of P are the same probability vector p, then X_1, X_2, … are i.i.d. with the law p.
If P is the identity matrix, each state is absorbing and the path stays at x0.
If the chain is irreducible and aperiodic, Pⁿ(x, ·) → π as n → ∞ for each start x, with π the unique stationary law.
If the chain is irreducible, periodic or not, the fraction of time in state j converges to π_j almost surely as n → ∞. This is the ergodic theorem for Markov chains.
If the chain has two or more closed classes, the long-run fraction of time in a state depends on the class that the path enters. So it depends on X_0, and from a transient start also on chance.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the state space is finite. The state numbers are labels. So the mean of X_n has a meaning only when the states have an order, such as ratings. The usual quantities are state probabilities and occupation fractions.

conditions.stationarity: A law π with π P = π is stationary. It is unique when the chain has exactly one closed communicating class. If the chain has two or more closed classes, each class has its own stationary law.
conditions.stability: If the chain is irreducible and aperiodic, Pⁿ(x, ·) → π for every start x at a geometric rate. The mixing time t_mix(1/4) is the first n with max over x of the TV distance ‖Pⁿ(x, ·) − π‖ ≤ 1/4. A periodic chain does not converge in law, but its time averages converge.
conditions.explosion: No explosion: the chain is in discrete time with finitely many states, so it makes exactly one transition in each unit of time.
conditions.boundary: A state i with P_ii = 1 is absorbing: a path that enters it stays there. A state outside the closed classes is transient: a path leaves it after a finite number of visits.
conditions.discretisation: None: the chain is in discrete time, and each method draws the exact transitions. A continuous-time chain observed at fixed times gives a discrete chain with P = exp(Q h).

methods: Exact (independent): for each row of P, an alias table (Walker, Vose) draws the next state with one integer and one uniform. The path law is exact.
Inverse transform: the next state is the first j with F_i(j) ≥ V. Here F_i is the cumulative sum of row i, and V is uniform. The path law is exact.
Rejection: not offered, because each row is a categorical law with cheap exact samplers.
Euler: the chain is in discrete time, so no time discretisation applies. The method uses the exact alias sampler.

links.relation: a continuous-state process that reverts to a level, which a chain on a fine grid of levels approximates
a Markov chain on the counts 0, 1, 2, …, with 0 absorbing
each step draws X_{n+1} from a law that reads the earlier variable X_n

laws.name: Galton–Watson branching process
laws.convention: Z_n counts the individuals of generation n. Each individual has an independent number of offspring with mean m, and the offspring form the next generation. With k = inf the offspring number is Poisson(m). With a finite k it is negative binomial with mean m and dispersion k, so its variance is m + m²/k. The process starts with z0 ancestors.
laws.formula: Z_{n+1} = \sum_{i=1}^{Z_n} \xi_{n,i}, \quad \xi_{n,i} \text{ i.i.d.}, \ \mathbb{E}\,\xi = m, \quad f(s) = \begin{cases} e^{m(s-1)} & k = \infty \\ \left(1 + m(1-s)/k\right)^{-k} & k < \infty \end{cases}
limits: m ≤ 1 (subcritical or critical): extinction is certain, except in the trivial case where each individual has exactly 1 offspring. The offspring laws of this page always give a positive probability to 0, so q = 1.
m > 1 (supercritical): the extinction probability q of one ancestor is the smallest root of f(s) = s in [0, 1], and q < 1. With z0 ancestors it is q^{z0}.
Critical case m = 1 with offspring variance σ²: P(Z_n > 0) ~ 2/(n σ²) as n → ∞ (Kolmogorov).
k → ∞ gives Poisson offspring. A small k gives superspreading: most individuals have no offspring, and a few have many.
Z_n / mⁿ converges almost surely to a limit W. If m > 1 and E ξ log ξ < ∞, then W > 0 on the event of survival (Kesten–Stigum).

moments.variance: \operatorname{Var} Z_n = Z_0\,\sigma^2 m^{n-1} \frac{m^{n} - 1}{m - 1} \ (m \ne 1), \quad Z_0\, n \sigma^2 \ (m = 1), \quad \sigma^2 = m + m^2/k
moments.existence: All moments exist for each finite n, because the Poisson and negative binomial offspring laws have all moments. The mean mⁿ can be large while P(Z_n = 0) is near 1. Then the mean comes from rare large families.

conditions.stationarity: The only stationary law is the point mass at 0. If m ≤ 1, the process reaches 0 with probability 1. If m > 1, it reaches 0 with probability q^{z0} and otherwise grows like mⁿ.
