models.dsl:
title: Which transit line takes a rider to work in the least time?
problem: A rider comes to the stop at a random time and waits for the next vehicle. Three lines have different headways and ride times. Find the line with the least mean time that is rarely late.
param headway = 12 {min} "time between two vehicles"
param ride = 22 {min} "ride time to the destination"
param deadline = 33 {min} "time the rider has before the start of work"
W ~ cuniform(a = 0, b = headway) {min} "wait at the stop"
total := W + ride {min} "wait and ride"
mean time = total {min}
prob late = total > deadline "the rider is late"
alt "Bus, every 12 min": headway = 12; ride = 22
alt "Tram, every 6 min": headway = 6; ride = 26
alt "Express, every 20 min": headway = 20; ride = 16
minimise time
require late <= 0.1
focus W

models.title: Round each invoice line or only the total?
models.decision: Decision: the rule that rounds the amounts of a 30-line invoice. Estimated quantity: the probability that the buyer rejects the invoice, the mean absolute error of the total, and the mean cost for each invoice.
models.reason: Each line amount has digits below the rounding step. Prices and quantities vary, so the part below one step is close to uniform. The error of one rounded line is then uniform between −0.5 and +0.5 steps, independently of the other lines.
models.inputs: The model uses illustrative values: 30 lines and a tolerance of 1 cent in the buyer's match. A rejected invoice costs 12 currency units of manual work. The new layouts cost 0.02 and 0.05 currency units for each invoice. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: the errors of different lines are independent. Lines that repeat one price, such as many units of one item at a price with 3 decimals, break this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of the 30 line errors and of the error of the total, each by a scaled uniform. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. For the first rule, the total error is a sum of 30 uniform values. Its law is the Irwin–Hall law, moved to the mean 0.
models.diagnostics: The page shows no reference values: the line errors are a repeated variable, and the quadrature does not integrate over 30 copies. For the sum S of 30 line errors, the Irwin–Hall law gives P(|S| > 1) = 0.5289 exactly. The CLT gives about 0.527. Other candidate models: a discrete error on a grid of 0.1 cent, and dependent errors for lines that repeat one price.
models.interpretation: Round each line fails the constraint: about 53 % of the invoices differ from the buyer's total by more than 1 cent. Its mean absolute error is about 1.26 cents. The page selects Lines to 0.1 cent, with the least mean cost: about 0.021 against 0.05 currency units for Round only the total. Its P(reject) is about 7 × 10⁻⁵. Reject the model if many lines repeat one price, because the errors are then dependent and not uniform.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Round each invoice line or only the total?
problem: An invoice has 30 lines. Each rounded line adds an error to the total. The buyer's system rejects an invoice whose total differs from its own exact total by more than 1 cent. Find the rule with the least cost.
param step = 1 {cents} "rounding step of each line, 0 if the lines keep all digits"
param round_total = 0 "1 if the total is rounded to the cent after the lines, else 0"
param tol = 1 {cents} "tolerance of the buyer's match"
param rework = 12 {currency units} "manual work for one rejected invoice"
param change = 0 {currency units per invoice} "cost of the new invoice layout"
U ~ cuniform(a = -0.5, b = 0.5) repeat 30 "error of one rounded line, in rounding steps"
V ~ cuniform(a = -0.5, b = 0.5) {cents} "error of the rounded total"
err := step*sum(U) + round_total*V {cents} "error of the invoice total"
prob reject = abs(err) > tol "the buyer rejects the invoice"
mean abs_err = abs(err) {cents}
mean cost = change + rework*(abs(err) > tol) {currency units per invoice}
alt "Round each line": step = 1; round_total = 0; change = 0
alt "Lines to 0.1 cent": step = 0.1; round_total = 1; change = 0.02
alt "Round only the total": step = 0; round_total = 1; change = 0.05
minimise cost
require reject <= 0.02
focus V

models.title: Which tolerance class fits a shaft to its hole at the least cost?
models.decision: Decision: the tolerance class of a shaft and its hole. Estimated quantity: the probability that the clearance is outside the functional range, and the mean cost for each pair of parts.
models.reason: Tool wear moves each diameter at a constant rate between two tool changes, from one end of its band to the other. A part made at a random time then has a uniform diameter on its band.
models.inputs: The nominal diameter is 20 mm. The bands follow the ISO 286 grades for 18 to 30 mm: IT8 = 33 µm, IT7 = 21 µm, IT6 = 13 µm and IT5 = 9 µm. The shaft band starts 7 µm below the nominal size. The functional range of 8 to 38 µm and all costs are illustrative values. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: the hole and the shaft come from different machines, so their diameters are independent. Selective assembly, which pairs large shafts with large holes, breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of H and S by scaled uniforms. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. The alternatives use common random numbers, but each class scales the uniforms in a different way. So the variance ratio against independent alternatives stays between 0.99 and 1.2.
models.diagnostics: Quadrature over the 2 uniform variables gives the reference values. P(misfit) is 0.3795, 0.0183 and 0.0043, and the mean cost is 12.89, 2.55 and 3.03 currency units. The clearance H − S has a trapezoidal law, so these values also have a closed form. Other candidate models: a normal law cut to each band for a centred process, and a triangular law for a process with little tool wear.
models.interpretation: The fine class IT6/IT5 is the only class that meets the constraint. Its P(misfit) is about 0.004, and its mean cost is about 3.03 currency units. The medium class costs less, about 2.55, but its P(misfit) of about 0.018 is above the limit 0.01. The coarse class scraps about 38 % of the pairs. Reject the model if the diameters gather near the centre of each band, because the misfit probabilities are then smaller.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Which tolerance class fits a shaft to its hole at the least cost?
problem: A shaft turns in a bored hole. The clearance must stay between 8 and 38 µm. Finer tolerance classes cost more to machine but scrap fewer pairs. Find the class with the least cost for each pair.
param th = 21 {µm} "tolerance band of the hole"
param ts = 13 {µm} "tolerance band of the shaft"
param fd = 7 {µm} "distance of the shaft band below the nominal size"
param cmin = 8 {µm} "least clearance that turns freely"
param cmax = 38 {µm} "largest clearance that stays quiet"
param machine = 2 {currency units per pair} "cost to machine one shaft and one hole"
param scrap = 30 {currency units} "cost of one pair that does not fit"
H ~ cuniform(a = 0, b = th) {µm} "hole diameter above the nominal size"
S ~ cuniform(a = -fd - ts, b = -fd) {µm} "shaft diameter above the nominal size"
clearance := H - S {µm}
prob misfit = clearance < cmin or clearance > cmax "the clearance is outside the functional range"
mean cost = machine + scrap*(clearance < cmin or clearance > cmax) {currency units per pair}
alt "Coarse IT8/IT7": th = 33; ts = 21; machine = 1.5
alt "Medium IT7/IT6": th = 21; ts = 13; machine = 2
alt "Fine IT6/IT5": th = 13; ts = 9; machine = 2.9
minimise cost
require misfit <= 0.01
focus H

models.title: The normal law and the 68–95–99.7 rule
models.observe: The estimates of upper and two_sided are near their references 0.1587 and 0.0455, and sq_dev is near σ² = 4. By symmetry, P(|X − μ| ≤ σ) = 1 − 2 × 0.1587 ≈ 0.683 and P(|X − μ| ≤ 2σ) ≈ 0.954. With 3σ the value is 0.997, so the rule reads 68–95–99.7 %. With antithetic variables, the variance ratio of two_sided and sq_dev is 0.50, a loss, and the ratio of upper is about 1.23. The partner X' = 2μ − X gives the same value of an even function of X − μ. So a pair costs 2 evaluations for the information of 1.
models.dsl:
title: The normal law and the 68–95–99.7 rule
problem: A normal value falls within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of its mean with probabilities near 0.68, 0.95 and 0.997. Estimate two tail probabilities and the variance.
param mu = 10 "mean μ"
param sigma = 2 "standard deviation σ"
X ~ normal(mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
prob two_sided = abs(X - mu) > 2*sigma "P(|X − μ| > 2σ)"
mean sq_dev = (X - mu)^2 "the variance σ² = 4"
prob upper = X > mu + sigma "P(X > μ + σ)"
focus X

models.title: How many loaves to bake for one day?
models.decision: Decision: the number of loaves to bake each morning. Estimated quantity: the mean profit for each day, and the probability that the demand is above the stock.
models.reason: The daily demand is the sum of the purchases of many customers who act independently. By the CLT, such a sum is close to normal when the mean count is large, here 400 loaves.
models.inputs: The mean demand of 400 loaves and its standard deviation of 80 loaves are illustrative values. So are the price of 3 and the cost of 1 currency unit for each loaf. Unsold loaves have no value. P(D < 0) = Φ(−5) ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁷ is negligible, and the model uses max(D, 0). There is no data.
models.dependence: None: the model looks at one day. Weather and the day of the week change the mean demand. A separate model for each type of day removes that dependence.
models.method: Independent draws of D. The estimators are means and fractions of replicates. The control C = D has the exact mean 400. With control variates, the variance ratio of profit is about 3.8 for 400 loaves, 7.4 for 440 and 17 for 480. The ratio is large because profit has a strong correlation with D. With the failure control_mean, the control mean is wrong by 0.1σ, and the estimates move 12 to 20 currency units above their references.
models.diagnostics: Quadrature over D gives the reference values: mean profit 704.25, 712.53 and 700.00, and P(short) = 0.5, 0.3085 and 0.1587. The closed form E[min(D, q)] = μ − σ[φ(z) − z(1 − Φ(z))], with z = (q − μ)/σ, gives the same values. With the failure control_mean, the estimates are 41 to 105 standard errors from their references at 2^16 replicates. Other candidate models: a negative binomial count for a small bakery, and a gamma demand with a long right tail.
models.interpretation: Without the constraint, 440 loaves give the largest mean profit, about 712.5 against 704.3 for 400 and 700.0 for 480. The constraint P(short) ≤ 0.25 removes 400 and 440 loaves, so the page selects 480 loaves. The constraint costs about 12.5 currency units of mean profit each day. Reject the model if the sales data show a skewed demand. Reject it also if many days end with an empty shelf, because the stock then cuts the observed demand.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: How many loaves to bake for one day?
problem: A bakery bakes bread each morning before it knows the demand. Unsold loaves have no value. Find the number of loaves that gives the most profit with few days of lost sales.
param price = 3 {currency units} "price of one loaf"
param cost = 1 {currency units} "cost to bake one loaf"
param q = 440 {loaves} "loaves baked"
D ~ normal(mu = 400, sigma = 80) {loaves} "daily demand"
sold := min(max(D, 0), q) {loaves} "loaves sold"
mean profit = price*sold - cost*q {currency units per day}
prob short = D > q "demand above the stock"
alt "Bake 400": q = 400
alt "Bake 440": q = 440
alt "Bake 480": q = 480
maximise profit
require short <= 0.25
focus D
control C = D "demand, with the known mean 400"

models.title: Does a stack of three parts fit its housing?
models.decision: Decision: a standard or a precision part C in a stack of three parts. Estimated quantity: the probability that the stack is longer than the housing gap, the mean slack, and the mean cost for each assembly.
models.reason: Each length is the result of many small independent effects of the machine, the tool and the material. By the CLT, each length is close to normal. The stack length is a sum of independent normal lengths, so it is also normal.
models.inputs: These values are illustrative: mean lengths of 20, 30 and 50 mm, and a gap of 100.15 mm. The standard deviations are σ_A = σ_B = 0.02 mm, and σ_C = 0.08 mm or 0.03 mm for the precision part. The precision part costs 1.2 currency units more, and one assembly that does not fit costs 30 currency units. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: the three parts come from different processes. Parts from one batch with the same tool offset have correlated lengths, and the stack variance is then larger.
models.method: Independent draws of A, B and C. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. Stratification helps only on the variable that drives the variance. With 16 strata of A, the variance ratio for the standard part is about 1.01 for no_fit and 1.06 for slack. A gives only 5.6 % of the stack variance. With 16 strata of C, which gives 89 %, the ratios are about 1.8 and 7.6.
models.diagnostics: Linearity gives the exact reference of the mean slack, 0.15 mm. The page has no reference for no_fit and cost, because the model has 3 continuous variables. For a sum of independent normal values, P(no_fit) = 1 − Φ(0.15/√0.0072) = 0.0385 for the standard part. For the precision part it is 1.4 × 10⁻⁴. Other candidate models: a worst-case stack of the tolerance limits, and a uniform law for parts from a process with tool wear.
models.interpretation: The standard part C fails the constraint: about 3.9 % of the assemblies do not fit. Its mean cost, about 1.16, is close to the 1.20 of the precision part. The precision part meets the constraint with P(no_fit) of about 0.00014, so the page selects it. Reject the model if the lengths of part C have heavier tails than a normal law, because the misfit rate then grows.

models.dsl:
title: Does a stack of three parts fit its housing?
problem: Three parts sit end to end in a housing gap. Part C varies much more than parts A and B. Find whether a precision part C is worth its extra cost.
param gap = 100.15 {mm} "length of the housing gap"
param sc = 0.08 {mm} "standard deviation of part C"
param extra = 0 {currency units per assembly} "extra cost of part C"
param rework = 30 {currency units} "cost of one assembly that does not fit"
A ~ normal(mu = 20, sigma = 0.02) {mm} "length of part A"
B ~ normal(mu = 30, sigma = 0.02) {mm} "length of part B"
C ~ normal(mu = 50, sigma = sc) {mm} "length of part C"
stack := A + B + C {mm} "length of the stack"
prob no_fit = stack > gap "the stack is longer than the gap"
mean slack = gap - stack {mm}
mean cost = extra + rework*(stack > gap) {currency units per assembly}
alt "Standard part C": sc = 0.08; extra = 0
alt "Precision part C": sc = 0.03; extra = 1.2
minimise cost
require no_fit <= 0.01
focus C

models.title: Cold drinks or hot drinks at a summer festival?
models.decision: Decision: the type of drinks stall to rent for a one-day festival. Estimated quantity: the mean profit of the day, and the probability of a loss.
models.reason: The maximum temperature T of the day is the forecast value plus a forecast error. The error of a forecast one or two days ahead is close to normal, so T is normal around the forecast.
models.inputs: These values are illustrative: a forecast of 22 °C with a standard deviation of 3 °C, and a stall fee of 600 currency units. Cold drinks sell 900 at 20 °C and 80 more for each °C above. Hot drinks sell 1000 at 20 °C and 60 less for each °C above. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: the model looks at one day, and the profit is a linear function of T. Sales that stop at the capacity of the stall break the linear form.
models.method: Independent draws of T. The estimators are means and fractions of replicates. Common random numbers fail here: the cold profit rises with T and the hot profit falls, so their covariance is negative. The variance ratio against independent alternatives for the profit difference is 0.51, a loss. With separate streams it is near 1.
models.diagnostics: Linearity gives the exact mean profit: 300 + 80 × 2 = 460 for cold drinks and 400 − 60 × 2 = 280 for hot drinks. Quadrature gives P(loss) = Φ((16.25 − 22)/3) = 0.0276 and 1 − Φ((26.67 − 22)/3) = 0.0599. Other candidate models: a forecast error with heavier tails, such as a Student t law, and sales that stop at the capacity of the stall.
models.interpretation: Cold drinks give the larger mean profit, about 460 against 280 currency units, and P(loss) ≈ 0.028 meets the limit 0.05. Hot drinks fail the constraint, with P(loss) ≈ 0.060. The paired interval separates the two stalls, but common random numbers make it wider. Reject the model if the sales do not follow the temperature in a straight line, for example when a cold day keeps visitors away.

models.dsl:
title: Cold drinks or hot drinks at a summer festival?
problem: A trader rents one stall at a one-day festival. Cold drinks sell better on a hot day, and hot drinks on a cool day. Find the stall with the larger mean profit and a small risk of a loss.
param fee = 600 {currency units} "stall fee"
param base = 900 {currency units} "sales at 20 °C"
param slope = 80 {currency units per °C} "change of the sales for each °C above 20 °C"
T ~ normal(mu = 22, sigma = 3) {°C} "maximum temperature of the day"
profit_day := base + slope*(T - 20) - fee {currency units}
mean profit = profit_day {currency units}
prob loss = profit_day < 0 "the day makes a loss"
alt "Cold drinks": base = 900; slope = 80
alt "Hot drinks": base = 1000; slope = -60
maximise profit
require loss <= 0.05
focus T

models.title: Correlation changes the spread of a sum and the joint tail
models.observe: The spread of S grows with ρ: Var S = 2 + 2ρ moves from 0.4 to 3.6, and P(S > 2) from about 0.0008 to 0.146. P(X[1] > 1 and X[2] > 1) is about 0.098 with ρ = 0.8, against 0.025 with ρ = 0. E[S] = 0 is exact by linearity, but the probabilities have no reference: the page does not integrate over a vector law. With ρ = 0.8, P(X[2] > t | X[1] > t) falls from about 0.62 at t = 1 to 0.35 at t = 2.5. It falls to 0 as t grows. So the normal joint law has no tail dependence. Group 5 adds copulas that have it.
models.dsl:
title: Correlation changes the spread of a sum and the joint tail
problem: X[1] and X[2] are standard normal values with the correlation rho. Compare the law of the sum S and the chance that both values are large, for 3 values of rho.
param rho = 0 "correlation of X[1] and X[2]"
X ~ mvnormal(mu = [0, 0], cov = [1, rho, rho, 1]) "a pair of standard normal values"
S := X[1] + X[2] "the sum"
prob sum_high = S > 2 "P(S > 2)"
prob both_high = X[1] > 1 and X[2] > 1 "P(X[1] > 1 and X[2] > 1)"
mean s = S "E[S], exact by linearity"
mean spread = S^2 "E[S^2] = Var S = 2 + 2 rho"
ratio tail1 = E[X[1] > 1 and X[2] > 1] / E[X[1] > 1] "P(X[2] > 1 | X[1] > 1)"
ratio tail25 = E[X[1] > 2.5 and X[2] > 2.5] / E[X[1] > 2.5] "P(X[2] > 2.5 | X[1] > 2.5)"
alt "rho = -0.8": rho = -0.8
alt "rho = 0": rho = 0
alt "rho = 0.8": rho = 0.8
focus X[1]

models.title: Which asset mix gives the best mean return with a limited loss risk?
models.decision: Decision: the weights of bonds, equities and property in a fund. Estimated quantity: the mean monthly return, and the probability of a monthly loss worse than 4 %.
models.reason: A monthly log return is the sum of many small log price changes, so a normal law is a common first model. For monthly changes of a few percent, the simple return that the weights add is close to the log return. The three assets react to the same economic news, so their returns are correlated. The multivariate normal law holds the means, the volatilities and the correlations in one covariance matrix.
models.inputs: The monthly means are 0.3, 0.8 and 0.6 % for bonds, equities and property, and the standard deviations are 1, 4.5 and 3.5 %. The correlations are −0.2 for bonds and equities, 0.1 for bonds and property, and 0.6 for equities and property. These values are illustrative, not market estimates. The loss limit is 4 % in one month.
models.dependence: The covariance matrix holds the dependence: [1, −0.9, 0.35; −0.9, 20.25, 9.45; 0.35, 9.45, 12.25] in %². The months are independent in this model. The normal law has no tail dependence, so in this model large losses do not come together more often than the correlations say.
models.method: Independent draws: R = μ + LZ, with L the Cholesky factor of the covariance matrix and Z a vector of standard normal values. The estimators are a sample mean and a fraction of replicates. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences of the mean return are precise.
models.diagnostics: The mean return has an exact reference by linearity: 0.43, 0.56 and 0.69 % a month. The loss probability has no reference on the page, because the page does not integrate over a vector law. The fund return is normal with a mean m and a standard deviation s. So Φ((−4 − m)/s) gives a check: about 0.0002, 0.022 and 0.085. Other candidate models: a multivariate Student t law for heavy tails, and a t copula for losses that come together.
models.interpretation: The growth mix has the largest mean, 0.69 % a month. But its probability of a loss worse than 4 % is about 0.085, above the limit 0.05. The balanced mix meets the limit with about 0.022, and its mean 0.56 % is the best of the admissible mixes. Reject the model if the returns show heavy tails, or if large losses come together more often than the normal law allows.

models.dsl:
title: Which asset mix gives the best mean return with a limited loss risk?
problem: Three assets have correlated monthly returns. Find the weights with the largest mean return, while a monthly loss worse than 4 % stays rare.
param w1 = 0.4 "weight of bonds"
param w2 = 0.4 "weight of equities"
param w3 = 0.2 "weight of property"
param limit = 4 {%} "monthly loss limit"
R ~ mvnormal(mu = [0.3, 0.8, 0.6], cov = [1, -0.9, 0.35, -0.9, 20.25, 9.45, 0.35, 9.45, 12.25]) {% per month} "returns of bonds, equities and property"
Rp := w1*R[1] + w2*R[2] + w3*R[3] {% per month} "return of the fund"
mean ret = Rp {% per month} "mean return of the fund"
prob loss = Rp < -limit "a monthly loss worse than the limit"
alt "Defensive 70/20/10": w1 = 0.7; w2 = 0.2; w3 = 0.1
alt "Balanced 40/40/20": w1 = 0.4; w2 = 0.4; w3 = 0.2
alt "Growth 10/60/30": w1 = 0.1; w2 = 0.6; w3 = 0.3
maximise ret
require loss <= 0.05
focus Rp

models.title: Which z-score rule should flag a child for a growth review?
models.decision: Decision: the z-score rule that flags a child for a growth review. Estimated quantity: the false-flag rate among healthy children, and the detection rate among children with a growth disorder.
models.reason: Growth references define the height and weight z-scores so that they are close to standard normal in healthy children. Tall children are also heavier, so the two z-scores are correlated. A bivariate normal law keeps both margins and the correlation.
models.inputs: The correlation 0.65 and the flag limit −2 are illustrative values. So are the mean z-scores with the disorder: −1.5 for height and −1.0 for weight. Both groups have the same covariance. The clinic accepts a false-flag rate of at most 0.03.
models.dependence: The covariance matrix [1, 0.65; 0.65, 1] holds the dependence of the two z-scores of one child. Each replicate draws one healthy child and one child with the disorder, independently.
models.method: Independent draws: μ + LZ with the Cholesky factor L of the covariance matrix. The estimators are fractions of replicates. All rules read the same draws, so the differences between the rules are paired.
models.diagnostics: No reference value: the page does not integrate over a vector law. A check: the height rule flags Φ(−2) ≈ 0.0228 of healthy children. With independent z-scores, the either rule would flag 0.045 and the both rule 0.0005. The correlation 0.65 gives about 0.039 and 0.0064. Other candidate models: a skewed law for the weight z-score, and a mixture with an unknown share of children with the disorder.
models.interpretation: The either rule detects the most, about 0.35, but it flags about 0.039 of healthy children, above 0.03. The height rule flags about 0.023 and detects about 0.31. The both rule detects only about 0.12. So the height rule is the best admissible rule. Reject the model if the z-scores of the local population are not near standard normal, or if the correlation differs much from 0.65.

title: Which z-score rule should flag a child for a growth review?
problem: A clinic flags a child for review when the height or the weight z-score is low. The two z-scores are correlated. Find the rule that detects the most children with a growth disorder and flags at most 3 % of healthy children.

param dw = -1 "mean weight z-score with the disorder"
param cut = -2 "flag limit of a z-score"

param uw = 1 "1 if the rule reads the weight z-score"
param need = 1 "number of low z-scores that flag a child"

models.title: How much weight to give each sensor when their errors are correlated
models.decision: Decision: the weight w of sensor 1 in the combined position estimate. Estimated quantity: the mean squared error of the combined estimate, and P(|error| > 4 m).
models.reason: Each sensor error is the sum of many small effects, so a normal law fits. The two sensors share some effects, such as the same atmospheric delay or the same map error, so their errors are correlated. A bivariate normal law describes this pair of errors.
models.inputs: Error standard deviations of 2 m and 3 m, a correlation of 0.5 and an error limit of 4 m are illustrative values. Both sensors have no bias. The combined estimate must have P(|error| > 4 m) of at most 0.05.
models.dependence: The covariance matrix [4, 3; 3, 9] in m² holds the correlation 0.5. With correlated errors, the inverse-variance weight 9/13 ≈ 0.69 is not optimal. The optimal weight is (σ2² − ρσ1σ2)/(σ1² + σ2² − 2ρσ1σ2) = 6/7 ≈ 0.86.
models.method: Independent draws of the error pair by μ + LZ, with the Cholesky factor L. The estimators are sample means of F and F² and a fraction of replicates. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences of the mean squared error are precise.
models.diagnostics: The mean error has the exact reference 0 by linearity. The mean squared error has no reference on the page, because the page does not integrate over a vector law. The formula w²σ1² + (1 − w)²σ2² + 2w(1 − w)ρσ1σ2 gives a check: 4.75, 4.05, 3.86 and 4.00 m². Other candidate models: errors with a heavy tail, such as a Student t law, and errors with a bias.
models.interpretation: The weight 6/7 gives the smallest mean squared error, about 3.86 m², with P(|error| > 4 m) of about 0.042. The inverse-variance weight gives about 4.05 m². This is worse than sensor 1 alone, 4.00 m². Equal weights give P(|error| > 4 m) of about 0.066, above the limit 0.05. Reject the model if the error correlation changes with the conditions, or if the errors have a bias.

models.title: The exponential law has no memory
models.observe: The reference P(X > 10) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.3679 comes from the survival function. The ratio P(X > 15)/P(X > 5) has the same reference value. So a unit of age 5 hours lasts 10 more hours with the chance of a new unit. The ratio estimator uses only the replicates with X > 5, so its interval is wider. On the log axis, the survival plot is a straight line, because ln P(X > x) = −λx with λ = 0.1 per hour. It falls by one decade every ln(10)/λ ≈ 23 hours. E[X] = 1/λ = 10 hours.
models.dsl:
title: The exponential law has no memory
problem: A unit fails at a constant rate of 0.1 per hour. Compare the chance that a new unit lasts 10 hours with the chance that a unit of age 5 hours lasts 10 more hours.
param rate = 0.1 {per hour} "failure rate"
X ~ exponential(rate = rate) {hours} "life of the unit"
prob over10 = X > 10 "P(X > 10)"
ratio after = E[X > 15] / E[X > 5] "P(X > 15 | X > 5)"
mean m = X {hours} "mean life"
focus X

models.title: How long a warranty to give on a power supply with a constant failure rate
models.decision: Decision: the warranty length of a power supply. Estimated quantity: the expected profit for each unit sold, and the probability of a claim.
models.reason: Electronic parts with no wear fail at random times, at a constant rate. A constant failure rate gives an exponential life, with P(T < w) = 1 − e^(−w/8). The law has no memory, so each year of warranty gives a claim to the same fraction of the units that still work.
models.inputs: A mean life of 8 years and a claim cost of 100 currency units are illustrative values. So are the profit of 40 for each unit and the extra prices of 15 and 25 for 2 and 3 years. The maker accepts at most 1 claim in 4 units.
models.dependence: None: units fail independently. The model counts at most one claim for each unit, because the new unit has no new warranty.
models.method: Independent draws by inversion of the survival function: T = −log(U)/λ. The estimators are a fraction and a sample mean. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences of the profit are precise.
models.diagnostics: Exact references for P(claim) from the survival function: 0.1175, 0.2212 and 0.3127. The expected profit has a quadrature reference: 28.25, 32.88 and 33.73. Other candidate models: a Weibull life with wear, and a failure rate that is high at the start for early failures.
models.interpretation: The 3-year warranty has the largest expected profit, 33.73, but its claim probability 0.31 is above the limit 0.25. The 2-year warranty meets the limit with 0.22 and gives 32.88 for each unit. Reject the model if the failure rate grows with age, because the exponential law then understates the late claims.

models.title: Wait at the taxi rank or walk to a busier road?
models.decision: Decision: where to wait for a taxi. Estimated quantity: the probability to be late for the appointment, and the mean time until the ride starts.
models.reason: Free taxis pass at random times, independently of each other, at a constant rate. These times form a Poisson process, so the wait for the next taxi is exponential. The law has no memory: after 5 minutes at the rank, the rest of the wait has the same law as at the start.
models.inputs: The taxi rates of 0.2, 0.6 and 1.5 a minute and the walks of 0, 4 and 8 minutes are illustrative values. The appointment starts in 15 minutes and the ride takes 6 minutes, so 9 minutes remain for the walk and the wait.
models.dependence: None: the taxis at each place form a Poisson process with a constant rate. A rate that changes in the hour, or taxis that come in groups after a train, break this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws by inversion of the survival function. The estimators are a fraction and a sample mean. The alternatives use the same uniform numbers, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: P(late) = e^(−λ(9 − walk)) gives 0.1653, 0.0498 and 0.2231. The mean time walk + 1/λ is exact by linearity: 5.00, 5.67 and 8.67 minutes. Other candidate models: a Poisson process with a rate that changes in the hour, and a ride time with a random delay.
models.interpretation: The rank gives the shortest mean time, 5 minutes, but P(late) is about 0.17, above the limit 0.1. The main road meets the limit with P(late) about 0.05 and a mean time of 5.67 minutes. With the station, P(late) is about 0.22, because the 8-minute walk uses most of the time. Reject the model if taxis come in groups, or if the rate at the rank is lower at this hour.

models.title: Which timeout for a call to a slow service?
models.decision: Decision: the timeout of a web page for its call to a service. Estimated quantity: the probability of a timeout, the mean user wait, and the expected cost of the wait and the cached results.
models.reason: The service works as a single queue with Poisson arrivals and exponential service times. In such a queue the response time is exponential. The law has no memory. A request that has waited 400 ms has the same law for the rest of its wait as a new request. So a timeout helps only against the requests that the service loses.
models.inputs: A mean response time of 250 ms and a loss probability of 0.02 are illustrative values. So is the cost of a cached result, equal to 2000 ms of user wait. The latency target is a wait of at most 1.5 s in 99 % of page views.
models.dependence: None: the response time and the loss are independent, and the requests are independent. A load peak breaks this assumption, because it makes slow answers and lost requests more frequent at the same time.
models.method: Independent draws: R by inversion of the survival function, and the loss as a Bernoulli value. The estimators are fractions and sample means. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
models.diagnostics: Quadrature reference values for every quantity, over R and the 2 values of the loss. P(timeout) = 0.02 + 0.98 e^(−τ/250) gives 0.218, 0.038 and 0.020. Other candidate models: a gamma or a log-normal response time with a heavier tail. Other candidate design: a second attempt after the timeout.
models.interpretation: A 400 ms timeout cuts the wait, but 22 % of requests give a cached result, so its expected cost is about 639 ms. A 2000 ms timeout has the least cost, about 326 ms, but 2.2 % of page views wait more than 1.5 s. The 1000 ms timeout meets the target with a cost of about 336 ms. Reject the model if the response time has a heavier tail than the exponential law.

title: Which timeout for a call to a slow service?

models.title: The gamma shape sets the skewness when the mean is fixed
models.observe: All three laws have E[X] = 4. But the variance kθ² = 16/k falls from 32 to 0.8, and the skewness 2/√k falls from 2.8 to 0.45. With k = 0.5 the density is unbounded at 0: P(X < 1) ≈ 0.383 and P(X > 8) ≈ 0.157. With k = 20 the law is nearly normal, and P(X > 8) is only about 0.00018. Rejection sampling from an exponential proposal is not available for k = 0.5. An exponential envelope is bounded, so it cannot cover a density that is unbounded at 0.
models.dsl:
title: The gamma shape sets the skewness when the mean is fixed
problem: Three gamma laws have the same mean 4, with the shapes k = 0.5, 2 and 20 and the scale theta = 4/k. Compare their tails and their spread.
param mean_x = 4 "mean k theta"
param k = 2 "shape"
param theta = mean_x / k "scale"
X ~ gamma(k = k, theta = theta) "a gamma value with the mean 4"
prob tail = X > 2*mean_x "P(X > 8)"
prob low = X < 0.25*mean_x "P(X < 1)"
mean m = X "E[X] = 4"
mean spread = (X - mean_x)^2 "Var X = k theta^2"
alt "k = 0.5": k = 0.5
alt "k = 2": k = 2
alt "k = 20": k = 20
focus X

models.title: Which deductible and cap to offer on a home contents contract
models.decision: Decision: the deductible and the cap of a home contents contract. Estimated quantity: the mean payout and the expected margin for each claim, and the probability that the payout reaches the cap.
models.reason: A claim size is positive and skewed to the right. A gamma law gives this shape with two parameters. With k = 2, it is the law of the sum of 2 independent exponential amounts of damage. The payout is the claim size above the deductible, cut at the cap.
models.inputs: A shape k = 2 and a scale θ = 2500 (a mean claim of 5000 currency units) are illustrative values. So are the deductibles, the caps and the premium income for each claim. The insurer accepts a payout at the cap in at most 2 % of claims.
models.dependence: None: the model looks at one claim at a time, with independent claim sizes. A storm that damages many homes at once makes the claims dependent, and this model does not cover it.
models.method: Independent draws by the Marsaglia–Tsang method. The estimators are sample means and a fraction. The antithetic method draws L by inversion, L = F⁻¹(U). The payout is monotone in L, so the antithetic pairs U and 1 − U give negatively correlated payouts. With the antithetic method, the variance ratio of the mean payout is about 14, 5 and 3 for the three contracts. The control C = L, with the exact mean 5000, gives variance ratios between about 11 and 100.
models.diagnostics: Quadrature reference values for every quantity. The mean payout is 4270.6, 3987.0 and 3141.2, and P(payout at the cap) is 0.0780, 0.0123 and 0.0015. Other candidate models: a log-normal or a Pareto claim size. They have heavier tails, so far above the mean they give larger exceedance probabilities. With the same mean and variance they give a larger P(payout at the cap) for the cap 20000, but not for the cap 10000.
models.interpretation: The contract with the deductible 500 has the largest margin, 729. But its payout reaches the cap in 7.8 % of claims, above the limit 2 %. Of the admissible contracts, the deductible 2000 with the cap 20000 gives the larger margin, 659 against 613. Reject the model if large claims are more frequent than the gamma tail allows, because the model then understates P(payout at the cap).

models.title: How large a street drain for the rain of one wet day
models.decision: Decision: the capacity of a street drain and its storage tank. Estimated quantity: the probability of an overflow on a wet day, the expected rain depth above the capacity, and the expected yearly cost.
models.reason: The rain depth of a wet day is positive and skewed: many light days and a few heavy ones. Hydrologists often fit a gamma law with a shape below 1 to it. A shape below 1 gives many small depths and a long right tail.
models.inputs: A shape of 0.8 and a scale of 12.5 mm (a mean of 10 mm on a wet day) are illustrative values. So are 100 wet days a year and a 2 ha catchment, which gives 20 m³ of flood for each mm. The damage cost of 30 for each m³ and the yearly drain costs are also illustrative. The city accepts an overflow on at most 5 % of wet days.
models.dependence: None: the wet days are independent, and the model uses the depth of one day. Storms of several days and water that stays in the pipes break this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws by the Marsaglia–Tsang method, with the step Gamma(k + 1)·U^(1/k) for k < 1. The estimators are a fraction and sample means. Rejection sampling from an exponential proposal is not available, because k < 1 makes the density unbounded at 0.
models.diagnostics: Quadrature reference values for every quantity. P(overflow) is 0.0943, 0.0403 and 0.0114, and the expected depth above the capacity is 1.12, 0.48 and 0.14 mm on a wet day. Other candidate models: a mixed exponential law, a Weibull law, and a generalised Pareto tail for the extreme days.
models.interpretation: The 35 mm drain has the least expected cost, about 73,900 a year, against 86,900 for 25 mm and 98,300 for 50 mm. Its overflow probability 0.040 meets the limit 0.05. Reject the model if heavy days are more frequent than the gamma tail allows. Fit the law to local rain records first.

models.title: Which repair-time guarantee to sell in a service contract
models.decision: Decision: the repair time that a service contract guarantees. Estimated quantity: the probability of a late repair, the expected time after the guarantee, and the expected margin for each repair.
models.reason: A repair is a sequence of phases: travel, diagnosis, parts and the fix. If each phase is exponential with the same rate, the total time is Erlang. When the phases differ in size, a gamma law with a shape that is not an integer is a flexible fit.
models.inputs: A shape of 2.5 and a scale of 1.6 hours (a mean repair time of 4 hours) are illustrative values. So are the fees 420, 300 and 220, a fixed penalty of 500 and 100 for each hour late. The provider accepts late repairs in at most 10 % of calls.
models.dependence: None: the repair times of different calls are independent. A shortage of spare parts or of staff makes several repairs late at the same time.
models.method: Independent draws by the Marsaglia–Tsang method. The estimators are a fraction and sample means of quantities with finite moments. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
models.diagnostics: Quadrature reference values for every quantity. P(late) is 0.186, 0.075 and 0.029, and the expected margin is 287.1, 247.1 and 200.2. Other candidate models: a log-normal repair time, and a mixture for the calls that wait for parts.
models.interpretation: The 6-hour guarantee has the largest margin, 287, but 18.6 % of repairs are late, above the limit 10 %. The 8-hour guarantee meets the limit with 7.5 % late repairs and a margin of 247. Reject the model if some repairs wait days for parts, because the gamma tail is then too light.

models.title: The Erlang law is the time of the k-th event of a Poisson process
models.observe: Each alternative keeps E[X] = 6 minutes, and Var X = 36/k falls as k grows. P(X > 12) falls from e^(−2) ≈ 0.1353 for k = 1 to 0.0620 for k = 3 and 0.0050 for k = 10. The k-th event comes after 12 minutes exactly when fewer than k events occur in 12 minutes: P(X > t) = P(N(t) < k). The reference values of the two probabilities are equal. The estimates differ a little, because X and N are independent draws in the model.

models.title: How many cold spare boards for a remote relay station
models.decision: Decision: the number of control boards that a remote relay station keeps as cold spares. Estimated quantity: the probability that the station works until the next service visit, and the expected cost of the boards and of a failure.
models.reason: A board in use fails at a constant rate, so its life is exponential. A cold spare does not age while it is off, and the switch is perfect. The station life is then the sum of k i.i.d. exponential lives: the Erlang(k, λ) law.
models.inputs: A failure rate of 0.0005 an hour gives a mean board life of 2000 hours. This rate, the 3000 hours to the next visit and the costs are illustrative values. A board costs 40 thousand currency units, and a station failure costs 500 thousand. The operator needs a survival probability of at least 0.9.
models.dependence: None: the board lives are independent. A switch that can fail, or spares that age while they are off, break the Erlang model.
models.method: Independent draws as the sum of k exponential phases: X = −Σ log(U_i)/λ. The estimators are a fraction and sample means. The alternatives use the same streams, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
models.diagnostics: Exact references for P(survive) and E[T] = k/λ from the Erlang law, and a quadrature reference for the cost. P(survive) = P(N < k) for a Poisson count N with the mean λt = 1.5: 0.809, 0.934 and 0.981. Other candidate models: a warm standby with spares that age at a lower rate, and an imperfect switch.
models.interpretation: 2 spares give a survival probability of about 0.81, below 0.9. 3 spares meet the target with 0.934 and give the least expected cost, about 192.8 thousand. 4 spares give an expected cost of 209.3 thousand, because the extra board costs more than the risk it removes. Reject the model if the failure rate grows with age, or if the switch can fail.

models.dsl:
title: How many cold spare boards for a remote relay station
problem: A relay station runs on one control board. Spare boards stay off until a switch puts one in service. Find the number of spares with the least expected cost and a survival probability of at least 0.9.
param lam = 0.0005 {per hour} "failure rate of a board in use"
param k = 4 {boards} "boards in all: the board in use and k - 1 spares"
param mission = 3000 {hours} "time until the next service visit"
param unit_cost = 40 {thousand currency units} "cost of one board"
param loss = 500 {thousand currency units} "cost of a station failure before the visit"
T ~ erlang(k = k, rate = lam) {hours} "life of the station"
prob survive = T > mission "the station works until the visit"
mean life = T {hours} "mean life of the station"
mean cost = unit_cost*k + loss*(T <= mission) {thousand currency units} "boards and failure cost"
alt "2 spares": k = 3
alt "3 spares": k = 4
alt "4 spares": k = 5
minimise cost
require survive >= 0.9
focus T

models.title: How many orders to put in one van trip
models.decision: Decision: the number of orders in one van trip. Estimated quantity: the probability that the first order of a batch waits more than 1 hour, and the expected cost for each order.
models.reason: Orders come from many independent customers, so they form a Poisson process. The first order of a batch waits for the k − 1 orders after it. That wait is the sum of k − 1 exponential gaps: an Erlang(k − 1, λ) law.
models.inputs: The order rate of 12 an hour is an illustrative value. So are the cost of 30 for each van trip and the wait cost of 6 an hour for each order. The depot accepts a wait of more than 1 hour for the first order in at most 10 % of batches.
models.dependence: None: the order times form a Poisson process with a constant rate. Peaks at lunch time or after an advertisement break this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws as sums of exponential gaps. The estimators are a fraction and a sample mean. Given W, the arrival times between the first and the last order are uniform. So the mean wait of an order in the batch is W/2 on average.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: P(W > 1 hour) = P(N < k − 1) for a Poisson count N with the mean 12, which gives 0.0005, 0.0458 and 0.3472. The cost is affine in W, so its reference 8.25, 5.50 and 5.25 is exact by linearity. Other candidate models: a Poisson process with daily peaks, and a dispatch rule with a time limit.
models.interpretation: Batches of 12 orders give the least cost, 5.25 for each order. But the first order waits more than 1 hour in 35 % of batches. Batches of 8 meet the limit, with 4.6 % of batches late, at a cost of 5.50 for each order. Reject the model if the order rate changes much during the day.

models.dsl:
title: How many orders to put in one van trip
problem: Orders arrive at random times. The depot sends a van when k orders wait. Find the batch size with the least cost for each order, while the first order of a batch rarely waits more than 1 hour.

param batch = 8 {orders} "orders in one van trip"

param trip = 30 {currency units} "cost of one van trip"
param hold = 6 {currency units per hour} "wait cost of one order"

prob late = W > limit "the first order waits more than the limit"

alt "12 orders": batch = 12

models.title: When to call a second doctor to the emergency department at night
models.decision: Decision: the number k of patients in 30 minutes that calls a second doctor to the emergency department at night. Estimated quantity: the probability of a call, the call rates on normal and surge nights, and the expected cost for each night.
models.reason: Patients arrive independently at a constant rate during the night, so the arrivals form a Poisson process. The time of the k-th arrival is then the sum of k exponential gaps: the Erlang(k, λ) law. The rate is higher on a surge night.
models.inputs: The arrival rates of 3 patients an hour on a normal night and 8 on a surge night are illustrative values. So are the surge probability 0.2, the call cost 400 and the cost 2000 of a surge night with one doctor. The window is the first 30 minutes of the night shift.
models.dependence: The night type S sets the rate, so T depends on S. Given S, the arrivals form a Poisson process. Ambulances that bring several patients at once break this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws: S as a Bernoulli value, then T as a sum of k exponential gaps with the rate of the night. The estimators are fractions, ratios of means and a sample mean.
models.diagnostics: Quadrature reference values over S and T. P(call | normal night) = P(N ≥ k) for a Poisson count N with the mean 1.5. The values for k = 2 to 5 are 0.442, 0.191, 0.066 and 0.019. Other candidate models: a rate that changes during the night, and a negative binomial count for nights with more spread.
models.interpretation: k = 3 gives the least expected cost, about 217 a night. It calls the second doctor on 76 % of surge nights and on 19 % of normal nights. A threshold of 2 calls too often. Thresholds of 4 and 5 leave too many surge nights with one doctor. Reject the model if patients arrive in groups, or if the surge rate differs much from 8 an hour.

models.dsl:
title: When to call a second doctor to the emergency department at night
problem: On some nights a surge of patients arrives. The rule calls a second doctor when the k-th patient arrives within 30 minutes. Find the threshold k with the least expected cost.
param psurge = 0.2 "probability of a surge night"
param normal_rate = 3 {patients per hour} "arrival rate on a normal night"
param surge_rate = 8 {patients per hour} "arrival rate on a surge night"
param k = 3 {patients} "threshold of the rule"
param window = 0.5 {hours} "time window"

param miss_cost = 2000 {currency units} "cost of a surge night with one doctor"

ratio false_call = E[(T <= window)*(1 - S)] / E[1 - S] "P(call | normal night)"
ratio detect = E[(T <= window)*S] / E[S] "P(call | surge night)"
mean cost = call_cost*(T <= window) + miss_cost*S*(T > window) {currency units per night}
alt "k = 2": k = 2
alt "k = 3": k = 3
alt "k = 4": k = 4
alt "k = 5": k = 5

models.title: Three shapes of the beta law with the same mean
models.observe: The three laws have the mean 0.3 but different shapes. Beta(0.3, 0.7) is U-shaped, with P(X < 0.1) about 0.43 and P(X > 0.5) about 0.27. Beta(1.5, 3.5) is skewed to the right, with P(X > 0.5) about 0.16, and Beta(30, 70) puts almost all its mass near 0.3. For the concentrated law, the interval for E[X] is about 7 times narrower than for the U-shaped law. Rejection sampling from the uniform proposal is not available when a < 1 or b < 1, because the density is then unbounded.

param b = 0.7 "shape b"

prob above_half = X > 0.5 "P(X > 0.5)"

focus X

models.title: How large an A/B test before the shop launches the new checkout page?
models.decision: Decision: the size of the A/B test before the shop launches page B. The launch rule is P(rate B > rate A) ≥ 0.95 and an expected loss of at most 0.0001. Estimated quantity: P(rate B > rate A) and the expected loss E[max(A − B, 0)] for each test size.
models.reason: Each visitor converts or not, with the rate of the page. After s conversions in n visits, the uniform prior Beta(1, 1) gives the posterior law Beta(1 + s, 1 + n − s). The beta law is the conjugate prior of a binomial count.
models.inputs: The observed rates 4.0 % on page A and 4.6 % on page B are illustrative. Each alternative assumes that a test of its size gives these rates, so the counts are illustrative too. They are 80 and 92 conversions for 2,000 visitors on each page, 200 and 230 for 5,000, and 400 and 460 for 10,000. The loss limit 0.0001 is 0.01 percentage points of conversion rate.
models.dependence: None between the pages: different visitors see A and B, so the two posteriors are independent. The model assumes that the rates do not change during the test. A weekly cycle in the traffic breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of A and B, each as a ratio of gamma values. P(B > A) is the fraction of replicates with B > A, and the expected loss is the mean of max(A − B, 0). The alternatives use the same streams.
models.diagnostics: The page shows no reference here: the quadrature over two concentrated posterior laws needs more work than its budget. A quadrature with a larger budget gives P(B > A) = 0.825, 0.930 and 0.982, and the expected losses 0.00061, 0.00013 and 0.000019, as checks. Other candidate models: a normal approximation of the difference of the rates, and a hierarchical prior from earlier tests.
models.interpretation: The 10,000 test is the smallest test that meets the launch rule. It gives P(B > A) about 0.98 and an expected loss of about 0.00002. The 5,000 test gives P(B > A) about 0.93 and an expected loss of about 0.00013, so it fails both parts of the rule. Reject the model if the conversion rate changes during the test, or if one visitor sees both pages.

models.title: How much buffer to plan for a task with a three-point estimate?
models.decision: Decision: the schedule buffer after the most likely duration of 14 days. Estimated quantity: P(the task ends after the deadline), the expected delay, and the expected cost of the buffer and the delay.
models.reason: PERT, the Program Evaluation and Review Technique, gives a task duration a beta law between the minimum and the maximum duration. This law has bounds, one mode at the most likely value, and a long tail toward the maximum. These properties fit a task that seldom ends early but can end much later.
models.inputs: The minimum 10 days, the most likely 14 days and the maximum 30 days are illustrative values. The PERT shapes are a = 1 + 4(mode − min)/(max − min) = 1.8 and b = 1 + 4(max − mode)/(max − min) = 4.2. The mean duration is (min + 4·mode + max)/6 = 16 days. A reserved day costs 1 and a late day costs 5 thousand currency units, also illustrative values.
models.dependence: None: the model has one task. In a project, the tasks on one path share causes of delay, so their durations are dependent. A sum of independent PERT durations then understates the spread of the project duration.
models.method: Independent draws of X ~ Beta(1.8, 4.2), and T = 10 + 20X days. The estimators are the fraction of late replicates and the means of the delay and the cost. The three buffers use the same streams.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by adaptive quadrature over the one beta variable. For the 6-day buffer, P(T > 20) = 0.142 and the expected delay is 0.30 days. Other candidate models: the triangular law on the same three points, with the larger mean 18 days, and a lognormal law with no upper bound.
models.interpretation: The 6-day buffer gives the least expected cost, about 7.5 thousand currency units, and its P(late) of about 0.14 meets the limit 0.2. The 2-day buffer is late with probability 0.45. The 10-day buffer is seldom late but costs about 10.1. Reject the model if past tasks of this kind often took longer than the stated maximum, because the beta law has no mass above it.

models.dsl:
title: How much buffer to plan for a task with a three-point estimate?
problem: The team gives a minimum, a most likely and a maximum duration for a task. A buffer after the most likely duration sets the deadline. Find the buffer that balances the cost of reserved days and the cost of a late task.
param tmin = 10 {days} "minimum duration"
param tmode = 14 {days} "most likely duration"
param tmax = 30 {days} "maximum duration"
param a = 1 + 4*(tmode - tmin)/(tmax - tmin) "PERT shape a"
param b = 1 + 4*(tmax - tmode)/(tmax - tmin) "PERT shape b"
param buffer = 6 {days} "buffer after the most likely duration"
param day_cost = 1 {thousand currency units per day} "cost of one reserved day"
param late_cost = 5 {thousand currency units per day} "penalty for each day after the deadline"
X ~ beta(a = a, b = b) {fraction of the range}
T := tmin + (tmax - tmin)*X {days} "task duration"
late := max(T - tmode - buffer, 0) {days} "days after the deadline"
prob overrun = T > tmode + buffer "the task ends after the deadline"
mean delay = late {days}
mean cost = day_cost*buffer + late_cost*late {thousand currency units}
alt "Buffer 2 days": buffer = 2
alt "Buffer 6 days": buffer = 6
alt "Buffer 10 days": buffer = 10
minimise cost
require overrun <= 0.2
focus T

models.title: Which inspection policy for the lots of a supplier?
models.decision: Decision: the inspection policy for each lot from the supplier. A bad lot has more than 5 % defects. Estimated quantity: the expected cost of a lot, the expected number of defective units at the customer, and P(a bad lot reaches the customer).
models.reason: The process of the supplier drifts, so the defect fraction p differs from lot to lot. The beta law is the usual model for a fraction on [0, 1] that varies between groups. Given p, the number of defects in a random sample is binomial.
models.inputs: Lots of 2,000 units and a defect fraction p ~ Beta(2, 98) with mean 0.02 are illustrative values. So are the inspection cost 0.5 for each unit and the cost 20 for each defective unit at the customer. Full inspection finds and replaces each defective unit. The sample rule inspects 50 units and sends the lot to full inspection when the sample has more than 1 defect.
models.dependence: The defect count K depends on p: K ~ Binomial(50, p) given p. The binomial count ignores the finite lot, a small error for 50 units out of 2,000. Lots are independent. A run of bad lots after a process change breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws: first p from the beta law, then K given p. The estimators are means and fractions over the replicates. In the model, the alternative with n = 0 and c = 0 accepts every lot. The alternative with n = 0 and c = −1 sends every lot to full inspection. The alternatives use the same streams.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over p and a sum over the values of K. P(p > 0.05) = 0.039 is the share of bad lots. Other candidate models: a hypergeometric sample count for small lots, and a mixture of two process states in place of the beta law.
models.interpretation: The rule 'sample 50, accept if K ≤ 1' gives the least expected cost, about 741 for each lot. No inspection costs 800 and full inspection costs 1,000. The rule sends a bad lot to the customer with probability 0.0075, below the limit 0.01. No inspection fails the limit, with 0.039. Reject the model if the defect fractions of consecutive lots are correlated.

models.dsl:
title: Which inspection policy for the lots of a supplier?
problem: The defect fraction changes from lot to lot. Inspection costs money, and a defective unit that reaches the customer costs more. Find the inspection policy with the least expected cost for each lot.
param N = 2000 {units} "units in one lot"
param a = 2 "beta shape a of the defect fraction"
param b = 98 "beta shape b; the mean fraction is a/(a + b) = 0.02"
param n = 50 {units} "units in the sample"
param c = 1 {defects} "largest defect count in the sample that accepts the lot"
param inspect_cost = 0.5 {currency units} "cost to inspect one unit"
param escape_cost = 20 {currency units} "cost of one defective unit at the customer"
p ~ beta(a = a, b = b) {fraction} "defect fraction of the lot"
K ~ binomial(n = n, p = p) {defects} "defects in the sample"
full := K > c "the lot goes to full inspection"
mean cost = inspect_cost*n + if(full, inspect_cost*(N - n), escape_cost*p*(N - n)) {currency units per lot}
mean escaped = if(full, 0, p*(N - n)) {units per lot} "defective units sent to the customer"
prob bad_accepted = (K <= c) and (p > 0.05) "a lot with more than 5 % defects goes to the customer"
alt "Inspect none": n = 0; c = 0
alt "Inspect all": n = 0; c = -1
alt "Sample 50, accept if K ≤ 1": n = 50; c = 1
minimise cost
require bad_accepted <= 0.01
focus p

models.title: The concentration of the Dirichlet law sets the spread
models.observe: The mean share E[X1] is 0.5 for each c, and the page computes this reference by linearity. The spread falls as c grows: P(X1 > 0.7) is about 0.37 for c = 1, 0.10 for c = 10 and near 0 for c = 100. With c = 1 a share is often almost 0, and P(X3 < 0.01) is about 0.37. The marginal law of X1 is Beta(0.5c, 0.5c). Its exact tail values are 0.369, 0.0988 and 0.0000156, and the first two agree with the estimates. For c = 100 a run of 65,536 replicates expects only about 1 hit, so its estimate is 0 or a small multiple of 0.000015. The page shows no reference for these probabilities, because it does not integrate over a vector law.

models.title: When can a news desk call a three-party race from a poll?
models.decision: Decision: the poll size that lets the news desk call the race for party A. The desk calls the race when P(A has the largest share) ≥ 0.95. Estimated quantity: P(A has the largest share), P(A > 50 %), and the expected cost of the poll and of a wrong call.
models.reason: Each respondent names one of three parties, so the poll counts are multinomial. With the uniform prior Dirichlet(1, 1, 1), the posterior law of the three vote shares is Dirichlet(1 + counts). The Dirichlet law is the conjugate prior of a multinomial count.
models.inputs: The poll shares 46 %, 42 % and 12 % are illustrative. Each alternative assumes that a poll of its size gives these shares, so the counts are illustrative too. An interview costs 20 and a wrong call costs 200,000 currency units, also illustrative values.
models.dependence: The three shares are negatively correlated, because they sum to 1. The Dirichlet law holds this dependence. The model assumes a simple random sample of voters who vote as they answer. Turnout and late changes of opinion break this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of the share vector as normalised gamma values. The estimators are fractions of replicates and means. The alternatives use the same streams.
models.diagnostics: The page has no quadrature for a vector law. Only the mean lead E[X1 − X2] has a reference, by linearity: (nA − nB)/(n + 3) for a poll of n, about 0.040. The marginal law Beta(1 + nA, 2 + nB + nC) of X1 gives the exact P(A > 50 %): 0.034, 0.0052, 0.00016 and 0.0000002. Other candidate models: a design effect for a cluster sample, and a model of turnout.
models.interpretation: The poll of 1,000 gives the least expected cost, about 38,000. But its P(A leads) of about 0.91 is below the threshold 0.95. The poll of 2,000 is the best poll that meets the threshold. It has P(A leads) of about 0.97 and a cost of about 45,600. P(A > 50 %) stays small, so the desk cannot report a majority. Reject the model if the poll misses groups of voters, because the posterior then has the wrong centre.

models.title: How much capacity to give the video queue of a backbone link?
models.decision: Decision: the capacity of the video queue at the daily peak: keep 6 Gbit/s, or upgrade to 6.5 or 7 Gbit/s. Estimated quantity: P(the video load is more than the queue capacity) on one day, the expected excess load, and the expected daily cost.
models.reason: The daily traffic mix is a vector of shares with the sum 1. The Dirichlet law is the usual model for random shares. Its mean gives the typical mix, and its concentration sets the change from day to day. Each share has a beta marginal law, and the shares are negatively correlated.
models.inputs: The total peak load of 10 Gbit/s and the concentration 40 are illustrative values. So is the mean mix: 55 % video, 25 % web, 5 % voice and 15 % backup. The upgrades cost 8 and 20 currency units a day. Each Gbit/s of video load above the capacity costs 100 currency units, also an illustrative value.
models.dependence: The shares of one day are dependent through their sum. The model fixes the total peak load at 10 Gbit/s and makes the days independent. A growth trend in the total load, or a week with a large sports event, breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of the share vector as normalised gamma values. The estimators are the fraction of days with an overflow and the means of the excess and the cost. The alternatives use the same streams.
models.diagnostics: The page has no quadrature for a vector law, so only the mean video load 10·E[X1] = 5.5 Gbit/s has a reference, by linearity. The video share alone has the law Beta(22, 18), which gives the exact overflow probabilities 0.265, 0.100 and 0.024 for the three capacities. Other candidate models: a random total load, and a time series of the mix with dependence between days.
models.interpretation: The upgrade to 6.5 Gbit/s gives the least expected cost, about 11.3 a day, but it overflows on about 10 % of days. Only the upgrade to 7 Gbit/s meets the limit of 5 %, with P(overflow) about 0.024 and a cost of about 20.6 a day. Reject the model if the video share of one day predicts the share of the next day.

models.dsl:
title: How much capacity to give the video queue of a backbone link?
problem: The shares of video, web, voice and backup traffic change from day to day. The video queue overflows when the video load at the daily peak is more than its capacity. Find the capacity upgrade with the least expected cost.
param load = 10 {Gbit/s} "total load at the daily peak"
param conc = 40 "concentration of the daily mix"
param cap = 6 {Gbit/s} "capacity of the video queue"
param upgrade = 0 {currency units per day} "cost of the upgrade"
param penalty = 100 {currency units per Gbit/s} "cost of each Gbit/s of video load above the capacity at the peak"

alt "Upgrade to 7 Gbit/s": cap = 7; upgrade = 20

models.title: Which measure protects juvenile salmon from a river predator?
models.decision: Decision: the measure that protects juvenile salmon from a river predator: no measure, a seasonal deterrent, or a covered bypass channel. Estimated quantity: P(the salmon take is more than the sustainable take) and the expected cost of the measure and of the excess take.
models.reason: Each prey item in a stomach is one of four prey types, so the counts are multinomial. With the uniform prior Dirichlet(1, 1, 1, 1), the posterior law of the four diet shares is Dirichlet(1 + counts). The shares have the sum 1, so a larger share of salmon leaves less for the other prey.
models.inputs: The counts of 18 salmon, 11 sculpin, 7 crayfish and 4 other prey items are illustrative. The predators eat 20,000 prey items in a season, and the salmon run can sustain a take of 7,000 fish. Each fish above that take costs 0.02 thousand currency units. The deterrent costs 20 and removes 30 % of the salmon take. The channel costs 60 and removes 60 %. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The four shares are dependent through their sum. The model assumes that each prey item is an independent draw from the diet. The prey items of one stomach often come from one meal, so they cluster, and the posterior is then too narrow.
models.method: Independent draws of the share vector as normalised gamma values. The estimators are fractions of replicates and the means of the take and the cost. The diet does not depend on the measure, so P(salmon share > 0.4) is the same for each alternative. The alternatives use the same streams.
models.diagnostics: The page has no quadrature for a vector law. Only the expected take has a reference, by linearity. It is 20,000·(19/44) times the fraction that the measure keeps: about 8,640, 6,050 and 3,450 fish. The salmon share alone has the law Beta(19, 25), which gives the exact P(X1 > 0.4) = 0.660. For the three measures, it gives P(take > 7,000) = 0.865, 0.180 and almost 0. Other candidate models: a Dirichlet-multinomial model with one cluster for each stomach, and diet shares that change with the season.
models.interpretation: The seasonal deterrent gives the least expected cost, about 22 thousand currency units. However, its P(take > 7,000) is about 0.18, above the limit 0.1. The covered channel meets the limit and costs 60. Salmon are more than 40 % of the diet with probability about 0.66, and the main prey with probability about 0.89. Reject the model if the stomach samples come from a few predators only, because the prey counts are then not independent.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Which measure protects juvenile salmon from a river predator?
problem: The stomach contents of a predator give counts of four prey types. The diet shares are uncertain, so the take of juvenile salmon is uncertain. Find the protection measure with the least expected cost and a small risk of an excess take.
param n1 = 18 {prey items} "juvenile salmon in the stomach samples"
param n2 = 11 {prey items} "sculpin in the samples"
param n3 = 7 {prey items} "crayfish in the samples"
param n4 = 4 {prey items} "other prey in the samples"
param eaten = 20000 {prey items per season} "prey items that the predators eat"
param safe = 7000 {fish per season} "largest take that the salmon run can sustain"
param reduction = 0 "fraction of the salmon take that the measure removes"
param measure_cost = 0 {thousand currency units} "cost of the measure for one season"
param damage = 0.02 {thousand currency units per fish} "cost of each fish above the sustainable take"
X ~ dirichlet(alpha = [1 + n1, 1 + n2, 1 + n3, 1 + n4]) {diet shares} "shares of salmon, sculpin, crayfish and other prey"
take := eaten*X[1]*(1 - reduction) {fish per season} "salmon that the predators eat"
prob over40 = X[1] > 0.4 "salmon are more than 40 % of the diet"
prob main_prey = X[1] > max(X[2], X[3], X[4]) "salmon are the main prey"
prob unsafe = take > safe "the take is more than the sustainable take"
mean take_mean = take {fish per season} "expected salmon take"
mean cost = measure_cost + damage*max(take - safe, 0) {thousand currency units}
alt "No measure": reduction = 0; measure_cost = 0
alt "Seasonal deterrent": reduction = 0.3; measure_cost = 20
alt "Covered bypass channel": reduction = 0.6; measure_cost = 60
minimise cost
require unsafe <= 0.1
focus X[1]

models.title: The chi-square law is a sum of squared normal values
models.observe: Under the normal approximation N(ν, 2ν), each tail beyond 2 standard deviations has the probability 0.0228. The exact upper tail is about 0.050 for ν = 1, 0.045 for ν = 5 and 0.035 for ν = 30. Thus the normal approximation is poor in the tails for small ν. For ν = 30 it is still too small for the upper tail and too large for the lower tail. The lower tail is 0 for ν = 1 and 5, because ν − 2√(2ν) is below 0, and about 0.008 for ν = 30. The page draws X as a sum of ν squared standard normal values, and the estimate of E[X] is near ν.
models.dsl:
title: The chi-square law is a sum of squared normal values
problem: The sum of ν squared standard normal values has the chi-square law with ν degrees of freedom. Compare its two tails with the normal approximation for ν = 1, 5 and 30.
param nu = 5 {degrees of freedom}
X ~ chisq(nu = nu)
prob upper = X > nu + 2*sqrt(2*nu) "P(X > ν + 2√(2ν)); the normal approximation gives 0.0228"
prob lower = X < nu - 2*sqrt(2*nu) "P(X < ν − 2√(2ν)); the normal approximation gives 0.0228"
mean m = X "E[X] = ν"
alt "ν = 1": nu = 1
alt "ν = 5": nu = 5
alt "ν = 30": nu = 30
focus X

models.title: Where to set the alarm limit of an S chart for a shaft grinder?
models.decision: Decision: the alarm limit on the sample standard deviation S of 5 parts. Estimated quantity: for one sample, P(false alarm) in control and P(alarm) after a fault that raises σ from 20 to 30 µm.
models.reason: Let the part dimensions be independent and normal with standard deviation σ. Then (n − 1)S²/σ² has the chi-square law with n − 1 degrees of freedom. Thus the alarm probability of an S chart is a chi-square tail probability.
models.inputs: Samples of n = 5 parts, σ = 20 µm in control and σ = 30 µm after a fault are illustrative values. The alternatives are the limits 35, 37, 40 and 43 µm on S. The limit on false alarms is 0.005 for each sample, about one false alarm in 200 hours.
models.dependence: None: the parts of one sample are independent, and the model looks at one sample. Tool wear makes consecutive parts dependent, and the chi-square law then does not hold.
models.method: One chi-square variable V gives both cases: S² = σ²V/(n − 1), with σ = 20 µm or 30 µm. The estimators are the fractions of replicates with S above the limit. The alternatives use the same streams.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over V. They agree with the closed form P(χ²(4) > 4L²/σ²) for the limit L. E[S²] = σ² = 400 µm² has a reference by linearity. For the 40 µm limit, P(false alarm) = 0.0030 and P(alarm after a fault) = 0.130. Other candidate models: a range chart, and a chart of the exponentially weighted mean of S².
models.interpretation: The 40 µm limit gives the best detection, P(alarm) about 0.13 after a fault, among the limits with P(false alarm) ≤ 0.005. The 35 and 37 µm limits detect more, but they give false alarms with probability 0.016 and 0.008. Reject the model if the part dimensions have a heavier tail than the normal law, because the chi-square law then understates the false alarms.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Where to set the alarm limit of an S chart for a shaft grinder?
problem: Every hour an operator measures 5 parts and computes the sample standard deviation S. An alarm stops the machine when S is more than a limit. Find the limit that detects a larger spread best with few false alarms.
param n = 5 {parts} "parts in each sample"
param sigma0 = 20 {µm} "process standard deviation in control"
param sigma1 = 30 {µm} "process standard deviation after a fault"
param limit = 40 {µm} "alarm limit on S"
V ~ chisq(nu = n - 1) "V = 4S²/σ², the same law in control and after a fault"
S2 := sigma0^2*V/(n - 1) {µm²} "sample variance in control"
S2f := sigma1^2*V/(n - 1) {µm²} "sample variance after a fault"
prob false_alarm = S2 > limit^2 "alarm when the process is in control"
prob detect = S2f > limit^2 "alarm after a fault"
mean var_in = S2 {µm²} "E[S²] = σ² in control"
alt "Limit 35 µm": limit = 35
alt "Limit 37 µm": limit = 37
alt "Limit 40 µm": limit = 40
alt "Limit 43 µm": limit = 43
maximise detect
require false_alarm <= 0.005
focus V

models.title: Which receiver class meets a 95 % position specification?
models.decision: Decision: the receiver class for a survey of 2,000 fixes. The specification asks for 95 % of the fixes within 5 m. Estimated quantity: P(error radius > 5 m), the mean squared error, and the expected cost of the rent and of the fixes measured again.
models.reason: The errors in the east, north and up directions are independent and normal, each with mean 0 and standard deviation σ. The squared error radius divided by σ² is then a sum of 3 squared standard normal values. This sum has the chi-square law with 3 degrees of freedom.
models.inputs: The classes with σ = 1.0, 1.5 and 2.5 m and their rents 1,200, 500 and 200 are illustrative values. So is the cost 3 of a fix measured again. The model assumes the same σ in the 3 directions. On real receivers the vertical error is larger.
models.dependence: None: the 3 coordinate errors are independent with equal σ, and the fixes are independent. The errors of real receivers are correlated in time, so fixes close in time fail together.
models.method: Independent draws of Q ~ χ²(3), and R = σ√Q. The estimators are the fraction of replicates with R > 5 m and the means of σ²Q and of the cost. The alternatives use the same streams.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over Q, and E[σ²Q] = 3σ² by linearity. The 95 % quantile of χ²(3) is 7.81, so the class with σ = 1.5 m puts 95 % of the fixes within 4.2 m. Other candidate models: a larger vertical σ, and a heavier tail from multipath errors.
models.interpretation: Class 2, with σ = 1.5 m, gives the least expected cost, about 567, and its P(R > 5 m) is about 0.011. Class 3 has the lowest rent but fails the specification with P(R > 5 m) about 0.26. Reject the model if the 3 errors have different σ or a common bias, because R²/σ² then does not have the chi-square law.
