models.dsl:
title: Which receiver class meets a 95 % position specification?
problem: A survey needs 95 % of its 3-D position fixes within 5 m of the true point. Each coordinate error is normal with standard deviation σ. Find the receiver class with the least cost that meets the specification.
param sigma = 1.5 {m} "standard deviation of each coordinate error"
param r = 5 {m} "radius of the specification"
param rent = 500 {currency units} "rent of the receiver for the project"
param points = 2000 {fixes} "fixes in the project"
param remeasure = 3 {currency units} "cost to measure one fix again"
Q ~ chisq(nu = 3) "squared 3-D error divided by σ²"
R := sigma*sqrt(Q) {m} "error radius"
prob outside = R > r "the fix is outside the specification"
mean mse = sigma^2*Q {m²} "mean squared error, 3σ²"
mean cost = rent + points*remeasure*(R > r) {currency units} "rent plus the cost of fixes measured again"
alt "Class 1: σ = 1.0 m": sigma = 1; rent = 1200
alt "Class 2: σ = 1.5 m": sigma = 1.5; rent = 500
alt "Class 3: σ = 2.5 m": sigma = 2.5; rent = 200
minimise cost
require outside <= 0.05
focus Q

models.title: Which turbine model gives the most value at a windy site?
models.decision: Decision: the turbine model for a site with a mean wind speed of about 7 m/s. Estimated quantity: the mean power, P(no output), and the expected net value for each year.
models.reason: In a common model, the two horizontal components of the wind are independent normal values with mean 0 and the same σ. Then V²/σ² is a sum of 2 squared standard normal values, which has the chi-square law with 2 degrees of freedom. Thus V = σ√W has the Rayleigh law, the Weibull law with shape 2.
models.inputs: σ = 5.6 m/s gives the mean wind speed σ√(π/2), about 7.0 m/s. The three power curves, the annual costs 300, 480 and 420 thousand currency units and the price 60 currency units/MWh are illustrative values. The power rises as V³ from the cut-in speed to the rated speed. It stays at the rated power up to the cut-out speed, and it is 0 above that speed.
models.dependence: None in this model: each replicate is one independent hour of wind. Real wind speeds are correlated over hours. This does not change the means, but it changes the variance of the energy of one year.
models.method: Independent draws of W ~ χ²(2), and V = σ√W. The estimators are the mean power, the fraction of replicates with no output, and the mean net value. The three models use the same streams.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over W. P(V < 3 m/s) = 1 − exp(−9/(2σ²)) = 0.134 is the no-output probability of Model A, with a very small addition above 25 m/s. Other candidate models: a Weibull law fitted to the measured wind of the site, and a mean wind that changes with the season.
models.interpretation: Model C, the low-wind turbine, gives the largest net value, about 80 thousand currency units a year. Its mean power is about 950 kW, and it gives no output in about 10 % of hours. Model B has the largest rated power but seldom reaches it, so its net value is negative. Reject the model if the measured wind speeds do not fit a Weibull law with a shape near 2.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Which turbine model gives the most value at a windy site?
problem: The two horizontal wind components are normal with mean 0, so the wind speed has the Rayleigh law. Each turbine has a power curve with a cut-in, a rated and a cut-out speed. Find the turbine with the largest net value.
param sigma = 5.6 {m/s} "standard deviation of each wind component"
param rated = 2000 {kW} "rated power"
param vin = 3 {m/s} "cut-in speed"
param vr = 12 {m/s} "rated speed"
param vout = 25 {m/s} "cut-out speed"
param annual = 300 {thousand currency units per year} "annual cost of the turbine"
param price = 60 {currency units per MWh} "price of energy"
W ~ chisq(nu = 2) "V²/σ², a sum of 2 squared standard normal values"
V := sigma*sqrt(W) {m/s} "wind speed"
power := if(V >= vout, 0, rated*min(max((V^3 - vin^3)/(vr^3 - vin^3), 0), 1)) {kW} "power output"
mean avg_power = power {kW} "mean power"
prob no_output = V < vin or V >= vout "the turbine gives no power"
mean net = 8.76*price*power/1000 - annual {thousand currency units per year} "value of the energy less the annual cost"
alt "Model A: 2.0 MW": rated = 2000; vin = 3; vr = 12; vout = 25; annual = 300
alt "Model B: 3.0 MW": rated = 3000; vin = 3.5; vr = 13; vout = 25; annual = 480
alt "Model C: 2.5 MW, low wind": rated = 2500; vin = 2.5; vr = 10.5; vout = 22; annual = 420
maximise net
focus V

models.title: Heavy tails of Student's t law
models.observe: On the log survival plot, P(|T| > 4) is about 0.090 for ν = 1.5, 0.028 for ν = 3 and 0.00038 for ν = 30. For ν = 30 the law is near the normal law, but this tail is still 6 times the normal value 0.000063. The mean of T exists for ν > 1, and the variance only for ν > 2. For ν = 3 and ν = 30 the page draws a CLT interval for m. For ν = 1.5 the variance is infinite, so the page draws no CLT interval for m. For ν = 1.5 the estimate of m jumps when a very large value comes, although its reference value is 0.
models.dsl:
title: Heavy tails of Student's t law
problem: The t law has polynomial tails. A small ν gives rare, very large values, and a large ν gives a law near the standard normal law.
param nu = 3 "degrees of freedom ν"
T ~ student(nu = nu) "standard t value"
mean m = T "sample mean of T"
prob far = abs(T) > 4 "P(|T| > 4)"
alt "ν = 1.5": nu = 1.5
alt "ν = 3": nu = 3
alt "ν = 30": nu = 30
focus T

models.title: Which outlier rule to apply to repeated length measurements?
models.decision: Decision: the rejection limit k, in units of the error scale s, for single measured values of a gauge block. Estimated quantity: P(the rule rejects a good value), and P(the rule keeps a value with a gross error of 4 µm).
models.reason: The error of one measured value is normal for a given precision. The precision changes between measurements with the temperature, the contact force and the operator. If the precision has a gamma law, the error has the t law: a scale mixture of normal laws, with heavier tails.
models.inputs: The block deviates by m = 0.2 µm from its nominal length. The error scale is s = 0.5 µm, with ν = 4 degrees of freedom. The rule must catch a gross error of g = 4 µm, which is 8 s. These values are illustrative. The rule compares each value with the reference value m, from the median of many values.
models.dependence: None: the errors of different measurements are independent. A temperature drift during one day breaks this assumption, because it moves many values together.
models.method: Independent draws of T. Each replicate gives one good value m + s·T and one value m + s·T + g with the gross error, from the same T. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams, so the paired differences between the limits are precise.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the quantile function of T: P(|T| > k) and P(|T + 8| ≤ k). A normal model gives P(|Z| > 3) = 0.0027 and P(|Z| > 4) = 0.00006. It understates the false rejections by a factor of about 15 at k = 3 and about 250 at k = 4. Other candidate models: the normal law, and a normal law with a mixture of gross errors of random size.
models.interpretation: k = 5 meets the limit of 1 % false rejections with the least risk to keep the gross error. P(the rule rejects a good value) is about 0.0075, and P(it keeps the gross error) about 0.020. Under the t model, k = 3 and k = 4 reject about 4.0 % and 1.6 % of good values. A normal model would accept k = 3. Reject the model if many repeated values show tails lighter than the t law, or if the values drift with time.

models.dsl:
title: Which outlier rule to apply to repeated length measurements?
problem: A laboratory measures the length of a gauge block many times, and a few measured values have a gross error. A rule rejects each value that is more than k·s from the reference value. Find the k that rejects few good values and still catches a gross error of 4 µm.
param m = 0.2 {µm} "deviation of the block from its nominal length"
param s = 0.5 {µm} "scale of the error of a good value"
param nu = 4 "degrees of freedom of the error law"
param g = 4 {µm} "smallest gross error that the rule must catch"
param k = 3 "rejection limit in units of s"
T ~ student(nu = nu) "standard error of one measured value"
good := m + s*T {µm} "a good measured value"
gross := m + s*T + g {µm} "a measured value with the gross error g"
prob false_reject = abs(good - m) > k*s "the rule rejects a good value"
prob gross_kept = abs(gross - m) <= k*s "the rule keeps a value with the gross error g"
alt "k = 3": k = 3
alt "k = 4": k = 4
alt "k = 5": k = 5
alt "k = 6": k = 6
minimise gross_kept
require false_reject <= 0.01
focus good

models.title: How large can a stock position be under a daily loss limit?
models.decision: Decision: the size of a stock position. Estimated quantity: P(the daily loss exceeds 250 thousand currency units), the expected loss beyond this limit, and the expected daily profit.
models.reason: The volatility of a stock changes from day to day. A normal daily return with a gamma law for its precision gives the t law. With ν = 4, the tail probability decreases as a power of the loss, as in many return series.
models.inputs: A mean return m = 0.0003 a day, a scale s = 0.0085 and ν = 4 are illustrative values. The standard deviation of the return is s·√2, about 1.2 % a day. The loss limit is 250 thousand currency units a day. The positions are 3, 5, 7 and 9 million currency units.
models.dependence: None in this model: it describes one day only. Real returns show volatility clusters, so a large loss makes the next large loss more likely. A model with a volatility that changes with time describes that.
models.method: Independent draws of T. The loss of the day is −V(m + s·T). The estimators are the fraction of days with a breach, and the means of the excess loss and of the profit. The alternatives share the streams, so one draw of T gives the loss of each position.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the quantile function of T for P(breach). The expected profit V·m is exact by linearity. The excess loss has no reference: the page cannot show that its moments exist, although its mean is finite for ν > 1. A normal model with the same standard deviation gives P(breach) = 0.0014 for 7 million, against 0.0066 for the t model. Other candidate models: the normal law, and a skewed t law for a market with crashes.
models.interpretation: 7 million is the largest position that meets the limit. Its P(breach) is about 0.0066, and its expected loss beyond the limit about 0.6 thousand currency units a day. 9 million gives P(breach) of about 0.015, above 0.01. A normal model would accept 9 million, with P(breach) = 0.0098. Reject the model if the past fraction of days beyond the limit is far from the model value, or if large losses come in clusters.

models.dsl:
title: How large can a stock position be under a daily loss limit?
problem: Daily returns of a stock have heavier tails than the normal law. A trader has a daily loss limit. Find the largest position whose loss exceeds the limit on at most 1 day in 100.
param V = 5000 {thousand currency units} "size of the position"
param m = 0.0003 "mean daily return"
param s = 0.0085 "scale of the daily return"
param nu = 4 "degrees of freedom of the return law"
param limit = 250 {thousand currency units} "daily loss limit"
T ~ student(nu = nu) "standard t value of the day"
loss := -V*(m + s*T) {thousand currency units} "loss of the day"
prob breach = loss > limit "the loss of the day exceeds the limit"
mean excess = max(loss - limit, 0) {thousand currency units} "expected loss beyond the limit"
mean pnl = V*(m + s*T) {thousand currency units} "expected profit of the day"
alt "3 million": V = 3000
alt "5 million": V = 5000
alt "7 million": V = 7000
alt "9 million": V = 9000
maximise pnl
require breach <= 0.01
focus loss

models.title: Which go threshold for a small pilot trial?
models.decision: Decision: the go threshold c for the t statistic of a pilot trial with 8 patients. Estimated quantity: P(go) when the treatment has no effect, and P(go) when the true effect is 0.8 standard deviations.
models.reason: The changes in blood pressure of the patients are independent normal values. The t statistic is the mean change divided by its standard error. With no effect, it has the t law with n − 1 = 7 degrees of freedom. This is the classical sampling law of t.
models.inputs: The values n = 8 patients, a true effect δ = 0.8 standard deviations and the thresholds 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 are illustrative. The limit for a false go is 0.1, a one-sided level that pilot trials often accept.
models.dependence: The changes of different patients are independent. The model draws T and U = Σz², the sum of squares of the standardised changes. With no effect, U has the χ²(8) law and is independent of T, because T depends only on the direction of the vector of changes.
models.method: Independent draws of T and U. The sum of squares about the mean is V = U/(1 + T²/7). The t statistic of the same patients with the effect is T + δ√n/√(V/7). The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: P(false go) = P(T > c) is an exact closed form from the t survival function, for example 0.089 at c = 1.5. P(true go) has no reference, because its quadrature over T and U exceeds the budget of the page. The noncentral t law gives 0.895, 0.776 and 0.618. A normal model of the statistic gives P(false go) = 0.067 at c = 1.5, so it understates the false go decisions. Other candidate models: the normal approximation of the statistic, and a sign test for changes that are not normal.
models.interpretation: c = 1.5 meets the limit of 0.1 with P(false go) of about 0.089. It gives a go for the true effect with a probability of about 0.78. c = 1.0 gives too many false go decisions, about 0.175. c = 2.0 gives a go for the true effect with a probability of only about 0.62. Reject the model if the changes are skewed or have outliers, because the t law then does not describe the statistic.

models.dsl:
title: Which go threshold for a small pilot trial?
problem: A pilot trial measures the change in blood pressure of 8 patients. The team starts a large trial when the t statistic exceeds a threshold. Find the threshold that limits false go decisions and keeps a good chance to detect a real effect.
param n = 8 {patients}
param delta = 0.8 "true effect, in standard deviations of the change"
param c = 1.5 "go threshold for the t statistic"
T ~ student(nu = n - 1) "t statistic of the trial when the treatment has no effect"
U ~ chisq(nu = n) "sum of squares of the standardised changes when there is no effect"
V := U/(1 + T^2/(n - 1)) "sum of squares about the mean, (n − 1)S²/σ²"
t_eff := T + delta*sqrt(n)/sqrt(V/(n - 1)) "t statistic of the same patients with the effect delta"
prob false_go = T > c "a go when the treatment has no effect"
prob true_go = t_eff > c "a go when the effect is delta"
alt "c = 1.0": c = 1
alt "c = 1.5": c = 1.5
alt "c = 2.0": c = 2
maximise true_go
require false_go <= 0.1
focus T

models.title: The heavy right tail of the F law
models.observe: The mean of F exists only for d₂ > 2, and the variance only for d₂ > 4. The reference means d₂/(d₂ − 2) are 3, 1.67 and 1.07. For d₂ = 5 and d₂ = 30 the page draws a CLT interval for m. For d₂ = 3 the variance is infinite, so the page draws no CLT interval for m. P(F > 3) is about 0.198, 0.118 and 0.0096. On the log axis the survival function of d₂ = 3 decreases slowly, as a power of x.
models.dsl:
title: The heavy right tail of the F law
problem: The F law with few denominator degrees of freedom d₂ has a heavy right tail. Its mean exists only for d₂ > 2, and its variance only for d₂ > 4.
param d1 = 10 "numerator degrees of freedom d₁"
param d2 = 5 "denominator degrees of freedom d₂"
F ~ fisher(d1 = d1, d2 = d2) "F value"
mean m = F "sample mean of F"
prob over3 = F > 3 "P(F > 3)"
alt "d₂ = 3": d2 = 3
alt "d₂ = 5": d2 = 5
alt "d₂ = 30": d2 = 30
focus F

models.title: Which critical value for the fertiliser trials of a research station?
models.decision: Decision: the critical value c of the F test in the fertiliser trials of a research station. Estimated quantity: P(a claim) for a fertiliser with no effect, and P(a claim) for a fertiliser with a real effect.
models.reason: In an analysis of variance with normal plot errors, the F statistic is the ratio of 2 independent mean squares. With no treatment effect, it has the F(3, 16) law for 4 treatments on 5 plots each. A real effect gives the noncentral F law. It is a Poisson mixture of the laws of ((3 + 2J)/3)·F(3 + 2J, 16), with J ~ Poisson(λ/2).
models.inputs: A real effect has the noncentrality λ = 9, for example treatment effects of −0.9, −0.3, 0.3 and 0.9 standard deviations of the plot yield. The station accepts at most 3 false claims in 100 trials of fertilisers with no effect. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The trials of different fertilisers are independent. Inside one trial the plots are independent, with one error variance for all treatments. A soil gradient across the field breaks this assumption, and a block design then removes it.
models.method: Independent draws of F0 for a trial with no effect. For a trial with an effect, independent draws of J ~ Poisson(λ/2) and of F with 3 + 2J numerator degrees of freedom. The statistic F·(3 + 2J)/3 then has the noncentral F law. The estimators are fractions of replicates, and the alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: P(F0 > c) is an exact closed form: 3.24 is the tabulated 5 % critical value, and 5.29 the 1 % value. P(a claim with an effect) has no reference, because its quadrature exceeds the budget of the page. A sum over J of F survival values gives 0.724, 0.594, 0.472 and 0.308. Other candidate models: a mixed model with random block effects, and the Kruskal–Wallis test of ranks for yields that are not normal.
models.interpretation: c = 4.0 detects the most real effects within the limit. P(a claim) is about 0.027 with no effect, and about 0.47 with the effect λ = 9. c = 3.24 gives about 0.050 false claims, above the limit of 0.03. If 30 % of the tested fertilisers work, about 1 claim in 9 is false at c = 4.0. Reject the model if the residuals are not normal, or if the error variance differs between treatments.

models.dsl:
title: Which critical value for the fertiliser trials of a research station?
problem: A research station tests many fertilisers each year, each in a trial of 4 treatments on 5 plots. It claims an effect when the F statistic of the analysis of variance exceeds a critical value. Find the critical value that limits false claims and still finds most real effects.
param lam = 9 "noncentrality of a real effect"
param d1 = 3 "treatment degrees of freedom: 4 treatments − 1"
param d2 = 16 "residual degrees of freedom: 20 plots − 4"
param c = 4 "critical value"
F0 ~ fisher(d1 = d1, d2 = d2) "F statistic of a trial with no treatment effect"
J ~ poisson(lambda = lam/2) "Poisson index of the noncentral chi-square law"
F ~ fisher(d1 = d1 + 2*J, d2 = d2) "F value with d₁ + 2J numerator degrees of freedom"
stat := F*(d1 + 2*J)/d1 "F statistic of a trial with a real effect"
prob false_claim = F0 > c "a claim for a fertiliser with no effect"
prob detect = stat > c "a claim for a fertiliser with a real effect"
alt "c = 2.5": c = 2.5
alt "c = 3.24": c = 3.24
alt "c = 4.0": c = 4
alt "c = 5.29": c = 5.29
maximise detect
require false_claim <= 0.03
focus F0

models.title: When to switch a supplier whose parts vary more?
models.decision: Decision: the switch rule, which is the number of parts to compare and the critical variance ratio c. Estimated quantity: P(a needless switch) when the variances are equal, and P(a switch) when supplier 1 has 3 times the variance.
models.reason: For normal part dimensions, each sample variance is a scaled chi-square value, and the 2 suppliers are independent. The ratio of the sample variances then has the F(n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1) law when the true variances are equal. With a true variance ratio ρ, the ratio is ρ times an F value.
models.inputs: 13 parts from each supplier each quarter, or 26 parts each half-year, are illustrative values. So are the variance ratio ρ = 3 to detect and the limit 0.05 for a needless switch.
models.dependence: None: the parts are independent, and the 2 suppliers are independent. Parts from one batch can share a cause and vary less, which breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of F with parts − 1 degrees of freedom in the numerator and the denominator. A needless switch is the event F > c, and a switch for the ratio ρ is the event ρF > c. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: P(F > c) is an exact closed form from the incomplete beta function, and P(ρF > c) comes from quadrature. The tabulated 5 % critical values are 2.69 for F(12, 12) and 1.96 for F(25, 25). Other candidate models: Levene's test for dimensions that are not normal, and a control chart of the sample standard deviation.
models.interpretation: The half-year rule with c = 2 detects the larger variance with a probability of about 0.84. Its probability of a needless switch is about 0.045. The quarterly rule with c = 3 also meets the limit, but it detects with a probability of only 0.50. The quarterly rule with c = 2.5 switches without need with a probability of 0.063, above the limit. The half-year rule decides later, so a bad supplier stays longer. Reject the model if the dimensions are not normal, because the F test is sensitive to the tails.

models.dsl:
title: When to switch a supplier whose parts vary more?
problem: A plant measures 13 parts from each of 2 suppliers each quarter and compares the sample variances. It can decide each quarter, or pool the parts of a half-year. A switch to the other supplier costs a requalification. Find the switch rule that seldom switches without need and still detects a variance 3 times larger.
param parts = 13 {parts} "parts measured from each supplier for one decision"
param rho = 3 "variance ratio that the rule must detect"
param c = 2.5 "critical variance ratio"
F ~ fisher(d1 = parts - 1, d2 = parts - 1) "ratio of the sample variances when the true variances are equal"
prob needless = F > c "a switch when the true variances are equal"
prob detect = rho*F > c "a switch when supplier 1 has rho times the variance"
alt "Each quarter, c = 2.5": parts = 13; c = 2.5
alt "Each quarter, c = 3": parts = 13; c = 3
alt "Each half-year, c = 2": parts = 26; c = 2
alt "Each half-year, c = 2.2": parts = 26; c = 2.2
maximise detect
require needless <= 0.05
focus F

models.title: How many repeats to compare the precision of 2 analysers?
models.decision: Decision: the number of repeats n on each analyser. Estimated quantity: P(the test rejects equal precision when it holds), P(the test accepts an analyser with 3 times the variance), and the cost.
models.reason: Repeated measurements of one control sample have independent normal errors. The ratio of the 2 sample variances, new over old, then has the F(n − 1, n − 1) law when the precision is equal. A new analyser with ρ times the variance gives ρ times an F value.
models.inputs: The limit L = 2, a worse analyser with ρ = 3 and a cost of 15 currency units for each measurement are illustrative values. The limits are 0.05 for a wrong rejection and 0.15 for a wrong acceptance.
models.dependence: None: the measurements are independent. A drift during the series breaks this assumption and makes the sample variance too large.
models.method: Independent draws of F. The estimators are the fractions of replicates with F > L and with ρF ≤ L. The cost 2·n·15 is a constant. The alternatives share the streams, but the law of F changes with n.
models.diagnostics: P(F > L) is an exact closed form, and P(ρF ≤ L) comes from quadrature. The cost is exact. With the tabulated 5 % critical value instead of L, for example 1.86 for F(29, 29), the wrong rejection would be 0.05 for each n. Other candidate models: errors with heavier tails than the normal law, which make the F law wrong, and Levene's test for such errors.
models.interpretation: 30 repeats is the least cost that meets both limits. It gives a wrong rejection of about 0.033 and a wrong acceptance of about 0.14, for 900 currency units. 20 repeats give a wrong rejection of about 0.070, above the limit. Reject the model if the measurements drift during the series, or if the errors have heavy tails.

models.dsl:
title: How many repeats to compare the precision of 2 analysers?
problem: A laboratory replaces an analyser only if the new one is at least as precise. It measures one control sample n times on each analyser and rejects the new analyser when the variance ratio new/old exceeds 2. Find the number of repeats that keeps both wrong decisions rare at the least cost.

param L = 2 "rejection limit for the variance ratio new/old"
param rho = 3 "variance ratio of a new analyser that is truly worse"
param cm = 15 {currency units} "cost of one measurement"

prob wrong_reject = F > L "the test rejects equal precision when it holds"
prob wrong_accept = rho*F <= L "the test accepts a new analyser with rho times the variance"
mean cost = 2*n*cm {currency units} "cost of the measurements"
alt "10 repeats": n = 10
alt "20 repeats": n = 20
alt "30 repeats": n = 30
alt "40 repeats": n = 40
minimise cost
require wrong_reject <= 0.05
require wrong_accept <= 0.15
focus F

models.title: Logistic tails against normal tails
models.observe: X has mean 0 and variance 1, as the standard normal law has. P(X > 3) = 1/(1 + e^(3/s)) is about 0.0043, about 3 times the normal value 0.00135. P(X > 1) is about 0.140, below the normal value 0.159, so the logistic law has less mass at the shoulders. On the log axis the survival function is almost a straight line, because the tail decreases as e^(−x/s). Change the plot to the CDF to see the sigmoid 1/(1 + e^(−x/s)).
models.dsl:
title: Logistic tails against normal tails
problem: The logistic law with variance 1 has a sharper peak and heavier tails than the standard normal law. Its CDF is the sigmoid function.
param s = sqrt(3)/pi "scale s, so that the variance s²π²/3 is 1"
X ~ logistic(mu = 0, s = s)
mean m = X "sample mean of X"
prob over1 = X > 1 "P(X > 1)"
prob over3 = X > 3 "P(X > 3)"
focus X

models.title: Which play-off format lets the stronger team win?
models.decision: Decision: the format of a play-off between 2 teams: one game, best of 3 or best of 5. Estimated quantity: the probability that the stronger team wins the series, and the expected number of games played.
models.reason: The Elo model gives each team a performance in each game. The logistic version takes the difference of the 2 performances as logistic, with location d and scale 400/ln 10. Then P(the stronger team wins one game) = 1/(1 + 10^(−d/400)), the Elo formula.
models.inputs: An Elo difference d = 120 points and a target probability of 0.7 are illustrative values. Basketball has no draws, so each game has a winner. The model has no home advantage.
models.dependence: The games are independent, with the same law. Fatigue, injuries and home advantage make the games of a series dependent. The model ignores them.
models.method: Independent draws of 5 performance differences, D repeat 5. The run counts the wins after each game and the games played until one team has the wins it needs. The estimators are means over replicates. The alternatives share the streams, so the same games decide each format.
models.diagnostics: No reference from the page, because D repeats. Closed forms: one game gives p = 1/(1 + 10^(−0.3)), about 0.666. Best of 3 gives p²(3 − 2p), about 0.740. Best of 5 gives p³(10 − 15p + 6p²), about 0.789. The expected numbers of games are 2.445 and 3.964. Other candidate models: the normal version of the Elo model, and a model with home advantage.
models.interpretation: Best of 3 is the shortest format that meets the target 0.7. The stronger team wins it with a probability of about 0.740, in about 2.45 games. One game gives only 0.666. Best of 5 raises the probability to about 0.789, but it takes about 1.5 more games. Reject the model if the results of past series differ from the Elo forecast, or if home games change the results.

models.dsl:
title: Which play-off format lets the stronger team win?
problem: Two basketball teams with an Elo difference of 120 points meet in a play-off. A longer series makes a win of the stronger team more likely, but it takes more games. Find the shortest format that the stronger team wins with a probability of at least 0.7.
param d = 120 {Elo points} "Elo difference of the 2 teams"
param sc = 400/log(10) {Elo points} "logistic scale of the performance difference"
param games = 3 {games} "length of the series: 1, 3 or 5"
param need = (games + 1)/2 {games} "wins needed to take the series"
D ~ logistic(mu = d, s = sc) repeat 5 {Elo points} "performance difference in each game"
w1 := D[1] > 0 {games} "wins of the stronger team after game 1"
w2 := w1 + (D[2] > 0) {games} "wins after game 2"
w3 := w2 + (D[3] > 0) {games} "wins after game 3"
w4 := w3 + (D[4] > 0) {games} "wins after game 4"
w5 := w4 + (D[5] > 0) {games} "wins after game 5"
played := 1 + (max(w1, 1 - w1) < need) + (max(w2, 2 - w2) < need) + (max(w3, 3 - w3) < need) + (max(w4, 4 - w4) < need) {games} "games played until one team has the wins it needs"
wins := if(games == 1, w1, if(games == 3, w3, w5)) {games} "wins of the stronger team if all games are played"
prob series_win = wins >= need "the stronger team wins the series"
mean games_played = played {games} "expected number of games played"
alt "One game": games = 1
alt "Best of 3": games = 3
alt "Best of 5": games = 5
minimise games_played
require series_win >= 0.7
focus D[1]

models.title: Which dose gives an effect in 90 % of patients with the least toxicity?
models.decision: Decision: the dose of a drug, from 20 to 60 mg. Estimated quantity: the probability of the effect, the probability of a toxic reaction, and the probability of the effect without toxicity.
models.reason: Each patient has a tolerance: the least log dose that gives the response. If the tolerances are logistic on the log-dose scale, the probability of a response is the logistic function of the log dose. This is the logit model of dose response.
models.inputs: The median effective dose is 15 mg, with a logistic scale of 0.35. The median toxic dose is 120 mg, with a scale of 0.4. These values are illustrative. The scales are on the natural log-dose scale. The target is an effect in at least 90 % of patients.
models.dependence: The model takes the 2 tolerances of one patient as independent. A patient who absorbs more drug has both responses at a lower dose, so the 2 tolerances can have a positive correlation. A correlation changes P(effect without toxicity), but not the 2 marginal probabilities.
models.method: Independent draws of the 2 tolerances. The estimators are the fractions of patients with each response. The alternatives share the streams, so each simulated patient receives each dose.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the 2 tolerances. Closed form for comparison: P(effect) = 1/(1 + exp(−(ln dose − ln 15)/0.35)), which is 0.943 at 40 mg. Other candidate models: the probit model with normal tolerances, and a model with correlated tolerances.
models.interpretation: 40 mg meets the target with P(effect) of about 0.943. Among the doses that meet it, 40 mg has the least toxicity: P(toxic) is about 0.060. 30 mg gives P(effect) of about 0.879, below 0.9. 60 mg raises P(toxic) to about 0.150. Reject the model if the observed response fractions at the tested doses do not follow a logistic curve in the log dose.

models.dsl:
title: Which dose gives an effect in 90 % of patients with the least toxicity?
problem: Each patient has a tolerance for the effect and a tolerance for toxicity on the log-dose scale. A dose acts when its logarithm exceeds the tolerance. Find the dose that gives an effect in at least 90 % of patients with the least toxicity.
param dose = 40 {mg} "dose"
param ld = log(dose) {log mg} "logarithm of the dose"
param ed50 = 15 {mg} "dose that gives the effect in half of the patients"
param td50 = 120 {mg} "dose that gives toxicity in half of the patients"
param se = 0.35 {log mg} "logistic scale of the effect tolerance"
param st = 0.4 {log mg} "logistic scale of the toxicity tolerance"
Te ~ logistic(mu = log(ed50), s = se) {log mg} "tolerance of the patient for the effect"
Tt ~ logistic(mu = log(td50), s = st) {log mg} "tolerance of the patient for toxicity"
prob effect = ld > Te "the patient has the effect"
prob toxic = ld > Tt "the patient has a toxic reaction"
prob success = ld > Te and ld <= Tt "the effect without toxicity"
alt "20 mg": dose = 20
alt "30 mg": dose = 30
alt "40 mg": dose = 40
alt "60 mg": dose = 60
minimise toxic
require effect >= 0.9
focus Te

models.title: Up to which main-road flow can side-road drivers enter without a signal?
models.decision: Decision: the largest main-road flow at which the junction stays without a signal. Estimated quantity: P(a side-road driver accepts the first gap), P(the driver rejects 4 or more gaps), and the mean number of rejected gaps.
models.reason: Data on gap acceptance often follow a binary logit model: P(accept a gap of length x) = 1/(1 + e^(−(x − μ)/s)). This is the same as a logistic critical gap with location μ and scale s. With Poisson traffic on the main road, the gaps are exponential. So a driver with the critical gap t accepts each gap with probability e^(−q·t).
models.inputs: A median critical gap of 6 s, a logistic scale of 0.6 s and flows of 400 to 700 vehicles per hour are illustrative values. The limit is 15 % of drivers who reject 4 or more gaps.
models.dependence: The model takes each driver as consistent: the same critical gap Tc for each gap. Given Tc, the gaps are independent, so the number of rejected gaps is geometric with p = e^(−q·Tc). The drivers are independent.
models.method: Independent draws of Tc, then of the geometric number N of rejected gaps. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over Tc, with a sum over N, for the probabilities. The mean number of rejected gaps has no reference. N has a geometric law with a random parameter, so the page cannot show that its moments exist. Its value is E[e^(q·Tc)] − 1, which is finite here because q·s < 1. Other candidate models: a log-normal critical gap, and the Cowan model of bunched traffic behind an upstream signal.
models.interpretation: 500 vehicles per hour is the largest flow that meets the limit. At this flow about 10.7 % of drivers reject 4 or more gaps, and about 44 % accept the first gap. At 600 vehicles per hour the share rises to about 16.4 %, above the limit. Above about 500 vehicles per hour the junction thus needs a signal or another measure. Reject the model if the observed gaps are not exponential, for example in platoons behind a signal.

problem: A driver on a side road waits for a gap in the main-road traffic that is longer than the critical gap of the driver. Critical gaps differ between drivers. Find the largest main-road flow at which few drivers must reject many gaps.

alt "700 veh/h": q = 700

models.title: The sharp peak and exponential tails of the Laplace law
models.observe: X has mean 0 and variance 1, as the standard normal law has. P(|X| < 0.1) is about 0.132 against 0.080 for the normal law, so the peak at 0 is sharper. P(|X| > 3) = e^(−3/b) is about 0.0144, about 5 times the normal value 0.0027. The estimate of E|X| is near b = 0.707, below the normal value 0.798.
models.dsl:
title: The sharp peak and exponential tails of the Laplace law
problem: The Laplace law with variance 1 has more mass near 0 and in the far tails than the standard normal law. Its tails decrease as e^(−|x|/b).
param b = 1/sqrt(2) "scale b, so that the variance 2b² is 1"
X ~ laplace(mu = 0, b = b)
prob near0 = abs(X) < 0.1 "P(|X| < 0.1)"
prob far = abs(X) > 3 "P(|X| > 3)"
mean abs_dev = abs(X) "mean absolute deviation E|X|"
focus X

models.title: How much reserve to hold against day-ahead load forecast errors?
models.decision: Decision: the reserve for one hour, from 300 to 750 MW. Estimated quantity: the expected cost of the hour (reserve plus unserved energy), the probability that the error exceeds the reserve, and the expected unserved energy.
models.reason: The weather changes the size of the forecast error from day to day. A normal error whose variance has an exponential law gives the Laplace law: a sharp peak at 0 and exponential tails. Errors of day-ahead load forecasts often show this shape.
models.inputs: A Laplace scale b = 100 MW gives a standard deviation of 141 MW. A reserve costs 5 currency units for each MW and hour, and lost load costs 3000 per MWh. These values are illustrative. The limit for P(error > reserve) is 0.01.
models.dependence: None in this model: it describes one hour only. The errors of adjacent hours have a strong positive correlation, so a shortfall often lasts several hours. A daily model needs a time series of errors.
models.method: Independent draws of the error. The estimators are the fraction of hours with a shortfall, and the means of the unserved energy and of the cost. The alternatives share the streams, so the paired differences of the cost are precise.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the quantile function of the error. Closed forms for comparison: P(error > r) = e^(−r/b)/2, and E[max(error − r, 0)] = (b/2)·e^(−r/b). A normal law with the same standard deviation gives P(error > 600 MW) of about 0.00001, against 0.0012 for the Laplace law. Other candidate models: the normal law, and a Student t law for heavier tails.
models.interpretation: 600 MW gives the least expected cost, about 3,370 currency units for the hour, with P(shortfall) of about 0.0012. 450 MW costs about 3,920, and 750 MW about 3,830. 300 MW does not meet the limit: its P(shortfall) is about 0.025. Reject the model if the history of forecast errors shows a bias, or tails that decrease at a different rate.

title: How much reserve to hold against day-ahead load forecast errors?

param r = 450 {MW} "reserve held for the hour"
param b = 100 {MW} "Laplace scale of the forecast error"
param cres = 5 {currency units per MW} "cost of 1 MW of reserve for 1 hour"
param voll = 3000 {currency units per MWh} "value of lost load"
Err ~ laplace(mu = 0, b = b) {MW} "actual load minus forecast load"

alt "300 MW": r = 300
alt "450 MW": r = 450
alt "600 MW": r = 600
alt "750 MW": r = 750

focus Err

models.title: Which privacy budget for a published count?
models.decision: Decision: the privacy budget ε of a published count. Estimated quantity: the probability that the noise exceeds 5 people, and the mean absolute error.
models.reason: The Laplace mechanism adds noise with scale Δ/ε to a query with the sensitivity Δ. The ratio of the noise densities at 2 counts that differ by Δ is at most e^ε, so the release has ε-differential privacy. Here the Laplace law is the mechanism itself, not a fit to data.
models.inputs: A count has the sensitivity Δ = 1, because one person changes it by at most 1. The privacy policy sets the upper bound 1 for ε. The tolerance of 5 people and the limit 0.05 are illustrative values.
models.dependence: None for one release. Several releases about the same people add their budgets: k releases with ε each give kε-differential privacy.
models.method: Independent draws of the noise. The estimators are the fraction of releases with an error above the tolerance, and the mean of |noise|. The budget ε is a constant. The alternatives share the streams, so each alternative scales the same draw by 1/ε.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the quantile function of the noise. Closed forms: P(|noise| > a) = e^(−aε/Δ), and E|noise| = Δ/ε. Other candidate models: the Gaussian mechanism for (ε, δ)-differential privacy, and the geometric mechanism, a discrete Laplace law for integer counts.
models.interpretation: ε = 0.75 is the smallest budget that meets the limit. Its P(error > 5) is about 0.024, and its mean absolute error about 1.33 people. ε = 0.5 gives P(error > 5) of about 0.082, above the limit. ε = 1 also meets the limit, but it gives weaker privacy. Reject the model if one person can add more than 1 to the count, because the sensitivity is then larger than 1.

models.title: Which hedge ratio keeps the daily currency loss within a limit?
models.decision: Decision: the hedge ratio h of a receivable in a foreign currency. Estimated quantity: the probability that the daily loss exceeds 100 thousand currency units, the expected daily loss, and the daily cost of the hedge.
models.reason: Daily log changes of exchange rates have a sharper peak and heavier tails than the normal law. A normal change whose variance has an exponential law from day to day gives the Laplace law. Its tails decrease as e^(−|x|/b).
models.inputs: The receivable is worth 20 million in the home currency. A Laplace scale b = 0.004 gives a standard deviation of 0.57 % a day. A hedge costs 0.0001 a day for each unit hedged. These values are illustrative. The daily loss limit is 100 thousand currency units.
models.dependence: None in this model: it describes one day only. The loss uses the first-order value −(1 − h)·V·R, which is accurate for small daily changes. Volatility clusters make large losses on successive days more likely.
models.method: Independent draws of R. The estimators are the fraction of days with a breach, and the means of the loss and of the hedge cost. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the quantile function of R. Closed forms: P(breach) = e^(−L/((1 − h)·V·b))/2 for the limit L, and E[max(loss, 0)] = (1 − h)·V·b/2. A normal law with the same standard deviation gives P(breach) of about 0.0002 for h = 0.75, against 0.0034 for the Laplace law. Other candidate models: the normal law, and a Student t law.
models.interpretation: A 75 % hedge is the least hedge that meets the limit. Its P(breach) is about 0.0034, its expected loss about 10 thousand currency units a day, and its cost 1.5 thousand a day. A 50 % hedge gives P(breach) of about 0.041, above 0.01. Reject the model if the daily changes have a trend, or if the tails in the history decrease more slowly than e^(−|x|/b).

param b = 0.004 "Laplace scale of the daily log change"

models.title: A finite variance does not make the sample mean behave
models.observe: For σ = 2.5, E[X] = e^(3.125) ≈ 22.76, but the standard deviation is about 518 and the skewness is about 11,800. All moments exist, so the CLT applies. But it applies only for very large samples. The page runs 64 blocks of 1,024 values. The 95 % CLT interval of one block contains 22.76 in only about 45 of 64 blocks, about 70 %. Most blocks miss the rare very large values. Thus their mean is too low and their interval is too narrow. For σ = 1 the coverage is about 61 of 64 blocks, near 95 %. P(X > 10) is 0.0107 for σ = 1 and 0.179 for σ = 2.5. On the log–log tail plot the survival curve bends down. It is not a straight line, so the tail is not regularly varying.

title: A finite variance does not make the sample mean behave
problem: A lognormal law with σ = 2.5 has all moments, but its variance is very large and its skewness is extreme. Compare the sample mean and its CLT interval with the law with σ = 1.
param mu = 0 "mean of log X"
param sigma = 2.5 "standard deviation of log X"
X ~ lognormal(mu = mu, sigma = sigma) "a lognormal value with the median 1"
mean m = X "E[X] = exp(μ + σ²/2)"
prob big = X > 10 "P(X > 10)"
alt "σ = 1": sigma = 1
alt "σ = 2.5": sigma = 2.5
focus X

models.title: When to send a second copy of a slow request?
models.decision: Decision: the delay d after which the client sends a second copy of a slow request. Estimated quantity: the fraction of requests with a second copy, which is the extra load, and P(latency > 250 ms).
models.reason: A response time is the product of many independent factors: queue lengths, cache misses and retries. The log of a product is a sum, so the response time is near lognormal. The lognormal law is a standard model of the body of server latency. A second copy cuts the slow requests, because two independent copies are rarely both slow.
models.inputs: A median response time of 40 ms and σ = 0.8 for the log response time are illustrative values. The latency target is at most 0.3 % of requests above 250 ms. There is no data.
models.dependence: The two copies go to two servers and are independent. A load peak on all servers breaks this assumption, because then both copies are slow together. The second copy also adds load, which this model does not feed back into the response time.
models.method: Independent draws of R1 and R2. The estimators are fractions and sample means. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
models.diagnostics: The extra load P(R1 > d) has an exact reference from the lognormal survival function: 0.306, 0.126, 0.049 and 0.022 for the 4 delays. The late fraction has a quadrature reference: it is P(R1 > 250) P(R2 > 250 − d) for d < 250. With no second copy, P(R1 > 250) = 0.011. Other candidate models: a gamma or Weibull response time, and a lognormal body with a Pareto tail for rare stalls.
models.interpretation: A delay of 150 ms meets the target with the least extra load. About 4.9 % of requests get a second copy, and about 0.14 % of requests are late. A delay of 200 ms gives 0.43 % late requests, which misses the target. A delay of 60 ms doubles the load of 30 % of requests for a small gain. Reject the model if the slow requests of the two servers occur together, or if the measured tail is heavier than the lognormal tail.

prob hedged = R1 > d "fraction of requests with a second copy: extra load"

alt "Delay 200 ms": d = 200

focus latency

models.title: Which daily dose for a drug with variable clearance?
models.decision: Decision: the daily dose of a drug given as a constant infusion. Estimated quantity: P(the mean concentration is in the window 2–6 mg/L) and P(the concentration is above the toxic limit 6 mg/L).
models.reason: The clearance of a drug differs between patients by factors: body size, liver function and enzyme genes. Population pharmacokinetics models such factors as a lognormal law of the clearance. Then the concentration dose/(24·CL) is also lognormal, because 1/CL is lognormal.
models.inputs: A median clearance of 5 L/h and a standard deviation 0.35 of the log clearance are illustrative values. The window 2–6 mg/L is also illustrative. The dose is in mg/day, so the dose rate is dose/24 in mg/h. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: one patient, one clearance. The model ignores the change of the clearance with time and with other drugs.
models.method: Independent draws of CL. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
models.diagnostics: Each probability reads only CL, so the page computes a quadrature reference. The exact value is a normal probability: for example, P(C > 6) = P(Z > (log(5) − log(dose/144))/0.35). It gives 0.047 for 400 mg/day. Other candidate models: a gamma law of the clearance, and a covariate model with the body weight.
models.interpretation: 400 mg/day puts about 88 % of patients in the window, with about 4.7 % above the toxic limit. 500 mg/day puts about 15 % above the toxic limit, which breaks the constraint. 300 mg/day is safe, but about 26 % of patients are below the window. Reject the model if the lognormal law does not fit the skewness of measured concentrations, or if a covariate explains much of the clearance.

title: Which daily dose for a drug with variable clearance?
problem: A drug is given as a constant infusion. The mean concentration at steady state is the dose rate divided by the clearance. The clearance differs between patients. Find the daily dose that puts most patients in the therapeutic window.

param dose = 500 {mg/day} "daily dose"

param high = 6 {mg/L} "toxic limit"
CL ~ lognormal(mu = log(cl_median), sigma = omega) {L/h} "clearance of one patient"
C := dose / (24*CL) {mg/L} "mean concentration at steady state"
prob in_window = C >= low and C <= high "the patient is in the therapeutic window"
prob toxic = C > high "the patient is above the toxic limit"
prob low_conc = C < low "the patient is below the window"
alt "300 mg/day": dose = 300
alt "400 mg/day": dose = 400
alt "500 mg/day": dose = 500
alt "600 mg/day": dose = 600

focus C

models.title: Which rule to declare a workplace compliant from 6 measurements?
models.decision: Decision: the rule constant c. A workplace passes if the geometric mean of 6 shift exposures is at most c times the exposure limit. Estimated quantity: P(a bad workplace passes) and P(a good workplace passes).
models.reason: Occupational exposures between shifts are close to lognormal, with a geometric standard deviation of about 2 to 3. Hygiene standards and their statistical tools use this model. The geometric mean is the natural statistic, because the log values are normal.
models.inputs: Exposures are fractions of the limit, so the limit is 1. The geometric standard deviation 2.5 is illustrative. A bad workplace has 10 % of shifts above the limit: its true geometric mean is 0.309. A good workplace has 1 % of shifts above the limit: its true geometric mean is 0.119. The rule must pass a bad workplace in at most 5 % of surveys. There is no data.
models.dependence: The 6 shifts are independent in this model. Shifts of the same worker or the same week are often correlated. Then the geometric mean of the sample varies more, and a bad workplace passes more often.
models.method: Independent draws of 6 exposures for each workplace. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
models.diagnostics: The page gives no reference, because the variables repeat. An exact check exists: the log of the sample geometric mean is N(log g, (log 2.5)²/6). It gives P(a bad workplace passes) = 0.0013, 0.027, 0.122 and 0.286 for c = 0.10, 0.15, 0.20 and 0.25. P(a good workplace passes) is 0.321, 0.732, 0.917 and 0.976. The estimate of P(one shift above the limit) in the bad workplace is about 0.10, as designed. Other candidate models: a gamma law of the exposure, and a random worker effect. Other candidate rule: an upper tolerance limit for the 95th percentile.
models.interpretation: c = 0.15 is the largest of the 4 constants that meets the 5 % limit. A bad workplace passes in about 2.6 % of surveys, and a good workplace passes in about 73 %. c = 0.20 passes a bad workplace in about 12 % of surveys. Six measurements cannot separate the two workplaces better. Reject the model if the log exposures are not near normal, or if the shifts of one worker show a strong correlation.

title: Which rule to declare a workplace compliant from 6 measurements?

alt "c = 0.15": c = 0.15
alt "c = 0.20": c = 0.20
alt "c = 0.25": c = 0.25

models.title: The Weibull shape sets the ageing
models.observe: All three laws give P(T > 1) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368. The ratio P(T > 2 | T > 1) = exp(−(2^k − 1)) shows the ageing. For k = 0.5 it is 0.661, larger than 0.368: an old unit is better than a new unit. For k = 1 it is 0.368: the exponential law has no memory. For k = 2 it is only 0.050: an old unit wears out. The mean life λΓ(1 + 1/k) is 2 for k = 0.5, 1 for k = 1 and 0.886 for k = 2. On the log survival plot, the curve for k = 0.5 is convex. The curve for k = 1 is a straight line. The curve for k = 2 falls faster and faster.
models.dsl:
title: The Weibull shape sets the ageing
problem: Three Weibull laws have the scale λ = 1, so P(T > 1) = e^(−1) for all three. Compare the chance that a new unit survives 1 unit of time with the chance that a unit of age 1 survives 1 more unit.
param k = 1 "shape"
T ~ weibull(k = k, lambda = 1) {years} "life of a unit"
prob new_unit = T > 1 "P(T > 1)"
ratio old_unit = E[T > 2] / E[T > 1] "P(T > 2 | T > 1)"
mean m = T {years} "mean life"
alt "k = 0.5": k = 0.5
alt "k = 1": k = 1
alt "k = 2": k = 2
focus T

models.title: When to replace a bearing that wears out?
models.decision: Decision: the age τ at which the team replaces a pump bearing before it fails. Estimated quantity: the long-run cost for each hour of operation, E[cost]/E[min(T, τ)], by the renewal–reward theorem.
models.reason: The Weibull law is the standard model of the fatigue life of rolling bearings. Wear-out gives a shape above 1. A shape above 1 means a growing hazard. Only then can a planned replacement lower the cost.
models.inputs: The shape k = 2.5 and the scale λ = 20,000 h are illustrative values. A failure costs 12,000 and a planned replacement 1,500 currency units, also illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: Successive bearings are independent and have the same law, which makes the replacements a renewal process. A misaligned shaft breaks this assumption, because it shortens all bearings on that pump.
models.method: Independent draws of T. The cost rate is a ratio of two means, with a delta-method interval. The alternatives use the same draws.
models.diagnostics: The page gives quadrature references for the cost rate, and exact references for P(T ≤ τ). The cost rate is 0.368, 0.323, 0.365 and 0.676 for τ = 5,000, 8,000 and 12,000 h and for no planned replacement. Other candidate models: a lognormal life, and a Weibull law with a minimum life (3 parameters).
models.interpretation: Replacement at 8,000 h gives the least cost rate of these ages, about 0.323 for each hour. Replacement only after a failure costs about 0.676 for each hour, more than twice as much. At 8,000 h about 9.6 % of bearings still fail before the planned replacement. Reject the model if the life data give a Weibull shape near 1 or below 1. Then a planned replacement does not help.

param tau = 10000 {h} "planned replacement age"
param cfail = 12000 {currency units} "cost of a replacement after a failure, with the lost production"

focus T

models.title: Which site gives more energy from the same turbine?
models.decision: Decision: the site for a 2 MW turbine. Estimated quantity: the mean power, and the capacity factor E[power]/2 MW.
models.reason: The hourly mean wind speed at a site is close to a Weibull law, often with a shape near 2. Wind resource assessments use this model. The power is a nonlinear function of the speed, so the mean power needs the whole law, not only the mean speed.
models.inputs: Site A has k = 2 and λ = 7.5 m/s. Site B has k = 1.6 and λ = 8 m/s. These values are illustrative. The power curve is a simple model. The power is 0 below 3 m/s and above 25 m/s. It increases as a cubic to 2 MW at 12 m/s, then stays at 2 MW. The project needs a capacity factor of at least 0.3.
models.dependence: The model uses the marginal law of one hour. The mean power needs only this law. The variability of the energy in one year depends on the correlation between hours, which this model does not give.
models.method: Independent draws of V. The estimators are sample means and fractions. The alternatives use the same uniform numbers.
models.diagnostics: Each quantity reads only V. Thus the page gives quadrature references. Site A gives a mean power of 0.523 MW and a capacity factor of 0.261. Site B gives 0.622 MW and 0.311. Other candidate models: a Rayleigh law (k = 2), a mixture of two Weibull laws for two seasons, and a measured power curve.
models.interpretation: Site B gives about 19 % more energy, and only site B meets the capacity factor 0.3. Its lower shape gives more hours above 12 m/s, about 14.6 % against 7.7 %. It also gives more idle hours, about 19 % against 15 %. Reject the model if a year of measured hourly speeds does not fit a Weibull law, for example with two modes.

title: Which site gives more energy from the same turbine?

alt "Site A: k = 2, λ = 7.5 m/s": k = 2; lambda = 7.5
alt "Site B: k = 1.6, λ = 8 m/s": k = 1.6; lambda = 8

models.title: Which design stress for a ceramic part?
models.decision: Decision: the design stress of a ceramic part. Estimated quantity: P(the part fails), the probability that the weakest of its 20 unit volumes is weaker than the stress.
models.reason: A brittle part fails at its weakest flaw. Weibull's weakest-link theory gives a Weibull law of the strength. The minimum of n independent Weibull(m, s0) values is Weibull(m, s0 n^(−1/m)). Thus a larger part is weaker.
models.inputs: The Weibull modulus m = 10 and the scale s0 = 400 MPa for one unit volume are illustrative values. The part has 20 unit volumes under the same stress. The load is 30 kN, and the cross-section is the load divided by the stress. The failure probability must be at most 0.001.
models.dependence: The flaws in different unit volumes are independent. A processing defect that affects the whole part breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of 20 strengths and their minimum. The estimator is a fraction of replicates. A probability near 0.001 needs many replicates, so check the width of the interval.
models.diagnostics: The minimum of a repeated variable has an exact reference: P(fail) = 1 − exp(−20 (s/400)^10). It gives 0.00012, 0.00055, 0.0021 and 0.0068 for the 4 stresses. A test bar of one unit volume fails at 140 MPa with probability 0.000028, 20 times less. Other candidate models: a lognormal strength, and a strength with a lower bound from proof testing.
models.interpretation: 140 MPa is the largest stress that meets the limit, with P(fail) about 0.00055 and a cross-section of 214 mm². 160 MPa gives P(fail) about 0.0021, which breaks the limit. A design from test bars alone would ignore the size effect. Reject the model if the test strengths do not lie on a straight line on a Weibull plot.

models.title: The same mean and variance, different tails
models.observe: X ~ IG(1, 1) and Y, a lognormal value with σ² = log 2, both have the mean 1 and the variance 1. The tails still differ. P(X > 4) = 0.0209 is larger than P(Y > 4) = 0.0187. But P(X > 8) = 0.00126 is smaller than P(Y > 8) = 0.00178. At 16 the lognormal tail is about 9.5 times the inverse Gaussian tail: 0.0000897 against 0.0000094. The inverse Gaussian tail is exponential, and the lognormal tail is subexponential. On the log survival plot the inverse Gaussian curve becomes a straight line, and the lognormal curve bends up and falls more slowly.

prob y4 = Y > 4 "P(Y > 4)"

prob y8 = Y > 8 "P(Y > 8)"
prob x16 = X > 16 "P(X > 16)"
prob y16 = Y > 16 "P(Y > 16)"
mean mx = X "E[X] = 1"
mean my = Y "E[Y] = 1"
focus X

models.title: How large a protection zone around a drinking-water well?
models.decision: Decision: the radius L of the protection zone around a drinking-water well. Estimated quantity: P(T < 50 days), the probability that water from the edge of the zone arrives in less than 50 days.
models.reason: In one dimension, a solute that moves with a mean velocity v and a dispersion D reaches the distance L at a first-passage time. This time has the inverse Gaussian law IG(L/v, L²/(2D)). Hydrogeologists use it for travel-time distributions.
models.inputs: A mean velocity v = 1 m/day and a dispersivity a = 5 m, with D = a·v, are illustrative values. The 50-day travel time is a common basis for the inner protection zone of a well. The probability limit 0.01 is a choice of this example.
models.dependence: None for one water particle. The model assumes a uniform aquifer in one dimension. Layers and fractures give fast paths that this model does not have.
models.method: Independent draws of T by the transformation of Michael, Schucany and Haas. The estimators are fractions and sample means.
models.diagnostics: T has constant parameters, so P(T < 50) has an exact reference from the inverse Gaussian CDF. It is 0.049, 0.017, 0.0051 and 0.0013 for L = 90, 100, 110 and 120 m. The mean travel time is L/v. Other candidate models: a lognormal travel time, and a model with two flow paths.
models.interpretation: L = 110 m is the smallest radius that meets the limit, with P(T < 50 days) about 0.005 and an area of 3.8 ha. A radius of 50 m, the mean travel distance in 50 days, would fail often. The dispersion spreads the arrivals, so the zone must be about twice that distance. Reject the model if tracer tests give a breakthrough curve with a long early tail or two peaks.

alt "L = 90 m": L = 90
alt "L = 100 m": L = 100
alt "L = 110 m": L = 110
alt "L = 120 m": L = 120
