require early <= 0.01
focus T

models.title: How often to inspect a part that wears with a drift?
models.decision: Decision: the inspection interval of a part that wears. Estimated quantity: the long-run cost for each month, E[cost]/E[cycle], by the renewal–reward theorem. Also P(the part fails before an inspection finds it).
models.reason: If the wear is a Brownian motion with a positive drift, the time to reach a fixed level is inverse Gaussian. The time to the alarm level and the further time to the failure level are independent, by the strong Markov property. Both are inverse Gaussian.
models.inputs: A drift of 0.1 mm/month and a standard deviation of 0.15 mm after one month are illustrative values. The alarm level is 1.5 mm and the failure level 2 mm. An inspection costs 100, a planned replacement 1,000 and a failure 10,000 currency units. There is no data.
models.dependence: The two passage times are independent, as the Brownian model implies. Successive parts are independent, which makes the replacements a renewal process.
models.method: Independent draws of A and G. Inspections are at dt, 2dt, …. The first inspection after A finds the part. The cost rate is a ratio of means with a delta-method interval.
models.diagnostics: The page gives no reference: the cost reads two variables, and its quadrature needs too much work. Checks: E[A] = 15 months and E[G] = 5 months are exact. The fraction of failures must grow with the interval. Other candidate models: a gamma wear process, which never decreases, and a random drift for each part.
models.interpretation: An inspection every 2 months gives the least cost rate, about 127 currency units for each month. About 2.6 % of parts then fail before an inspection finds them. Monthly inspections cost about 165, and inspections every 4 months about 172, with about 17 % failures. Reject the model if the measured wear decreases between inspections more than the measurement error allows. Then the gamma process is a better model.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: How often to inspect a part that wears with a drift?
problem: The wear of a part grows with a constant drift and random fluctuations. An inspection finds the part if its wear has passed the alarm level, and the part is then replaced. If the wear reaches the failure level before an inspection finds it, the part fails. Find the inspection interval with the least cost for each month.
param drift = 0.1 {mm/month} "mean wear rate"
param vol = 0.15 {mm/sqrt(month)} "standard deviation of the wear after one month"
param alarm = 1.5 {mm} "alarm level of the wear"
param fail_level = 2 {mm} "failure level of the wear"
param dt = 2 {months} "inspection interval"
param cinsp = 100 {currency units} "cost of one inspection"
param cprev = 1000 {currency units} "cost of a planned replacement"
param cfail = 10000 {currency units} "cost of a failure"
A ~ invgauss(mu = alarm/drift, lambda = alarm^2/vol^2) {months} "time until the wear reaches the alarm level"
G ~ invgauss(mu = (fail_level - alarm)/drift, lambda = (fail_level - alarm)^2/vol^2) {months} "further time from the alarm level to the failure level"
found := ceil(A/dt)*dt {months} "first inspection after the alarm"
failed := A + G < found "the part fails before an inspection finds it"
cycle := min(A + G, found) {months} "time until the replacement"
cost := cinsp*floor(cycle/dt) + if(failed, cfail, cprev) {currency units} "cost of one cycle"
ratio cost_rate = E[cost] / E[cycle] {currency units per month}
prob fail = failed "the part fails before it is found"
alt "Every month": dt = 1
alt "Every 2 months": dt = 2
alt "Every 3 months": dt = 3
alt "Every 4 months": dt = 4
minimise cost_rate
focus A

models.title: Which lead time to quote for a batch of 20 jobs?
models.decision: Decision: the lead time quoted to the customer for a batch of 20 jobs. Estimated quantity: P(the batch is late) and the expected cost of the quote and the penalty.
models.reason: A job ends when its accumulated work reaches a fixed amount, and the work rate fluctuates. A first-passage time of a Brownian motion with drift is inverse Gaussian. Sums stay in the family: the sum of 20 IG(μ, λ) times is IG(20μ, 400λ).
models.inputs: A mean job time of 1 h and a shape λ = 4 h are illustrative values, so the coefficient of variation of one job is 0.5. Each hour of quoted lead time costs 50, and a late batch costs 2,000 currency units. There is no data.
models.dependence: The 20 job times are independent. A slow operator or a worn tool makes all jobs of a batch slow, which breaks this assumption and makes the batch time more variable.
models.method: Independent draws of 20 job times and their sum. The estimators are a fraction and a sample mean. The alternatives use the same draws.
models.diagnostics: The sum has an exact law. Thus the page shows exact references for P(S > quote): 0.181, 0.045, 0.0079 and 0.0010 for the 4 quotes. The expected cost has a quadrature reference. Other candidate models: gamma or lognormal job times. Their sum has no simple closed form.
models.interpretation: A quote of 24 h has the least expected cost, about 1,291 currency units, and the batch is late with probability about 0.045. A quote of 22 h costs about 1,463 because 18 % of batches are late. Reject the model if the job times of one batch show a correlation. Then the batch time has a larger variance than 20μ³/λ = 5 h².

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Which lead time to quote for a batch of 20 jobs?
problem: A machine does 20 jobs of a batch one after the other. Each job ends when the accumulated work reaches a fixed amount, and the work rate fluctuates. The customer gets a penalty if the batch is late. Find the quoted lead time with the least expected cost.
param mu = 1 {h} "mean time of one job"
param lambda = 4 {h} "shape of the job time"
param n = 20 "jobs in the batch"
param quote = 24 {h} "quoted lead time"
param hold = 50 {currency units per hour} "cost of each hour of quoted lead time"
param penalty = 2000 {currency units} "penalty for a late batch"
J ~ invgauss(mu = mu, lambda = lambda) repeat 20 {h} "time of each job"
S := sum(J) {h} "time to finish the batch: IG(20μ, 400λ)"
prob late = S > quote "the batch is late"
mean cost = hold*quote + penalty*(S > quote) {currency units} "quoted time cost plus the expected penalty"
alt "Quote 22 h": quote = 22
alt "Quote 24 h": quote = 24
alt "Quote 26 h": quote = 26
alt "Quote 28 h": quote = 28
minimise cost
focus S

models.title: The hazard doubles every 8 years
models.observe: The hazard starts at 0.001 per year at age 30 and doubles every 8 years, so b = log(2)/8 ≈ 0.0866. The chance to live 10 more years is 0.984 at age 30. It falls to 0.601 at age 70, 0.298 at age 80 and 0.056 at age 90. The mean life after age 30 is e^η E1(η)/b ≈ 45.5 years. On the log survival plot the curve falls faster and faster, because log S(t) = −η(e^(bt) − 1). The ratio estimators use only the replicates that survive to the given age, so their intervals are wider at old ages.
models.dsl:
title: The hazard doubles every 8 years
problem: An adult has the hazard 0.001 per year at age 30, and the hazard doubles every 8 years. T is the life after age 30. Compare the chance to live 10 more years at the ages 30, 70, 80 and 90.
param h0 = 0.001 {per year} "hazard at age 30"
param b = log(2)/8 {per year} "growth rate of the hazard"
T ~ gompertz(eta = h0/b, b = b) {years} "life after age 30"
prob at30 = T > 10 "P(10 more years at age 30)"
ratio at70 = E[T > 50] / E[T > 40] "P(10 more years | alive at 70)"
ratio at80 = E[T > 60] / E[T > 50] "P(10 more years | alive at 80)"
ratio at90 = E[T > 70] / E[T > 60] "P(10 more years | alive at 90)"
mean life = T {years} "mean life after age 30"
focus T

models.title: Which anti-ageing intervention to take forward in mice?
models.decision: Decision: which of two interventions in mice to take forward to a larger study. Estimated quantity: the mean lifespan, and P(a mouse lives more than 1,000 days).
models.reason: Adult mortality of mice, like that of humans, is close to the Gompertz law over most adult ages: the log hazard grows linearly with age. The two parameters separate two effects. η·b is the initial hazard, and b is the rate of ageing.
models.inputs: An initial hazard of 0.000014 per day and a doubling time of the hazard of 100 days are illustrative values. They give a mean lifespan of about 814 days. One intervention halves the initial hazard. The other lowers b by 15 % with the same initial hazard, so η = h0/b grows. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: the mice are independent. A cage effect or an infection breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of T by inversion of the survival function. The estimators are a sample mean and a fraction. The alternatives use the same uniform numbers.
models.diagnostics: The mean e^η E1(η)/b and the survival function give exact references: 813.8, 913.0 and 930.2 days, and P(T > 1000) = 0.127, 0.356 and 0.424. A halved initial hazard adds about log(2)/b ≈ 100 days to the mean. It moves the survival curve by one doubling time of the hazard. Other candidate models: the Gompertz–Makeham law with a constant term, and the logistic hazard, which levels off at old ages.
models.interpretation: The 15 % slower ageing gives the larger gain, about 116 days against about 99 days, and more mice past 1,000 days. A real study measures the effect with a sample, not with the exact law. Reject the model if the log hazard of the control group is not linear in age, for example if it levels off at old ages.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Which anti-ageing intervention to take forward in mice?
problem: A laboratory tests two interventions in mice. One halves the initial hazard. The other slows the growth of the hazard by 15 %. Find the intervention with the larger gain in mean lifespan, and compare the survival to 1,000 days.
param h0 = 0.000014 {per day} "initial hazard"
param b = log(2)/100 {per day} "growth rate of the hazard: it doubles every 100 days"
param fh = 1 "factor on the initial hazard"
param fb = 1 "factor on the growth rate"
T ~ gompertz(eta = fh*h0/(fb*b), b = fb*b) {days} "lifespan of a mouse"
mean life = T {days} "mean lifespan"
prob old = T > 1000 "the mouse lives more than 1,000 days"
alt "Control": fh = 1; fb = 1
alt "Initial hazard halved": fh = 0.5; fb = 1
alt "Growth rate 15 % lower": fh = 1; fb = 0.85
maximise life
focus T

models.title: Which price for a life annuity sold to 100 people aged 65?
models.decision: Decision: the loading on the expected present value of a life annuity sold to 100 people aged 65. Estimated quantity: P(the present value of the group is more than the premiums).
models.reason: Adult mortality from age 30 to age 95 is close to the Gompertz law. Actuaries use Gompertz and Gompertz–Makeham laws for annuity values. The present value of a continuous annuity of 1 for each year is (1 − e^(−δT))/δ.
models.inputs: A hazard of 0.01 per year at age 65 and b = 0.1 per year are illustrative values. They give a mean remaining life of about 20.1 years. The force of interest δ = 0.03 is also illustrative. The expected present value of 14.42 comes from the integral of e^(−δt) S(t). There is no data.
models.dependence: The 100 lives are independent in this model. A common improvement of mortality, the longevity risk, makes all lives longer together. This model does not have that risk, so it understates the risk of the insurer.
models.method: Independent draws of 100 lifetimes. The estimators are a sample mean and a fraction. The alternatives use the same draws.
models.diagnostics: The page gives no reference, because T repeats. The expected present value for one life is 14.42 by quadrature, and the estimate is about 14.43. Its standard deviation is 5.29, so the group mean has a standard deviation of about 0.53. Other candidate models: the Gompertz–Makeham law, and a model with a random trend of mortality.
models.interpretation: A loading of 7 % is the smallest of these loadings that keeps the chance of a loss below 5 %, at about 2.5 %. A loading of 5 % gives a loss in about 8.3 % of groups. The loading falls as 1/√n for a larger group of independent lives, but not for the common longevity risk. Reject the model if the hazards of the group do not grow by a near-constant factor each year.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Which price for a life annuity sold to 100 people aged 65?
problem: An insurer sells a life annuity to 100 people aged 65. The annuity pays 1 currency unit per year, continuously, until death. Find the smallest loading on the expected present value that keeps the chance of a loss on the group below 5 %.
param h65 = 0.01 {per year} "hazard at age 65"
param b = 0.1 {per year} "growth rate of the hazard"
param delta = 0.03 {per year} "force of interest"
param loading = 0.07 "loading on the expected present value"
param epv = 14.42 {currency units} "expected present value of the annuity for one life"
T ~ gompertz(eta = h65/b, b = b) repeat 100 {years} "remaining life of each annuitant"
pv := (1 - exp(-delta*T[1]))/delta {currency units} "present value for one annuitant"
group := mean((1 - exp(-delta*T))/delta) {currency units} "mean present value in the group"
mean one = pv {currency units} "expected present value for one life"
prob loss = group > (1 + loading)*epv "the group costs more than the premiums"
mean premium = (1 + loading)*epv {currency units} "premium for one life"
alt "Loading 3 %": loading = 0.03
alt "Loading 5 %": loading = 0.05
alt "Loading 7 %": loading = 0.07
alt "Loading 9 %": loading = 0.09
minimise premium
require loss <= 0.05
focus pv

models.title: How many care places for a cohort after 3 years?
models.decision: Decision: the number of long-term care places for a cohort after 3 years. Estimated quantity: P(the survivors are more than the places), the mean number of survivors, and the care-years in the 3 years.
models.reason: The hazard of death at old ages grows by a near-constant factor each year, as the Gompertz law states. The number of survivors after 3 years is then binomial with the probability S(3).
models.inputs: The cohort has 200 people aged 80 who need care now. A hazard of 0.25 per year at entry and b = 0.1 per year are illustrative values. They give S(3) = 0.417. The planner accepts a 5 % risk of too few places. There is no data.
models.dependence: The 200 lives are independent in this model. An epidemic or a heat wave breaks this assumption, because it raises the hazard of all residents together. New people who enter care are not in this cohort.
models.method: Independent draws of 200 lifetimes, then the count of survivors and the sum of min(T, 3). The estimators are a fraction and sample means.
models.diagnostics: The page gives no reference, because T repeats. An exact check: the survivors are Binomial(200, 0.417). This gives a mean of 83.4 and P(more than 90, 95 and 100) = 0.154, 0.042 and 0.0074. The care-years have the exact mean 200 ∫_0^3 S(t) dt = 408.6. Other candidate models: the Gompertz–Makeham law, and a frailty model with a random hazard factor for each person.
models.interpretation: 95 places meet the 5 % risk, with P(too few) about 0.042. 90 places are too few in about 15 % of runs. The cohort uses about 409 care-years in the 3 years. Reject the model if the deaths in the first year differ much from 200(1 − S(1)) ≈ 46. Also reject it if the health of the residents differs much.

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: How many care places for a cohort after 3 years?
problem: A district has 200 people aged 80 who need long-term care now. Plan the care places that this cohort needs after 3 years, and the care-years in these 3 years.
param n = 200 "people in the cohort"
param h80 = 0.25 {per year} "hazard of death at age 80 in this population"
param b = 0.1 {per year} "growth rate of the hazard"
param places = 95 "care places planned for year 3"
T ~ gompertz(eta = h80/b, b = b) repeat 200 {years} "remaining life of each person"
alive := sum(T > 3) {people} "people alive after 3 years"
prob short = alive > places "the planned places are too few"
mean survivors = alive {people} "mean number alive after 3 years"
mean care_years = sum(pmin(T, 3)) {person-years} "care-years in the first 3 years"
alt "90 places": places = 90
alt "95 places": places = 95
alt "100 places": places = 100
mean planned = places "places planned"
minimise planned
require short <= 0.05
focus alive

models.title: A hazard that rises and then falls
models.observe: For α = 1 and β = 3, the hazard rises to a maximum at x = 2^(1/3) ≈ 1.26 and then falls. The chance to fail in the next 0.5 time units is 0.286 at the age 0.25. It is 0.543 at the age 1 and 0.362 at the age 3. The run gives about the same values. A unit that is alive at the age 3 is thus safer than a unit at the age 1. The Weibull law cannot show this, because its hazard is monotone.
models.dsl:
title: A hazard that rises and then falls
problem: For β > 1 the log-logistic hazard rises to a maximum and then falls. Compare the chance to fail in the next 0.5 time units at an early, a middle and a late age.
param alpha = 1 "scale, the median"
param beta = 3 "shape"
param h = 0.5 "length of the next interval"
X ~ loglogistic(alpha = alpha, beta = beta) "time to failure"
ratio early = E[(X > 0.25)*(X <= 0.25 + h)] / E[X > 0.25] "P(fail in the next interval | alive at 0.25)"
ratio middle = E[(X > 1)*(X <= 1 + h)] / E[X > 1] "P(fail in the next interval | alive at 1)"
ratio late = E[(X > 3)*(X <= 3 + h)] / E[X > 3] "P(fail in the next interval | alive at 3)"
focus X

models.title: A transfer budget that closes the poverty gap
models.decision: Decision: the yearly budget of a cash transfer that lifts each poor household to the poverty line. Estimated quantity: the headcount ratio P(X < z) and the poverty gap per household E[max(z − X, 0)].
models.reason: The Fisk (log-logistic) law is a standard model of household income. Its Gini coefficient is 1/β, so one shape parameter sets the inequality. The poverty gap depends on the lower part of the law, which the median α and the shape β set.
models.inputs: The unit of the income X is k$ per year. The median income is α = 30. The shape is β = 3, which gives a Gini coefficient of 0.33. The poverty line is z = 18, which is 60 % of the median. There are 100,000 households. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: the incomes of households are independent in this model. The model ignores a change of behaviour that the transfer can cause.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The headcount estimator is a fraction of replicates. The gap estimator is a sample mean of max(z − X, 0). This value is between 0 and z.
models.diagnostics: The headcount ratio has a closed-form reference, 1/(1 + (α/z)^β). The page computes the gap by quadrature. For β = 3 the headcount is 0.178 and the gap is 0.868 k$ per household. All moments of max(z − X, 0) exist, because it is between 0 and z. Other candidate models: the lognormal law, the Singh–Maddala (Burr XII) law and the Dagum law.
models.interpretation: For a Gini coefficient of 0.33, 17.8 % of households are poor, and the transfer costs 86.8 M$ per year. With β = 2.5 (Gini 0.40) the cost is 124 M$, and with β = 4 (Gini 0.25) it is 43.6 M$. Thus the budget depends strongly on the inequality, at the same median. Reject the model if household survey data show a lower tail that the Fisk law does not fit, for example many zero incomes.
models.dsl:
title: A transfer budget that closes the poverty gap
problem: A government plans a transfer that brings each household below the poverty line up to the line. Estimate the share of poor households and the yearly cost.
param alpha = 30 {k$ per year} "median household income"
param beta = 3 "shape; the Gini coefficient is 1/β"
param z = 18 {k$ per year} "poverty line, 60 % of the median"
param households = 100000 {households}
X ~ loglogistic(alpha = alpha, beta = beta) {k$ per year} "income of one household"
prob poor = X < z "headcount ratio"
mean gap = max(z - X, 0) {k$ per household} "poverty gap per household"
mean budget = (households/1000)*max(z - X, 0) {M$ per year} "cost of the perfectly targeted transfer"
alt "Gini 0.40 (β = 2.5)": beta = 2.5
alt "Gini 0.33 (β = 3)": beta = 3
alt "Gini 0.25 (β = 4)": beta = 4
focus X

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.title: When to refer a patient who has not recovered after surgery
models.decision: Decision: the day d after surgery at which a patient who has not recovered goes to a specialist clinic. Estimated quantity: the chance to recover in the next 7 days, for a patient who has not recovered at day d. Also the mean time to recovery or referral E[min(X, d)].
models.reason: The chance to recover first rises as the wound heals, and then falls for patients with a complication. The log-logistic law has this hazard shape for β > 1. It is a standard accelerated failure time model in survival analysis.
models.inputs: The time to recovery X is in days. The median is α = 14 days and the shape is β = 2.5. Thus the hazard is largest near day 16.5. The clinic wants to refer only patients whose chance to recover in the next 7 days without help is at most 0.35. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: patients are independent. The model has no covariates. A real study adds the age of the patient and the type of surgery.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The conditional chance is a ratio estimator: the fraction of replicates that recover in (d, d + 7], over the fraction alive at d. The mean is a sample mean of min(X, d).
models.diagnostics: The page computes the references by quadrature. The chance to recover in the next 7 days is 0.467 at day 14 and 0.436 at day 21. It is 0.388 at day 28 and 0.344 at day 35. This chance falls after the peak of the hazard. Other candidate models: the Weibull law, whose hazard cannot rise and then fall, and the lognormal law.
models.interpretation: Only day 35 meets the limit of 0.35. At day 35, the clinic refers 9.2 % of patients, and the mean time to recovery or referral is 16.2 days. An earlier day refers patients who still have a good chance to recover alone. Reject the model if a Kaplan–Meier estimate from recovery records shows a monotone hazard.
models.dsl:
title: When to refer a patient who has not recovered after surgery
problem: Patients who have not recovered at day d go to a specialist clinic. Refer early, but only when the chance to recover in the next week without help is small.
param alpha = 14 {days} "median time to recovery"
param beta = 2.5 "shape"
param d = 21 {days} "day of the referral"
X ~ loglogistic(alpha = alpha, beta = beta) {days} "time to recovery"
prob referred = X > d "share of patients referred"
ratio next_week = E[(X > d)*(X <= d + 7)] / E[X > d] "P(recover in the next 7 days | not recovered at day d)"
mean wait = min(X, d) {days} "time to recovery or referral"
alt "Day 14": d = 14
alt "Day 21": d = 21
alt "Day 28": d = 28
alt "Day 35": d = 35
minimise wait
require next_week <= 0.35
focus X

models.title: A time limit for video sessions
models.decision: Decision: the time limit T after which the service ends a free video session. Estimated quantity: the share of sessions that the limit cuts P(X > T), and the mean number of open sessions, which sets the server capacity. At most 2 % of sessions may be cut.
models.reason: Session durations have a power-law tail, and the log-logistic law is a common model of call and session holding times. For β ≤ 2 the variance is infinite, so a few very long sessions use a large part of the server time.
models.inputs: The duration X is in minutes. The median is α = 12 minutes and the shape is β = 1.8. Thus the mean is finite but the variance is infinite. Sessions start at a rate of 50 per minute. At most 2 % of sessions may be cut. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: session durations are independent. By Little's law, the mean number of open sessions is the start rate times the mean held time E[min(X, T)].
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The share is a fraction of replicates. The load and the saved time are sample means. The objective is the smallest load that meets the limit on cut sessions.
models.diagnostics: P(X > T) = 1/(1 + (T/α)^β) is exact. The page computes the load by quadrature. The saved time max(X − T, 0) has a finite mean but an infinite variance for β ≤ 2, so the page shows no interval for it. Without a limit, the mean duration is απ/β / sin(π/β) ≈ 21.3 min, and the load is about 1,063 sessions. Other candidate models: the lognormal law and Pareto II.
models.interpretation: T = 60 min cuts 5.2 % of sessions, which is too many. T = 120 min cuts 1.6 % of sessions, and the mean load is 945 open sessions. T = 240 min cuts only 0.45 % but gives a load of 995 sessions. Thus T = 120 min saves about 2.4 min of server time per session, which is about 11 % of the mean duration. Reject the model if a log–log plot of the survival function of real durations is not straight in the tail.
models.dsl:
title: A time limit for video sessions
problem: A free video service ends each session after T minutes. Cut few sessions but save server time.
param alpha = 12 {min} "median session duration"
param beta = 1.8 "shape; the variance is infinite for β ≤ 2"
param rate = 50 {sessions per min} "start rate of sessions"
param T = 120 {min} "time limit"
X ~ loglogistic(alpha = alpha, beta = beta) {min} "duration that the user wants"
prob cut = X > T "share of sessions that the limit cuts"
mean saved = max(X - T, 0) {min per session} "server time saved"
mean load = rate*min(X, T) {sessions} "mean number of open sessions (Little's law)"
alt "T = 60 min": T = 60
alt "T = 120 min": T = 120
alt "T = 240 min": T = 240
minimise load
require cut <= 0.02
focus X

models.title: The same tail at every scale
models.observe: For x_m = 1 and α = 1.2, P(X > 2t)/P(X > t) = 2^(−1.2) ≈ 0.435 at every level t. The run gives about 0.435 for t = 2, 0.434 for t = 20 and 0.43 for t = 200. The interval for t = 200 is wider, because fewer values pass 200. On the tail plot, the log–log survival function is a straight line with the slope −1.2.
models.dsl:
title: The same tail at every scale
problem: The Pareto I tail has no scale. Doubling a level divides the tail probability by the same factor 2^α at every level.
param xm = 1 "least value"
param alpha = 1.2 "tail index"
X ~ pareto1(xm = xm, alpha = alpha)
ratio r2 = E[X > 4] / E[X > 2] "P(X > 4)/P(X > 2)"
ratio r20 = E[X > 40] / E[X > 20] "P(X > 40)/P(X > 20)"
ratio r200 = E[X > 400] / E[X > 200] "P(X > 400)/P(X > 200)"
focus X

models.title: A wealth tax threshold for a revenue target
models.decision: Decision: the threshold t of a 2 % yearly tax on net wealth above t. Estimated quantity: the revenue τ N E[max(X − t, 0)] and the number of taxed households N P(X > t). The revenue must be at least 2,000 M$ per year.
models.reason: The top of the wealth distribution follows a Pareto law with good accuracy. Pareto I describes wealth above a high lower limit x_m. The tax base above t depends only on the tail index α.
models.inputs: Wealth X is in M$. The model covers N = 200,000 households with a wealth of at least x_m = 1 M$. The tail index is α = 1.5. The tax rate is τ = 2 %. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: households are independent. The model ignores avoidance, which reduces the base, and a change of wealth over time.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The estimators are sample means and a fraction of replicates.
models.diagnostics: The number of taxed households has the reference N (t/x_m)^(−α). The revenue has the exact value τ N x_m^α t^(1 − α)/(α − 1) for α > 1. The page has no reference for the revenue. Its variance is infinite for α ≤ 2, so its interval is not reliable, and a run usually gives less than the exact value. The very rich households, which pay most of the tax, are rare in a run. Other candidate models: Pareto II and the generalised Pareto law above a threshold.
models.interpretation: The exact revenue is 3,578, 2,530, 1,789 and 1,131 M$ per year for t = 5, 10, 20 and 50 M$. Thus t = 10 M$ meets the target and taxes 6,325 households. A run of 2^18 households gave about 2,340 M$ for t = 10 M$, below the exact value. Use the exact formula for the decision, and use the run only as a check. Reject the model if a Pareto quantile plot of tax or rich-list data is not straight above x_m.
models.dsl:
title: A wealth tax threshold for a revenue target
problem: A 2 % yearly tax applies to the part of net wealth above a threshold t. Raise at least 2,000 M$ per year and tax as few households as possible.
param xm = 1 {M$} "least wealth in the model"
param alpha = 1.5 "tail index of wealth"
param households = 200000 {households} "households with a wealth of at least x_m"
param tau = 0.02 "tax rate"
param t = 10 {M$} "threshold"
X ~ pareto1(xm = xm, alpha = alpha) {M$} "net wealth of one household"
mean revenue = tau*households*max(X - t, 0) {M$ per year}
mean taxed = households*(X > t) {households}
alt "t = 5 M$": t = 5
alt "t = 10 M$": t = 10
alt "t = 20 M$": t = 20
alt "t = 50 M$": t = 50
minimise taxed
require revenue >= 2000
focus X

models.title: A policy limit for data-breach costs
models.decision: Decision: the policy limit L for the notification cost of a data breach. Estimated quantity: the expected payment per breach E[min(cX, L)], and the probability P(cX > L) that a breach uses all of the limit. At most 0.5 % of breaches may use all of the limit.
models.reason: Some studies of breach records find a Pareto tail with an index below 1 (Maillart and Sornette, Physica A, 2010). This model uses α = 0.7. For α < 1 the mean of X is infinite. Thus the price of the cover exists only because of the limit, and it grows without bound with L.
models.inputs: X is the number of records in a breach, at least x_m = 1,000 records. The tail index is α = 0.7. The cost is c = 2 $ per record. The limits are 1, 5 and 20 M$. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: one breach. The real cost per record falls with the size of the breach, which this linear cost ignores.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The payment estimator is a sample mean of a bounded value, so its variance is finite. The exhaustion estimator is a fraction of replicates.
models.diagnostics: The page computes the references by quadrature. The exact form is E[min(X, M)] = x_m(1 + ((M/x_m)^(1 − α) − 1)/(1 − α)), with M = L/c. Without the limit, the expected payment is infinite. Other candidate models: a lognormal law, a truncated Pareto law with a finite upper limit, and Pareto II.
models.interpretation: 1.3 % of breaches use all of L = 1 M$, which is too often. 0.42 % of breaches use all of L = 5 M$, and its pure premium is 65,000 $ per breach. L = 20 M$ costs 101,000 $ per breach. The premium grows as L^(1 − α) = L^0.3 and has no upper bound. Reject the model if breach records above x_m show a tail that bends down on a log–log plot.
models.dsl:
title: A policy limit for data-breach costs
problem: A cyber policy pays the notification cost of a breach, up to a limit L. The records lost in a breach have a Pareto tail with an infinite mean. Choose the cheapest limit that few breaches use up.
param xm = 1000 {records} "least breach size in the model"
param alpha = 0.7 "tail index; the mean is infinite for α ≤ 1"
param cost = 2 {$ per record} "notification cost"
param L = 5000000 {$} "policy limit"
X ~ pareto1(xm = xm, alpha = alpha) {records} "records in one breach"
mean payment = cost*min(X, L/cost) {$ per breach} "expected payment, the pure premium"
prob exhaust = cost*X > L "the breach uses all of the limit"
alt "L = 1 M$": L = 1000000
alt "L = 5 M$": L = 5000000
alt "L = 20 M$": L = 20000000
minimise payment
require exhaust <= 0.005
focus X

models.title: How much of a fire season is one fire?
models.decision: Decision: the share r of the seasonal suppression budget that a fire agency keeps in reserve for the largest fire. Estimated quantity: P(the largest fire needs more than the reserve) = P(max(X)/sum(X) > r). Also the unused reserve E[max(r − max(X)/sum(X), 0)].
models.reason: Burned areas of wildfires have a power-law tail with an index often below 1. For α < 1 the share of the largest fire does not tend to 0 as the number of fires grows: E[sum/max] tends to 1/(1 − α). Pareto I is the simplest law with this tail above a least size.
models.inputs: A season has 100 fires, each with a burned area of at least x_m = 10 ha. The tail index is α = 0.7. The cost to fight a fire is proportional to its burned area. The reserve may be too small in at most 25 % of seasons. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: the fires are independent, and the model uses a constant number of fires. Real fires in one season share the weather, which makes large fires come together.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform, 100 for each season. The estimators are a fraction of seasons and a sample mean.
models.diagnostics: P(max(X) > 100,000 ha) = 1 − (1 − (10^4)^(−0.7))^100 = 0.147 is an exact reference. The share max(X)/sum(X) is between 0 and 1, so all its moments exist, but the page has no reference for it. For α < 1, a theorem of Bingham and Teugels gives E[sum/max] → 1/(1 − α) ≈ 3.3 as the number of fires grows. Thus the largest fire stays a large share of the season. For α > 1, max/sum tends to 0. Other candidate models: a truncated Pareto law with the largest possible fire size, and a lognormal law.
models.interpretation: The largest fire is about 48 % of the season on average. It is more than half of the season with a probability of about 0.41. A reserve of r = 0.7 is too small in about 22 % of seasons, and r = 0.8 in about 15 %. r = 0.7 meets the limit with the least unused reserve. Reject the model if the largest fires of past seasons are a much smaller share of the burned area.
models.dsl:
title: How much of a fire season is one fire?
problem: A fire agency keeps a share r of its seasonal budget for the largest fire. With a tail index below 1, one fire can be a large part of the season.
param xm = 10 {ha} "least burned area in the model"
param alpha = 0.7 "tail index"
param r = 0.5 "reserve share of the budget"
X ~ pareto1(xm = xm, alpha = alpha) repeat 100 {ha} "burned areas of the fires of a season"
share := max(X)/sum(X) "share of the largest fire"
prob short = share > r "the largest fire needs more than the reserve"
mean unused = max(r - share, 0) "unused reserve, as a share of the budget"
M := max(X) {ha} "the largest fire"
mean expected_share = share "E[max/sum]"
prob huge = M > 100000 "a fire larger than 100,000 ha"
alt "r = 0.5": r = 0.5
alt "r = 0.7": r = 0.7
alt "r = 0.8": r = 0.8
minimise unused
require short <= 0.25
focus share

models.title: One big jump makes a large sum
models.observe: The 10 values are Pareto II with σ = 1 and α = 1.5, so the mean of the sum S is 20. At x = 300, P(M > x) = 0.00191 and 10 P(X > x) = 0.00191 (exact references). The run gives P(S > x) ≈ 0.0022, near these values. About 91 % of the sums above 300 have one value above 300: one big jump makes the large sum. At x = 20, which is only the mean of S, P(S > x) ≈ 0.26 is far from P(M > x) = 0.099. Only about 39 % of these sums have a value above 20. The approximation P(S > x) ≈ n P(X > x) is a limit as x → ∞, and its convergence is slow.
models.dsl:
title: One big jump makes a large sum
problem: For a subexponential law, a large sum of 10 values comes from one large value. Then P(S > x) ≈ P(M > x) ≈ 10 P(X > x) for a large x.
param sigma = 1 "scale"
param alpha = 1.5 "tail index"
param x = 300 "large level"
X ~ pareto2(mu = 0, sigma = sigma, alpha = alpha) repeat 10 "10 independent values"
Y ~ pareto2(mu = 0, sigma = sigma, alpha = alpha) "one value"
S := sum(X) "sum"
M := max(X) "maximum"
prob sum_big = S > x "P(S > x)"
prob max_big = M > x "P(M > x)"
mean ten_one = 10*(Y > x) "10 P(X > x)"
ratio one_jump = E[(M > x)*(S > x)] / E[S > x] "P(M > x | S > x)"
alt "x = 20": x = 20
alt "x = 300": x = 300
focus S

models.title: Price an excess-of-loss reinsurance layer
models.decision: Decision: the priority d of a reinsurance layer that pays 5,000 k€ in excess of d for each claim. Estimated quantity: the layer loss per claim E[min(max(X − d, 0), L)], the premium, and the retained loss per claim. The premium must be at most 8,000 k€ per year.
models.reason: Large property claims have a power-law tail, and reinsurers price layers with Pareto laws. Pareto II also follows from a gamma mixture of exponential claim sizes over a varied portfolio. The mean excess over d grows linearly in d.
models.inputs: The claim X is in k€. The scale is σ = 100 k€ and the tail index is α = 1.8, so the mean is 125 k€ and the variance is infinite. There are 400 claims per year. The layer limit is L = 5,000 k€. The premium loading is 30 %. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: claims are independent. One event that causes many claims breaks this assumption. Then the insurer needs an event cover.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The estimators are sample means. The layer loss is between 0 and L, so its variance is finite. The mean claim does not change with d, so the most cover (the largest layer loss) within the budget gives the smallest retained loss.
models.diagnostics: The page computes the references by quadrature. The exact layer loss is σ/(α − 1) ((1 + d/σ)^(1 − α) − (1 + (d + L)/σ)^(1 − α)). The retained loss has an infinite variance for α ≤ 2, so its interval is not reliable. Its exact mean is 125 k€ minus the layer loss. Other candidate models: the generalised Pareto law above a threshold, the lognormal law and Burr XII.
models.interpretation: The premium is 12,906 k€ for d = 500 k€. It is 7,121 k€ for d = 1,000 k€ and 3,543 k€ for d = 2,000 k€. Thus d = 1,000 k€ is the lowest priority within the budget. Then 1.3 % of claims reach the layer, and the insurer keeps 111.3 k€ of the mean claim of 125 k€. Reject the model if the mean excess plot of large claims is not near a straight line.
models.dsl:
title: Price an excess-of-loss reinsurance layer
problem: An insurer buys a layer that pays the part of each claim between d and d + L. A lower priority d gives more cover but costs more. Choose d within the premium budget.
param sigma = 100 {k€} "scale of the claim size"
param alpha = 1.8 "tail index"
param claims = 400 {claims per year}
param L = 5000 {k€} "layer limit"
param load = 0.3 "premium loading"
param d = 1000 {k€} "priority"
X ~ pareto2(mu = 0, sigma = sigma, alpha = alpha) {k€} "size of one claim"
layer := min(max(X - d, 0), L) {k€} "the part of the claim that the layer pays"
mean layer_loss = layer {k€ per claim}
mean premium = (1 + load)*claims*layer {k€ per year}
mean retained = X - layer {k€ per claim} "the part of the claim that the insurer keeps"
prob hit = X > d "the claim reaches the layer"
alt "d = 500 k€": d = 500
alt "d = 1,000 k€": d = 1000
alt "d = 2,000 k€": d = 2000
maximise layer_loss
require premium <= 8000
focus X

models.title: How large a file to keep in an edge cache
models.decision: Decision: the size limit B of files that an edge cache stores. Estimated quantity: the share of requested bytes that the cache serves, E[X·1(X ≤ B)]/E[X]. Also the memory for 1,000,000 files. The memory must be at most 70 GB.
models.reason: Some measurements of web traffic find file sizes with a power-law tail and an index between 1 and 1.5 (Crovella and Bestavros, 1997). Pareto II is a heavy-tailed law of sizes from 0 up. With α near 1, a few large files hold a large share of the bytes.
models.inputs: The size X is in kB. The scale is σ = 20 kB and the tail index is α = 1.2, so the mean is 100 kB and the variance is infinite. Users request each of the 1,000,000 files with the same probability. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: file sizes are independent. Real requests prefer some files, so a model of popularity (for example the Zipf law) changes the result.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The byte share is a sample mean of X·1(X ≤ B), divided by the exact mean E[X] = σ/(α − 1). This value has the bound B, so its variance is finite. The ratio of two sample means would be very noisy, because X has an infinite variance. The memory is a sample mean of the same value.
models.diagnostics: The page computes the references by quadrature. A cache of files up to 1 MB stores 99.1 % of the files but serves only 45.5 % of the bytes. Other candidate models: the lognormal law for the body with a Pareto tail, and Pareto I.
models.interpretation: B = 10 MB serves 65.4 % of the bytes with 65.4 GB of memory. B = 100 MB serves 78.2 % but needs 78.2 GB, which is more than 70 GB. The last 0.06 % of the files hold about a third of the bytes. Reject the model if a log–log plot of the size distribution of the real catalogue is not straight in the tail.
models.dsl:
title: How large a file to keep in an edge cache
problem: An edge cache stores each file that is not larger than B. A larger B serves more bytes but needs more memory.
param sigma = 20 {kB} "scale of the file size"
param alpha = 1.2 "tail index"
param files = 1000000 {files}
param B = 10000 {kB} "largest file that the cache stores"
X ~ pareto2(mu = 0, sigma = sigma, alpha = alpha) {kB} "size of one file"
prob stored = X <= B "share of files that the cache stores"
mean byte_share = (alpha - 1)/sigma*min(X, B)*(X <= B) "share of requested bytes that the cache serves, X·1(X ≤ B)/E[X]"
mean memory = files/1000000*min(X, B)*(X <= B) {GB} "memory of the cache"
alt "B = 1 MB": B = 1000
alt "B = 10 MB": B = 10000
alt "B = 100 MB": B = 100000
maximise byte_share
require memory <= 70
focus X

models.title: When to send a reminder to a customer who has not come back
models.decision: Decision: the day r after a purchase at which a shop sends a reminder to a customer who has not come back. Estimated quantity: the share of wasted reminders, which go to customers who come back in the next 30 days without them. Also the share of customers who get a reminder.
models.reason: The model assumes that each customer comes back after an exponential time with a personal rate, and that the rates differ between customers. If the rates have a gamma law, the time to return has the Pareto II law. Its hazard α/(σ + x) falls with time, because the frequent customers come back first.
models.inputs: The time X is in days. The rates have a gamma law with the shape α = 2 and the scale 1/σ, with σ = 60 days. Thus the mean time to return is 60 days. At most 30 % of the reminders can go to waste. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: customers are independent. The model ignores customers who never come back. A Pareto/NBD model adds them.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The wasted share is a ratio estimator. The reach is a fraction of replicates.
models.diagnostics: The wasted share is 1 − ((σ + r)/(σ + r + 30))^α, and the reach is ((σ + r)/σ)^(−α). The page computes them by quadrature and in closed form. Other candidate models: the exponential law with one rate for all customers, and the Pareto/NBD model.
models.interpretation: The wasted share is 0.44 at day 30, 0.36 at day 60, 0.31 at day 90 and 0.27 at day 120. Only day 120 meets the limit of 0.3, and then 11 % of customers get a reminder. With one rate for all customers, the wasted share does not change with r, and no day would be better. Reject the model if the return hazard of real customers does not fall with time.
models.dsl:
title: When to send a reminder to a customer who has not come back
problem: A shop sends a reminder to each customer who has not come back r days after a purchase. A reminder is wasted if the customer comes back in the next 30 days without it.
param sigma = 60 {days} "scale"
param alpha = 2 "shape of the gamma law of the rates"
param r = 60 {days} "day of the reminder"
X ~ pareto2(mu = 0, sigma = sigma, alpha = alpha) {days} "time to the next purchase"
prob reach = X > r "share of customers who get a reminder"
ratio wasted = E[(X > r)*(X <= r + 30)] / E[X > r] "P(come back in the next 30 days | not back at day r)"
alt "Day 30": r = 30
alt "Day 60": r = 60
alt "Day 90": r = 90
alt "Day 120": r = 120
maximise reach
require wasted <= 0.3
focus X

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.title: Two shapes: the body and the tail
models.observe: The three laws have ck = 3, so their tails decay as x^(−3). The ratio P(X > 10)/P(X > 5) is 0.162 for c = 1, 0.126 for c = 3 and 0.125 for c = 6. For c = 3 and c = 6 they are near the limit 2^(−3) = 0.125. For c = 1 the ratio at these levels is still far from its limit. The bodies differ much: P(X ≤ 0.5) is 0.704, 0.111 and 0.0077. The means are 0.50, 1.21 and 1.40. On the tail plot, the three curves become parallel lines on the right.
models.dsl:
title: Two shapes: the body and the tail
problem: In Burr XII, c sets the body near 0 and the product ck sets the tail index. Compare three laws with ck = 3 and different c.
param c = 3 "first shape, the body"
param k = 1 "second shape"
param lambda = 1 "scale"
X ~ burr12(c = c, k = k, lambda = lambda)
prob small = X <= 0.5 "the body: P(X ≤ 0.5)"
mean m = X "mean"
ratio tail = E[X > 10] / E[X > 5] "P(X > 10)/P(X > 5), near 2^(−ck) = 0.125"
alt "c = 1, k = 3": c = 1; k = 3
alt "c = 3, k = 1": c = 3; k = 1
alt "c = 6, k = 0.5": c = 6; k = 0.5
focus X

models.title: A taper rate for a housing allowance
models.decision: Decision: the taper rate r of a housing allowance max(A − rX, 0), with A = 8 k$ per year. Estimated quantity: the share of households that get the allowance P(X < A/r), and the mean cost per household E[max(A − rX, 0)]. The cost must be at most 1 k$ per household.
models.reason: The Singh–Maddala (Burr XII) law fits household income well over the whole range. It has one shape for the lower part and the tail index ck for the top. The allowance depends on the lower part, which a one-shape law fits less well.
models.inputs: The income X is in k$ per year. The shapes are c = 2.8 and k = 1.4, and the scale is λ = 50 k$. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: households are independent. The model ignores a change of work hours that the taper can cause.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The estimators are a fraction of replicates and a sample mean of a bounded value.
models.diagnostics: P(X < A/r) has a closed-form reference, and the page computes the cost by quadrature. The cost is between 0 and A, so all its moments exist. The median income of the model is 42.6 k$ and the mean is 49.0 k$. Other candidate models: the Fisk (log-logistic) law, the Dagum law and the lognormal law.
models.interpretation: r = 0.25 reaches 29.7 % of households at a cost of 0.708 k$ per household. r = 0.2 reaches 45.1 % but costs 1.17 k$, which is more than the limit. Reject the model if survey incomes show a lower part that differs from the fitted law, for example a large atom at 0.
models.dsl:
title: A taper rate for a housing allowance
problem: A housing allowance pays A − rX to a household with income X, and 0 when this is negative. A lower taper r reaches more households but costs more.
param c = 2.8 "first shape"
param k = 1.4 "second shape"
param lambda = 50 {k$ per year} "scale"
param A = 8 {k$ per year} "allowance at zero income"
param r = 0.25 "taper rate"
X ~ burr12(c = c, k = k, lambda = lambda) {k$ per year} "income of one household"
prob reach = X < A/r "share of households that get the allowance"
mean cost = r*max(A/r - X, 0) {k$ per household}
alt "r = 0.4": r = 0.4
alt "r = 0.25": r = 0.25
alt "r = 0.2": r = 0.2
maximise reach
require cost <= 1
focus X

models.title: A deductible for motor damage claims
models.decision: Decision: the deductible d of a motor damage policy. Estimated quantity: the reduction of the pure premium E[min(X, d)]/E[X]. Also the share of claims that the deductible removes, P(X ≤ d). The premium must fall by at least 25 %.
models.reason: Motor damage claims have many small amounts, a mode above 0 and a moderately heavy tail. Burr XII fits these claim sizes well, because c sets the body and ck sets the tail.
models.inputs: The claim X is in $. The shapes are c = 1.5 and k = 2, so the tail index is 3. The scale is λ = 2,000 $. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: claims are independent. A deductible also stops policyholders from reporting some small claims. This model ignores that effect.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform. The reduction is a ratio estimator. The removed share is a fraction of replicates.
models.diagnostics: The page computes E[min(X, d)] by quadrature, and the mean claim is 1,612 $. The ratio has no reference, but the exact values are 0.150, 0.282 and 0.488 for d = 250, 500 and 1,000 $. Other candidate models: the lognormal law, the gamma law and Pareto II.
models.interpretation: d = 500 $ cuts the pure premium by 28 %, and the policyholder pays 455 $ of each claim on average. The deductible removes 21 % of claims, which also saves handling costs. d = 250 $ cuts only 15 %. Reject the model if the claim amounts show many claims near the old deductible, which shows a reporting effect.
models.dsl:
title: A deductible for motor damage claims
problem: The policyholder pays the first d $ of each claim. Choose the smallest deductible that cuts the pure premium by at least 25 %.
param c = 1.5 "first shape"
param k = 2 "second shape"
param lambda = 2000 {$} "scale"
param d = 500 {$} "deductible"
X ~ burr12(c = c, k = k, lambda = lambda) {$} "damage of one claim"
ratio cut = E[min(X, d)] / E[X] "reduction of the pure premium"
mean own = min(X, d) {$ per claim} "the part that the policyholder pays"
prob removed = X <= d "share of claims below the deductible"
alt "d = 250 $": d = 250
alt "d = 500 $": d = 500
alt "d = 1,000 $": d = 1000
minimise own
require cut >= 0.25
focus X

models.title: A design depth for daily rainfall
models.decision: Decision: the daily rainfall depth h that a storm-water tank must hold. Estimated quantity: the probability that the largest daily rainfall of a year is more than h, P(max(X) > h). It must be at most 0.1, which is a return period of 10 years.
models.reason: Global studies of daily rainfall on wet days find Burr XII among the best fits. It has a body near 0 and a power-law tail with the index ck, which a gamma law does not have.
models.inputs: X is the rainfall on one wet day, in mm. The shapes are c = 0.9 and k = 6, so the tail index is 5.4. The scale is λ = 30 mm. A year has 100 wet days. These values are illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: None: wet days are independent and the law does not change with the season. In real records, wet days come in spells, and their amounts have a correlation.
models.method: Independent draws by the closed-form inverse transform, 100 for each year. The estimator is a fraction of years.
models.diagnostics: P(max(X) > h) = 1 − (1 − P(X > h))^100 is an exact reference. The mean rainfall of a wet day is 5.35 mm. Other candidate models: the gamma law, the generalised Pareto law above a threshold, and the GEV law for the annual maximum.
models.interpretation: P(the largest daily rainfall of a year > h) is 0.165 for 60 mm, 0.061 for 80 mm and 0.026 for 100 mm. Thus 80 mm is the smallest of these depths that meets the limit, with a return period of about 16 years. Reject the model if the annual maxima of the station record exceed the design depths more often than the model says.
models.dsl:
title: A design depth for daily rainfall
problem: A storm-water tank holds the rainfall of one day up to the depth h. Choose the smallest h that a year exceeds with a probability of at most 0.1.
param c = 0.9 "first shape"
param k = 6 "second shape"
param lambda = 30 {mm} "scale"
param h = 80 {mm} "design depth"
X ~ burr12(c = c, k = k, lambda = lambda) repeat 100 {mm} "rainfall of the 100 wet days of a year"
M := max(X) {mm} "the largest daily rainfall of the year"
prob over = M > h "the largest daily rainfall of the year is more than h"
mean depth = h {mm} "design depth"
mean wet_mean = mean(X) {mm} "mean rainfall of a wet day"
alt "h = 60 mm": h = 60
alt "h = 80 mm": h = 80
alt "h = 100 mm": h = 100
minimise depth
require over <= 0.1
focus X

data.text: Synthetic: the illustrative parameters above define the model that makes the data. These values are illustrative and not calibrated evidence.

models.title: Maxima of Pareto draws become Fréchet
models.observe: M is the largest of 100 Pareto I draws with x_m = 1, divided by 100^(1/α). Its exact law is P(M ≤ x) = (1 − x^(−α)/100)^100. For α = 1.5, P(M ≤ 0.5) = 0.0567 and P(M > 4) = 0.1176. The Fréchet law gives 0.0591 and 0.1175. For α = 3, P(M ≤ 0.5) = 0.00024 against 0.00034, and P(M > 4) = 0.0155 for both laws. The two laws differ most in the lower part, where n = 100 is still small. On the tail plot both curves fall with the slope −α.
models.dsl:
title: Maxima of Pareto draws become Fréchet
problem: The largest of n Pareto draws, divided by n^(1/α), has a law near the Fréchet law with the same α.
param a = 1.5 "tail index α"
X ~ pareto1(xm = 1, alpha = a) repeat 100 "one Pareto draw"
M := max(X)/100^(1/a) "the normalised maximum of 100 draws"
F ~ frechet(alpha = a, s = 1, m = 0) "a Fréchet draw for comparison"
prob m_low = M <= 0.5 "P(M ≤ 0.5)"
prob f_low = F <= 0.5 "P(F ≤ 0.5)"
prob m_high = M > 4 "P(M > 4)"
prob f_high = F > 4 "P(F > 4)"
alt "α = 1.5": a = 1.5
alt "α = 3": a = 3
focus M

models.title: Retention of a cover for the largest claim of a year
models.decision: Decision: the retention R of a cover that pays the part of the largest claim of the year above R. Estimated quantity: the premium 1.3·E[max(M − R, 0)], the retained part E[min(M, R)] and P(M > R).
models.reason: Single claims of a property portfolio often have a Pareto-type tail. The maximum of many such claims is near the Fréchet law, by the Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem. The tail index α of the claims is also the tail index of the maximum.
models.inputs: The tail index is α = 2.5 and the scale is s = 2 million. The premium loading is 1.3, and the budget for the premium is 0.5 million per year. These values are illustrative. The model assumes many claims each year and the same claim law every year.
models.dependence: None inside the model: M is one value for one year. A storm that causes many large claims together changes the law of the maximum, and an aggregate cover is then a better tool.
models.method: Independent draws of M by the inverse transform. The estimators are sample means of min(M, R) and 1.3·max(M − R, 0), and a fraction of replicates for P(M > R). The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: P(M > R) has a closed form: 0.304, 0.162, 0.096 and 0.062 for R = 3, 4, 5 and 6. E[min(M, R)] has a reference by quadrature. The page shows the moment status of the premium as unknown and gives it no reference. Check it with E[max(M − R, 0)] = E[M] − E[min(M, R)]. Here E[M] = sΓ(1 − 1/α) = 2.978. This gives premiums of 0.884, 0.593, 0.430 and 0.330 million. The variance of M is finite because α > 2. Other candidate models: a GEV law with a free shape ξ, and a Gumbel law, which has a light tail.
models.interpretation: R = 5 million is the lowest retention whose premium fits the budget. Its premium is about 0.43 million, and the cover pays in about 1 year in 10. R = 4 costs about 0.59 million. A smaller α makes the premium much larger. Reject the model if past yearly maxima show a lighter tail on a Fréchet plot. Also reject it if the claim count changes much between years.

models.dsl:
title: Retention of a cover for the largest claim of a year
problem: An insurer buys a cover that pays the part of the largest claim of the year above a retention R. Find the lowest retention whose premium fits the budget.

mean premium = load*payout {million per year} "premium of the cover"

alt "R = 3": R = 3
alt "R = 4": R = 4
alt "R = 5": R = 5
alt "R = 6": R = 6

focus M

models.title: Capital buffer for the worst daily loss of a year
models.decision: Decision: the size L of a capital buffer for the worst daily loss of an equity index in one year. Estimated quantity: P(W > L), and the unused part E[L − min(W, L)] of the buffer.
models.reason: Daily losses of equity indices have a power tail with an index near 3 in some studies (Gopikrishnan and others, 1998). The worst of about 250 daily losses is then near the Fréchet law with the same index.
models.inputs: The tail index is α = 3 and the scale is s = 2.5 %. The losses are in % of the index value. These values are illustrative. The worst day may exceed the buffer in at most 1 year in 20.
models.dependence: The model treats the days as independent. Real losses come in clusters, because the volatility changes slowly. Clusters reduce the effective number of days, and the extremal index θ < 1 measures this effect.
models.method: Independent draws of W by the inverse transform. The estimators are a fraction of replicates for P(W > L) and a sample mean for the unused buffer. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: P(W > L) has a closed form: 0.118, 0.045, 0.021 and 0.012 for L = 5, 7, 9 and 11 %. The 20-year return level is the 0.95 quantile, 6.73 %. The mean E[W] = 3.39 % and the variance 5.28 are finite, but E[W³] is infinite. Other candidate models: a GEV law with a free ξ, and a model of the daily losses with changing volatility.
models.interpretation: L = 7 % is the smallest buffer with P(W > L) at most 0.05: the value is 0.045. On average the worst day leaves about 3.8 percentage points of this buffer unused. A buffer of 5 % fails in about 1 year in 8. Reject the model if past yearly worst losses show a tail index far from 3. Also reject it if the losses depend strongly on the volatility of the previous days.

title: Capital buffer for the worst daily loss of a year

alt "L = 5 %": L = 5

alt "L = 11 %": L = 11

models.title: Server capacity for the daily peak request rate
models.decision: Decision: the capacity C of a web service, in requests per second. Estimated quantity: the daily cost of capacity and overload, P(an overload day), and P(a month with at least one overload day).
models.reason: The peak request rate of a day is the largest of many bursts. The burst sizes have a power tail, so the daily peak is near the Fréchet law. The maximum of 30 independent Fréchet values is again Fréchet, with the scale 30^(1/α)s.
models.inputs: The tail index is α = 4. The scale is s = 1,500 requests/s above the base load m = 2,000 requests/s. Capacity costs 1 currency unit per 1,000 requests/s each day. An overload day costs 50 currency units. At most 1 month in 5 may have an overload day. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The 30 daily peaks of a month are independent with the same law. A trend in the traffic, or a weekly pattern, breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws by the inverse transform: one daily peak D, and 30 daily peaks Q for the month. The estimators are sample means and fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: All three quantities have references. P(D > C) and P(max(Q) > C) have closed forms. For C = 7,500 they are 0.0055 and 0.153. The monthly maximum has the law Fréchet(4, 3,510, 2,000). Its 0.8 quantile, 7,108 requests/s, is the least capacity that meets the monthly limit. Other candidate models: a GEV law with a free shape, and a lognormal law for the daily peak.
models.interpretation: C = 7,500 requests/s is the cheapest capacity that meets the limit. Its daily cost is about 7.78 currency units, and a month has an overload day with probability 0.153. C = 6,500 costs less, about 7.11, but 0.31 of the months have an overload day. Reject the model if past monthly maxima do not follow the Fréchet law with the scale 30^(1/α)s. Also reject it if the traffic has a trend.

title: Server capacity for the daily peak request rate

models.title: The mean of Cauchy values is no better than one value
models.observe: A is the mean of 100 standard Cauchy values, and Y is one value. P(A > 1) = P(Y > 1) = 0.25 exactly, and the run gives about 0.251 and 0.247. P(|A| > 10) = 0.0635 is the same as for one value. The mean of the values does not reduce the spread. E[Y] does not exist, so the page shows no interval and says that the mean does not exist. The sample mean of Y jumps each time a very large value comes.
models.dsl:
title: The mean of Cauchy values is no better than one value
problem: The mean of n independent Cauchy values has the same law as one value, so averaging does not reduce the spread.
X ~ cauchy(x0 = 0, gamma = 1) repeat 100 "one Cauchy value"
A := mean(X) "mean of 100 values"
Y ~ cauchy(x0 = 0, gamma = 1) "one value"
prob a_big = A > 1 "P(A > 1)"
prob y_big = Y > 1 "P(Y > 1)"
prob a_far = abs(A) > 10 "P(|A| > 10)"
mean avg = Y "sample mean of Y"
focus A

models.title: Lighthouse position from flashes on the shore
models.decision: Decision: estimate the position x_0 of a lighthouse along the shore by the mean or by the median of 50 flash positions. Estimated quantity: P(the estimate is within 0.5 km of x_0) for each estimator.
models.reason: The lighthouse sends each flash in a uniform random direction towards the shore. The flash arrives at x_0 + d tan(θ), with θ uniform on (−π/2, π/2). This position has exactly the law Cauchy(x_0, d).
models.inputs: The lighthouse is d = 2 km from the shore. The true position is x_0 = 0 km. The accepted error is 0.5 km. These values are illustrative. The detectors record the position of each flash without error.
models.dependence: None: the directions of the flashes are independent.
models.method: Independent draws of 50 positions in each replicate. The estimators are fractions of replicates in which each estimate is within 0.5 km of x_0.
models.diagnostics: The mean of the 50 positions has the law Cauchy(x_0, d), so P(|mean − x_0| ≤ 0.5) = (2/π) arctan(0.25) = 0.156. The median has no exact reference on the page. Its normal approximation has the standard deviation πd/(2√50) = 0.44 km, which gives about 0.74. The maximum likelihood estimator of x_0 is more precise than the median. Other candidate models: a normal law for the positions, and a Student's t law.
models.interpretation: The median is within 0.5 km of x_0 in about 74 % of the samples. The mean is within 0.5 km in only about 16 %. More flashes do not improve the mean, but they improve the median. Reject the model if the positions have a finite spread, for example if the shore is short or the detectors miss far flashes.

models.title: Width of a detector strip for diffusing particles
models.decision: Decision: the half-width w of a detector strip on a flat wall. Estimated quantity: P(the strip catches a particle), and the cost for each particle of the strip and of the missed particles.
models.reason: A particle that diffuses from a distance h above a flat wall first hits the wall at a random position. Along one axis of the wall, this position has exactly the law Cauchy(x_0, h). This follows from the harmonic measure of a half-space.
models.inputs: The source is h = 0.5 mm from the wall, above x_0 = 0. The strip costs 0.02 currency units per mm of width for each particle. A missed particle costs 1 currency unit. The strip must catch 90 % of the particles. These values are illustrative. The particles diffuse freely until they hit the wall.
models.dependence: None: the particles do not interact.
models.method: Independent draws of the hit position X. The estimators are a fraction of replicates and a sample mean of the cost. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: The page computes references by quadrature. The exact value is P(|X − x_0| ≤ w) = (2/π) arctan(w/h). This gives 0.844, 0.895, 0.921 and 0.947 for w = 2, 3, 4 and 6 mm. The least half-width for 90 % is h tan(0.45π) = 3.16 mm. w = 3 mm misses 90 % by only 0.005, so a short run can show it as not separable. A normal law with the same quartiles would give a much smaller strip. Other candidate models: a model with drift towards the wall, and a model with absorption before the wall.
models.interpretation: w = 4 mm is the cheapest strip that catches at least 90 % of the particles: about 92 %. Its cost is about 0.239 for each particle. w = 3 mm costs less, but it catches only about 89.5 %. Reject the model if the measured hit positions have a tail that falls faster than x^(−2). A flow or a drift can cause this.

alt "w = 4 mm": w = 4

models.title: Diversification with Cauchy returns
models.decision: Decision: whether an equal-weight portfolio of 10 assets reduces the risk of a monthly loss larger than 5 %. Estimated quantity: P(loss > 5 %) for one asset and for the portfolio.
models.reason: Mandelbrot and Fama proposed stable laws for returns. The Cauchy law is the symmetric stable law with α = 1 and β = 0. It is the boundary case in which the mean of n independent values has the same law as one value. This model shows the limit of diversification under very heavy tails.
models.inputs: Each monthly return has the law Cauchy(0.5 %, 2 %). The loss level is 5 %. The normal comparison model has the standard deviation 2.965 %, so it has the same quartiles. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The 10 returns are independent. Real returns are dependent, which makes diversification less effective still.
models.method: Independent draws of 1 and 10 returns in each replicate. The estimators are fractions of replicates.
models.diagnostics: The portfolio return has the law Cauchy(0.5, 2), the same as one asset. Thus P(loss > 5 %) = 1/2 − arctan(2.75)/π = 0.111 for both, with closed references. Under the normal model the probability falls from 0.032 for one asset to 2.2·10^(−9) for the portfolio. The run gives no loss of the normal portfolio, and the page shows a zero-hit bound. Other candidate models: a stable law with 1 < α < 2, a Student's t law, and a model with dependence.
models.interpretation: Under the Cauchy model the portfolio does not reduce P(loss > 5 %): it is about 0.111 for one asset and for the portfolio. For a stable law with α > 1 diversification reduces the scale by n^(1/α − 1). Reject the model if returns have a finite variance, or if their tail index is clearly above 1.

models.title: Averaging Lévy first-passage times makes large values more likely
models.observe: T is the first-passage time of a Brownian motion with no drift to the level 1, with the law Lévy(0, 1). A is the mean of 10 such times, with the law Lévy(0, 10). P(T > 100) = 0.080 and P(A > 100) = 0.248. Thus a large value is more likely for the mean of 10 times than for one time. E[T] is infinite, so the page shows no interval. The sample mean of T grows without limit when very long times come.
models.dsl:
title: Averaging Lévy first-passage times makes large values more likely
problem: A Brownian motion with no drift and unit variance per unit time starts at 0. Its first-passage time to the level 1 has the Lévy law with c = 1. The mean of 10 such times has the Lévy law with c = 10, so the mean is stochastically larger than one time: P(A > t) ≥ P(T > t) for all t.
X ~ levy(mu = 0, c = 1) repeat 10 "first-passage time to the level 1"
A := mean(X) "mean of 10 first-passage times"
T ~ levy(mu = 0, c = 1) "one first-passage time"
prob t_big = T > 100 "P(T > 100)"
prob a_big = A > 100 "P(A > 100)"
mean avg = T "sample mean of T"
focus A

models.title: Planned length of play in a fair game
models.decision: Decision: the planned number of rounds N for a player with a stake of 20 units in a fair game. Estimated quantity: P(the player loses the stake before round N), and the expected number of rounds played.
models.reason: In a fair game the fortune of the player is a random walk with no drift. For a large stake it is near a Brownian motion, and the time to lose the stake a has the law Lévy(0, a²). The player loses the stake with probability 1, but the mean time is infinite.
models.inputs: The stake is a = 20 units. Each round has the stake 1 unit and the variance 1. The risk to lose the stake may be at most 0.2. These values are illustrative. The Brownian approximation ignores the discrete steps.
models.dependence: The rounds are independent. The model has no upper target: the player stops only at round N or when the player loses the stake.
models.method: Independent draws of T by the inverse transform. The estimators are a fraction of replicates for the ruin and a sample mean of min(T, N). The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: P(T ≤ N) = 2(1 − Φ(a/√N)) has a closed form: 0.046, 0.157, 0.317 and 0.527 for N = 100, 200, 400 and 1,000. E[min(T, N)] has a reference by quadrature. The longest session with a risk of at most 0.2 is the 0.2 quantile of T, 244 rounds. Other candidate models: the exact random walk, and a game with a negative drift, which gives an inverse Gaussian time.
models.interpretation: N = 200 rounds is the longest planned session with a ruin risk below 0.2: about 0.157. The player then plays about 189 rounds on average. N = 400 doubles the ruin risk. The median time to lose the stake is about 879 rounds, but the mean is infinite. Reject the model if the game has an edge for the house, because the time then has a finite mean.

models.title: Recording window for the next spike of a neuron
models.decision: Decision: the length W of the recording window after a spike of a neuron. Estimated quantity: P(the next spike comes in the window), and the expected recording time for each trial.
models.reason: In the perfect integrate-and-fire model of Gerstein and Mandelbrot (1964), the membrane potential is a Brownian motion that starts at the reset value. A spike comes when it first reaches the threshold. With no drift, the interspike interval has the Lévy law with c = (θ/σ)².
models.inputs: The threshold is θ = 10 mV above the reset value. The noise is σ = 2 mV per √ms, so c = 25 ms. The window must hold the next spike in at least 80 % of the trials. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The intervals are independent, because the potential resets after each spike. Adaptation currents break this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of T by the inverse transform. The estimators are a fraction of replicates and a sample mean of min(T, W). The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: P(T ≤ W) = erfc(√(c/(2W))) has a closed form: 0.617, 0.752, 0.823 and 0.874 for W = 100, 250, 500 and 1,000 ms. The least window for 80 % is the 0.8 quantile, 390 ms. The median interval is 55 ms, but the mean interval is infinite. Other candidate models: the inverse Gaussian law for a positive drift, and a gamma law.
models.interpretation: W = 500 ms is the shortest window in the list that holds the next spike in at least 80 % of the trials: about 82 %. Each trial then uses about 155 ms on average. The mean of measured intervals does not estimate a firing rate under this model, because it has no finite limit. Reject the model if the sample mean of the intervals settles to a finite value as the record grows. A positive drift then gives the inverse Gaussian law.

models.title: Stop-loss level for a stock with no drift
models.decision: Decision: the fall L of the price that triggers a stop-loss order, for a holding period of one year. Estimated quantity: P(the stop triggers in the year), and P(the stop triggers in the first quarter).
models.reason: If the log price is a Brownian motion with no drift, the time until the price first falls by L is a first-passage time. It has the law Lévy(0, c), with c = (log(1/(1 − L))/σ)².
models.inputs: The volatility of the log price is σ = 0.3 per √year. The holding period is 1 year. The stop may trigger in at most 25 % of the years. These values are illustrative. The model assumes no drift of the log price and no price jumps.
models.dependence: The increments of the log price are independent. Volatility clusters and jumps break this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of T by the inverse transform. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: Both probabilities have a closed form: P(T ≤ H) = erfc(√(c/(2H))). For L = 10, 20, 30 and 40 %, P(T ≤ 1) is 0.725, 0.457, 0.234 and 0.089. The mean time to a fall is infinite, so a mean holding time is not a useful summary. Other candidate models: a Brownian motion with drift, which gives an inverse Gaussian time, and a model with jumps.
models.interpretation: L = 30 % is the tightest stop that triggers in at most 25 % of the years: the value is 0.234. A stop at 20 % triggers in about 46 % of the years, and in about 14 % in the first quarter. Reject the model if the log price has a clear drift, or if large falls come as jumps.

alt "L = 30 %": L = 0.3
alt "L = 40 %": L = 0.4
maximise trigger
require trigger <= 0.25
focus T

models.title: Sums of stable values keep the shape
models.observe: A is the sum of 16 values of S(1.5, 0, 1, 0; 0), divided by 16^(1/1.5). A has the law of one value Y. P(A > 3) = P(Y > 3) = 0.0516, and P(A > 30) = P(Y > 30) = 0.00123. These references are numerical. The run gives about 0.052 and 0.0012 for A. On the tail plot the curve falls with the slope −1.5. The tail formula c_α x^(−α) gives 0.00121 at x = 30. E[Y] = 0 exists, but the variance is infinite, so the page shows no interval.
models.dsl:
title: Sums of stable values keep the shape
problem: The sum of n independent symmetric stable values, divided by n^(1/α), has the law of one value. The tail of this law falls like x^(−α).
X ~ stable(alpha = 1.5, beta = 0, gamma = 1, delta = 0) repeat 16 "one stable value"
A := sum(X)/16^(1/1.5) "the scaled sum of 16 values"
Y ~ stable(alpha = 1.5, beta = 0, gamma = 1, delta = 0) "one value"
prob a_big = A > 3 "P(A > 3)"
prob y_big = Y > 3 "P(Y > 3)"
prob a_far = A > 30 "P(A > 30)"
prob y_far = Y > 30 "P(Y > 30)"
mean avg = Y "sample mean of Y"
focus A

models.title: Daily loss limit for a stock index
models.decision: Decision: whether a daily loss limit of 4 % for a stock index position is a rare event. Estimated quantity: P(a daily loss larger than 4 %) and P(a daily loss larger than 3 %). The models are stable laws with α = 1.7 and 1.9, and the normal law α = 2.
models.reason: Mandelbrot (1963) and Fama (1965) proposed stable laws for price changes. A daily return is a sum of many small changes. If these changes have a power tail with an index below 2, the generalised central limit theorem gives a stable law. With a finite variance it gives the normal law. Some early estimates of α for daily returns were between 1.6 and 1.9 (Fama, 1965).
models.inputs: The scale is γ = 0.6 % and the location is δ = 0.03 %, with β = 0. The normal model α = 2 has the standard deviation √2·γ = 0.85 %. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: One day only. Real returns have volatility clusters, which a stable law for single days does not describe.
models.method: Independent draws by the Chambers–Mallows–Stuck method. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: The references come from the numerical CDF. P(loss > 4 %) is 0.0059 for α = 1.7, 0.0015 for α = 1.9 and 1.0·10^(−6) for α = 2. For α = 2 the run usually sees no losses, and the page shows a zero-hit bound. Other candidate models: a Student's t law with ν near 3, which has a finite variance, and a GARCH model.
models.interpretation: Under α = 1.7 a loss larger than 4 % comes on about 1.5 days of 250 trading days. Under the normal model it comes about once in 4,000 years. The value of α changes the answer by more than three orders of magnitude. Reject the stable model if the sample has a finite variance, for example if a Hill estimate of the tail index is clearly above 2.

param mu = 0.03 {%} "location δ of the daily return"

models.title: Search radius for an animal that moves along a river
models.decision: Decision: the search radius r along a river around the release point of a tagged animal. Estimated quantity: P(the animal is within r after 100 steps), and the expected cost of one search.
models.reason: Some studies model animal movement as a Lévy flight, with step lengths that have a power tail. This model assumes stable steps, so the sum of 100 steps is again stable with the same α. Its scale grows like 100^(1/α), faster than the √100 of normal diffusion.
models.inputs: Each step along the river has the law S(1.5, 0, 10 m, 0; 0). The search costs 0.01 currency units per metre of the river. A failed search costs 100 currency units. The search must find the animal with probability at least 0.9. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The steps are independent with the same law. Real animals have a home range and a memory of places, which limit the long steps.
models.method: Independent draws of 100 steps by the Chambers–Mallows–Stuck method. The estimators are fractions of replicates and a sample mean of the cost. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: D has the law S(1.5, 0, 215 m, 0; 0). The page gives P(D > r) a numerical reference, but not P(|D| ≤ r). By symmetry P(|D| ≤ r) = 1 − 2P(D > r), which checks the run: for r = 750 m it gives 1 − 2·0.0393 = 0.921. Under normal steps with the same γ, D has the standard deviation 141 m, and P(|D| > 750 m) is about 10^(−7). Other candidate models: a truncated stable step law, and a correlated random walk.
models.interpretation: r = 750 m is the cheapest radius in the list that finds the animal with probability at least 0.9: about 0.92. The expected cost is about 22.8 currency units. A normal diffusion model would choose a much smaller radius and fail often. Reject the model if the measured step lengths have a finite variance, or if the displacement grows like √n.

param r = 2000 {m} "search radius"

alt "r = 2,000 m": r = 2000
