models.title: Detector threshold for impulsive radio noise
models.decision: Decision: the threshold t of a pulse detector in impulsive noise. Estimated quantity: P(false alarm) = P(N > t), and P(detection) = P(15 + N > t).
models.reason: Atmospheric and man-made radio noise is impulsive. Each sample is the sum of many independent pulses with a symmetric power-law size whose tail index is below 2, so the noise is near a symmetric stable law. Nikias and Shao (1995) use symmetric stable noise for this reason.
models.inputs: The noise has the law S(1.5, 0, 1 µV, 0; 0). The pulse has the amplitude 15 µV. The false-alarm rate may be at most 1 %. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: One sample only. Real impulsive noise often comes in bursts.
models.method: Independent draws by the Chambers–Mallows–Stuck method. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: The references come from the numerical CDF. The false-alarm rate is 0.043, 0.021, 0.0078 and 0.0050 for t = 3.3, 5, 9 and 12 µV. The 0.99 quantile of the noise is 7.74 µV. A normal noise model with the same γ gives the threshold 3.3 µV for 1 %. Under the stable noise this threshold has a false-alarm rate of 0.043. Other candidate models: Middleton class A noise, and a Gaussian mixture.
models.interpretation: t = 9 µV meets the false-alarm limit with the most detections: about 98.5 %. The threshold from the normal model gives about 4 times too many false alarms. Reject the model if the noise samples have a finite variance, or if the tail slope on a log–log plot is far from −1.5.

models.title: The maximum of GEV values is a GEV value
models.observe: The largest of 50 GEV(ξ, 0, 1) values is GEV(ξ, (50^ξ − 1)/ξ, 50^ξ): the shape ξ stays, and only the location and the scale change. For ξ = −0.2 the location is 2.71 and the scale 0.457, and the maximum cannot pass the end point 5, so P(M > 5) = 0. For ξ = 0 the location moves by log 50 = 3.91 and the scale stays 1. For ξ = 0.2 the location is 5.93 and the scale 2.19, so the tail grows with the block. The exact values are P(M > 5) = 0, 0.286 and 0.790, and E[M] = 2.90, 4.49 and 7.73. The CDF plot shows the run on the exact law of M for each alternative.
models.dsl:
title: The maximum of GEV values is a GEV value
problem: The GEV laws are the only laws of maxima that keep their shape: the maximum of n independent GEV values is again a GEV value, with the same ξ and a new location and scale.
param xi = 0.2 "shape ξ"
X ~ gev(xi = xi, mu = 0, sigma = 1) repeat 50 "one value of each of 50 blocks"
M := max(X) "the largest of the 50 values"
prob over5 = M > 5 "P(M > 5)"
prob over2 = M > 2 "P(M > 2)"
mean level = M "mean of the largest value"
alt "ξ = −0.2": xi = -0.2
alt "ξ = 0": xi = 0
alt "ξ = 0.2": xi = 0.2
focus M

models.title: Design depth for a storm drain at Fort Collins
models.decision: Decision: the daily rainfall depth d that a storm drain must carry. Estimated quantity: P(the annual maximum daily rainfall passes d), and P(it passes d at least once in a design life of 50 years).
models.reason: The data are annual maxima: the largest daily rainfall of each year. The Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem gives the GEV law as the only possible limit law of a normalised maximum. Thus the GEV law is the standard first model for annual maxima.
models.inputs: Real data: 128 annual maxima of daily rainfall at Fort Collins, Colorado, from 1896 to 2025, in mm. The maximum likelihood fit gives μ = 34.6 mm, σ = 13.1 mm and ξ = 0.124 (standard error 0.075). The model uses these estimates as fixed values, so it does not include their uncertainty. The model takes the years as independent, with one law and no trend.
models.dependence: Annual maxima of different years are independent in the model. Over 50 years the model takes the largest of 50 independent annual maxima. A climate trend or a multi-year cycle breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of the annual maximum Z and of 50 annual maxima L. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The page has exact references: the GEV survival function, and 1 − F(d)^50 for the largest of 50 years.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: P(Z > d) = 1 − F(d), and P(M > d) = 1 − F(d)^50. The data panel shows the maximum likelihood fit, its standard errors and a probability plot. The deviance test of ξ = 0 gives 3.28 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.070. Thus the data do not exclude the Gumbel law, but the GEV fit has the heavier tail. Other candidate models: the Gumbel law (ξ = 0), with μ = 35.5 mm and σ = 13.8 mm, and a GEV law with a trend in μ.
models.interpretation: Under the GEV fit, d = 100 mm passes the annual maximum with probability 0.020: about the 50-year level. Over 50 years the drain overflows at least once with probability 0.64. d = 125 mm gives 0.0068 a year and 0.29 over 50 years, so it is the least depth that meets the limit of 0.3. Under the Gumbel fit the same depths give 0.37 and 0.073 over 50 years. Thus the choice of ξ changes the overflow probability by a factor of about 4, much more than the Monte Carlo error. In this list, d = 125 mm is still the least depth that meets the limit. The estimates also omit the uncertainty of the fitted parameters: the standard error of ξ is 0.075. Reject the model if the annual maxima show a trend, or if a longer record gives a clearly different ξ.
models.dsl:
title: Design depth for a storm drain at Fort Collins
problem: A storm drain must carry the rainfall of one day. Choose the design depth from the annual maxima of daily rainfall at Fort Collins, Colorado, for a design life of 50 years.
param mu = 34.6 {mm} "location, maximum likelihood estimate"
param sigma = 13.1 {mm} "scale, maximum likelihood estimate"
param xi = 0.124 "shape, maximum likelihood estimate (standard error 0.075)"
param d = 100 {mm} "design depth"
Z ~ gev(xi = xi, mu = mu, sigma = sigma) {mm} "annual maximum of daily rainfall"
L ~ gev(xi = xi, mu = mu, sigma = sigma) repeat 50 {mm} "annual maxima of 50 years"
M := max(L) {mm} "largest daily rainfall in 50 years"
prob annual = Z > d "the drain overflows in one year"
prob life = M > d "the drain overflows at least once in 50 years"
alt "d = 100 mm": d = 100
alt "d = 125 mm": d = 125
alt "d = 150 mm": d = 150
require life <= 0.3
focus Z

models.title: Crest height of a sea wall with a bounded tide
models.decision: Decision: the crest height h of a sea wall, in metres above the datum. Estimated quantity: P(the annual maximum sea level passes h), and P(it passes h at least once in 100 years).
models.reason: The annual maximum sea level is a maximum of many tides and surges. The GEV law is its limit law. Sea levels often have ξ < 0: the tide and the depth of the sea limit the surge, so the law has a finite upper end point.
models.inputs: Illustrative values: μ = 3.9 m, σ = 0.2 m and ξ = −0.1. The upper end point is μ − σ/ξ = 5.9 m. Candidate heights are 4.6 m, 4.8 m and 5.0 m. The design life is 100 years.
models.dependence: The annual maxima are independent and have one law in the model. A rise of the mean sea level moves μ with time and breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of the annual maximum Z and of 100 annual maxima. The estimators are fractions of replicates. Exact references come from the GEV survival function and from 1 − F(h)^100.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: 1 − F(h) for one year and 1 − F(h)^100 for 100 years. For ξ < 0 the law has the end point μ − σ/ξ = 5.9 m, so no value of the run passes it. Other candidate models: the Gumbel law (ξ = 0), and a GEV law with μ that increases with time. The Gumbel law has no end point, so it gives larger probabilities for high crests.
models.interpretation: h = 4.6 m fails in a year with probability 0.013, and at least once in 100 years with probability 0.74. h = 4.8 m gives 0.0025 and 0.22. h = 5.0 m gives 0.00034 and 0.033, so it is the only height that meets the limit of 0.1 over 100 years. The end point of 5.9 m comes from the assumed ξ = −0.1. A small error in ξ moves it far, so the design must not rely on it. Reject the model if the record shows a rise of the annual maxima, or if a storm passes the end point of the assumed law.

models.title: Cooling capacity of a hospital ward for the hottest day of a year
models.decision: Decision: the outdoor design temperature c of the cooling system of a hospital ward. Estimated quantity: P(the hottest day of a year passes c). Also the mean number of degrees above c on that day, E[max(Z − c, 0)].
models.reason: The hottest day of a year is a maximum of 365 daily maxima. The GEV law is its limit law. Annual maximum temperatures usually have ξ < 0: a finite upper end point.
models.inputs: Illustrative values: μ = 36 °C, σ = 1.5 °C and ξ = −0.25. The upper end point is μ − σ/ξ = 42 °C. Candidate design temperatures are 38 °C, 39 °C and 40 °C.
models.dependence: Years are independent and have one law in the model. A warming trend moves μ with time and breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of the annual maximum Z. The estimators are a fraction of replicates and a sample mean. References: the exact GEV survival function, and quadrature over the quantile function for the mean excess.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: P(Z > c) = 1 − F(c). The mean excess E[max(Z − c, 0)] has a numerical reference by quadrature over the quantile function of Z. The upper end point is μ − σ/ξ = 42 °C. Other candidate models: the Gumbel law, with no end point, and a GEV law with μ that increases with time.
models.interpretation: The hottest day passes 38 °C in about 18 % of years, and 39 °C in about 6.1 %. Thus only c = 40 °C meets the limit of 5 %. With c = 40 °C the hottest day passes the design temperature in about 1.2 % of years, by a mean of 0.0049 °C over all years. The finite end point of 42 °C limits the excess, but it depends on the fitted ξ. Reject the model if the annual maxima increase with time, or if the excess above 40 °C does not fall as the fit says.

models.title: Threshold stability of the generalised Pareto law
models.observe: For ξ = 0.25 and y = 1, P(X > u + 1 | X > u) is 0.410, 0.482 and 0.540 for u = 0, 1 and 2 (exact references). The excess over u is GPD(ξ, σ + ξu), so a higher threshold gives a larger excess. For ξ = 0 all three ratios are e^(−1) = 0.368, because the exponential law has no memory. For ξ = −0.25 they fall to 0.316, 0.198 and 0.0625, because the end point 4 comes nearer. The mean excess (σ + ξu)/(1 − ξ) is linear in u. Its exact values are 1.33, 1.67 and 2.00 for ξ = 0.25, 1 for ξ = 0, and 0.8, 0.6 and 0.4 for ξ = −0.25. The page shows the mean excess as a Monte Carlo estimate with no reference value, and the estimates agree with these values.
models.dsl:
title: Threshold stability of the generalised Pareto law
problem: The excess of a GPD value over a threshold u is again GPD, with the same shape ξ and the scale σ + ξu. The conditional tail and the mean excess show this.
param xi = 0.25 "shape ξ"
param sigma = 1 "scale σ"
param y = 1 "excess level y"
X ~ gpd(xi = xi, sigma = sigma, mu = 0) "a GPD value with threshold 0"
ratio tail0 = E[X > 0 + y] / E[X > 0] "P(X > u + y | X > u) for u = 0"
ratio tail1 = E[X > 1 + y] / E[X > 1] "P(X > u + y | X > u) for u = 1"
ratio tail2 = E[X > 2 + y] / E[X > 2] "P(X > u + y | X > u) for u = 2"
ratio excess0 = E[pmax(X - 0, 0)] / E[X > 0] "mean excess over u = 0"
ratio excess1 = E[pmax(X - 1, 0)] / E[X > 1] "mean excess over u = 1"
ratio excess2 = E[pmax(X - 2, 0)] / E[X > 2] "mean excess over u = 2"
alt "ξ = 0.25": xi = 0.25
alt "ξ = 0 (exponential)": xi = 0
alt "ξ = −0.25 (end point 4)": xi = -0.25
focus X

models.title: Attachment point of an operational-loss insurance layer
models.decision: Decision: the attachment point a of an insurance layer that pays up to 20 M€ above a, for each operational loss. Estimated quantity: the annual premium 1.5 · 5 · E[min(max(L − a, 0), 20)], and the annual loss that the bank keeps.
models.reason: Banks record operational losses only above a collection threshold. By the Pickands–Balkema–de Haan theorem, the excess over a high threshold has a law near the GPD, for most continuous laws. The peaks-over-threshold method of operational risk uses this model. The shape ξ sets the tail: ξ > 0 gives a power tail with the index 1/ξ.
models.inputs: Losses above u = 1 M€ have the excess law GPD(ξ = 0.4, σ = 2 M€). A mean of n = 5 such losses occurs in one year. The layer pays at most 20 M€ for each loss. The premium is 1.5 times the expected payment. The budget is 6 M€ for each year. These values are illustrative. Real estimates of ξ for operational losses are often larger, and they are very uncertain.
models.dependence: The losses are independent, and their number does not depend on their sizes. The annual values multiply the mean for one loss by n = 5, so they need only the mean number of losses. A common cause, such as one system failure, can make several large losses together. This breaks the assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of L by inversion of the survival function. The estimators are sample means and fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams, so the differences between the attachment points are precise.
models.diagnostics: The page computes exact references for P(L > a), and references by quadrature for the payment and the premium. E[L] = u + σ/(1 − ξ) = 4.33 M€. Thus the bank keeps an annual loss of 5 · (4.33 − payment): E[L] is exact, and the payment comes from quadrature. This is 16.0, 19.0, 20.2 and 21.2 M€ for a = 5, 10, 15 and 30. The variance of L is finite only for ξ < 0.5. The fourth moment is infinite for ξ = 0.4, so the interval of the kept loss can have a poor coverage. Other candidate models: a lognormal or a Burr XII law for the loss sizes, and a GPD with a larger ξ.
models.interpretation: a = 10 M€ is the lowest attachment point in the budget. Its premium is 3.93 M€ (reference), and the bank keeps 19.0 M€ for each year (from the exact E[L] and the quadrature reference of the payment). a = 5 M€ costs 8.56 M€, more than the budget. For a = 10 M€, 7.6 % of the losses above 1 M€ reach the layer. The result is sensitive to ξ: a larger ξ puts more mass above the layer, and the bank keeps that mass. Reject the model if the mean excess plot of the data is not near a straight line above u. Also reject it if the estimate of ξ changes much with the threshold.

models.dsl:
title: Attachment point of an operational-loss insurance layer
problem: A bank records operational losses above 1 M€. It buys insurance that pays the part of one loss above the attachment point a, up to a cover of 20 M€. Find the lowest a whose premium fits the budget.
param xi = 0.4 "GPD shape of the loss excess"
param sigma = 2 {M€} "GPD scale of the loss excess"
param u = 1 {M€} "collection threshold"
param a = 10 {M€} "attachment point"
param cover = 20 {M€} "cover of the layer"
param n = 5 {losses per year} "mean number of losses above u in one year"
param load = 1.5 "premium loading on the expected payment"

prob hit = L > a "the loss reaches the layer"
mean paid = pmin(pmax(L - a, 0), cover) {M€} "insurance payment for one loss"

alt "a = 5 M€": a = 5
alt "a = 10 M€": a = 10
alt "a = 15 M€": a = 15
alt "a = 30 M€": a = 30

require premium <= 6
focus L

models.title: Per-day rate for long-stay outlier payments
models.decision: Decision: the payment rate for each outlier day, from a fixed annual fund of €300,000. Estimated quantity: P(the annual payment exceeds the fund), and the mean annual payment.
models.reason: Lengths of stay have a long right tail. The insurer pays only the days beyond a trim point of 30 days, so the payment depends only on the excess over this threshold. The GPD is the standard approximation for the excess over a high threshold (Pickands–Balkema–de Haan). A positive ξ gives the heavy tail of very long stays.
models.inputs: 40 long stays (beyond day 30) occur in each year. The days beyond day 30 of each stay have the law GPD(ξ = 0.2, σ = 12 days), with the mean σ/(1 − ξ) = 15 days. The fund is €300,000. The rates are €300, €325, €350 and €400 for each day. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The stays are independent. The model uses a fixed number of 40 long stays. A Poisson number would add variance. An epidemic can cause more long stays in one year, which breaks the assumption.
models.method: 40 independent GPD draws in each replicate. The annual payment is the rate times the sum of the days. The estimators are a fraction of replicates and sample means. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: The expected sum of days is 40 · 15 = 600 days, and the page shows this exact reference. The estimate of the mean days agrees with it, which checks the sampler. The probability of a shortfall has no reference, because the law of a sum of GPD values has no closed form. The variance of each excess is finite for ξ < 0.5: σ²/((1 − ξ)²(1 − 2ξ)) = 375 days². Other candidate models: a lognormal or a gamma law for the excess days, and a negative binomial number of long stays.
models.interpretation: €350 for each day is the highest rate with a shortfall probability of at most 5 %: about 0.030. The mean annual payment is then €210,000 (exact). At €400 the probability of a shortfall is about 0.11. The fund is 43 % above the mean payment, because the sum of 40 heavy-tailed values has a wide spread. Reject the model if the excess days of past years show a tail much heavier or lighter than ξ = 0.2. Also reject it if the number of long stays changes much from year to year.

models.title: Design magnitude for a 50-year life with a bounded magnitude law
models.decision: Decision: the design magnitude md for a plant with a 50-year service life. Estimated quantity: P(the largest magnitude in 50 years > md).
models.reason: The Gutenberg–Richter law makes the magnitudes above a threshold exponential: the GPD with ξ = 0. The finite size of the faults gives a maximum magnitude. A GPD with ξ < 0 has a finite end point, and it is a standard model for magnitudes above a threshold.
models.inputs: The magnitudes above m0 = 6 have the law GPD(ξ = −0.18, σ = 0.45). The end point is m0 + σ/|ξ| = 8.5. 10 events above magnitude 6 occur in 50 years: this is the mean count. The values are illustrative and do not come from a seismic hazard study.
models.dependence: The magnitudes are independent. Aftershocks break this assumption, so remove them from the catalogue first. The model uses a fixed count of 10 events.
models.method: 10 independent GPD draws in each replicate, and their maximum. The estimator is a fraction of replicates. The law of the maximum is exact, P(max ≤ m) = F(m)^10, so the page shows a reference.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: P(exceed) = 1 − F(md)^10 is 0.453, 0.193, 0.0599 and 0.0013 for md = 7.0, 7.25, 7.5 and 8.0. A Poisson count with the mean 10 gives 1 − exp(−10(1 − F(md))) = 0.0597 for md = 7.5, nearly the same value. The unbounded exponential model (ξ = 0, σ = 0.45) gives 0.305 for md = 7.5 and 0.111 for md = 8.0. Other candidate models: the exponential (Gutenberg–Richter) law, and a tapered Pareto law of the seismic moment.
models.interpretation: md = 7.5 is the lowest design magnitude in the list with an exceedance probability of at most 10 %: 0.060 (exact). The choice depends strongly on ξ. With ξ = 0 the same rule needs md above 8.0. The end point 8.5 is a model assumption, and data of a few decades cannot confirm it. Reject the model if the catalogue has magnitudes near or above 8.5, or if the excess magnitudes are not near a GPD.

models.title: The maximum of exponential values tends to the Gumbel law
models.observe: M is the maximum of 100 standard exponential values minus log 100. Its exact law is P(M ≤ x) = (1 − e^(−x)/100)^100. P(M ≤ −1) = 0.0636, and the Gumbel limit gives P(G ≤ −1) = 0.0660. P(M ≤ 2) = 0.8733, and P(G ≤ 2) = 0.8734. E[M] = H_100 − log 100 = 0.5822, and E[G] = γ = 0.5772. On the CDF plot the two curves are near for n = 100. The largest difference is in the left tail.

models.title: Design wind speed for a 50-year service life
models.decision: Decision: the design wind speed v for a tower with a 50-year service life. Estimated quantity: P(the highest wind speed in 50 years > v).
models.reason: The annual maximum wind speed is the maximum of many wind values in a year. The parent law has a light tail, so the annual maximum is in the Gumbel domain of attraction. Design codes fit the Gumbel law to annual maxima of wind speed.
models.inputs: The annual maxima have the law Gumbel(μ = 28 m/s, β = 3 m/s). The service life is 50 years. The target is a probability of exceedance of at most 10 % in the life. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The annual maxima are independent and have the same law. A climate trend breaks the assumption of the same law.
models.method: 50 independent Gumbel draws in each replicate, and their maximum. The estimator is a fraction of replicates. By max-stability the maximum has the exact law Gumbel(μ + β log 50, β), so the page shows a reference.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: P(exceed) = 1 − exp(−50 e^(−(v − μ)/β)) is 0.375, 0.159, 0.0616 and 0.0231 for v = 42, 45, 48 and 51 m/s. The mean highest speed in 50 years is μ + β(log 50 + γ) = 41.5 m/s. The 50-year return value is 39.7 m/s. The probability that the highest speed in 50 years exceeds it is 1 − 0.98^50 = 0.64. Other candidate models: a GEV law with ξ ≠ 0, and a Weibull law for the parent wind speed.
models.interpretation: v = 48 m/s is the lowest speed in the list with a probability of at most 10 %: 0.062 (exact). v = 45 m/s gives 0.159. The highest speed would exceed the 50-year return value in 64 % of the service lives. Reject the model if a GEV fit of the annual maxima gives a shape ξ clearly different from 0, or if the record shows a trend.

models.title: Rating load for the heaviest truck in 100 years
models.decision: Decision: the rating load R for the assessment of a bridge over a 100-year reference period. Estimated quantity: P(the heaviest truck in 100 years > R).
models.reason: The heaviest truck in a year is the maximum of a very large number of truck weights, with a light upper tail. Thus its law is near the Gumbel law. The Gumbel law is max-stable: the maximum of N annual values is Gumbel(μ + β log N, β). Bridge load models use this to extrapolate from measured traffic.
models.inputs: The heaviest truck in one year has the law Gumbel(μ = 60 t, β = 4 t). The reference period is N = 100 years. The target is a probability of at most 5 %. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The annual maxima are independent and have the same law. A growth of traffic or a change of the legal weight limits breaks this.
models.method: Two methods in the same model: one Gumbel draw W of the 100-year law by max-stability, and the maximum of 100 annual draws. The estimators are fractions of replicates.
models.diagnostics: Both methods have the same exact references: 0.0872, 0.0422, 0.0201 and 0.0096 for R = 88, 91, 94 and 97 t. The two estimates agree within their intervals, which checks max-stability. The mean heaviest truck in 100 years is μ + β(log 100 + γ) = 80.7 t. Other candidate models: a GEV law with ξ < 0, because the weight of a truck has a physical upper limit.
models.interpretation: R = 91 t is the lowest rating load in the list with a probability of at most 5 %: 0.042 (exact). R = 88 t gives 0.087. Reject the model if a GEV fit of the annual maxima gives ξ clearly below 0. Also reject it if overloaded trucks form a separate group in the data.

models.title: Installed capacity for the annual peak electricity demand
models.decision: Decision: the installed capacity K of a power system. Estimated quantity: P(the annual peak demand exceeds the available capacity), the loss-of-load probability at the peak.
models.reason: The annual peak demand is the maximum of the hourly demand in a year. The hourly demand has light tails, so the law of the annual maximum is near the Gumbel law. The Gumbel law is a common model for annual peak loads.
models.inputs: The peak demand has the law Gumbel(μ = 9 GW, β = 0.3 GW). The system has 10 large units of 0.6 GW. Each one is out of service at the peak with the probability 0.05. The rest of the capacity comes from small units that the model takes as always available. The target is a shortfall in at most 1 year in 20. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The demand and the outages are independent, and the outages of the units are independent. A heat wave raises the demand and can also reduce the output of thermal units. This breaks the assumption.
models.method: Independent draws of the demand D and of the binomial number of units out of service. The estimators are fractions of replicates and a sample mean.
models.diagnostics: The page computes a numerical reference by summation over the outages and quadrature over D. Without outages, P(D > K) has an exact reference: 0.0067 for K = 10.5 GW and 0.0013 for K = 11 GW. The outages raise the loss-of-load probability to 0.053 and 0.014. Other candidate models: a GEV law for the peak, and a demand model with a temperature variable.
models.interpretation: K = 11 GW is the lowest capacity in the list with a loss-of-load probability of at most 0.05: 0.014 (reference). The mean reserve margin is then 1.53 GW. A plan that ignores the outages would accept K = 10.5 GW, but its true probability is 0.053. Reject the model if the annual peaks show a trend, or if the peak demand and the outages are dependent in the data.

models.title: The maximum of values with a finite end point
models.observe: X has the GPD law with ξ = −0.5 and σ = 1, so P(X > 2 − s) = s²/4 near the end point 2. The normalised maximum M = (max(X) − 2)·√50 of 200 values has P(M ≤ −s) = (1 − s²/200)^200, which tends to e^(−s²). P(M ≤ −1) = 0.3670, and the limit gives P(W ≤ −1) = e^(−1) = 0.3679. P(M ≤ −0.5) = 0.7787, and P(W ≤ −0.5) = 0.7788. E[M] = −0.8846 (numerical reference), and E[W] = −Γ(1.5) = −0.8862. The maximum comes near the end point at the rate n^(−1/2). For the uniform law (α = 1) the rate is 1/n.

models.title: Which long jumper to select for one place in a championship?
models.decision: Decision: select athlete A or athlete B for one place in the long jump. Estimated quantity: P(the best mark ≥ 8.35 m, a medal mark), with the condition P(the best mark ≥ 8.15 m, a final mark) ≥ 0.35.
models.reason: The best mark in a competition is a maximum of several jumps. Human performance has a physical upper limit, so the law of the best mark has a finite end point. The reverse Weibull law is the extreme-value law with a finite end point. Studies of best marks in athletics use this law to estimate the ultimate record.
models.inputs: Athlete A: upper limit μ = 8.40 m, σ = 0.30 m, α = 3. Athlete B: μ = 8.70 m, σ = 0.70 m, α = 3. These values are illustrative. Real values come from a fit to the best marks of each athlete in the season.
models.dependence: None between the athletes. The fit assumes that the competitions of the season are independent and have the same law. A change of form during the season breaks this.
models.method: Independent draws of B by inversion of the CDF. The estimators are fractions of replicates and a sample mean.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: P(B ≥ 8.15) = 0.439 for A and 0.384 for B. P(B ≥ 8.35) = 0.0046 for A and 0.1175 for B. The mean best marks are 8.132 m for A and 8.075 m for B. Thus the mean puts A first, but the tail near the medal mark puts B first. Other candidate models: a GEV law with a free shape, and a normal law for the best mark, which has no upper limit.
models.interpretation: Select athlete B. B reaches the medal mark with the probability 0.118 (exact), and A with 0.0046. Both athletes meet the condition for the final. A selection by the mean mark would choose A. Reject the model if an athlete jumps beyond the fitted upper limit μ, or if the marks of the season show a trend.

models.title: Drawdown of a reservoir before the flood season
models.decision: Decision: the drawdown d of the reservoir before the flood season. Estimated quantity: P(the annual maximum level > the spillway crest at 415.5 m), and the stored energy lost.
models.reason: The annual maximum level is a maximum over a year. The volume of the largest possible flood and the operation of the outlets bound the level above. Fits of the GEV law to annual maximum lake and reservoir levels can give ξ < 0. The reverse Weibull law is this case of the GEV law, written with its end point μ.
models.inputs: With no drawdown, the annual maximum level H has the reverse Weibull law with α = 2.5, the upper end 417.0 m and σ = 2.0 m. A drawdown d lowers the whole law by d. Each metre of drawdown loses 1.2 GWh of stored energy. The target is spillway use in at most 1 year in 10. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The annual maxima are independent. The shift by d assumes that the flood volume does not depend on the start level. Droughts of several years break the independence.
models.method: Independent draws of H by inversion of the CDF. The estimator is a fraction of replicates. The energy lost is a constant for each alternative.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: P(H > 415.5) = 1 − exp(−((1.5 − d)/2)^2.5) is 0.386, 0.162, 0.083 and 0.031 for d = 0, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 m. The mean annual maximum is 417.0 − d − σΓ(1.4) = 415.23 − d m. Other candidate models: a GEV law with a free shape, and the Gumbel law, which has no upper end.
models.interpretation: d = 0.75 m is the smallest drawdown in the list with spillway use in at most 1 year in 10: 0.083 (exact). It loses 0.9 GWh in each year. The answer depends on the end point, which a short record estimates badly. Reject the model if a level above the fitted end point occurs. Also reject it if the annual maxima show a trend after a change of the operation rules.

models.title: Closing age of a life table
models.decision: Decision: the closing age ω of the life table of a pension fund. Estimated quantity: P(a death older than ω occurs in the next 30 years).
models.reason: The oldest age at death in a year is a maximum over many lives. An extreme-value study of Dutch data found a finite upper end of the age at death (Einmahl, Einmahl and de Haan, 2019). Its estimates were near 114 to 116 years. The reverse Weibull law is the extreme-value law with a finite end point.
models.inputs: The oldest age at death in one year has the reverse Weibull law with α = 8, the upper end μ = 115.7 years and σ = 7 years. The table looks 30 years ahead. The target is a probability of at most 10 %. The values are illustrative and are not a fit to data.
models.dependence: The years are independent and have the same law. A rise of the oldest ages with time breaks this, because then μ is not constant.
models.method: 30 independent reverse Weibull draws in each replicate, and their maximum. The estimator is a fraction of replicates. The law of the maximum is exact, so the page shows a reference.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: P(pass) = 1 − exp(−30((μ − ω)/σ)^α) is 0.710, 0.167, 0.0146 and 0.0004 for ω = 111, 112, 113 and 114. The mean oldest age in 30 years is 111.4 years (numerical reference). Other candidate models: the Gumbel law, which has no upper end, and a GPD fit to the ages above 98 years.
models.interpretation: ω = 113 years is the lowest closing age in the list that meets the target: 0.015 (exact). ω = 112 gives 0.167. The result depends on the finite end point, which is a model assumption. Reject the model if a death above the fitted end point occurs, or if the oldest ages increase with time.

models.title: Censoring biases the naive estimate, and the Kaplan–Meier estimate corrects it
models.observe: The true survival probability is S(10) = e^(−1) = 0.368. The naive estimate mean(T_obs > 10) estimates S_T(10)·S_C(10), not S_T(10). Its exact mean is 0.189 for the mean censoring time 15 h and 0.287 for 40 h. The Kaplan–Meier estimate has a mean of about 0.367 for both: a bias of about −0.0006, near 0. This small bias comes from the finite sample of 50 units. The fraction of censored units is 0.411 and 0.193 (exact, by quadrature). The page has no reference value, because T and C repeat 50 times. The parameter S_true holds the exact S(10), and the bias quantities compare each estimate with it.

title: Censoring biases the naive estimate, and the Kaplan–Meier estimate corrects it
problem: 50 units have Weibull lifetimes, and an independent exponential censoring time hides some failures. Estimate the survival probability S(t) at t = 10 from the observed data.
param k = 1.5 "Weibull shape of the lifetime"
param lambda = 10 {h} "Weibull scale of the lifetime"
param cmean = 15 {h} "mean censoring time"

models.title: Extrapolation of a censored reliability test
models.decision: Decision: accept the units if the estimated reliability at 500 h is at least 0.55. Estimated quantity: the mean of the exponential estimate of S(500), its bias, and P(the rule accepts).
models.reason: A test that stops at 300 h gives right-censored lifetimes: for a unit that survives the test, the data give only a lower bound. The exponential law gives a simple estimate from censored data: the number of failures divided by the total time on test. Lifetimes with wear-out often have a Weibull law with k > 1.
models.inputs: 30 units, with the test duration c = 300 h (Type I censoring). True law: Weibull(k = 1.8, λ = 600 h), so S(300) = 0.750 and S(500) = 0.487 (exact). The second alternative is an exponential law with the same S(300) = 0.750, so S(500) = 0.620. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The units fail independently. The censoring time is a constant, so it is independent of the lifetimes.
models.method: 30 independent Weibull draws in each replicate, censored at 300 h. The rate estimate sum(T_event)/sum(T_obs) is the exponential maximum likelihood estimate. The estimate of S(500) is exp(−500 · rate). The estimators are sample means and a fraction of replicates.
models.diagnostics: The quantities read 30 lifetimes, so the page has no reference value. The parameter S_true holds the exact S(500), so the bias quantity compares the estimate with the truth. The Kaplan–Meier estimate of S(300) has a bias near 0, which checks the censoring. As the number of units grows, the exponential estimate tends to exp(−500 F(300)/∫₀³⁰⁰ S(t) dt) = 0.632 under the Weibull law. The test expects only 7.5 failures out of 30, too few to separate the two laws. Other candidate models: the Weibull law fitted by maximum likelihood to the censored data, and the lognormal law.
models.interpretation: Under the Weibull law the exponential estimate has a mean of about 0.636, and the true value is 0.487: a bias of about +0.150. The rule accepts the units in about 80 % of the tests, although the true reliability is below 0.55. Under the exponential law the bias is about +0.004. The two laws give nearly the same data up to 300 h, and only the model makes the difference at 500 h. Do not extrapolate a censored test beyond its duration with the exponential law when wear-out is possible. Reject the exponential model if a Weibull fit of the censored data gives k clearly above 1.

models.title: Go/no-go rule from the 2-year survival in a trial with dropout
models.decision: Decision: continue the drug (go) if the Kaplan–Meier estimate of the 2-year progression-free survival is at least 0.52. Estimated quantity: P(go) when the drug works (true S(2) = 0.60) and when it fails (true S(2) = 0.45).
models.reason: In a trial the follow-up ends at a fixed time, and some patients leave early. Their times to progression are right-censored. The Kaplan–Meier estimator uses the censored patients while they are at risk. It is consistent when the censoring is independent of the time to progression. The lognormal law is a standard parametric model of a time to progression.
models.inputs: 100 patients. The time to progression has the law lognormal(μ, σ = 1) in years. μ = 0.9465 gives S(2) = 0.60, and μ = 0.5675 gives S(2) = 0.45, from μ = log 2 − σΦ^(−1)(1 − S(2)). The dropout times are exponential with the rate 0.15 for each year, and 0.30 in the third alternative. The follow-up ends at 3 years. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The patients are independent. The dropout is independent of the time to progression. If patients with a worse state leave early, the censoring is informative, and the Kaplan–Meier estimate has an upward bias.
models.method: In each replicate, 100 lognormal times and 100 exponential dropout times. The censoring time is min(dropout, 3). The page computes km(T_obs, T_event, 2). The estimators are a fraction of replicates and sample means.
models.diagnostics: T and Drop repeat 100 times, so the page has no reference value. The parameter S2 holds the true S(2), which is exact for the given μ and σ. The bias quantities compare the estimates with it. The bias of the Kaplan–Meier estimate is near 0: about −0.0002, with an interval that contains 0. The fraction of patients observed beyond 2 years has a bias of about −0.16 when the drug works, and of about −0.27 with double dropout. It counts the patients censored before 2 years as if they progressed. Other candidate models: a Weibull or a log-logistic law for the time to progression.
models.interpretation: The rule goes with a probability of about 0.93 when the drug works, and of about 0.10 when it fails. Double dropout reduces the first value to about 0.91, because fewer patients stay at risk. It does not bias the Kaplan–Meier estimate. Reject the model if the dropout depends on the state of the patients. Also reject it if the Kaplan–Meier curve of the data is far from the lognormal curve.

models.title: Values below the detection limit and the mean concentration
models.decision: Decision: the substitution factor f for values below the limit of detection (LOD). Estimated quantity: the mean squared error of the estimate of the mean concentration from 20 samples.
models.reason: Concentrations of trace substances are positive and skewed to the right, and the lognormal law is a standard model for them. A value below the LOD is left-censored: the laboratory reports only that it is below 1.5 µg/L. Substitution by LOD/2 is a common practice, but its error depends on the law and on the fraction below the LOD.
models.inputs: 20 samples. The concentration has the law lognormal(μ = 0, σ = 1) in µg/L, so the true mean is e^0.5 = 1.649 µg/L. LOD = 1.5 µg/L, so P(X < LOD) = Φ(log 1.5) = 0.657. The action level is 2.5 µg/L. These values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The samples are independent. Samples from the same well at near times are often correlated, which breaks this.
models.method: 20 independent lognormal draws in each replicate, censored on the left at the LOD. The estimate is mean(if(X_event, X_obs, f·LOD)). The estimators are sample means and fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
models.diagnostics: The quantities read 20 draws, so the page has no reference value. The parameter true_mean holds the exact mean, so the bias and the squared error compare the estimate with the truth. A check: the exact mean of the estimate is E[X; X ≥ LOD] + f·LOD·P(X < LOD) = 1.194 + 0.986f. This gives the biases −0.455, +0.038, +0.242 and +0.531 for f = 0, 0.5, 0.71 and 1, and the simulation agrees. Other candidate models: a gamma or a Weibull law for the concentration. Other candidate methods: the maximum likelihood estimate of the lognormal law with left censoring, and the Kaplan–Meier estimate on a reversed scale.
models.interpretation: f = 0.5 (LOD/2) has the least mean squared error, about 0.228 (µg/L)². Its bias is +0.038 µg/L (exact). P(the estimate > 2.5) is about 0.057, near the value 0.053 of the full data. f = 1 raises it to about 0.18, so it flags too many sites. The good result of LOD/2 holds only for these σ and LOD: a different fraction below the LOD can change the order. Reject the model if a lognormal fit of the detected values is poor, or if the fraction below the LOD changes much between sites.

models.dsl:
title: Values below the detection limit and the mean concentration

param mu = 0 "lognormal μ of the concentration"
param sigma = 1 "lognormal σ of the concentration"
param LOD = 1.5 {µg/L} "limit of detection"
param f = 0.5 "substitution factor"
param action = 2.5 {µg/L} "action level for the mean concentration"

alt "f = 0": f = 0
alt "f = 0.5 (LOD/2)": f = 0.5
alt "f = 0.71 (LOD/√2)": f = 0.7071
alt "f = 1": f = 1

focus X_obs

models.title: A mixture of two Poisson laws
models.observe: With the weights 0.7 and 0.3 and the means 2 and 9, E[X] = 4.1 but Var X = 14.39, more than 3 times the mean. One Poisson law with mean 4.1 has the variance 4.1. The PMF has two modes, near 2 and near 9. P(X ≥ 10) = 0.124, but a Poisson law with mean 4.1 gives about 0.0095. Equal weights give the mean 5.5 and the variance 17.75. A count with a variance above its mean can come from a mixture. But overdispersion alone does not prove a finite mixture: a gamma mixture (the negative binomial law) also has it.
models.dsl:
title: A mixture of two Poisson laws
problem: Counts come from one of two groups, but the group is not observed. The law of a count is then a finite mixture of two Poisson laws. Compare its mean, its variance and its shape with one Poisson law.
param w1 = 0.7 "weight of the first group"
param l1 = 2 {events} "mean count of the first group"
param l2 = 9 {events} "mean count of the second group"
X ~ mixture_poisson(w = [w1, 1 - w1], lambda = [l1, l2]) {events} "a count from an unknown group"
mean m = X {events} "E[X] = w1 λ1 + w2 λ2"
mean spread = (X - (w1*l1 + (1 - w1)*l2))^2 "Var X"
prob big = X >= 10 "P(X ≥ 10)"
alt "Weights 0.7 and 0.3": w1 = 0.7
alt "Weights 0.5 and 0.5": w1 = 0.5
focus X

models.title: How many agents for calls on normal and promotion days?
models.decision: Decision: the number of agents for each 15-minute interval. Estimated quantity: P(more calls than the agents handle) and the expected cost of the agents and of the calls that wait.
models.reason: On a normal day the calls of an interval are Poisson. On a promotion day the rate is higher. The plan does not know the day type in advance. Thus the law of the calls is a mixture of two Poisson laws, with the fraction of promotion days as a weight.
models.inputs: 80 % normal days with 22 calls and 20 % promotion days with 40 calls in 15 minutes are illustrative values. So are the costs: 30 for one agent for 15 minutes and 12 for each call that waits. One agent handles 3 calls in 15 minutes. There is no data.
models.dependence: Calls in one interval are independent given the day type. Intervals of the same day share the day type, so the overload of consecutive intervals is dependent. This model looks at one interval only.
models.method: Independent draws: the alias method picks the day type, then a Poisson count. The estimators are a fraction and a sample mean. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences have a smaller variance.
models.diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration of the mixture: P(overload) = 0.430, 0.220, 0.142 and 0.068 for 8, 10, 12 and 14 agents. Other candidate models: one Poisson law with the mean rate 25.6, and a negative binomial law fitted to the variance. The Poisson law gives P(N > 36) = 0.020 for 12 agents, so it hides the risk of the promotion days.
models.interpretation: 12 agents meet the overload limit of 15 % at the least cost, about 372 for each interval. 10 agents cost less but overload 22 % of the intervals, mostly on promotion days. Reject the model if the plan knows the day type in advance. Then use a Poisson law for each day type, which needs fewer agents on normal days.

models.title: Which alarm threshold for a decline in seabird nests?
models.decision: Decision: the threshold t below which the total count of 40 plots triggers a decline alarm. Estimated quantity: P(false alarm), the probability of an alarm in a year with no decline.
models.reason: A plot is either empty, because it has no suitable ground, or it holds a Poisson number of nests. The count of a plot then has a zero-inflated Poisson law. This is a mixture of a point mass at 0 (Poisson with λ = 0) and a Poisson law.
models.inputs: 35 % empty plots and a mean of 4.2 nests on an occupied plot are illustrative values. The survey has 40 plots. The alarm limit of 5 % false alarms is a policy choice. There is no data.
models.dependence: The 40 plots are independent. Plots near each other can share a colony. Then the counts are positively dependent, and the total varies more than this model says.
models.method: Independent draws of 40 counts, each by the alias method and a Poisson draw. The estimator is a fraction of replicates. The total of 40 plots has no enumeration here, so the page shows no reference value.
models.diagnostics: The total has the mean 40 × 0.65 × 4.2 = 109.2 and the variance 40 × 6.74 = 270. The CLT then gives P(total < 80) ≈ 0.04, close to the simulated 0.033. Other candidate models: a negative binomial law for each plot, and a model with dependence between plots.
models.interpretation: t = 80 keeps false alarms near 3 %. t = 90 gives about 11 % false alarms. A higher threshold finds a real decline sooner. Thus the choice is a balance between an early alarm and fewer false alarms. Reject the model if the fraction of empty plots changes between years. Then a drop of the total can come from the habitat and not from the birds.

title: Which alarm threshold for a decline in seabird nests?

models.title: Which acceptance number for parts from two suppliers?
models.decision: Decision: the acceptance number c: a lot goes to full inspection when the sample of 50 parts has more than c defective parts. Estimated quantity: the fraction of lots sent to full inspection, and the expected defective parts that pass, for each lot.
models.reason: Lots come from two suppliers with different defect rates, and the lot label does not name the supplier. Given the supplier, the defective parts in a sample of 50 are binomial. The count is then a mixture of two binomial laws.
models.inputs: 70 % of lots from supplier A with a defect rate of 1 % and 30 % from supplier B with 6 % are illustrative values. Each defective part of the sample stands for 20 parts of the lot. The inspection team can take at most 20 % of the lots. There is no data.
models.dependence: Parts in one lot are independent given the supplier. A process fault that damages a run of parts breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws: the alias method picks the supplier, then a binomial count. The estimators are a fraction and a sample mean. Exact references come from the enumeration of the sample count.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: the full-inspection fraction is 0.306, 0.185 and 0.107 for c = 1, 2 and 3. Other candidate models: one binomial law with the mean rate 2.5 %, and a beta-binomial law if the defect rate varies within each supplier. The binomial law gives too few lots with many defects.
models.interpretation: c = 2 meets the 20 % limit of the team, with about 10 defective parts that pass for each lot. c = 1 passes fewer defects but needs the team for 31 % of the lots. Reject the model if the inspector can identify the supplier of a lot. Then use one plan for each supplier.

models.title: Clusters of events: the compound Poisson law
models.observe: 3 clusters of mean 2 give E[S] = 6 and Var S = 3 × E[Y²] = 3 × 6 = 18. This is three times the variance of a Poisson law with mean 6. P(S = 0) = exp(−3(1 − e^(−2))) = 0.0747, against e^(−6) = 0.0025 for the Poisson law. 6 clusters of mean 1 give the same mean but the variance 12. The total varies more when events come in larger clusters. Panjer's recursion gives the law of S, exact up to round-off and a cut mass below 10^-12.

models.title: How much stock of a product for one day?
models.decision: Decision: the stock of one product at the start of the day. Estimated quantity: P(a shortage) and the expected cost of the units left and of the units that customers cannot buy.
models.reason: Customers come at random, so their number is Poisson. Each customer takes a random number of units, possibly none, and the numbers are independent. The total is a compound Poisson sum with geometric terms.
models.inputs: 12 customers a day and a geometric number of units with p = 0.4 (a mean of 1.5 units) are illustrative values. So are the costs: 1 for each unit left and 6 for each unit not sold. There is no data.
models.dependence: Customers act independently. A promotion or a group of customers that buy together breaks this assumption.
models.method: Independent draws: a Poisson number of customers, then their geometric numbers of units. The estimators are a fraction and a sample mean. Exact references come from Panjer's recursion.
models.diagnostics: Exact references: P(D > 30) = 0.083 and P(D > 35) = 0.034. E[D] = 18 and Var D = 12 × E[Y²] = 12 × 6 = 72, much above the mean. Other candidate models: a Poisson law of units with mean 18, and a negative binomial law of customers on busy days. The Poisson law gives P(D > 30) = 0.003, so it gives too little stock.
models.interpretation: 35 units meet the 5 % shortage limit with the least cost, about 18.3 a day. 30 units cost less but give shortages on 8 % of days. Reject the model if the units of one customer depend on the stock on the shelf.
