models.dsl:
title: Shelf split for two substitute products
problem: A shop sells two brands of the same product on one shelf of 60 places. A customer who buys one brand often does not buy the other, so the two daily demands are negatively dependent. Choose how to split the shelf.
param theta = -5 "Frank parameter θ, negative for substitutes"
param s1 = 32 {units} "shelf places for brand A"
param s2 = 28 {units} "shelf places for brand B"
param margin = 3 {currency units per unit} "margin of one unit sold"
U ~ frankcopula(theta = theta, d = 2) "copula of the two daily demands"
D1 ~ poisson(lambda = 27, u = U[1]) {units per day} "daily demand, brand A"
D2 ~ poisson(lambda = 23, u = U[2]) {units per day} "daily demand, brand B"
sales := pmin(D1, s1) + pmin(D2, s2) {units per day} "units sold"
mean profit = margin*sales {currency units per day} "daily margin"
prob both_out = D1 > s1 and D2 > s2 "both brands sell out"
prob any_out = (D1 > s1) + (D2 > s2) >= 1 "at least one brand sells out"
alt "Split 30 / 30": s1 = 30; s2 = 30
alt "Split 34 / 26": s1 = 34; s2 = 26
alt "Split 38 / 22": s1 = 38; s2 = 22
maximise profit
require any_out <= 0.35
focus sales

models.title: Backup contract for a wind and solar plant
models.decision: Decision: the size of a backup power contract for a wind and solar plant (0, 40 or 80 megawatt hours per day). Estimated quantity: the probability that the plant misses its commitment, and the expected daily cost.
models.reason: Days with strong wind are often cloudy, and calm days are often sunny. So the two outputs are negatively dependent. The Frank copula with θ < 0 gives this without a tail effect.
models.inputs: The Weibull wind output with k = 2 and λ = 220 and the gamma solar output with k = 9 and θ = 12 are illustrative. The Frank copula with θ = −4, the commitment of 220, the fee of 0.8 and the penalty of 3 are also illustrative. There is no data.
models.dependence: A Frank copula with θ = −4 in d = 2 joins the two daily outputs. Days are independent in this model, and the margins do not change with the season.
models.method: The method independent uses the exact copula sampler and the inverse transform of each margin at u = U[j]. The estimators are sample means. All alternatives use the same streams, so the paired differences have a smaller variance. For θ < 0 the copula sampler is conditional inversion in closed form.
models.diagnostics: Reference value: P(W < 80 and S < 70) = 0.002154. Under independence it is 0.017, so the negative dependence makes a joint low day 8 times rarer. Other candidate models: the Gaussian copula with ρ < 0, and a Clayton copula with θ < 0.
models.interpretation: No backup fails the constraint P(miss) ≤ 0.1. A contract of 40 meets it at a lower cost than 80. The negative dependence is a natural hedge: under independence a contract of 40 fails. Reject the model if wind and solar are often low on the same day.

models.dsl:
title: Backup contract for a wind and solar plant
problem: A plant has wind turbines and solar panels. Days with strong wind are often cloudy, so the two daily outputs are negatively dependent. Choose the size of a backup power contract that meets a delivery commitment.
param theta = -4 "Frank parameter θ, negative dependence"
param commit = 220 {megawatt hours per day} "delivery commitment"
param backup = 40 {megawatt hours per day} "backup contract"
param fee = 0.8 {thousand currency units per megawatt hour of contract} "daily fee of the contract"
param penalty = 3 {thousand currency units per megawatt hour} "penalty for energy not delivered"
U ~ frankcopula(theta = theta, d = 2) "copula of wind and solar output"
W ~ weibull(k = 2, lambda = 220, u = U[1]) {megawatt hours per day} "daily wind energy"
S ~ gamma(k = 9, theta = 12, u = U[2]) {megawatt hours per day} "daily solar energy"

prob miss = gap > 0 "the plant misses the commitment"

alt "Backup 80": backup = 80

models.title: Departure buffer for a trip with two legs
models.decision: Decision: the departure buffer for a courier trip with a road leg and a ferry leg (30, 45 or 60 minutes). Estimated quantity: the probability of a late delivery, and the expected cost of a trip.
models.reason: Bad weather slows the two legs together, so the times are positively dependent. Extreme delays on the two legs have different causes, so there is no tail dependence. The Frank copula with θ > 0 fits this.
models.inputs: The gamma road time with k = 9 and θ = 8 minutes and the lognormal ferry time with μ = 3.8 and σ = 0.25 are illustrative. The Frank copula with θ = 4 and the planned time of 120 are also illustrative. So are the cost of 0.5 for each minute of buffer and the late cost of 80. There is no data.
models.dependence: A Frank copula with θ = 4 joins the two leg times. Kendall's tau is 0.39. The model ignores the timetable of the ferry.
models.method: The method independent uses the exact copula sampler and the inverse transform of each margin at u = U[j]. The estimators are sample means. All alternatives use the same streams, so the paired differences have a smaller variance. The method inverse gives the same law by conditional inversion in closed form.
models.diagnostics: Reference value: P(T1 > 90 and T2 > 60) = 0.06223. Under independence it is 0.025. Other candidate models: a Gumbel copula, if one storm can cause extreme delays on the two legs, and the Gaussian copula.
models.interpretation: A buffer of 30 fails the constraint P(late) ≤ 0.1. A buffer of 45 meets it at a lower cost than 60. Tail dependence would matter if storms delayed both legs: a Gumbel copula then puts more mass on joint long delays. Reject the model if extreme delays on the two legs often occur on the same trip.

title: Departure buffer for a trip with two legs
problem: A courier trip has a road leg and a ferry leg. Bad weather slows both legs, but it does not cause extreme delays on both at once. Choose how early to start so that the courier is rarely late.

param plan = 120 {minutes} "planned travel time without buffer"
param wage = 0.5 {currency units per minute} "cost of one minute of buffer"
param late_cost = 80 {currency units} "cost of a late delivery"

T1 ~ gamma(k = 9, theta = 8, u = U[1]) {minutes} "road leg time"
T2 ~ lognormal(mu = 3.8, sigma = 0.25, u = U[2]) {minutes} "ferry leg time"

alt "Buffer 60": buffer = 60

models.title: First passage of Brownian motion and the monitoring bias
models.observe: The reference of hit is 2(1 − Φ(1)) = 0.3173, from the reflection principle in continuous time. With 16 steps the grid estimate is near 0.26, lower than the reference. The difference is a discretisation bias of order √h, not Monte Carlo error: the interval does not cover the reference. Set steps to 256, and the estimate rises to about 0.30. The bias shrinks but stays. The estimate of end_above is near its reference 0.1587, because X_T is exact on any grid. Thus hit ≈ 2 × end_above only in continuous time.
models.dsl:
title: First passage of Brownian motion and the monitoring bias
problem: Find the probability that a standard Brownian motion reaches the level 1 before time 1. Compare the grid estimate with the continuous-time value.
param steps = 16 "grid steps; the step is h = 1/steps"
param b = 1 "level"
W ~ brownian(x0 = 0, mu = 0, sigma = 1, T = 1, steps = steps) "standard Brownian motion"
M := max(W) "largest grid value"
prob hit = M >= b "the grid path reaches b; the reference is continuous"
prob end_above = last(W) >= b "W_1 ≥ b, exact on the grid"
mean end = last(W) "E W_1 = 0"
initial: W_0 = 0 at t = 0
dynamics: dW_t = dB_t, a standard Brownian motion observed at t_k = k/steps
focus M

models.title: How long can a drifting sensor run before recalibration?
models.decision: Decision: recalibrate a sensor every 10, 20 or 30 days. Estimated quantity: the probability that the calibration error reaches the alarm level before the recalibration.
models.reason: The calibration error of the sensor is the sum of many small independent changes, with a slow mean drift. A Brownian motion with drift is the simplest model of this sum.
models.inputs: Illustrative values: error drift 0.03 units for each day, volatility 0.2 units for each √day, alarm level 1.5 units, start at 0 after a recalibration. The grid has 16 steps. MLMC refines it.
models.dependence: The error X is a Brownian motion with drift. It has no stationary law and no mean reversion. The alarm is a first passage of the level, so the quantity reads the whole path. The page monitors the path only at the grid times.
models.method: Euler steps, exact on the grid for this process. The alarm probability has a monitoring bias of order √h. MLMC estimates the continuous limit: it adds level corrections of coupled paths (coarsen = 2). Here the alarm is a discontinuous functional, so the level variances decay slowly, about as √h, and MLMC gains little.
models.diagnostics: The page gives the continuous-time reference by the reflection principle with drift. The grid estimate is below it. The MLMC run should come near it. Watch the level variances: a slow decay is the failure example of MLMC. Other candidate models: an OU error with mean reversion, and a model with jumps for shocks.
models.interpretation: Choose the longest interval that keeps the alarm probability at most 0.1. The continuous reference is the relevant value, because a real sensor fails between checks. Reject the model if the error increments of past cycles are not near normal or not independent.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative values, not calibrated evidence. The example invents the drift and the volatility.

models.dsl:
title: How long can a drifting sensor run before recalibration?
problem: The calibration error of a sensor drifts as a Brownian motion. Choose the recalibration interval with an alarm probability at most 0.1.
param steps = 16 "grid steps, the coarsest level of MLMC"
param coarsen = 1 "fine increments for each step (MLMC coupling)"
param days = 20 {days} "recalibration interval"
param level = 1.5 {units} "alarm level of the error"
X ~ brownian(x0 = 0, mu = 0.03, sigma = 0.2, T = days, steps = steps, coarsen = coarsen) {units} "calibration error"
prob alarm = any(X >= level) "the error reaches the alarm level"
Err := last(X) "error at recalibration"
mean final = Err {units} "mean error at recalibration"
mean interval = days {days} "days between recalibrations"
alt "10 days": days = 10
alt "20 days": days = 20
alt "30 days": days = 30
maximise interval
require alarm <= 0.1
initial: X_0 = 0 at t = 0, after a recalibration
dynamics: dX_t = μ dt + σ dW_t with μ = 0.03 and σ = 0.2 for each day
focus Err

models.title: How much cash buffer for the next quarter?
models.decision: Decision: hold a cash buffer of 30, 40 or 50 at the start of the quarter. Estimated quantity: the probability that the cash balance falls to 0 before the end of the quarter.
models.reason: The cash balance changes by many receipts and payments of moderate size. Their sum over weeks is near a Brownian motion with a small drift. Large single payments are not in this model.
models.inputs: Illustrative values in thousands of currency units: drift +1 for each week, volatility 5 for each √week, horizon 13 weeks, weekly grid. Idle cash costs 0.5 % for the quarter.
models.dependence: The balance C is a Brownian motion with drift. It is not stationary. The shortfall is the first passage of 0 from above, a path quantity. The weekly grid misses a dip between two weeks.
models.method: Independent exact increments on the weekly grid. The shortfall probability is a fraction of replicates. The page gives the continuous-time reference by the reflection principle with drift.
models.diagnostics: Compare the weekly estimate with the continuous reference. The weekly estimate is lower by the monitoring bias. If the bank checks the balance each day, use more steps. Other candidate models: a compound Poisson model with large single payments, and an OU balance with a target level.
models.interpretation: Choose the smallest buffer with a shortfall probability at most 0.05. The cost of idle cash is small next to a missed payment. Reject the model if weekly changes show heavy tails or strong seasonal patterns.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative values, not calibrated evidence. The example invents the cash flows.

models.dsl:
title: How much cash buffer for the next quarter?
problem: The cash balance of a firm moves as a Brownian motion with drift. Choose the starting buffer so that the balance stays above 0 for one quarter.
param c0 = 30 {thousand currency units} "starting cash buffer"
C ~ brownian(x0 = c0, mu = 1, sigma = 5, T = 13, steps = 13) {thousand currency units} "cash balance, weekly"
prob shortfall = min(C) <= 0 "the balance reaches 0"
CT := last(C) "balance at the end of the quarter"
mean end = CT {thousand currency units} "mean balance at the end of the quarter"
mean idle_cost = 0.005 * c0 {thousand currency units} "cost of the idle buffer"
alt "Buffer 30": c0 = 30
alt "Buffer 40": c0 = 40
alt "Buffer 50": c0 = 50
minimise idle_cost
require shortfall <= 0.05
initial: C_0 = c0 at t = 0
dynamics: dC_t = μ dt + σ dW_t with μ = 1 and σ = 5 for each week
focus CT

models.title: Keep a gas plant available for next winter?
models.decision: Decision: keep unit A, B or C of a gas plant available for one delivery month in six months. Estimated quantity: the mean value of the option to run, E[max(X_T − c, 0)], with c the cost to run the unit.
models.reason: The spark spread is a price difference, so it can be negative. A Brownian motion (the Bachelier model) allows negative values, but a GBM does not. The plant runs only when the spread is above its cost: the value is a call payoff.
models.inputs: Illustrative values: spread today 6 currency units for each MWh, no drift, volatility 10 for each √year, horizon 0.5 years. Costs to run units A, B and C: 2, 6 and 10. Availability costs: 4.5, 2.5 and 1.0.
models.dependence: The spread X is a Brownian motion with drift 0. It is not stationary, and it has no boundary. The value depends only on X_T, so the grid has no monitoring bias for it.
models.method: Independent exact increments. X_T does not need 26 weekly steps, but the page draws the path. The page gives the Bachelier reference for E[max(X_T − c, 0)] and for P(X_T < 0).
models.diagnostics: Compare the estimates of run_value and negative with their references. Other candidate models: a mean-reverting OU spread, and two correlated GBM prices for power and gas.
models.interpretation: Keep the unit with the largest net value, if this value is positive. A negative spread has a large probability, which a lognormal model would hide. Reject the model if the spread shows strong mean reversion in past data.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative values, not calibrated evidence. The example invents the spreads and costs.

models.dsl:
title: Keep a gas plant available for next winter?
problem: The value of a gas unit is the option to run when the spark spread is above its running cost. Choose the unit to keep available.
param c = 6 {currency units per MWh} "running cost"
param fixed = 2.5 {currency units per MWh} "cost to keep the unit available"
X ~ brownian(x0 = 6, mu = 0, sigma = 10, T = 0.5, steps = 26) {currency units per MWh} "spark spread"
V := max(last(X) - c, 0) "value of the option to run"
mean run_value = V {currency units per MWh} "value of the option to run"
mean net = V - fixed {currency units per MWh} "value after the availability cost"
prob negative = last(X) < 0 "negative spread at delivery"
alt "Unit A": c = 2; fixed = 4.5
alt "Unit B": c = 6; fixed = 2.5
alt "Unit C": c = 10; fixed = 1.0
maximise net
initial: X_0 = 6 at t = 0
dynamics: dX_t = σ dW_t with σ = 10 for each year (the Bachelier model)
focus V

models.title: Ensemble average and time average of a GBM
models.observe: Here μ = 0.05 < σ²/2 = 0.125. The estimate of mean_ST is near the reference E S_T = e^{0.5} = 1.649: the ensemble average grows. The estimate of below is near its reference Φ(0.474) = 0.682: most paths end below S_0. The median is e^{−0.75} = 0.472, and log S_T / T is near μ − σ²/2 = −0.075. The mean is high because of a few large paths. Its interval is wide. This is the contrast of the ergodicity panel: the time average of one path differs from the ensemble average.
models.dsl:
title: Ensemble average and time average of a GBM
problem: A GBM has a mean that grows and a typical path that decays. Estimate E S_T and the probability that S_T ends below S_0.
param s0 = 1 "initial value"
param mu = 0.05 "drift of the mean"
param sigma = 0.5 "volatility"
S ~ gbm(s0 = s0, mu = mu, sigma = sigma, T = 10, steps = 50) "geometric Brownian motion"
ST := last(S) "value at T = 10"
mean mean_ST = ST "the ensemble average E S_T"
prob below = ST < s0 "the path ends below S_0"
prob below_half = ST < 0.5 * s0 "the path loses half its value"
mean growth = log(ST / s0) / 10 "time-average growth rate of one path"
initial: S_0 = 1 at t = 0
dynamics: dS_t = μ S_t dt + σ S_t dW_t with μ = 0.05 and σ = 0.5
focus ST

models.title: Which strike for a cap on a fuel price?
models.decision: Decision: buy a cap on the fuel price in one year with a strike of 90, 100 or 110. Estimated quantity: the mean payoff E[max(S_T − K, 0)] and the probability that the cap pays.
models.reason: A price that changes by many small independent percentage moves has a lognormal law. A GBM gives this law and stays positive. Under the risk-neutral measure, its drift is the interest rate.
models.inputs: Illustrative values: price today 100 currency units, rate 0.03 for each year, volatility 0.2 for each √year, one year. The budget for the payoff is 10 currency units. The grid has 4 Euler steps. MLMC refines it.
models.dependence: The price S is a GBM with μ = r. It is not stationary, and it stays in (0, ∞). The payoff reads only S_T. The Euler scheme can leave (0, ∞) with a very small probability here.
models.method: Euler steps with coarsen for the coupled MLMC pair. With 4 steps the Euler mean has a bias of order h. The MLMC run removes it with corrections on finer levels. The target RMSE is 0.05, about 0.5 % of the value. The call payoff is Lipschitz, so the level variances decay as h.
models.diagnostics: The page gives the Black–Scholes references: 15.90, 9.700 and 5.455 for the strikes 90, 100 and 110 (no discount). The 4-step Euler estimate differs a little. The MLMC estimate should come within the target RMSE. Other candidate models: a GBM with stochastic volatility, and a lognormal law for S_T only.
models.interpretation: Choose the lowest strike whose mean payoff stays within the budget. The cap then pays most often. Multiply the payoff by e^{−rT} for the price today. Reject the model if past log returns show heavy tails or a volatility that changes over time.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative values, not calibrated evidence. The example invents the price, rate and volatility.

models.dsl:
title: Which strike for a cap on a fuel price?
problem: A firm buys a cap on its fuel price in one year. Choose the strike that pays most often within a budget for the mean payoff.
param steps = 4 "Euler steps, the coarsest level of MLMC"
param coarsen = 1 "fine increments for each step (MLMC coupling)"
param K = 100 {currency units} "strike of the cap"
param r = 0.03 "interest rate for each year"
S ~ gbm(s0 = 100, mu = r, sigma = 0.2, T = 1, steps = steps, coarsen = coarsen) {currency units} "fuel price"
pay := max(last(S) - K, 0) "payoff of the cap"
mean payoff = pay {currency units} "E[max(S_T − K, 0)]"
prob pays = last(S) > K "the cap pays"
alt "Strike 90": K = 90
alt "Strike 100": K = 100
alt "Strike 110": K = 110
maximise pays
require payoff <= 10
initial: S_0 = 100 at t = 0
dynamics: dS_t = r S_t dt + σ S_t dW_t with r = 0.03 and σ = 0.2 for each year
focus pay

models.title: Which asset mix reaches a pension target?
models.decision: Decision: invest a pension fund in a low-risk, balanced or growth mix for 20 years. Estimated quantity: the probability that the fund ends below the target 150, and the probability of a loss below 80.
models.reason: A fund that reinvests its returns changes by percentage moves. Many small moves give a lognormal value. A GBM is the simplest model with this property.
models.inputs: Illustrative values: fund 100 today, target 150 in 20 years, annual grid. Mixes: low-risk with μ = 0.03 and σ = 0.05, balanced with μ = 0.05 and σ = 0.12, and growth with μ = 0.07 and σ = 0.20. No contributions and no withdrawals.
models.dependence: The fund F is a GBM. It is not stationary. Its typical path grows at μ − σ²/2, which is 0.0288, 0.0428 and 0.05 for the three mixes. The volatility cost σ²/2 reduces the advantage of the growth mix.
models.method: Independent exact log-steps, so the annual grid has no discretisation bias for F_T. The page gives lognormal references for the probabilities and for E F_T.
models.diagnostics: Compare the estimates with the lognormal references: P(F_T < 150) is 0.224, 0.201 and 0.253. Other candidate models: a model with fat-tailed annual returns, and a model with mean reversion of returns.
models.interpretation: The balanced mix has the lowest shortfall probability here, although the growth mix has the largest mean. The require line excludes a large loss. Reject the model if the annual returns are far from independent or normal in their logarithm.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative values, not calibrated evidence. The example invents the returns and volatilities.

models.dsl:
title: Which asset mix reaches a pension target?
problem: A pension fund of 100 must reach 150 in 20 years. Choose the asset mix with the lowest probability of a shortfall.
param mu = 0.05 "drift for each year"
param sigma = 0.12 "volatility for each year"
F ~ gbm(s0 = 100, mu = mu, sigma = sigma, T = 20, steps = 20) {currency units} "fund value"
FT := last(F) "fund value in 20 years"
prob shortfall = FT < 150 "below the target"
prob loss = FT < 80 "below 80 % of today"
mean final = FT {currency units} "mean fund value"
alt "Low risk": mu = 0.03; sigma = 0.05
alt "Balanced": mu = 0.05; sigma = 0.12
alt "Growth": mu = 0.07; sigma = 0.20
minimise shortfall
require loss <= 0.05
initial: F_0 = 100 at t = 0
dynamics: dF_t = μ F_t dt + σ F_t dB_t, with B a Brownian motion, for each year
focus FT

models.title: How large a loan against a share position?
models.decision: Decision: lend 50 %, 60 % or 70 % of the value of a share position for 6 months. Estimated quantity: the probability of a margin call, when the share price falls to the call level before the end.
models.reason: A share price changes by percentage moves and stays positive. A GBM gives this behaviour. The margin call reads the lowest price on the path, so the model must give the path.
models.inputs: Illustrative values: share price 50, drift 0.06 and volatility 0.35 for each year, 6 months with 126 trading days. A margin call happens when the loan reaches 80 % of the position value, so the call level is 50 × LTV / 0.8.
models.dependence: The price S is a GBM. It stays in (0, ∞). The margin call is a first passage below the call level. The lender checks the price once each trading day, which is the grid.
models.method: Independent exact log-steps on the daily grid. The page gives the continuous-time reference by the reflection principle for log S. The daily estimate is lower by the monitoring bias, of order √h.
models.diagnostics: The continuous reference is an upper bound for a daily check. The difference shows the monitoring bias. The bias shrinks with more steps. Other candidate models: a GARCH-type volatility, and a model with price jumps, which give calls without warning.
models.interpretation: Choose the largest loan with a margin-call probability at most 0.1. A call with a jump in price can lose money, which this model does not show. Reject the model if the share has large overnight gaps.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative values, not calibrated evidence. The example invents the share and its volatility.

models.dsl:
title: How large a loan against a share position?
problem: A lender gives a loan against a share position. Choose the largest loan-to-value ratio with a low margin-call probability.
param ltv = 0.6 "loan-to-value ratio at the start"
S ~ gbm(s0 = 50, mu = 0.06, sigma = 0.35, T = 0.5, steps = 126) {currency units} "share price, daily"
low := min(S) "lowest daily price"
prob margin_call = low <= 50 * ltv / 0.8 "the price reaches the call level"
mean loan = 1000 * ltv {currency units} "loan for a position of 1,000"
alt "LTV 50 %": ltv = 0.5
alt "LTV 60 %": ltv = 0.6
alt "LTV 70 %": ltv = 0.7
maximise loan
require margin_call <= 0.1
initial: S_0 = 50 at t = 0
dynamics: dS_t = μ S_t dt + σ S_t dW_t with μ = 0.06 and σ = 0.35 for each year
focus low

models.title: Mean reversion of the OU process and the unstable Euler scheme
models.observe: The exact transition (the comparison method) shows mean reversion. The estimate of end is near θ = 1, and the estimate of var_end is near σ²/(2κ) = 0.4. The reference of above is 1 − Φ(1/√0.4) = 0.0569. Here κ = 5 and h = 0.5, so κh = 2.5 and the Euler factor is 1 − κh = −1.5. The Euler paths oscillate and grow by a factor of 1.5 in each step. Thus var_end is in the thousands, not 0.4, and end is near 2 × 1.5¹⁰ ≈ 115, not 1. The exact process is stable. Only the scheme fails. Set steps to 100 (κh = 0.25): Euler is stable, with the stationary variance σ²/(κ(2 − κh)) = 0.457.
models.dsl:
title: Mean reversion of the OU process and the unstable Euler scheme
problem: An OU process reverts to θ. Show its stationary law with the exact transition, and the instability of the Euler scheme when κh ≥ 2.
param steps = 10 "grid steps; h = 5/steps"
param kappa = 5 "rate of mean reversion"
param theta = 1 "long-run mean"
param sigma = 2 "volatility"
X ~ ou(x0 = 3, kappa = kappa, theta = theta, sigma = sigma, T = 5, steps = steps) "OU process"
XT := last(X) "value at T = 5"
mean end = XT "E X_T, near θ"
mean var_end = (XT - theta)^2 "near the stationary variance σ²/(2κ) = 0.4"
prob above = XT > 2 "X_T > 2"
mean avg = mean(X) "average of the grid values"
initial: X_0 = 3 at t = 0
dynamics: dX_t = κ(θ − X_t) dt + σ dW_t with κ = 5, θ = 1 and σ = 2
focus XT

models.title: Borrow at a floating rate or fix the rate?
models.decision: Decision: borrow for 3 years at a floating short rate, or fix the rate at 1.3 %. Estimated quantity: the mean average rate of the floating loan, and the probability that the short rate is negative at the end.
models.reason: A short interest rate moves randomly but returns to a long-run level set by policy. The OU process (the Vasicek model) has this mean reversion and allows negative rates.
models.inputs: Illustrative values in percent: rate today 0.5, long-run mean 1.5, κ = 0.4 for each year, σ = 0.8 for each √year, 3 years. The grid starts with 8 Euler steps. MLMC refines it. The cost of the floating loan is the average of the grid rates.
models.dependence: The rate r is an OU process with κ > 0: it approaches the stationary law N(1.5, 0.8) with the time constant 2.5 years. It has no boundary, so negative rates are possible.
models.method: Euler steps with coarsen for the coupled MLMC pair. κh = 0.15 with 8 steps, so the scheme is stable, with a bias of order h. The page gives exact references for E r_T, P(r_T < 0) and the mean of the grid average.
models.diagnostics: Compare the estimates with the references. The Euler bias is small here. Check that the MLMC level variances decay as h. Other candidate models: the CIR process, which stays positive, and a model with regime changes of policy.
models.interpretation: The floating loan is cheaper on average, but its average rate is uncertain. The require line limits the probability of a high average rate. Reject the model if past rates show jumps at policy meetings.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative values, not calibrated evidence. The example invents the rates and parameters.

models.dsl:
title: Borrow at a floating rate or fix the rate?
problem: A firm borrows for 3 years. Compare a floating short rate, modelled as an OU process, with a fixed rate of 1.3 %.
param steps = 8 "Euler steps, the coarsest level of MLMC"
param coarsen = 1 "fine increments for each step (MLMC coupling)"
param fix = 0 "1 when the rate is fixed"
r ~ ou(x0 = 0.5, kappa = 0.4, theta = 1.5, sigma = 0.8, T = 3, steps = steps, coarsen = coarsen) {percent} "short rate"
cost := if(fix == 1, 1.3, mean(r)) "average rate paid"
mean avg_cost = cost {percent} "mean average rate"
mean avg_float = mean(r) {percent} "mean of the grid average of the floating rate"
prob negative = last(r) < 0 "negative rate at the end"
prob high = cost > 2 "average rate above 2 %"
alt "Floating": fix = 0
alt "Fixed at 1.3 %": fix = 1
minimise avg_cost
require high <= 0.1
initial: r_0 = 0.5 at t = 0
dynamics: dr_t = κ(θ − r_t) dt + σ dW_t with κ = 0.4, θ = 1.5 and σ = 0.8 for each year
focus cost

models.title: How much heating fuel for a winter month?
models.decision: Decision: order fuel for 430, 470 or 510 heating degree days for one winter month. Estimated quantity: the probability that the heating degree days exceed the order, and the mean cost.
models.reason: The mean temperature of a day varies around a seasonal level and returns to it in a few days. An OU process gives this mean reversion and the correlation of nearby days.
models.inputs: Illustrative values: 30 days, a seasonal level of 5 °C, κ = 0.3 for each day, σ = 2.5 °C for each √day, 4 °C on day 0. The base temperature is 18 °C. Fuel costs 1 currency unit for each degree day in advance and 3 in an emergency delivery.
models.dependence: The temperature X is an OU process. Its stationary law is N(5, 10.4), with a correlation e^{−0.3} = 0.74 between consecutive days. The degree days add 30 correlated terms, so their variance is much larger than with independent days.
models.method: Independent exact transitions on the daily grid. The degree days are sum(pmax(18 − X, 0)) over days 1 to 30. The page has exact references for the mean temperature, not for the degree days.
models.diagnostics: Check the reference of mean_temp. Compare the spread of the degree days with the spread for independent days. The variance ratio is near (1 + 0.74)/(1 − 0.74) ≈ 6.7. Other candidate models: an OU process with a seasonal θ(t), and a model with cold spells as jumps.
models.interpretation: Choose the order with the lowest mean cost that keeps the shortage probability at most 0.1. The correlation of days makes a cold month likely enough to matter. Reject the model if the residual temperatures have a correlation that does not decay as e^{−κ}.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative values, not calibrated evidence. The example invents the temperature parameters and costs.

models.dsl:
title: How much heating fuel for a winter month?
problem: A building orders heating fuel for one winter month. Choose the order in heating degree days with a low mean cost.
param Q = 470 {degree days} "fuel order"
X ~ ou(x0 = 4, kappa = 0.3, theta = 5, sigma = 2.5, T = 30, steps = 30) {°C} "daily mean temperature"
hdd := sum(pmax(18 - X, 0)) - max(18 - X[1], 0) "heating degree days, days 1 to 30"
prob shortage = hdd > Q "demand above the order"
mean cost = Q + 3 * max(hdd - Q, 0) {currency units} "fuel and emergency delivery"
mean degree_days = hdd {degree days} "mean heating degree days"
mean mean_temp = mean(X) {°C} "mean of the grid temperatures"
alt "Order 430": Q = 430
alt "Order 470": Q = 470
alt "Order 510": Q = 510
minimise cost
require shortage <= 0.1
initial: X_0 = 4 °C on day 0
dynamics: dX_t = κ(θ − X_t) dt + σ dW_t with κ = 0.3, θ = 5 and σ = 2.5 for each day
focus hdd

models.title: How strong a controller for a heated bath?
models.decision: Decision: set the gain of a temperature controller to 0.5, 1 or 2 for each minute. Estimated quantity: the probability that the deviation from the set point is above 1 °C after 10 minutes.
models.reason: A controller pushes the temperature back to the set point in proportion to the deviation. Small random heat losses add noise. This is the mechanism of an OU process with κ equal to the gain.
models.inputs: Illustrative values: deviation 3 °C at the start after a load change, noise σ = 0.6 °C for each √minute, 10 minutes, 100 steps. The energy cost is proportional to the gain: 2 units for each unit of gain.
models.dependence: The deviation X is an OU process with θ = 0. For κ > 0 its stationary law is N(0, σ²/(2κ)), with the standard deviation 0.60, 0.42 and 0.30 for the three gains.
models.method: Independent exact transitions, so the result has no discretisation bias. The page gives an exact reference for P(X_T > 1) and E X_T.
models.diagnostics: Compare with the references. The fraction of time out of tolerance has no reference. It is a finite-run estimate. Other candidate models: a model with a delay in the controller, and a model with a heater limit.
models.interpretation: Choose the lowest gain that keeps the end deviation above 1 °C with a probability at most 0.02. A higher gain uses more energy and can make a real controller oscillate. Reject the model if the measured deviation does not decay as e^{−κt}.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative values, not calibrated evidence. The example invents the noise and costs.

models.dsl:
title: How strong a controller for a heated bath?
problem: A controller returns the temperature of a bath to its set point. Choose the lowest gain that keeps the deviation small after 10 minutes.
param kappa = 1 "controller gain for each minute"
X ~ ou(x0 = 3, kappa = kappa, theta = 0, sigma = 0.6, T = 10, steps = 100) {°C} "deviation from the set point"
XT := last(X) "deviation after 10 minutes"
prob out_end = XT > 1 "deviation above 1 °C at the end"
mean end = XT {°C} "mean deviation at the end"
mean frac_out = mean(abs(X) > 1) "fraction of grid times out of tolerance"
mean energy = 2 * kappa {units} "energy cost"
alt "Gain 0.5": kappa = 0.5
alt "Gain 1": kappa = 1
alt "Gain 2": kappa = 2
minimise energy
require out_end <= 0.02
initial: X_0 = 3 °C at t = 0, after a load change
dynamics: dX_t = −κ X_t dt + σ dW_t with σ = 0.6 for each minute
focus XT

models.title: A Poisson process with a periodic rate
models.observe: The rate is λ(t) = 2(1 + 0.8 sin(2πt)), so Λ(1) = 2 and Λ(0.5) = 2(0.5 + 0.8/π) = 1.509. The estimate of count is near its reference E N(1) = 2, and the estimate of half is near 1.509. The first half of the period has 75 % of the events. The estimate of none is near P(N(1) = 0) = e^{−2} = 0.1353, and five_plus near P(N(1) ≥ 5) = 0.0527. Thinning with λ̄ = max λ(t) = 3.6 gives the same law. With method = rejection and failure = envelope, thinning uses λ̄ = 1.8, which is half of max λ(t). Then λ(t)/λ̄ is above 1 for most of the period, and the page counts the violations. The count is too low: in one run its mean is near 1.35, not 2, and P(N(1) = 0) is near 0.26. The law is wrong.
models.dsl:
title: A Poisson process with a periodic rate
problem: Events come at a rate that rises and falls once in each unit of time. Check the count law Poisson(Λ(T)) and the probability of no event.
param lambda = 2 {events per unit time} "mean rate λ"
param amp = 0.8 "relative amplitude a of the rate"
N ~ poissonprocess(lambda = lambda, amp = amp, period = 1, T = 1, steps = 24) {events} "count of events"
events := last(N)
mean count = last(N) "E N(1) = Λ(1) = 2"
mean half = N[13] "E N(0.5) = Λ(0.5) = 1.509"
prob none = last(N) == 0 "P(N(1) = 0) = e^{−Λ(1)}"
prob five_plus = last(N) >= 5 "P(N(1) ≥ 5)"
initial: N(0) = 0 at t = 0
dynamics: P(one event in [t, t + h]) = λ(t)h + o(h), with λ(t) = λ(1 + a sin(2πt)) and independent increments
focus events

models.title: Staff a service desk for the midday peak
models.decision: Decision: put 3, 4 or 5 agents on the desk from 10:00 to 14:00. Estimated quantity: the probability that the arrivals in these 4 hours exceed the capacity of the agents, and the mean excess.
models.reason: Many customers decide independently to come, and each customer is a small part of the population. Such arrivals form a Poisson process. The daily cycle enters as a periodic rate, so the counts in different hours have different means.
models.inputs: Time in hours from 06:00. Mean rate λ = 6 arrivals per hour over the day, relative amplitude a = 0.8 and period 24 hours, so the rate is highest at 12:00. One agent serves 3 customers per hour. One agent costs 30 currency units for each hour. These are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.
models.dependence: A Poisson process with the rate λ(t) = λ(1 + a sin(2πt/24)). Counts in disjoint intervals are independent. The model assumes no groups of customers and no effect of the queue length on the arrivals.
models.method: Exact on the grid: each hourly increment is Poisson(Λ(t_{k+1}) − Λ(t_k)). The estimators are means of replicates. The thinning method is also exact and gives a check.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: E N(24) = Λ(24) = 144 arrivals in the day, and E(N[9] − N[5]) = Λ(8) − Λ(4) = 42.33 arrivals in the peak. Compare the hourly counts of past days with Poisson laws of these means. Other candidate models: a Cox process (a random daily level), with a variance above the mean.
models.interpretation: The model compares the 4-hour demand with the 4-hour capacity. It does not model the queue inside the 4 hours, so it is optimistic about the time that customers wait. The smallest staff that meets the constraint is the choice. Reject the model if the peak counts of past days have a variance much above their mean.

data.text: Synthetic: a daily arrival cycle with illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Staff a service desk for the midday peak
problem: Customers arrive at a desk with a daily cycle. Find the smallest number of agents for 10:00 to 14:00 that keeps the overload probability at 5 % or less.
param lambda = 6 {arrivals per hour} "mean rate over the day"
param amp = 0.8 "relative amplitude of the daily cycle"
param agents = 4 {agents} "agents from 10:00 to 14:00"
param serve = 3 {customers per agent-hour} "service capacity of one agent"
param wage = 30 {currency units per agent-hour} "cost of one agent"
N ~ poissonprocess(lambda = lambda, amp = amp, period = 24, T = 24, steps = 24) {arrivals} "arrivals from 06:00"
peak := N[9] - N[5]
prob overload = peak > agents*serve*4 "the peak demand exceeds the capacity"
mean excess = max(peak - agents*serve*4, 0) {customers} "customers above the capacity"
mean peak_mean = N[9] - N[5] {arrivals} "E(peak) = Λ(8) − Λ(4)"
mean day = last(N) {arrivals} "E N(24) = Λ(24)"
mean cost = wage*agents*4 {currency units}
alt "3 agents": agents = 3
alt "4 agents": agents = 4
alt "5 agents": agents = 5
minimise cost
require overload <= 0.05
initial: N(0) = 0 at t = 0 (06:00)
dynamics: arrivals at the rate λ(t) = λ(1 + a sin(2πt/24)), independent increments
focus peak

models.title: Spare pumps for a year of failures
models.decision: Decision: hold 8, 10 or 12 spare pumps at the start of the year. Estimated quantity: the probability of a stockout, P(N(12) > s), and the mean cost of the spares in stock and the emergency orders.
models.reason: A large fleet of pumps fails at random. Each pump has a small failure probability in a month, and the failures are independent. The total count of failures is then near a Poisson process. Hot months raise the rate, so the rate is periodic.
models.inputs: Time in months. Mean failure rate λ = 0.5 failures per month for the fleet, relative amplitude a = 0.3 and period 12 months. A spare in stock costs 40 currency units for each year. An emergency order costs 500 currency units for each pump that the stock cannot supply. These are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.
models.dependence: A Poisson process with the rate λ(t) = λ(1 + a sin(2πt/12)). The operator replaces a failed pump at once, so the fleet size and the rate do not change. The model assumes that failures do not cause other failures.
models.method: Exact on the grid: the monthly increments are independent Poisson counts. The stockout probability has an exact reference. The thinning method gives a second exact sampler.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: E N(12) = Λ(12) = 6 failures, because 12 months is one whole period. P(N(12) > 10) = 0.0426 and P(N(12) > 12) = 0.0088. Compare the yearly failure counts of past years with Poisson(6). Other candidate models: a negative binomial count if the pumps differ in age, and a Weibull renewal process if failures depend on age.
models.interpretation: More spares lower the stockout risk, but each spare costs 40 a year. The choice is the stock with the lowest mean cost that keeps the stockout probability at 5 % or less. Reject the model if the failures come in groups, for example after a power surge.

data.text: Synthetic: failure counts of a pump fleet with illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Spare pumps for a year of failures
problem: A fleet of pumps fails at a seasonal rate. Find the number of spare pumps that gives the lowest mean cost with a stockout probability of 5 % or less.
param lambda = 0.5 {failures per month} "mean failure rate of the fleet"
param amp = 0.3 "relative amplitude of the seasonal rate"
param s = 10 {pumps} "spare pumps at the start of the year"
param hold = 40 {currency units per pump-year} "holding cost"
param urgent = 500 {currency units per pump} "cost of an emergency order"
N ~ poissonprocess(lambda = lambda, amp = amp, period = 12, T = 12, steps = 12) {failures} "failures from the start of the year"
failures := last(N)
prob stockout = last(N) > s "P(N(12) > s)"
mean expected = last(N) {failures} "E N(12) = 6"
mean cost = hold*s + urgent*max(last(N) - s, 0) {currency units}
alt "8 spares": s = 8
alt "10 spares": s = 10
alt "12 spares": s = 12
minimise cost
require stockout <= 0.05
initial: N(0) = 0 at t = 0 (start of the year)
dynamics: failures at the rate λ(t) = λ(1 + a sin(2πt/12)), independent increments
focus failures

models.title: A trigger for a junction safety review
models.decision: Decision: start a safety review of a junction after 5, 6 or 7 accidents in 3 years. Estimated quantity: the false alarm probability at the normal rate and the detection probability at a doubled rate.
models.reason: Accidents at one junction are rare, and many independent trips each carry a small risk. The accident count is then near a Poisson process. Winter raises the rate, so the rate has a yearly cycle.
models.inputs: Time in years. Normal rate 1.2 accidents per year. A dangerous junction has 2.4 accidents per year. Relative amplitude a = 0.2 and period 1 year. These are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.
models.dependence: Two Poisson processes with the rates λ(1 + a sin(2πt)): one for a normal junction (N0) and one for a dangerous junction (N1). The model assumes a constant traffic volume for the 3 years.
models.method: Exact on the grid: monthly increments are independent Poisson counts. Both probabilities have exact references, because 3 years is a whole number of periods and Λ(3) = 3λ.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: E N0(3) = 3.6 and E N1(3) = 7.2. P(N0(3) ≥ 6) = 0.156 and P(N1(3) ≥ 6) = 0.725. Check the counts of many normal junctions against Poisson(3.6). Other candidate models: a negative binomial count with a random junction rate (an empirical Bayes model), which corrects regression to the mean.
models.interpretation: A low trigger finds more dangerous junctions but starts more reviews at normal junctions. The choice is the highest trigger with a detection probability of 0.7 or more, which gives the fewest false alarms. Reject the model if the traffic volume changed in the 3 years.

data.text: Synthetic: accident rates for a junction with illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: A trigger for a junction safety review
problem: A review starts when a junction has many accidents in 3 years. Find the trigger with the fewest false alarms that still detects a doubled rate with probability 0.7.
param base = 1.2 {accidents per year} "normal rate"
param high = 2.4 {accidents per year} "rate of a dangerous junction"
param trig = 6 {accidents} "trigger for a review"
N0 ~ poissonprocess(lambda = base, amp = 0.2, period = 1, T = 3, steps = 36) {accidents} "normal junction"
N1 ~ poissonprocess(lambda = high, amp = 0.2, period = 1, T = 3, steps = 36) {accidents} "dangerous junction"
count0 := last(N0)
prob false_alarm = last(N0) >= trig "P(N0(3) ≥ trigger)"
prob detect = last(N1) >= trig "P(N1(3) ≥ trigger)"
mean mean_normal = last(N0) {accidents} "E N0(3) = 3.6"
alt "Trigger 5": trig = 5
alt "Trigger 6": trig = 6
alt "Trigger 7": trig = 7
minimise false_alarm
require detect >= 0.7
initial: N0(0) = N1(0) = 0 at t = 0
dynamics: accidents at the rate λ(1 + 0.2 sin(2πt)), independent increments, λ = 1.2 or 2.4 per year
focus count0

models.title: Ruin of an insurer in the Cramér–Lundberg model
models.observe: The surplus is R_t = u + c t − S_t with u = 10 and the premium rate c = 6. The claims come at the rate λ = 1 and are exponential with mean 5. The safety loading is θ = c/(λ × 5) − 1 = 0.2. The estimate of final is near its reference E R_10 = u + (c − λ × 5) × 10 = 20. For exponential claims, ruin in infinite time has the probability ψ(10) = e^{−θu/((1 + θ) × 5)}/(1 + θ) = 0.597. Ruin by T = 10 has a lower probability. The page checks for ruin at the 200 grid times only. The grid can miss a drop below 0 between two grid times, so the estimate is a little low. More steps reduce this bias. With a premium rate c = 5, θ = 0 and ruin in infinite time is certain.
models.dsl:
title: Ruin of an insurer in the Cramér–Lundberg model
problem: An insurer starts with capital u, receives premiums at a constant rate and pays exponential claims at random times. Estimate the probability of ruin before T = 10 and the mean final surplus.
param u = 10 {currency units} "initial capital"
param c = 6 {currency units per year} "premium rate"
param lambda = 1 {claims per year} "claim rate"
param m = 5 {currency units} "mean claim"
R ~ compoundprocess(x0 = u, drift = c, lambda = lambda, jump = -m, T = 10, steps = 200) {currency units} "surplus"
final := last(R)
prob ruin = min(R) < 0 "ruin before T, on the grid"
mean final_mean = last(R) {currency units} "E R_10 = u + (c − λm)T = 20"
mean loading = c/(lambda*m) - 1 "safety loading θ = 0.2"
initial: R_0 = u at t = 0
dynamics: R_t = u + c t − S_t, with S a compound Poisson process of rate λ and exponential claims of mean m
focus final

models.title: Choose a quota share retention for 5 years
models.decision: Decision: keep 100 %, 60 % or 40 % of each claim and cede the rest to a reinsurer under a quota share. Estimated quantity: the probability of ruin before 5 years and the mean final surplus.
models.reason: Claims of a large portfolio come at random times, independently of each other. Their times form a Poisson process and their sizes are i.i.d., so the aggregate claims are a compound Poisson process. The premium comes in at a constant rate, which gives the Cramér–Lundberg surplus.
models.inputs: Initial reserve u = 20, claim rate λ = 10 per year, mean claim 2 (in millions of currency units). Premium rate c = 24, so the safety loading is 0.2. The reinsurer charges a loading ξ = 0.3 on the ceded claims. These are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.
models.dependence: With the retention q, the net surplus is R_t = u + (c − (1 − q)(1 + ξ)λm)t − q S_t. S is a compound Poisson process with exponential claims. The model assumes a constant portfolio and no interest on the reserve.
models.method: Exact on the grid: the claims in each step are Poisson(λh) in number, with a Gamma sum. The page checks for ruin at 250 grid times, so the estimate is a little low: the grid can miss a short drop below 0.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: E R_5 = u + (c − (1 − q)(1 + ξ)λm − qλm) × 5, that is 40, 28 and 22 for q = 1, 0.6 and 0.4. Check the net safety loading of each retention: it must be positive. Other candidate models: an excess-of-loss treaty, and claims with a heavier tail (lognormal or Pareto).
models.interpretation: Reinsurance lowers the ruin probability, but the insurer pays the reinsurer's loading, so the mean of the final surplus is lower. The choice is the highest retention that keeps the ruin probability at 5 % or less. Reject the model if the claim sizes have a heavier tail than the exponential law.

data.text: Synthetic: an insurance portfolio with illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Choose a quota share retention for 5 years
problem: An insurer cedes a fraction of each claim to a reinsurer. Find the highest retention that keeps the ruin probability before 5 years at 5 % or less.
param u = 20 {million currency units} "initial reserve"
param c = 24 {million currency units per year} "premium rate"
param lambda = 10 {claims per year} "claim rate"
param m = 2 {million currency units} "mean claim"
param xi = 0.3 "loading of the reinsurer"
param q = 0.6 "retained fraction of each claim"
R ~ compoundprocess(x0 = u, drift = c - (1 - q)*(1 + xi)*lambda*m, lambda = lambda, jump = -q*m, T = 5, steps = 250) {million currency units} "net surplus"
final := last(R)
prob ruin = min(R) < 0 "ruin before 5 years, on the grid"
mean final_mean = last(R) {million currency units} "E R_5"
alt "Keep 100 %": q = 1
alt "Keep 60 %": q = 0.6
alt "Keep 40 %": q = 0.4
maximise final_mean
require ruin <= 0.05
initial: R_0 = u at t = 0
dynamics: R_t = u + (c − (1 − q)(1 + ξ)λm)t − q S_t, with S a compound Poisson process of exponential claims
focus final

models.title: Plan irrigation for a season of rain
models.decision: Decision: plan 60, 90 or 120 mm of irrigation for a 90-day season. Estimated quantity: the probability that rain plus irrigation is below the crop need, and the water cost.
models.reason: Rain comes in separate storms at random times. The storm depths are positive and vary. The season total is then a sum of a random number of random depths, a compound Poisson process with upward jumps.
models.inputs: Storms at the rate λ = 0.2 per day, mean storm depth 8 mm, season of 90 days. The crop needs 200 mm. Water costs 2 currency units for each mm and hectare. These are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.
models.dependence: A compound Poisson process with drift 0 and exponential jumps of mean 8 mm. Storm times are independent, and depths are independent of the times. The model ignores wet and dry spells, which cluster the storms.
models.method: Exact on the grid: the storms in each day are Poisson(λ) in number, with a Gamma sum of depths. The estimators are means of replicates.
models.diagnostics: Reference value: E R_90 = λ × 8 × 90 = 144 mm, with a standard deviation √(2 × 18 × 64) = 48 mm. Compare the season totals of past years with this mean and spread. Other candidate models: a Markov chain for wet and dry days (clustered storms), and gamma or mixed-exponential storm depths.
models.interpretation: More irrigation lowers the risk of a shortfall but costs more water. The choice is the lowest amount with a shortfall probability of 10 % or less. Reject the model if wet and dry spells make the variance of the season totals much larger than 2λm²T.

data.text: Synthetic: a storm model for one season with illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Plan irrigation for a season of rain
problem: Rain comes in random storms. Find the smallest irrigation plan that meets the crop need with probability 0.9.
param lambda = 0.2 {storms per day} "storm rate"
param depth = 8 {mm} "mean storm depth"
param need = 200 {mm} "water need of the crop"
param irr = 90 {mm} "planned irrigation"
param price = 2 {currency units per mm-hectare} "water cost"
R ~ compoundprocess(x0 = 0, drift = 0, lambda = lambda, jump = depth, T = 90, steps = 90) {mm} "cumulative rain"
rain := last(R)
prob shortfall = last(R) + irr < need "rain and irrigation below the need"
mean season = last(R) {mm} "E R_90 = 144 mm"
mean cost = price*irr {currency units per hectare}
alt "Irrigate 60 mm": irr = 60
alt "Irrigate 90 mm": irr = 90
alt "Irrigate 120 mm": irr = 120
minimise cost
require shortfall <= 0.1
initial: R_0 = 0 at t = 0 (start of the season)
dynamics: R_t = sum of the storm depths up to day t; storms at the rate λ, depths exponential with mean 8 mm
focus rain

models.title: Buy a maintenance contract or pay for each repair
models.decision: Decision: pay for each repair, buy a basic contract or buy a full contract for one year. Estimated quantity: the mean yearly cost and the probability that the cost exceeds the budget of 45.
models.reason: Breakdowns of a machine line come at random times, and each repair has a random cost. The cost to date is a compound Poisson process with upward jumps. A contract fee is a constant cost rate, the drift, and preventive work lowers the breakdown rate.
models.inputs: Time in months, costs in thousands of currency units. Without a contract: 1.5 breakdowns per month, mean repair cost 2. Basic contract: fee 0.8 per month, 1.1 breakdowns per month. Full contract: fee 1.5 per month, 0.7 breakdowns per month. Budget 45 for the year. These are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.
models.dependence: A compound Poisson process with drift = fee, rate λ and exponential repair costs of mean 2. Breakdowns are independent. The model assumes that the contract changes the rate but not the repair cost.
models.method: Exact on the grid: the breakdowns in each month are Poisson(λ) in number, with a Gamma sum of costs. The mean cost has an exact reference.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: E C_12 = 12(fee + 2λ), that is 36.0, 36.0 and 34.8 for the three options. Check the monthly breakdown counts of past years against a Poisson law. Other candidate models: a lognormal repair cost, and a rate that grows with the age of the machines.
models.interpretation: The full contract has the lowest mean cost here. It also has less spread, because the fee, which does not depend on the breakdowns, is a larger part of the cost. The choice is the option with the lowest mean cost that keeps the budget risk at 15 % or less. Reject the model if a breakdown makes more breakdowns likely in the next weeks.

data.text: Synthetic: breakdowns and repair costs of a machine line with illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Buy a maintenance contract or pay for each repair
problem: Repairs come at random times with random costs. Compare the yearly cost of three maintenance options and the risk of exceeding the budget.
param fee = 0 {thousand currency units per month} "contract fee"
param lambda = 1.5 {breakdowns per month} "breakdown rate"
param m = 2 {thousand currency units} "mean repair cost"
param budget = 45 {thousand currency units} "yearly budget"
C ~ compoundprocess(x0 = 0, drift = fee, lambda = lambda, jump = m, T = 12, steps = 48) {thousand currency units} "cost to date"
year_cost := last(C)
mean cost = last(C) {thousand currency units} "E C_12 = 12(fee + λm)"
prob over_budget = last(C) > budget "cost above the budget"
alt "Pay for each repair": fee = 0; lambda = 1.5
alt "Basic contract": fee = 0.8; lambda = 1.1
alt "Full contract": fee = 1.5; lambda = 0.7
minimise cost
require over_budget <= 0.15
initial: C_0 = 0 at t = 0 (start of the year)
dynamics: C_t = fee × t + sum of the repair costs up to month t; breakdowns at the rate λ
focus year_cost

models.title: Time average and ensemble average of a Markov chain
models.observe: The ergodic chain has the unique stationary law π = (6/13, 5/13, 2/13) ≈ (0.4615, 0.3846, 0.1538) and mixes fast, with t_mix(1/4) = 3. The time average time1, the fraction of the 201 states equal to 1, has the reference 0.4688 from start 1 and 0.4535 from start 3. Both are near π_1, and the difference comes from the first few steps. The ensemble average ens1 = P(X_200 = 1) has the reference 0.4615 = π_1 for both starts. But early1 = P(X_5 = 1) is 0.5158 from start 1 and 0.3808 from start 3. The histogram of occ1 is narrow around π_1: one long path gives the same answer as many paths. The reducible chain has the closed classes {1, 2} and {3}. From start 1, time1 is near 4/7 ≈ 0.5714, and from start 3 it is 0. So the time average depends on the start.
models.dsl:
title: Time average and ensemble average of a Markov chain
problem: A chain with 3 states runs for 200 steps. Compare the fraction of time in state 1 with the probability of state 1 at the last step, and with the stationary law.
param x0 = 1 "initial state"
param Q = [0.8, 0.15, 0.05, 0.2, 0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.6] "transition matrix, row by row"
X ~ markovchain(P = Q, x0 = x0, steps = 200) {state}
occ1 := mean(X == 1)
mean time1 = mean(X == 1) "time average: fraction of the 201 states equal to 1"
prob ens1 = last(X) == 1 "ensemble average: P(X_200 = 1)"
mean time3 = mean(X == 3) "fraction of time in state 3"
prob early1 = X[6] == 1 "P(X_5 = 1), before the chain mixes"
alt "Ergodic chain, start in 1": x0 = 1
alt "Ergodic chain, start in 3": x0 = 3
alt "Reducible chain, start in 1": x0 = 1; Q = [0.7, 0.3, 0, 0.4, 0.6, 0, 0, 0, 1]
alt "Reducible chain, start in 3": x0 = 3; Q = [0.7, 0.3, 0, 0.4, 0.6, 0, 0, 0, 1]
initial: X_0 = x0
dynamics: P(X_{n+1} = j | X_n = i) = Q_ij, independent of the earlier states
focus occ1

models.title: Which borrower rating gives the best return after credit losses?
models.decision: Decision: offer the 5-year loan to a borrower rated A, B or C, at the margin of that rating class. Estimated quantity: the probability of default within 5 years, the expected loss EAD × LGD × PD, and the expected income minus the credit loss.
models.reason: Ratings move between yearly reviews, and the next rating depends mainly on the present rating. A Markov chain on the ratings with an absorbing default state is the usual migration model. It gives the probability of default for each term from the powers of one matrix.
models.inputs: Four states: 1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C, 4 = default. An illustrative yearly migration matrix with yearly default probabilities 0.5 %, 2 % and 10 % from A, B and C. Exposure at default EAD = 100 currency units, loss given default LGD = 0.45, margins 1 %, 2.5 % and 6 % a year. The values are illustrative, not from a rating agency.
models.dependence: A time-homogeneous Markov chain in yearly steps: the next rating depends only on the present rating. Default (state 4) is absorbing, so the only closed class is {4}, and each path ends in default when the term is long enough. The model has no rating momentum and no economic cycle.
models.method: Exact sampling of the chain with an alias table for each row. The estimators are fractions and means over replicates. The page computes the exact reference of pd from e_{x0} P⁵, and of time_def from the average of the state probabilities.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: pd = 0.0495 (A), 0.134 (B) and 0.355 (C) from the matrix powers. The estimates must agree within their intervals. Check that each row of the matrix adds to 1. Other candidate models: a chain with an extra state for a recent downgrade (rating momentum), or a chain whose matrix follows the economy. A continuous-time chain with a generator matrix is a third candidate.
models.interpretation: The C loan has the largest mean profit, but its default probability 0.36 breaks the limit of 0.15. The B loan meets the limit and has a larger profit than the A loan, so it is the choice in this illustration. The result depends on the margin of each class. Reject the model if observed migrations show momentum, or if default rates change with the economic cycle.

data.text: Synthetic: an illustrative yearly migration matrix of four states and illustrative loan terms. Illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Which borrower rating gives the best return after credit losses?
problem: A lender offers a 5-year loan to one borrower. The rating moves each year by a migration matrix, and default is absorbing. Choose the rating class to lend to.
param x0 = 2 "initial rating: 1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C"
param n = 5 {years} "loan term"
param ead = 100 {currency units} "exposure at default"
param lgd = 0.45 "loss given default"
param margin = 0.025 "annual interest margin"
R ~ markovchain(P = [0.90, 0.08, 0.015, 0.005, 0.05, 0.85, 0.08, 0.02, 0.01, 0.09, 0.80, 0.10, 0, 0, 0, 1], x0 = x0, steps = n) {rating}
income := margin * ead * (n - sum(R == 4))
loss := lgd * ead * (last(R) == 4)
net := income - loss
prob pd = last(R) == 4 "probability of default within the term"
mean el = lgd * ead * (last(R) == 4) {currency units} "expected loss EAD × LGD × PD"
mean profit = net {currency units} "income minus credit loss"
mean time_def = mean(R == 4) "fraction of the 6 yearly states in default"
alt "Lend to an A borrower": x0 = 1; margin = 0.01
alt "Lend to a B borrower": x0 = 2; margin = 0.025
alt "Lend to a C borrower": x0 = 3; margin = 0.06
maximise profit
require pd <= 0.15
initial: R_0 = x0, the rating at the start of the loan
dynamics: P(R_{n+1} = j | R_n = i) = M_ij each year; state 4 (default) is absorbing
focus net

models.title: How often should a worn machine get maintenance?
models.decision: Decision: run the machine to failure, or do maintenance on 20 %, 50 % or 80 % of the days when it is worn. Estimated quantity: the fraction of failed days and the expected cost for each day over 250 days.
models.reason: Each day the machine is in one of three conditions: good, worn or failed. Wear and failure depend mainly on the present condition. A three-state Markov chain gives the long-run fraction of days in each condition, and the policy changes one row of the matrix.
models.inputs: Daily probabilities: good → worn d = 0.05, worn → failed f = 0.1, repair of a failed machine g = 0.5. Maintenance makes a worn machine good with probability r. Costs: 1,000 currency units for each failed day and 1,500 for each maintenance. All values are illustrative.
models.dependence: A time-homogeneous Markov chain with the matrix [1 − d, d, 0; r, 1 − r − f, f; g, 0, 1 − g]. It is irreducible and aperiodic, so a unique stationary law π exists, and the time averages converge to π. No state is absorbing.
models.method: Exact sampling of the chain with an alias table for each row. The daily cost is an affine function of the occupation fractions mean(M == 2) and mean(M == 3). So the page computes its exact reference from the state probabilities e_1 Pⁿ.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: downtime = 0.0605, 0.0273, 0.0149 and 0.0103 for r = 0, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8, and daily_cost = 60.5, 68.5, 71.4 and 72.5. The panel of conditions shows the stationary law and the mixing time at each r. Other candidate models: a semi-Markov model, where the time in the worn state is not geometric, or a model with a lead time for maintenance.
models.interpretation: Run to failure has the lowest cost, but its fraction of failed days, about 0.06, breaks the limit of 0.05. Maintenance on 20 % of worn days meets the limit at the lowest cost. Reject the model if the time from wear to failure is not near geometric. This occurs, for example, when the failure risk grows with the age of the wear.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative daily transition probabilities and costs of a single machine. Illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: How often should a worn machine get maintenance?
problem: A machine is good, worn or failed on each day. Maintenance of a worn machine makes it good again. Choose the daily maintenance probability that gives the lowest cost.
param r = 0.2 "probability of maintenance on a worn day"
param d = 0.05 "probability that a good machine becomes worn in one day"
param f = 0.1 "probability that a worn machine fails in one day"
param g = 0.5 "probability that a repair ends in one day"
param cf = 1000 {currency units} "cost of one day of failure"
param cm = 1500 {currency units} "cost of one maintenance"
M ~ markovchain(P = [1 - d, d, 0, r, 1 - r - f, f, g, 0, 1 - g], x0 = 1, steps = 250) {state}
down := mean(M == 3)
mean downtime = mean(M == 3) "fraction of days failed"
mean daily_cost = cf * mean(M == 3) + cm * r * mean(M == 2) {currency units per day} "expected cost for each day"
prob failed_end = last(M) == 3 "P(failed on day 250)"
alt "Run to failure": r = 0
alt "Maintenance on 20 % of worn days": r = 0.2
alt "Maintenance on 50 % of worn days": r = 0.5
alt "Maintenance on 80 % of worn days": r = 0.8
minimise daily_cost
require downtime <= 0.05
initial: M_0 = 1, a good machine on day 0
dynamics: good → worn with probability d; worn → good with r, worn → failed with f; failed → good with g
focus down

models.title: How much water can a reservoir supply in a dry season?
models.decision: Decision: supply 2.5, 3 or 3.5 megalitres a day for the 90 days of the dry season. Estimated quantity: the probability that the storage goes below 0 on some day, and the storage at the end of the season.
models.reason: Rain occurs in spells: a wet day is more probable after a wet day. A two-state Markov chain of dry and wet days keeps this persistence. Independent days would give too few long dry spells, and the shortages come from long dry spells.
models.inputs: P(wet tomorrow | dry today) = 0.2, P(dry tomorrow | wet today) = 0.5. Inflow of 15 ML on a wet day and 0 on a dry day. Storage at the start 80 ML. The model has no evaporation and no spill. All values are illustrative.
models.dependence: A two-state Markov chain W with the stationary fraction of wet days π_wet = 0.2/(0.2 + 0.5) = 2/7 ≈ 0.286. Dry spells have a geometric length with mean 5 days. The storage is the start value plus the cumulative inflow minus the cumulative supply.
models.method: Exact sampling of the chain with an alias table for each row. The shortage indicator reads the whole storage path. The fraction of wet days has an exact reference from the state probabilities.
models.diagnostics: Reference value: wet = 0.281, slightly below 2/7, because the chain starts on a dry day. The estimate of p_short has no closed-form reference. Check it with a larger run. Other candidate models: a second-order chain, a chain with seasonal probabilities, or a model with random inflow on wet days.
models.interpretation: In this illustration a supply of 3 ML a day keeps the shortage probability near 0.04, below the limit of 0.05. A supply of 3.5 ML a day gives a shortage probability near 0.11. Reject the model if the observed dry spells are longer than geometric, or if the probability of rain changes during the season.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative wet and dry transition probabilities and an illustrative reservoir. Illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: How much water can a reservoir supply in a dry season?
problem: Wet days follow wet days more often than dry days. A reservoir gets inflow on wet days and supplies a fixed amount each day. Choose the largest daily supply with a small shortage risk.
param a = 0.2 "P(wet tomorrow | dry today)"
param b = 0.5 "P(dry tomorrow | wet today)"
param inflow = 15 {megalitres} "inflow on a wet day"
param s0 = 80 {megalitres} "storage at the start"
param supply = 4 {megalitres per day} "daily supply"
W ~ markovchain(P = [1 - a, a, b, 1 - b], x0 = 1, steps = 90) {1 = dry, 2 = wet}
store := s0 + cumsum(inflow * (W == 2) - supply)
shortage := any(store < 0)
mean wet = mean(W == 2) "fraction of wet days"
prob p_short = shortage "storage below 0 on some day"
mean final = s0 + sum(inflow * (W == 2) - supply) {megalitres} "storage after day 90 (no spill)"
mean delivered = supply {megalitres per day} "daily supply"
alt "Supply 2.5 ML a day": supply = 2.5
alt "Supply 3 ML a day": supply = 3
alt "Supply 3.5 ML a day": supply = 3.5
maximise delivered
require p_short <= 0.05
initial: W_0 = 1 (a dry day), storage s0
dynamics: P(W_{n+1} = 2 | W_n = 1) = a, P(W_{n+1} = 1 | W_n = 2) = b; storage S_{n+1} = S_n + inflow 1{W = 2} − supply
focus final

models.title: Extinction of a Galton–Watson process
models.observe: The page computes P(Z_n = 0) = f(f(…f(0)…)), with n applications of the offspring PGF f(s) = e^{m(s − 1)}. For m = 1, the reference of ext = P(Z_20 = 0) is 0.912, and ext5 = P(Z_5 = 0) is 0.732. The mean of zn stays at mⁿ = 1. So most families die, and a few large families keep the mean at 1. For m = 0.8, ext is 0.996 and E Z_20 = 0.8^20 = 0.0115. For m = 1.5, ext is 0.417, near the extinction probability q ≈ 0.417, the smallest root of f(s) = s. But E Z_20 = 1.5^20 ≈ 3,325. The histogram of size shows a large mass at 0 and a long right tail in each case.
models.dsl:
title: Extinction of a Galton–Watson process
problem: One ancestor has a Poisson number of children with mean m, and each child does the same. Find the probability that the family is extinct by generation 20.
param m = 1 "mean number of offspring"
param n = 20 "number of generations"
Z ~ branching(z0 = 1, m = m, steps = n) {individuals}
size := last(Z)
prob ext = Z[n + 1] == 0 "P(Z_20 = 0)"
prob ext5 = Z[6] == 0 "P(Z_5 = 0)"
mean zn = last(Z) {individuals} "E Z_20 = m^20"
alt "Subcritical, m = 0.8": m = 0.8
alt "Critical, m = 1": m = 1
alt "Supercritical, m = 1.5": m = 1.5
initial: Z_0 = 1
dynamics: Z_{n+1} = sum of Z_n independent Poisson(m) offspring counts
focus size

models.title: Which control measures stop chains of infection?
models.decision: Decision: no control, contact tracing, or contact tracing with the closure of large events. Estimated quantity: the probability of 100 or more cases in 10 generations from one imported case, and the expected cost of control and cases.
models.reason: At the start of an outbreak, almost all contacts are susceptible, so each case infects others independently of the other cases. A branching process is the standard model for this phase. A negative binomial offspring law with a small dispersion k gives superspreading.
models.inputs: Reproduction number R = 1.3 without control, 0.9 with contact tracing, 0.7 with the closure of large events. Dispersion k = 0.2. Costs: 20 and 60 units for the measures, 1 unit for each case. All values are illustrative.
models.dependence: A Galton–Watson process with negative binomial offspring of mean R and dispersion k, from one case. If R ≤ 1, extinction is certain. If R > 1, the chain survives with a positive probability and grows like Rⁿ. The model has no depletion of susceptible people, so it holds only for the first generations.
models.method: Exact sampling generation by generation: Z_{n+1} ~ Poisson(Λ) with Λ ~ Gamma(k Z_n, R/k). The probability of extinction by generation 10 has an exact reference by the iterated PGF.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: extinct = 0.911, 0.980 and 0.996 for R = 1.3, 0.9 and 0.7. The probability of a large outbreak has no closed-form reference. Compare the run with k = inf (Poisson offspring) to see the effect of superspreading. Other candidate models: an SIR model with depletion, or a Hawkes process in continuous time.
models.interpretation: Without control, about 8 % of chains reach 100 cases, above the limit of 5 %. Contact tracing keeps the large outbreaks near 2 % at the lowest expected cost. With k = 0.2 most chains end fast, so a few early chains do not show the risk. Reject the model if the number of cases is a large fraction of the population, or if the cases are not independent.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative reproduction numbers, dispersion and costs. Illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Which control measures stop chains of infection?
problem: Imported cases start chains of infection. Each case infects a negative binomial number of others with mean R and dispersion k. Choose the cheapest control that keeps large outbreaks rare.
param R = 1.3 "reproduction number"
param k = 0.2 "dispersion of the number of secondary cases"
param cc = 0 {currency units} "cost of the control measures"
param cpc = 1 {currency units} "cost of one case"
Z ~ branching(z0 = 1, m = R, k = k, steps = 10) {cases}
total := sum(Z)
prob large = total >= 100 "100 or more cases in 10 generations"
prob extinct = Z[11] == 0 "chain extinct by generation 10"
mean cases = total {cases} "expected number of cases"
mean cost = cc + cpc * total {currency units} "control cost plus case cost"
alt "No control, R = 1.3": R = 1.3; cc = 0
alt "Contact tracing, R = 0.9": R = 0.9; cc = 20
alt "Contact tracing and closure of large events, R = 0.7": R = 0.7; cc = 60
minimise cost
require large <= 0.05
initial: Z_0 = 1, one imported case
dynamics: Z_{n+1} ~ negative binomial(k Z_n, k/(k + R)), the cases of generation n + 1
focus total

models.title: How many animals must a reintroduction release?
models.decision: Decision: release 5, 10, 20 or 30 founders. Estimated quantity: the probability that the population is extinct by generation 30, and the expected total cost. The total cost is the cost of the release plus the cost of a failed program.
models.reason: A small population is at risk from chance in births and deaths, even when its mean growth rate is above 1. A branching process shows this demographic risk. The extinction probability of z0 independent founders is q^{z0}, so more founders reduce the risk fast.
models.inputs: The mean number of offspring that live to breed is m = 1.1 for each animal and generation. Dispersion k = 2, so some animals have many offspring and many have none. Cost 5 units for each founder and 200 units for a failed program. All values are illustrative.
models.dependence: A supercritical Galton–Watson process (m = 1.1 > 1) with negative binomial offspring. The founders act independently. The model has no limit from the habitat and no environmental variation between years.
models.method: Exact sampling generation by generation. The extinction probabilities by generations 10 and 30 have exact references by the iterated PGF, and the mean population has the reference z0 · 1.1^30.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: ext = 0.510, 0.260, 0.068 and 0.018 for 5, 10, 20 and 30 founders, and pop = 87.2, 174, 349 and 524. Check that ext is near q^{z0} with the single-founder value q. Other candidate models: a model with a carrying capacity, or a model with random good and bad years, which increases the extinction risk.
models.interpretation: A release of 10 animals has the lowest expected cost, but its extinction probability 0.26 breaks the limit of 0.1. A release of 20 animals meets the limit. Reject the model if the population reaches the capacity of the habitat, or if bad years affect all animals at the same time.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative offspring mean, dispersion and costs of a reintroduction program. Illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: How many animals must a reintroduction release?
problem: A program releases founders of a rare species into a habitat. Each animal leaves a random number of breeding offspring. Choose the smallest release with a small risk of extinction in 30 generations.
param z0 = 10 {animals} "number of founders"
param m = 1.1 "mean number of breeding offspring of one animal"
param k = 2 "dispersion of the offspring number"
param cr = 5 {currency units} "cost of one founder"
param cfail = 200 {currency units} "cost of a failed program"
Z ~ branching(z0 = z0, m = m, k = k, steps = 30) {animals}
gone := last(Z) == 0
prob ext = Z[31] == 0 "extinct by generation 30"
prob ext10 = Z[11] == 0 "extinct by generation 10"
mean pop = last(Z) {animals} "E Z_30 = z0 m^30"
mean cost = cr * z0 + cfail * gone {currency units} "release cost plus the cost of failure"
alt "Release 5 animals": z0 = 5
alt "Release 10 animals": z0 = 10
alt "Release 20 animals": z0 = 20
alt "Release 30 animals": z0 = 30
minimise cost
require ext <= 0.1
initial: Z_0 = z0 founders
dynamics: Z_{n+1} ~ negative binomial(k Z_n, k/(k + m)); no limit from the habitat
focus pop

models.title: Which seeding plan gives the largest reach for a viral campaign?
models.decision: Decision: send a plain message to 50 or 100 seed accounts, or send a message with a share reward to 20 seed accounts. Estimated quantity: the total reach in 12 steps, the probability of a reach below 150 accounts, and the value after costs.
models.reason: Each account that shares the message shows it to its contacts, and some of them share it again. Shares by different accounts are near independent while the reach is small. A branching process with seed accounts as ancestors models this cascade.
models.inputs: Mean new sharers for each sharer: m = 0.6 for the plain message and 0.9 with the reward. Dispersion k = 0.5. Value 1 unit for each sharer, cost 2 units for each seed and 0.3 units for each rewarded share. All values are illustrative.
models.dependence: A Galton–Watson process with z0 seed accounts and negative binomial offspring. With m < 1 the cascade is subcritical: it ends with probability 1, and the mean total reach is z0/(1 − m) in the long run. The model has no saturation of the audience.
models.method: Exact sampling generation by generation. The probability that the cascade has ended by step 12 has an exact reference by the iterated PGF. The mean size of the last step has the exact reference z0 m^12.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: dead = 0.966, 0.577 and 0.934, and last_gen = 0.109, 5.65 and 0.218. The mean reach is near z0/(1 − m) = 125, 200 and 250 before the cut at 12 steps. Other candidate models: a Hawkes process of shares in continuous time, or a model on a contact network with saturation.
models.interpretation: The reward plan has the largest mean value, but its reach varies much: about 60 % of runs have a reach below 150. The plan with 100 plain seeds meets the limit of 20 % and is the choice in this illustration. Reject the model if the audience saturates, or if the share rate falls in time.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative share rates, dispersion and campaign costs. Illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Which seeding plan gives the largest reach for a viral campaign?
problem: A campaign sends a message to seed accounts. Each account that shares it makes a random number of new accounts share it. Choose the plan with the largest value after costs.
param z0 = 50 {accounts} "seed accounts"
param m = 0.6 "mean number of new sharers for each sharer"
param k = 0.5 "dispersion of the number of new sharers"
param cs = 2 {currency units} "cost of one seed account"
param reward = 0 {currency units} "reward for each share after the seeds"
param v = 1 {currency units} "value of one sharer"
Z ~ branching(z0 = z0, m = m, k = k, steps = 12) {accounts}
reach := sum(Z)
prob flop = reach < 150 "reach below 150 accounts"
prob dead = Z[13] == 0 "cascade ended by step 12"
mean last_gen = last(Z) {accounts} "E Z_12 = z0 m^12"
mean value = v * reach - cs * z0 - reward * (reach - z0) {currency units} "value minus costs"
alt "50 seeds, plain message": z0 = 50; m = 0.6; reward = 0
alt "20 seeds, share reward": z0 = 20; m = 0.9; reward = 0.3
alt "100 seeds, plain message": z0 = 100; m = 0.6; reward = 0
maximise value
require flop <= 0.2
initial: Z_0 = z0 seed accounts
dynamics: Z_{n+1} ~ negative binomial(k Z_n, k/(k + m)), the new sharers in step n + 1
focus reach

models.title: Clustering in a Hawkes process
models.observe: With μ = 1, α = 1 and β = 2, the branching ratio is n = α/β = 0.5. The estimate of count is near its reference E N(20) = 39.0. The estimate of sq_dev, the variance, is far above the mean. In one run it is near 150. The long-run value is μT/(1 − n)³ = 160, so the dispersion index is near 1/(1 − n)² = 4. A Poisson process has a dispersion index 1. With the alternative n = 0.9 (α = 1.8), E N(20) = 155.8. The variance is much larger (near 9,600 in one run), because the clusters are larger.
