A stationary version exists only for n < 1. For n ≥ 1, E N(t) grows as t² (n = 1) or exponentially (n > 1). These variance values are finite-run observations, not references.
models.dsl:
title: Clustering in a Hawkes process
problem: Each event raises the rate of further events for a short time. Compare the mean and the variance of the count for a branching ratio of 0.5 and of 0.9.
param mu = 1 {events per unit time} "baseline rate μ"
param alpha = 1 {events per unit time} "rise α of the rate at each event"
param beta = 2 {per unit time} "decay rate β"
param T = 20 {time units} "horizon"
param mN = beta*mu*T/(beta - alpha) + alpha*mu*(exp(-(beta - alpha)*T) - 1)/(beta - alpha)^2 {events} "E N(T) for the current parameters"
N ~ hawkes(mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, T = T, steps = 100) {events} "count of events"
events := last(N)
mean count_mean = last(N) {events} "E N(T)"
mean sq_dev = (last(N) - mN)^2 "the variance of N(T)"
mean disp = (last(N) - mN)^2 / mN "the dispersion index Var N(T) / E N(T)"
mean half = N[51] {events} "E N(T/2)"
alt "n = 0.5": alpha = 1
alt "n = 0.9": alpha = 1.8
initial: N(0) = 0 and λ(0) = μ at t = 0, no history
dynamics: λ(t) = μ + Σ α e^{−β(t − t_i)} over past events t_i; P(event in [t, t + h]) = λ(t)h + o(h)
focus events

models.title: Inspection teams for 30 days of aftershocks
models.decision: Decision: plan 3 or 8 teams that inspect buildings for 30 days after a large earthquake. Compare the plans under a branching ratio n = α/β of 0.4 and of 0.8. Estimated quantity: the probability that the felt aftershocks exceed the inspection capacity.
models.reason: Each aftershock can trigger more aftershocks, so the events cluster in time. A self-exciting point process models this: each event raises the rate for a short time. The ETAS model of seismology is of this type. This model is a simplified version of ETAS.
models.inputs: Time in days. The baseline rate of felt aftershocks is μ = 0.5 per day, the decay rate is β = 1 per day, and α = 0.4 or 0.8 per day. One team can do the inspections that follow 15 felt events in 30 days. A team costs 20 currency units (thousands) for 30 days. These are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.
models.dependence: A Hawkes process with an exponential kernel. A stationary version exists only for n = α/β < 1, and both scenarios have n < 1. The model is a simplification. ETAS uses a power-law (Omori) kernel, and in ETAS a larger magnitude triggers more events. Also, the direct aftershocks of the main shock decay in time, but here the baseline rate μ is constant.
models.method: Exact: the sampler uses the cluster representation. It draws immigrant events at the rate μ and Poisson(n) children for each event. The estimators are means of replicates. The Ogata thinning method is a second exact sampler.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: E N(30) = 24.4 events for n = 0.4 and 65.0 events for n = 0.8. Fit α and β to the first days of the sequence and check the residual times Λ(t_i), which must look like a unit-rate Poisson process. Other candidate models: the ETAS model with an Omori kernel and magnitudes, and a Poisson process with the Omori rate.
models.interpretation: A plan that is enough for n = 0.4 can fail for n = 0.8, because the clusters are larger and the count varies more. If the data are consistent with n = 0.8, choose the plan that meets the constraint in that scenario. Reject the model if the rate decays as a power law and not exponentially.

data.text: Synthetic: an aftershock sequence with illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Inspection teams for 30 days of aftershocks
problem: Felt aftershocks trigger further aftershocks. Compare 3 and 8 inspection teams under a branching ratio of 0.4 and 0.8.
param mu = 0.5 {events per day} "baseline rate of felt aftershocks"
param alpha = 0.8 {events per day} "rise of the rate at each event"
param beta = 1 {per day} "decay rate"
param teams = 8 {teams} "inspection teams"
param per_team = 15 {events} "events one team can follow up in 30 days"
param team_cost = 20 {thousand currency units} "cost of one team for 30 days"
N ~ hawkes(mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, T = 30, steps = 120) {events} "felt aftershocks"
events := last(N)
prob overload = last(N) > teams*per_team "events above the capacity"
mean expected = last(N) {events} "E N(30)"
mean cost = team_cost*teams {thousand currency units}
alt "3 teams, n = 0.4": teams = 3; alpha = 0.4
alt "3 teams, n = 0.8": teams = 3; alpha = 0.8
alt "8 teams, n = 0.8": teams = 8; alpha = 0.8
minimise cost
require overload <= 0.1
initial: N(0) = 0 at t = 0 (just after the main shock), no earlier aftershocks
dynamics: λ(t) = μ + Σ α e^{−β(t − t_i)} over the past aftershocks t_i
focus events

models.title: Promote a message on a social network or not
models.decision: Decision: promote a public safety message or not, under a branching ratio n of 0.6 or 0.9. Estimated quantity: the mean number of reposts in 24 hours and the probability that the reposts exceed the review capacity of 600.
models.reason: Each repost shows the message to new readers, who can repost it again. So each repost can cause more reposts, and the excitation fades as the message ages. A Hawkes process with an exponential kernel models this.
models.inputs: Time in hours. Baseline rate μ = 2 reposts per hour without promotion and 4 with promotion. Decay rate β = 2 per hour. α = 1.2 (n = 0.6) or 1.8 (n = 0.9). The moderation team can review 600 reposts in a day. These are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.
models.dependence: A Hawkes process with an exponential kernel. A stationary version exists only for n < 1. With n near 1 the clusters are very large, and for n ≥ 1 the count can grow without a limit. The model assumes one community with no saturation of readers.
models.method: Exact: the cluster representation, with Poisson(n) children for each repost. The estimators are means of replicates. The Euler method is available for a check of the discretisation bias.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: E N(24) = 116.2 without promotion at n = 0.6, 232.5 with promotion at n = 0.6, and 781.5 with promotion at n = 0.9. Fit μ, α and β to the repost times of earlier messages. Other candidate models: a Hawkes process with a power-law kernel, and an SIR epidemic model with a finite population.
models.interpretation: Promotion doubles the reach for n = 0.6, but for n = 0.9 the reposts can exceed the review capacity. The decision depends strongly on n, so estimate n before the promotion. Reject the model if the repost rate falls because most readers have already seen the message.

data.text: Synthetic: repost times of a message with illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Promote a message on a social network or not
problem: Reposts of a message excite further reposts. Compare the reach and the review load with and without promotion, for two branching ratios.
param mu = 4 {reposts per hour} "baseline rate"
param alpha = 1.2 {reposts per hour} "rise of the rate at each repost"
param beta = 2 {per hour} "decay rate"
param review = 600 {reposts} "review capacity in 24 hours"
N ~ hawkes(mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, T = 24, steps = 96) {reposts} "reposts"
reposts := last(N)
mean reach = last(N) {reposts} "E N(24)"
prob overload = last(N) > review "reposts above the review capacity"
alt "No promotion, n = 0.6": mu = 2; alpha = 1.2
alt "Promotion, n = 0.6": mu = 4; alpha = 1.2
alt "Promotion, n = 0.9": mu = 4; alpha = 1.8
maximise reach
require overload <= 0.05
initial: N(0) = 0 at t = 0 (the message is posted), no earlier reposts
dynamics: λ(t) = μ + Σ α e^{−β(t − t_i)} over the past reposts t_i
focus reposts

models.title: Alarm floods in a control room
models.decision: Decision: staff 1 operator with alarm shelving, 1 operator without shelving, or 2 operators without shelving. Shelving lowers α. Estimated quantity: the probability of an alarm flood and the probability that the hourly alarms exceed the operator capacity. A flood is 10 or more alarms in a fixed 10-minute window.
models.reason: One process upset sets off several related alarms, and a chattering alarm repeats itself. So each alarm raises the alarm rate for a short time, and the alarms come in bursts. A Hawkes process models these bursts. Shelving of chattering alarms lowers the self-excitation α.
models.inputs: Time in minutes. Baseline rate μ = 0.1 alarms per minute, decay rate β = 0.5 per minute. α = 0.4 without shelving (n = 0.8) and α = 0.2 with shelving (n = 0.4). One operator can handle 20 alarms in an hour. These are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.
models.dependence: A Hawkes process with an exponential kernel. Both scenarios have n < 1, so a stationary version exists. The model treats all alarms as one type. The related alarms of one upset are part of one cluster.
models.method: Exact: Ogata's thinning, with candidates at the intensity just after the last alarm. The estimators are means of replicates. The flood rule uses 6 fixed 10-minute windows, so it misses floods that cross a window edge. A sliding window gives a higher probability.
models.diagnostics: Reference values: E N(60) = 26.0 alarms without shelving and 9.8 alarms with shelving. Check the alarm log: the dispersion of the 10-minute counts must be above 1. Other candidate models: a multivariate Hawkes process with one type for each alarm group, and a Markov-modulated Poisson process for upset states.
models.interpretation: Shelving lowers the flood probability more than a second operator does, because it makes the clusters smaller. A second operator only adds capacity. Reject the model if the alarms follow a fixed sequence after each trip, which a Hawkes process does not describe.

data.text: Synthetic: an alarm log of a control room with illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Alarm floods in a control room
problem: Alarms come in bursts. Compare alarm shelving and a second operator by the flood probability and the hourly load.
param mu = 0.1 {alarms per minute} "baseline rate"
param alpha = 0.4 {alarms per minute} "rise of the rate at each alarm"
param beta = 0.5 {per minute} "decay rate"
param ops = 1 {operators} "operators on shift"
param per_op = 20 {alarms per hour} "capacity of one operator"
N ~ hawkes(mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, T = 60, steps = 60) {alarms} "alarms in the hour"
peak := max(N[11] - N[1], N[21] - N[11], N[31] - N[21], N[41] - N[31], N[51] - N[41], N[61] - N[51])
prob flood = peak >= 10 "10 or more alarms in a fixed 10-minute window"
prob overload = last(N) > ops*per_op "alarms above the hourly capacity"
mean alarms = last(N) {alarms} "E N(60)"
mean staff = ops {operators}
alt "1 operator, shelving (n = 0.4)": ops = 1; alpha = 0.2
alt "1 operator, no shelving (n = 0.8)": ops = 1; alpha = 0.4
alt "2 operators, no shelving (n = 0.8)": ops = 2; alpha = 0.4
minimise flood
require overload <= 0.05
initial: N(0) = 0 at t = 0 (start of the hour), no earlier alarms
dynamics: λ(t) = μ + Σ α e^{−β(t − t_i)} over the past alarms t_i
focus peak

models.title: Heavier tails than Brownian motion with the same variance
models.observe: X is a VG process with θ = −0.1, σ = 0.2 and ν = 0.5. B is a Brownian motion with the same mean −0.1 and the same variance σ² + θ²ν = 0.045 at T = 1. The mean of X_T agrees with the reference x0 + θT = −0.1. The kurtosis E[(X_T − θT)⁴]/Var² of X is near 3 + κ₄/Var² ≈ 4.81, while the value for B is near 3. The lower tail P(X_T < −0.7) is near 0.012, about 5 times the Brownian reference 0.0023. With ν = 0.1 the kurtosis falls to about 3.31, and with ν = 1 it rises to about 7.08. The grid values of the VG process are exact, so no discretisation error enters these estimates.
models.dsl:
title: Heavier tails than Brownian motion with the same variance
problem: A variance-gamma process and a Brownian motion have the same mean and variance at T = 1. Compare their kurtosis and a lower tail probability.
param theta = -0.1 "drift θ of the time-changed Brownian motion"
param sigma = 0.2 "volatility σ"
param nu = 0.5 "variance rate ν of the gamma time change"
X ~ variancegamma(x0 = 0, theta = theta, sigma = sigma, nu = nu, T = 1, steps = 50)
B ~ brownian(x0 = 0, mu = theta, sigma = sqrt(sigma^2 + theta^2 * nu), T = 1, steps = 50)
xT := last(X)
mean mean_vg = last(X) "E X_T = x0 + θT"
mean kurt_vg = (last(X) - theta)^4 / (sigma^2 + theta^2 * nu)^2 "E[(X_T − θT)^4] / Var²"
mean kurt_bm = (last(B) - theta)^4 / (sigma^2 + theta^2 * nu)^2 "the same for Brownian motion: 3"
prob tail_vg = last(X) < -0.7 "P(X_T < −0.7)"
prob tail_bm = last(B) < -0.7 "P(B_T < −0.7)"
alt "ν = 0.1": nu = 0.1
alt "ν = 0.5": nu = 0.5
alt "ν = 1": nu = 1
initial: X_0 = 0 and B_0 = 0
dynamics: X_t = θ G_t + σ W(G_t), with G a gamma process of mean t and variance ν t
focus xT

models.title: How large can an equity position be for a 5-day loss limit?
models.decision: Decision: hold a position of 5, 10, 15 or 20 million currency units for 5 trading days. Estimated quantity: the probability of a loss above 0.8 million, and the expected gain.
models.reason: Daily equity returns have heavier tails than the normal law, and large moves come as jumps. The VG process has jumps and a kurtosis above 3, but it keeps independent increments. A normal model with the same variance gives too small a probability of a large loss.
models.inputs: Log-return parameters for each day: θ = 0.0002, σ = 0.012, ν = 1.5 days. Horizon 5 days on a grid of 20 steps. Loss limit 0.8 million. The values are illustrative, not fitted to a real asset.
models.dependence: The log-return X is a VG Lévy process with stationary and independent increments. The position value is V0 exp(X_T). The model has no volatility clustering, so the risk does not depend on the recent returns.
models.method: Exact sampling at the grid times: gamma time steps, then normal increments on the gamma clock. The estimators are fractions and means over replicates. The mean log-return has the exact reference θT = 0.001.
models.diagnostics: Reference value: ret = 0.001. Compare the breach probability with a Brownian model of the same variance: the Brownian model gives a smaller value. Other candidate models: a GARCH model with volatility clustering, a normal inverse Gaussian process, or a jump-diffusion model.
models.interpretation: A position of 10 million keeps the breach probability near 0.003, and a position of 15 million breaks the limit of 0.01 in this illustration. The expected gain grows with the size, so the constraint decides. Reject the model if the returns show volatility clustering, or if the tails are heavier than the VG fit.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative VG parameters of a log-return and illustrative position sizes. Illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: How large can an equity position be for a 5-day loss limit?
problem: A fund holds one equity position for 5 trading days. The log-return has jumps and heavy tails. Choose the largest position with a small chance of a loss above the limit.
param V0 = 10 {million currency units} "position size"
param L = 0.8 {million currency units} "loss limit"
param theta = 0.0002 "drift θ of the log-return for each day"
param sigma = 0.012 "volatility σ for each day"
param nu = 1.5 {days} "variance rate ν"
X ~ variancegamma(x0 = 0, theta = theta, sigma = sigma, nu = nu, T = 5, steps = 20) {log-return}
loss := V0 * (1 - exp(last(X)))
prob breach = loss > L "loss above the limit"
mean ret = last(X) "E X_T = θT"
mean gain = V0 * (exp(last(X)) - 1) {million currency units} "expected gain"
alt "Position 5": V0 = 5
alt "Position 10": V0 = 10
alt "Position 15": V0 = 15
alt "Position 20": V0 = 20
maximise gain
require breach <= 0.01
initial: X_0 = 0, the log-return at the start
dynamics: X_t = θ G_t + σ W(G_t), with G a gamma process of mean t and variance ν t (t in days)
focus loss

models.title: How much of a foreign-currency receipt should a firm hedge?
models.decision: Decision: sell 0 %, 50 % or 100 % of a 10-million foreign-currency receipt forward for 90 days. Estimated quantity: the probability that the proceeds are below the budget of 11.4 million home units, and the expected proceeds.
models.reason: Exchange rates move with sudden jumps after news, and their returns have heavy tails. A VG process for the log rate gives these jumps with few parameters. The forward contract fixes the rate for the hedged part.
models.inputs: Spot rate 1.2 and forward rate 1.195 home units for each foreign unit. Log-rate parameters for each day: θ = 0, σ = 0.006, ν = 5 days. Receipt 10 million foreign units, budget 11.4 million home units. All values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The log rate change X is a VG Lévy process with stationary and independent increments. The rate in 90 days is S0 exp(X_T). The proceeds are h N F + (1 − h) N S0 exp(X_T). The model has no interest rates and no credit risk of the forward.
models.method: Exact sampling of the VG process at 90 daily grid times. The estimators are fractions and means over replicates. The mean log rate change has the exact reference θT = 0.
models.diagnostics: Reference value: drift = 0. Compare the shortfall probability with a Brownian model of the same variance. Other candidate models: a GARCH model, a regime-switching model, or the empirical distribution of 90-day rate changes.
models.interpretation: Without a hedge, the shortfall probability is near 0.18, above the limit of 0.05. A 50 % hedge gives about 0.04 and keeps most of the expected proceeds, so it is the choice in this illustration. A full hedge removes the shortfall but gives the lowest expected proceeds. Reject the model if the rate shows a trend or volatility clusters over the period.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative spot and forward rates and illustrative VG parameters of an exchange rate. Illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: How much of a foreign-currency receipt should a firm hedge?
problem: A firm will receive 10 million units of a foreign currency in 90 days. The log exchange rate moves with jumps. Choose the hedge ratio with a forward contract.
param h = 0.5 "fraction sold forward"
param N = 10 {million foreign units} "amount to receive"
param S0 = 1.2 {home units per foreign unit} "spot rate today"
param F = 1.195 {home units per foreign unit} "forward rate for 90 days"
param budget = 11.4 {million home units} "budget value of the receipt"
param theta = 0 "drift θ of the log rate for each day"
param sigma = 0.006 "volatility σ for each day"
param nu = 5 {days} "variance rate ν"
X ~ variancegamma(x0 = 0, theta = theta, sigma = sigma, nu = nu, T = 90, steps = 90) {log rate change}
proceeds := h * N * F + (1 - h) * N * S0 * exp(last(X))
prob short = proceeds < budget "proceeds below the budget"
mean value = proceeds {million home units} "expected proceeds"
mean drift = last(X) "E X_T = θT"
alt "No hedge": h = 0
alt "Hedge 50 %": h = 0.5
alt "Hedge 100 %": h = 1
maximise value
require short <= 0.05
initial: X_0 = 0, the spot rate S0 today
dynamics: S_t = S0 exp(X_t), X_t = θ G_t + σ W(G_t), with G a gamma process of mean t and variance ν t (t in days)
focus proceeds

models.title: Which stop-loss level limits the trading loss best?
models.decision: Decision: set the stop-loss at a log-return of −2 %, −4 %, −6 % or −8 %, checked at each daily close for 20 days. Estimated quantity: the probability of a log-return below −8 %, the probability of a gap through the stop, and the mean log-return.
models.reason: A stop-loss sells at the first daily close below the stop level. A price with jumps can move from above the stop to far below it in one step. The VG process has jumps, so it shows this gap risk, which a continuous model does not show.
models.inputs: Log-return parameters for each day: θ = 0.0005, σ = 0.015, ν = 2 days. The rule checks the position at 20 daily closes. All values are illustrative.
models.dependence: The log-return X is a VG Lévy process with stationary and independent increments. The exit value is X at the first grid time with X ≤ −b, or X_T if no such time exists. The model sells at the close and has no transaction costs.
models.method: Exact sampling of the VG process at the 20 daily closes. The function first() finds the exit day. The estimators are fractions and means over replicates. The mean log-return without a stop has the exact reference θT = 0.01.
models.diagnostics: Reference value: ret = 0.01. The grid values are exact, but the model does not see the path between two closes. This matches a rule that checks only at the close. Other candidate models: a jump-diffusion model, or a model with intraday checks.
models.interpretation: A tight stop gives a small probability of a large loss, but it sells often and lowers the mean log-return. The stop at 6 % keeps the probability of a log-return below −8 % under 0.05 with the largest mean of the allowed levels in this illustration. Reject the model if the returns show volatility clustering or momentum after a fall.

data.text: Synthetic: illustrative VG parameters of a daily log-return and illustrative stop levels. Illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

models.dsl:
title: Which stop-loss level limits the trading loss best?
problem: A trader holds a position for 20 days and checks it at the end of each day. A stop-loss closes the position at the first daily close below −b. Jumps can make the loss larger than b. Choose b.
param b = 0.04 "stop-loss level for the log-return"
param theta = 0.0005 "drift θ for each day"
param sigma = 0.015 "volatility σ for each day"
param nu = 2 {days} "variance rate ν"
X ~ variancegamma(x0 = 0, theta = theta, sigma = sigma, nu = nu, T = 20, steps = 20) {log-return}
hit := first(X <= -b)
pnl := if(hit > 0, X[max(hit, 1)], last(X))
prob stopped = hit > 0 "the stop-loss closes the position"
prob gap = pnl < -1.5 * b "exit loss larger than 1.5 b (a gap through the stop)"
prob big = pnl < -0.08 "log-return below −8 %"
mean ret = last(X) "E X_T = θT without a stop"
mean result = pnl "mean log-return with the stop"
alt "Stop at 2 %": b = 0.02
alt "Stop at 4 %": b = 0.04
alt "Stop at 6 %": b = 0.06
alt "Stop at 8 %": b = 0.08
maximise result
require big <= 0.05
initial: X_0 = 0 at the open of the position
dynamics: X_t = θ G_t + σ W(G_t), with G a gamma process of mean t and variance ν t; the stop reads X at the daily closes only
focus pnl

methods.name: Independent sampling
methods.estimatorText: The sample mean of the quantity over n independent replicates. For an event, it is the fraction of replicates with the event. Each value comes from the reference sampler of its law, which the law card names.
assumptions: The sampler of each law draws exactly from that law, up to floating-point round-off. A sampler labelled approximate (a tabulated custom law, say) adds a numerical error that the interval does not include.
Replicates use different streams, so they are independent.
E|g(X)| < ∞ for consistency, and Var g(X) < ∞ for the CLT interval.
settings: Sample size n, a power of 2.
Seed, an integer from 0 to 2^32 − 1.
Each law uses its reference sampler, which the law panel names.

suitable.text: The quantities of the flight workflow have bounds, and their probabilities are not small. 65,536 replicates give intervals much narrower than the differences between the alternatives.

failure.text: For the zeta law with s = 1.8, E[X] is infinite. The sample mean tends to ∞, so it has no finite limit, and no number of replicates gives a valid estimate of a mean.

comparison.text: Both methods draw from the same law. The inverse transform maps one uniform to one value by a monotone function. Thus the alternatives with the same streams stay closely coupled, and the paired differences usually have a smaller variance.

methods.name: Inverse transform
methods.estimatorText: Each value is the quantile function at one uniform. The estimator of the quantity is the same sample mean.
assumptions: U is uniform on (0, 1), with 53 random bits.
The page computes F with an error much smaller than the Monte Carlo error.
The search reaches the whole support: a cut table loses the tail.
settings: A CDF table with binary search for a support of at most 65,536 points.
A sequential search from the mode for the binomial, Poisson, negative binomial and hypergeometric laws.
For the zeta law, a table to rank 4,096, then bisection on the survival function with the Hurwitz zeta function.

suitable.text: The geometric law has a closed-form inverse: X = ⌊log U / log(1 − p)⌋. This equals F⁻¹(1 − U), which has the same law as F⁻¹(U). 1 uniform gives 1 value at a fixed cost.

failure.text: A table that stops at the 0.99 quantile returns the last table value for every U above 0.99. The estimate of P(N > 10) is then 0, although the true value is about 0.002.

comparison.text: The inverse transform uses 1 uniform for each value. The rejection method uses a random number of uniforms, with mean 2M. Thus the inverse transform costs less here. Also, the same uniform gives the same value in each alternative, which keeps the alternatives coupled.

methods.name: Rejection sampling
methods.estimatorText: Each accepted proposal is one value of the target law. The estimator of the quantity is the same sample mean. The acceptance rate estimates 1/M.
assumptions: p(k) ≤ M q(k) for every k: the envelope M q dominates the target p.
The proposal and the acceptance uniform are independent.
M is finite. The page refuses the method when 1/M < 0.001.
settings: Finite support: the uniform proposal on the support, with M = (number of points) × max p.
Poisson and negative binomial laws: a geometric proposal, with M at the maximum of p/q.
Geometric law: a geometric proposal with success probability p/2, M = 2.
Zeta law: the Pareto proposal of Devroye, with acceptance probability above 1/2.

suitable.text: The zeta law has no closed-form inverse, and a CDF table cannot hold its long tail. The Pareto proposal of Devroye covers the whole tail and accepts more than half of the proposals.

failure.text: With the envelope constant halved, the envelope no longer covers the target. The accepted values then follow min(p, Mq) after normalisation, not p. The page counts the proposals where p/(Mq) > 1.

comparison.text: Both methods are exact. Rejection costs about 2M uniforms for each value, against 1 for the inverse transform. Compare the time for each replicate in the comparison table.

methods.name: Stratification
methods.estimatorText: The page divides the first uniform of one variable into K equal intervals, the strata, and draws n/K replicates in each stratum. Each stratum has the probability 1/K, so the mean of the stratum means is unbiased. The variance uses only the spread inside each stratum, so the part of the variance that the strata explain disappears.
assumptions: The stratum probabilities are exact: each stratum is an interval of length 1/K of the uniform, so its probability is 1/K.
The stratified variable uses the inverse transform, so a stratum of U is an interval between two quantiles of the variable.
Each stratum holds at least 2 replicates, for its variance. Each block of 1,024 replicates holds 1024/K ≥ 16 in each stratum.
With this proportional allocation the variance is never larger than the variance of independent sampling: (1/n) Σ w_k σ_k² ≤ σ²/n.
settings: The number of strata K = 2^s, with s from 1 to 6.
The stratified variable: the focus variable, or a scalar variable that the reader selects.
Every variable uses the inverse transform and the common streams.

suitable.text: The height √(1 − U²), whose mean is the area, is a smooth and monotone function of the one uniform U. With 16 strata the variance ratio against independent sampling is about 75: one stratified replicate gives the precision of about 75 independent ones.

failure.text: The stack has 3 lengths, and length A gives only about 6 % of the variance of the stack. Thus 16 strata of A give a variance ratio of about 1.01 for the misfit probability. Stratification removes only the variance that the stratified input explains. Select C, which gives 89 % of the variance, to see a ratio of about 7.6 for the mean slack.

comparison.text: Both methods use n replicates. Independent sampling gives the variance σ²/n. Stratification gives (1/n) Σ w_k σ_k², with σ_k² the variance inside stratum k. The comparison table shows both variances and their ratio.

methods.name: Antithetic variables
methods.estimator: \hat\theta_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{j=1}^{m} \frac{g(X_j) + g(X_j')}{2}, \quad X_j = F^{-1}(U_j), \ X_j' = F^{-1}(1 - U_j), \quad m = \frac{n}{2}
methods.estimatorText: Each pair of replicates uses the uniforms U and 1 − U for every draw, through the inverse transform. The estimator is the mean of the m = n/2 pair means. The interval uses the variance of the pair means, because the pairs are independent of each other.
assumptions: Each draw uses the inverse transform, a non-decreasing function of its uniform.
The variance of the estimate is (σ²/n)(1 + ρ), with ρ the correlation inside a pair. It is smaller than with independent sampling only when ρ < 0.
If g is monotone in each uniform, then ρ ≤ 0 by the association inequality of independent variables. For one uniform it is Chebyshev's inequality. An even function of a symmetric input gives ρ = 1.
settings: The pairs are the replicates 2j and 2j + 1 of each block.
Every variable uses the inverse transform. The second member of a pair takes the complement of every 32-bit random number, so its uniform is exactly 1 − U.

suitable.text: The payout min(max(L − d, 0), cap) increases with the claim size L. So a large claim and its antithetic small claim pull the pair mean towards the mean. The variance ratio of the mean payout is about 14 for the contract with deductible 500. It is about 5 and 3 for the other two contracts.

failure.text: The event |X − μ| > 2σ and the squared deviation (X − μ)² are even functions of X − μ. The antithetic partner of X is 2μ − X, which gives the same value. Thus ρ = 1, and the variance ratio is 0.5: a pair costs 2 evaluations for the information of 1. The one-sided event X > μ + σ still gains, with a ratio of about 1.23.

comparison.text: Both methods evaluate the model n times. The comparison table shows the variance of each estimate. The ratio of the two variances is 1/(1 + ρ).

methods.name: Control variates
methods.estimatorText: C is a control: an expression of the model with a mean μ_C that the page knows exactly. The estimator corrects the sample mean of the quantity by β̂ times the error of the sample mean of C. The interval uses the residual variance of the regression of Y on C.
assumptions: μ_C is exact. The page computes it by linearity of expectation from the laws of the variables in C.
Var C is finite and positive, and Var Y is finite.
The variance of the estimate is about (σ²/n)(1 − ρ²), with ρ the correlation of Y and C. Thus the gain is about 1/(1 − ρ²).
β̂ comes from the same replicates. This gives a bias of order 1/n, which is very small at the sample sizes of this page.
settings: The control is a line of the model text: control C = expression.
The expression is an affine function of its terms. Each term is a variable with constant parameters, a component of a vector law, or sum() or mean() of a repeated variable.
Every variable uses its reference sampler.

suitable.text: The profit of a bakery is a function of the demand D, and the page knows E[D] = 400 exactly. With the control C = D, the variance ratio of the mean profit is about 4 for 400 loaves and 17 for 480 loaves. These gains occur because the profit and D have a high correlation.

failure.text: The estimator uses the control mean 408 instead of 400: 0.1 standard deviation too high. Each estimate of the profit then moves 12 to 20 currency units above its reference, more than 40 standard errors at 65,536 replicates. More replicates make the interval narrower, but they do not correct the estimate.

comparison.text: Both methods use the same replicates. The comparison table shows the variance of each estimate. Their ratio is about 1/(1 − ρ²).

methods.name: Common random numbers
methods.estimatorText: Each alternative uses the same streams for the same variable in the same replicate. The estimate of a difference between two alternatives is the mean of the paired differences. Its variance is smaller than with separate streams when the outputs of the two alternatives have a positive covariance.
assumptions: The page synchronises the streams: one stream for each replicate and each variable, the same in each alternative.
The two outputs have a positive covariance. Outputs that move in the same direction with the inputs give it. With the inverse transform, each value is a monotone function of its uniform.
With separate streams the alternatives are independent, and the variance is (σ_a² + σ_b²)/n.
settings: Alternatives use: common random numbers (the default for every method) or separate streams.
The decision report shows each paired difference with the variance ratio (se_a² + se_b²)/se_d².

suitable.text: The wait at each line is the headway times the same uniform U. So a rider who waits long for one line also waits long for the others. The paired differences of the mean time then have variance ratios of 2.2 to 8.5 against independent alternatives.

failure.text: The profit of the cold-drinks stall increases with the temperature T, and the profit of the hot-drinks stall decreases. With the same T for both stalls their covariance is negative. The paired difference then has a larger variance than with separate streams: the variance ratio is about 0.51, a loss.

comparison.text: Independent sampling with separate streams draws each alternative from its own streams. The paired differences then have the variance (σ_a² + σ_b²)/n, and the ratio in the decision report is near 1.

methods.name: Euler time discretisation
methods.estimator: \hat X_{k+1} = \hat X_k + a(\hat X_k)\, h + b(\hat X_k)\, \Delta W_k, \quad \Delta W_k \sim N(0, h); \qquad \hat\theta_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f\left(\hat X^{(i)}\right), \quad \mathbb{E}\hat\theta_n - \theta = O(h)
methods.estimatorText: On each step of length h, the scheme freezes the drift and the volatility of a diffusion. For a point process, it freezes the intensity. The estimator is the sample mean of the quantity of the discrete path. Its error has two parts: the discretisation bias, which does not decrease with n, and the Monte Carlo error, of order n^(−1/2).
assumptions: The coefficients a and b are Lipschitz and grow at most linearly. Then the Euler–Maruyama scheme has strong order 1/2 and, for a smooth f, weak order 1.
The step h satisfies the stability condition of the scheme. For the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, |1 − κh| < 1, so 0 < κh < 2.
The scheme keeps the state space only when the step allows it. The Euler step of geometric Brownian motion can give a value below 0.
Some laws have an exact transition on the grid: Brownian motion, a Markov chain, a branching process and the variance-gamma process. Under this method, such a law uses its exact sampler.
settings: Diffusions: Euler–Maruyama with the normal increments of the exact sampler, so the comparison with independent sampling uses the same Brownian path.
Poisson and compound Poisson processes: at most one event in each step, with probability λh.
Hawkes process: Poisson(λ(t_k)h) events in each step with the intensity frozen at the start of the step.
With coarsen = c, the coarse path adds the fine increments in groups of c. This gives the coupled coarse path of multilevel Monte Carlo.

suitable.text: The payoff of the option is a Lipschitz function of the value at T. The Euler bias of its mean is of order h, and with a few hundred steps it is below the Monte Carlo error. The multilevel panel then lowers the cost to reach a given root mean square error.

failure.text: With κh ≥ 2 the Euler scheme multiplies the distance to θ by 1 − κh ≤ −1 in each step, so its paths oscillate and grow. The exact process is stable and stationary. The exact transition does not have this condition.

comparison.text: Independent sampling uses the exact lognormal transition on the same normals. The difference of the two estimates is the discretisation bias of the Euler scheme, because both use the same Brownian increments. The Monte Carlo error of each estimate does not include it.

methods.name: Multilevel Monte Carlo
methods.estimatorText: Level l estimates the correction E[P_l − P_(l−1)] between the grids of n0 · 2^l and n0 · 2^(l−1) steps. The two paths use the same Brownian increments. The sum of the level means is an unbiased estimate of E P_L. The levels are independent, so its variance is Σ V_l/N_l. The bias E P_L − E P remains, and the page estimates it apart from the Monte Carlo error.
assumptions: Each level couples its coarse and fine paths: the coarse path adds the fine Brownian increments in pairs (coarsen = 2).
The weak error decays as |E[P_l − P]| ≤ c 2^(−αl). The level variance decays as V_l ≤ c 2^(−βl), with α ≥ min(β, γ)/2 (Giles, 2015, theorem 1).
The levels use independent streams: level l takes the seed of the run plus (l + 1) · 2654435769.
The bias estimate max(|Y_(L−1)|/2^α, |Y_L|)/(2^α − 1) assumes that the decay of the level means has started. It is an estimate, not a bound.
settings: The target for the root mean square error is ε. The sample sizes are N_l = ⌈2 ε^(−2) √(V_l/C_l) Σ √(V_j C_j)⌉, in whole blocks of 1,024.
The run starts with levels 0, 1 and 2, with 2 blocks each. It adds one level while the bias test max(|Y_(L−1)|/2^α, |Y_L|) < (2^α − 1) ε/√2 fails, up to level 8.
The model declares the parameters steps (n0, the steps of level 0) and coarsen, and passes them to its diffusion.

suitable.text: The payoff is Lipschitz, so the Euler level variance decays as 2^(−l) (β = 1) and the means as 2^(−l) (α = 1). The cost for an error ε is then of order ε^(−2)(log ε)^2, against ε^(−3) for plain Monte Carlo on the finest grid.

failure.text: The indicator that the path reaches a level is a discontinuous function of the path. A fine and a coarse path disagree with a probability of order 2^(−l/2). Thus V_l decays only as 2^(−l/2) (β = 1/2), and the monitoring bias also decays as 2^(−l/2). The multilevel run needs many levels and gives a small gain.

comparison.text: The panel compares the cost of the multilevel run with the cost of plain Euler sampling on the finest grid. For the same Monte Carlo variance, the plain run needs N V_L/(Σ V_l/N_l) samples of n0 · 2^L steps each.

theory.title: The strong law of large numbers
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} X_1, X_2, \dots \ \text{i.i.d.}, \quad \mathbb{E}|X_1| < \infty \\ \Longrightarrow \ \bar X_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \to \mathbb{E} X_1 \ \text{almost surely} \end{gathered}
assumptions: The X_i have the same law.
The X_i are pairwise independent (Etemadi). Full independence is the classical condition.
theory.proof: Truncate: Y_k = X_k 1{|X_k| ≤ k}. Integrability gives Σ P(X_k ≠ Y_k) < ∞, so X_k = Y_k for all large k (Borel–Cantelli). Chebyshev's inequality on a geometric subsequence n_j = ⌊α^j⌋ with α > 1 gives almost sure convergence of the truncated means. For X ≥ 0, monotonicity covers the indices between the n_j. Then split X = X⁺ − X⁻.
theory.reference: R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Cambridge University Press, 2019, Theorem 2.4.1. N. Etemadi, An elementary proof of the strong law of large numbers, Z. Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie verw. Gebiete 55 (1981) 119–122.
theory.counterexample: The zeta law with s = 1.8 has E[X] = ∞. Then X̄_n → ∞ almost surely, so no finite limit exists.

theory.title: The central limit theorem and the CLT interval
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} X_i \ \text{i.i.d.}, \quad 0 < \sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var} X_1 < \infty \\ \Longrightarrow \ \frac{\sqrt{n}\,(\bar X_n - \mu)}{\sigma} \Rightarrow N(0, 1) \end{gathered}
assumptions: The X_i are i.i.d.
The variance σ² is finite and positive.
The coverage 0.95 of the interval X̄_n ± 1.96 s_n/√n is a limit as n → ∞. A bound for a given n needs more, for example E|X|³ < ∞ (Berry–Esseen).
theory.proof: Let φ be the characteristic function of X_1 − μ. Then φ(u) = 1 − σ²u²/2 + o(u²), and the characteristic function of the normalised sum is φ(t/(σ√n))^n. Its limit is e^(−t²/2). Lévy's continuity theorem gives convergence in law. Slutsky's lemma replaces σ by s_n.
theory.reference: R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., 2019, Theorem 3.4.1. B. V. Gnedenko and A. N. Kolmogorov, Limit Distributions for Sums of Independent Random Variables, Addison-Wesley, 1954.
theory.counterexample: The zeta law with s = 2.5 has a finite mean and an infinite variance. Then (S_n − nμ)/n^(2/3) converges in law to a stable law with index 1.5, not to a normal law. Thus the CLT interval has no coverage guarantee. The block coverage in the diagnostics shows the effect in a run.

theory.title: Consistency of the estimator and exactness of rejection
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \mathbb{E}|g(X)| < \infty \ \Rightarrow \ \mathbb{E}\hat\theta_n = \theta, \ \hat\theta_n \to \theta \ \text{a.s.} \\ p \le M q \ \Rightarrow \ Y \mid \text{accept} \sim p \end{gathered}
assumptions: Each replicate draws exactly from the model law.
For rejection: p and q each sum to 1, and p(k) ≤ M q(k) for every k. The acceptance uniform is independent of the proposal.
theory.proof: Unbiasedness follows from the linearity of expectation, and consistency from the strong law. For rejection, P(accept, Y = k) = q(k) p(k)/(M q(k)) = p(k)/M. The sum over k gives P(accept) = 1/M. Divide to get P(Y = k | accept) = p(k).
theory.reference: L. Devroye, Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation, Springer, 1986, chapter II. S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation: Algorithms and Analysis, Springer, 2007, chapter II.
theory.counterexample: If M is too small, the accepted values follow min(p, Mq) after normalisation, not p. The estimator is then consistent for the wrong quantity.

theory.title: Monte Carlo error and the zero-hit bound
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Var}\hat\theta_n = \frac{\sigma_g^2}{n} \\ 0 \ \text{hits in} \ n \ \Rightarrow \ p \le 1 - \alpha^{1/n} \ \text{at confidence} \ 1 - \alpha, \quad 1 - 0.05^{1/n} \approx \frac{3}{n} \end{gathered}
assumptions: The replicates are independent.
σ_g² = Var g(X) is finite for Var θ̂_n = σ_g²/n.
For the zero-hit bound, each replicate shows the event independently with the same probability p.
theory.proof: The variance of a sum of independent terms is the sum of their variances, so Var θ̂_n = σ_g²/n for any dimension of X. For the bound: P(0 hits) = (1 − p)^n, which is at most α if and only if p ≥ 1 − α^(1/n). Thus a test at level α rejects every p above the bound.
theory.reference: S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation, 2007, chapter III. J. A. Hanley and A. Lippman-Hand, If nothing goes wrong, is everything all right? JAMA 249 (1983) 1743–1745.
theory.counterexample: If replicates reuse 16 streams, the draws repeat and are not independent. The formula s/√n then understates the error by a factor near √(n/16), and the intervals cover the reference less often.

theory.title: Variance reduction: when each method lowers the variance
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Var}\hat\theta_{\mathrm{st}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k w_k \sigma_k^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_k w_k (\mu_k - \mu)^2 \\ \operatorname{Var}\hat\theta_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}(1 + \rho), \quad \rho \le 0 \ \text{if} \ g \ \text{is monotone} \\ \min_{\beta} \operatorname{Var}(Y - \beta C) = \sigma_Y^2 \left(1 - \rho_{YC}^2\right) \\ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y^{(a)} - Y^{(b)}\right) = \sigma_a^2 + \sigma_b^2 - 2\operatorname{Cov}\left(Y^{(a)}, Y^{(b)}\right) \end{gathered}
assumptions: Stratification: the allocation n_k = w_k n is proportional to the exact stratum probabilities w_k.
Antithetic variables: X = F⁻¹(U) and X' = F⁻¹(1 − U), and g is non-decreasing or non-increasing in each uniform.
Control variates: 0 < Var C < ∞, Var Y < ∞, and μ_C is exact.
Common random numbers: the same uniforms drive both alternatives. The gain needs a positive covariance of the outputs.
theory.proof: Stratification: the law of total variance splits σ² into the mean of the variances inside the strata and the variance of the stratum means. Proportional allocation removes the second part. Antithetic pairs: Var((Y + Y')/2) = (σ²/2)(1 + ρ) for one pair. If g is monotone, then one of g(U) and g(1 − U) increases with U and the other decreases. So their covariance is at most 0 (Chebyshev's association inequality). Control variates: Var(Y − βC) = σ_Y² − 2β Cov(Y, C) + β² Var C is smallest at β* = Cov(Y, C)/Var C, with the value σ_Y²(1 − ρ²). Common random numbers: the variance of a difference follows from the bilinearity of the covariance.
theory.reference: S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation: Algorithms and Analysis, Springer, 2007, chapter V. P. Glasserman, Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering, Springer, 2004, chapter 4. A. B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, 2013, chapters 8 and 10.
theory.counterexample: Let g be an even function of a symmetric input, such as (X − μ)² for a normal X. Then g(X') = g(X) for the antithetic partner X' = 2μ − X. Thus ρ = 1, and the pairs double the variance for the same number of evaluations.

theory.title: Regular variation and subexponentiality
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \bar F(x) = x^{-\alpha}\ell(x), \ \ \frac{\ell(tx)}{\ell(x)} \to 1 \ (x \to \infty) \ \text{for every} \ t > 0 \ \ \Longrightarrow \\ \mathbb{P}(X_1 + \dots + X_n > x) \sim n\,\bar F(x) \sim \mathbb{P}\left(\max_{i \le n} X_i > x\right) \ \ (x \to \infty) \end{gathered}
assumptions: X_1, …, X_n are nonnegative and i.i.d. with the law F, for a fixed n.
The tail is regularly varying with an index α > 0: F̄(x) = x^(−α) ℓ(x) with ℓ slowly varying. Then F is subexponential.
A subexponential law has P(X_1 + X_2 > x) ~ 2 F̄(x), by definition. It includes the lognormal law and the Weibull law with k < 1, which are not regularly varying.
theory.proof: The lower bound: {max X_i > x} ⊂ {S_n > x} when the X_i are positive, and P(max X_i > x) = 1 − F(x)^n ~ n F̄(x). The upper bound for n = 2: if X_1 + X_2 > x, then X_1 > (1 − ε)x, or X_2 > (1 − ε)x, or both are above εx. The first two events have probability at most 2 F̄((1 − ε)x) ~ 2(1 − ε)^(−α) F̄(x). The third has probability F̄(εx)², which is o(F̄(x)). Let ε → 0. Induction on n gives the general case.
theory.reference: P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance, Springer, 1997, section 1.3 and appendix A3. N. H. Bingham, C. M. Goldie and J. L. Teugels, Regular Variation, Cambridge University Press, 1987.
theory.counterexample: For the standard exponential law, P(X_1 + X_2 > x) = (1 + x) e^(−x), so the ratio to 2 P(X > x) is (1 + x)/2 → ∞. A large sum of light-tailed values comes from many moderate values, not from one large value.

theory.title: Extreme-value limits and domains of attraction
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}\left(\frac{M_n - b_n}{a_n} \le x\right) = F(a_n x + b_n)^n \to G(x) \ \text{non-degenerate} \ \Longrightarrow \\ G(x) = \exp\left(-(1 + \xi x)^{-1/\xi}\right), \ 1 + \xi x > 0, \ \text{for some} \ \xi \in \mathbb{R} \end{gathered}
assumptions: M_n is the maximum of n i.i.d. values with the law F, and a_n > 0 and b_n are constants.
G is non-degenerate: it is not a point mass. Then G is a GEV law, up to a change of location and scale (Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko).

Domains of attraction: ξ > 0 if and only if F̄ is regularly varying with index 1/ξ. ξ < 0 if and only if the end point x_F is finite and F̄(x_F − 1/x) is regularly varying with index −1/ξ. ξ = 0 holds for laws such as the normal, exponential, Gompertz and lognormal laws.
theory.proof: Max-stability: let F^n(a_n x + b_n) → G. Then for each k, the maximum of k blocks of n values gives G^k(α_k x + β_k) = G(x). By the convergence of types (Khinchine), G is max-stable. Take logarithms: −log G is a positive decreasing function that satisfies a Cauchy-type functional equation. Its only solutions are (1 + ξx)^(−1/ξ) and e^(−x) (the case ξ = 0).
theory.reference: P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance, Springer, 1997, theorems 3.2.3 and 3.3.7. L. de Haan and A. Ferreira, Extreme Value Theory: An Introduction, Springer, 2006, theorem 1.1.3. S. Coles, An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values, Springer, 2001, chapter 3.
theory.counterexample: The Poisson law is in no domain of attraction. P(X = k)/P(X ≥ k) does not tend to 0, so no constants a_n and b_n give a non-degenerate limit of its maxima. The geometric law has the same problem. A discrete law needs this jump condition before the theorem can apply.

theory.title: Threshold exceedances, maxima and sums
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} F \in \mathrm{MDA}(G_\xi) \iff \lim_{u \to x_F} \ \sup_{0 < y < x_F - u} \left| \mathbb{P}(X - u \le y \mid X > u) - H_{\xi, \sigma(u)}(y) \right| = 0 \\ H_{\xi,\sigma}(y) = 1 - (1 + \xi y/\sigma)^{-1/\xi}, \qquad \text{for } X \sim H_{\xi,\sigma}: \ \mathbb{E}[X - u \mid X > u] = \frac{\sigma + \xi u}{1 - \xi} \ (\xi < 1) \end{gathered}
assumptions: X has the law F with the upper end point x_F, which can be ∞.
F is in the maximum domain of attraction of the GEV law G_ξ, for a suitable function σ(u) > 0 (Pickands–Balkema–de Haan).
The GPD H_ξ,σ is threshold stable: its excess over u is GPD with the same ξ and the scale σ + ξu. Thus its mean excess is linear in u for ξ < 1.
theory.proof: Take logarithms of F^n(a_n x + b_n) → G_ξ(x): n F̄(a_n x + b_n) → (1 + ξx)^(−1/ξ). Divide the value at x + y by the value at x. Put u = a_n x + b_n. Then F̄(u + a_n y)/F̄(u) → (1 + ξy/(1 + ξx))^(−1/ξ). This is the GPD survival function with the scale σ(u) = a_n(1 + ξx). Monotonicity of F̄ makes the convergence uniform in y.
theory.reference: A. A. Balkema and L. de Haan, Residual life time at great age, Annals of Probability 2 (1974) 792–804. J. Pickands, Statistical inference using extreme order statistics, Annals of Statistics 3 (1975) 119–131. P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance, Springer, 1997, theorem 3.4.13.
theory.counterexample: The theorem is a limit. At a fixed threshold the excess law of the lognormal law is not a GPD law. The lognormal law is in the domain ξ = 0, but its mean excess still increases with u. Thus a fit at a practical threshold often shows an apparent ξ > 0. The Poisson law, which is in no domain of attraction, has no GPD limit at all.

theory.title: Ergodicity, mixing, and time and ensemble averages
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} (X_n) \text{ irreducible, positive recurrent with stationary law } \pi: \quad \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(X_k) \to \sum_x \pi(x) f(x) \ \text{a.s. for every } X_0 \\ \text{and, if also aperiodic:} \quad \lVert P^n(x, \cdot) - \pi \rVert_{TV} \to 0 \end{gathered}
assumptions: The chain is irreducible: each state reaches each other state.
It is positive recurrent. A finite irreducible chain always is. Then the stationary law π is unique.
f has a finite mean under π. The convergence of the law Pⁿ(x, ·) needs aperiodicity. The convergence of the time average does not.
For a general stationary process, Birkhoff's theorem gives the limit E[f | invariant σ-field] of the time average. This limit equals the ensemble average when the process is ergodic.
theory.proof: Split the path at the returns to a state x. The excursions between returns are i.i.d. (strong Markov property), and positive recurrence gives them a finite mean length E_x τ_x = 1/π(x). The strong law of large numbers applies to the sums of f over the excursions and to their lengths. The ratio of the two sums gives Σ π f. For the law, couple two copies of the chain, one started from π, until they meet at a time T. Aperiodicity and irreducibility make T finite, and ‖Pⁿ(x, ·) − π‖_TV ≤ P(T > n).
theory.reference: J. R. Norris, Markov Chains, Cambridge University Press, 1997, theorems 1.8.3 and 1.10.2. D. A. Levin and Y. Peres, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, 2nd ed., American Mathematical Society, 2017, chapter 4. G. D. Birkhoff, Proof of the ergodic theorem, PNAS 17 (1931) 656–660.
theory.counterexample: Geometric Brownian motion is not stationary. Let μ < σ²/2. Then (log S_t)/t → μ − σ²/2 < 0 almost surely, so almost every path tends to 0. But when μ > 0, the ensemble average E S_t = S_0 e^(μt) grows. The mean of many paths and the long-run growth of one path differ. A reducible chain with two closed classes also has a time average that depends on X_0.

theory.title: Sklar's theorem and copulas
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} F(x_1, \dots, x_d) = C\left(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d)\right) \text{ for a copula } C, \text{ unique on } \operatorname{Ran} F_1 \times \dots \times \operatorname{Ran} F_d \\ U \sim C, \ X_j = F_j^{-1}(U_j) \ \Longrightarrow \ X \sim F, \qquad \tau, \ \lambda_U, \ \lambda_L \text{ depend on } C \text{ only} \end{gathered}
assumptions: F is a d-dimensional CDF with the margins F_1, …, F_d.
A copula is a CDF on [0, 1]^d with uniform margins.
C is unique when every margin is continuous. A discrete margin leaves C free outside the range of the margins, so discrete data do not identify their copula.
λ_U = lim_{q→1} P(U_2 > q | U_1 > q) and λ_L = lim_{q→0} P(U_2 ≤ q | U_1 ≤ q), where the limits exist.
theory.proof: For continuous margins, U_j = F_j(X_j) is uniform, and C is the CDF of U. Then F(x) = P(U_j ≤ F_j(x_j) for all j) = C(F_1(x_1), …). Conversely, F_j^(−1)(U_j) ≤ x_j if and only if U_j ≤ F_j(x_j), so the quantile transform of U ~ C has the CDF C(F_1, …, F_d). Kendall's tau and the tail coefficients are invariant under strictly increasing maps of the components, so they depend only on C. For discrete margins, extend F by interpolation to a continuous CDF on the range.
theory.reference: A. Sklar, Fonctions de répartition à n dimensions et leurs marges, Publ. Inst. Statist. Univ. Paris 8 (1959) 229–231. R. B. Nelsen, An Introduction to Copulas, 2nd ed., Springer, 2006, theorems 2.10.9 and 5.1.9. A. J. McNeil, R. Frey and P. Embrechts, Quantitative Risk Management, revised ed., Princeton University Press, 2015, chapter 7.
theory.counterexample: The Gaussian and the Student t copula with the same correlation ρ = 0.5 have the same Kendall's tau, (2/π) arcsin ρ = 1/3. But λ_U = 0 for the Gaussian copula, and λ_U is about 0.25 for the t copula with ν = 4. The same margins and the same tau thus give different probabilities of joint extremes.

theory.title: Multilevel Monte Carlo and discretisation bias
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} |\mathbb{E}[P_l - P]| \le c_1 2^{-\alpha l}, \ V_l \le c_2 2^{-\beta l}, \ C_l \le c_3 2^{\gamma l}, \ \alpha \ge \tfrac12 \min(\beta, \gamma) \\ \Longrightarrow \ \exists L, N_l: \ \mathbb{E}\left[(\hat\theta - \mathbb{E}P)^2\right] < \varepsilon^2 \ \text{with cost} \ \le c_4 \begin{cases} \varepsilon^{-2} & \beta > \gamma \\ \varepsilon^{-2} (\log \varepsilon)^2 & \beta = \gamma \\ \varepsilon^{-2 - (\gamma - \beta)/\alpha} & \beta < \gamma \end{cases} \end{gathered}
assumptions: P_l is the quantity on the grid of level l, and P is its limit. The correction Y_l = P_l − P_(l−1) uses P_l and P_(l−1) on the same Brownian path.
The rates α, β and γ hold for every level. For the Euler–Maruyama scheme and a Lipschitz payoff, α = β = γ = 1.
The levels are independent, so the variance of the estimator is Σ V_l/N_l.
The mean square error is the sum of the Monte Carlo variance and the squared bias: E[(θ̂ − EP)²] = Σ V_l/N_l + (E P_L − E P)².
theory.proof: Choose L with c_1 2^(−αL) ≤ ε/√2, so the squared bias is at most ε²/2. Minimise the cost Σ N_l C_l under the constraint Σ V_l/N_l ≤ ε²/2 with a Lagrange multiplier: N_l ∝ √(V_l/C_l). The cost is then 2ε^(−2)(Σ √(V_l C_l))². The sum Σ 2^((γ−β)l/2) stays bounded when β > γ, grows as L when β = γ, and grows as 2^((γ−β)L/2) when β < γ. With L ≈ log2(1/ε)/α this gives the three cases.
theory.reference: M. B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo path simulation, Operations Research 56 (2008) 607–617. M. B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, theorem 1. P. E. Kloeden and E. Platen, Numerical Solution of Stochastic Differential Equations, Springer, 1992, chapters 10 and 14.
theory.counterexample: Take the indicator that Brownian motion reaches a level, checked only at the grid times. A fine and a coarse path disagree with a probability of order 2^(−l/2), so β = 1/2 < γ = 1. The cost then grows as ε^(−3) up to a log factor, near the cost of plain Monte Carlo. The interval of a plain run on one grid also says nothing about its bias: a smaller interval does not reduce the monitoring bias.

theory.title: Large deviations and the rate function
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \Lambda(\theta) = \log \mathbb E\, e^{\theta X_1}, \quad I(a) = \sup_{\theta} \left(\theta a - \Lambda(\theta)\right) \\ \Longrightarrow \ \frac{1}{n}\log \mathbb P(S_n \ge na) \to -I(a) \ \text{and} \ \mathbb P(S_n \ge na) \le e^{-n I(a)} \ \text{for } a > \mathbb E X_1 \end{gathered}
assumptions: X_1, X_2, … are i.i.d. real random variables, and S_n = X_1 + … + X_n.
Λ(θ) < ∞ for θ in a neighbourhood of 0, and a is inside the range of Λ'. The upper bound (Chernoff) holds for every n.
For exponential jumps with mean μ, I(a) = a/μ − 1 − log(a/μ) and θ* = 1/μ − 1/a. Bahadur and Rao refine the limit: P(S_n ≥ na) ~ e^(−nI(a)) / (θ* σ_a √(2πn)).
theory.proof: Upper bound: for θ ≥ 0, Markov's inequality gives P(S_n ≥ na) ≤ E e^(θS_n) e^(−θna) = e^(−n(θa − Λ(θ))). Take the best θ. Lower bound: change the measure to the tilted law dF_θ* = e^(θ*x − Λ(θ*)) dF, under which the mean is a. Then P(S_n ≥ na) = E_θ*[e^(−θ*S_n + nΛ(θ*)); S_n ≥ na]. Under the tilted law, S_n stays within √n of na with a probability bounded below (CLT). This gives the rate −I(a).
theory.reference: A. Dembo and O. Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, theorem 2.2.3. R. R. Bahadur and R. Ranga Rao, Ann. Math. Statist. 31 (1960) 1015–1027.
theory.counterexample: For Pareto II jumps, Λ(θ) = ∞ for every θ > 0, so I(a) = 0 above the mean. P(S_n > na) then decays as a power of n, about n P(X > n(a − μ)), not exponentially. The Chernoff bound gives only the value 1.

theory.title: Change of measure and exponential tilting
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \mathbb E_f\!\left[h(X)\right] = \mathbb E_g\!\left[h(X)\,\frac{f(X)}{g(X)}\right] \ \text{when } g > 0 \text{ wherever } h f \ne 0; \\ \operatorname{Var}_g = \mathbb E_g\!\left[h^2 \tfrac{f^2}{g^2}\right] - \left(\mathbb E_f h\right)^2, \quad g^* = \frac{|h| f}{\mathbb E_f |h|} \ \text{has zero variance for } h \ge 0 \end{gathered}
assumptions: The proposal g is positive wherever h f is not zero: then the weighted estimator has no bias.
The variance is finite only if E_g[h² f²/g²] < ∞. A proposal with a lighter tail than f can make it infinite.

An exponential tilt dF_θ = e^(θx − Λ(θ)) dF exists only when Λ(θ) < ∞. For the tail of a sum it is logarithmically efficient: the second moment decays at twice the rate of p (Sadowsky and Bucklew, 1990).
theory.proof: The identity is ∫ h f = ∫ h (f/g) g on the set where g > 0. This set contains every point where h f ≠ 0. The zero-variance law follows from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: E_g[h² f²/g²] ≥ (E_f |h|)², with equality when g ∝ |h| f. For the tail of a sum, the tilt θ* makes the weight e^(nΛ(θ*) − θ*S_n) at most e^(−nI(a)) on the event. Thus the second moment is at most e^(−2nI(a)).
theory.reference: S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation: Algorithms and Analysis, Springer, 2007, chapter VI. J. S. Sadowsky and J. A. Bucklew, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 36 (1990) 579–588. D. Siegmund, Ann. Statist. 4 (1976) 673–684.
theory.counterexample: For Pareto II claims, an exponential proposal with any mean gives f/g → ∞ as x → ∞, and E_g[f²/g²; S > b] = ∞. The estimator has no bias, but its variance is infinite. Most replications give a value below p, and a few replications give very large values.

theory.title: Ruin theory: the Cramér–Lundberg model
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} U(t) = u + ct - \sum_{i=1}^{N(t)} X_i, \quad \psi(u) = \mathbb P\!\left(\inf_{t \ge 0} U(t) < 0\right), \quad \lambda\left(\mathbb E e^{RX} - 1\right) = cR \\ \Longrightarrow \ \psi(u) \le e^{-Ru} \ \text{(Lundberg)}, \qquad \psi(u) \sim C e^{-Ru} \ \text{(Cramér)}, \qquad \psi(u) = \rho\, e^{-(1-\rho)u/\mu} \ \text{for exponential } X \text{ with mean } \mu \end{gathered}
assumptions: The claims arrive as a Poisson process with rate λ, and their sizes X_i are i.i.d., positive and independent of the arrivals.
The net profit condition ρ = λ E X / c < 1 holds. Else ψ(u) = 1 for every u.
The equation λ(E e^(RX) − 1) = cR has a positive root R, the adjustment coefficient. This needs E e^(θX) < ∞ for some θ > 0, but that alone is not enough. No root exists for heavy-tailed claims.
theory.proof: The process e^(−R U(t)) is a martingale when λ(E e^(RX) − 1) = cR. At the time of ruin τ, U(τ) < 0. The optional stopping theorem then gives e^(−Ru) = E[e^(−RU(τ)); τ < ∞] ≥ P(τ < ∞), which is the Lundberg inequality. Under the measure tilted by R, ruin is certain, and ψ(u) = e^(−Ru) E_R[e^(−Rξ)] with the overshoot ξ. The renewal theorem gives the constant C. For exponential claims, the overshoot is exponential, and this gives the exact formula.
theory.reference: S. Asmussen and H. Albrecher, Ruin Probabilities, 2nd ed., World Scientific, 2010, chapters I and IV. D. Siegmund, Ann. Statist. 4 (1976) 673–684.
theory.counterexample: With Pareto II claims (α = 2.5), E e^(θX) = ∞ for every θ > 0, so no R exists and no exponential bound holds: ψ(u) decays as u^(−1.5). Double the capital, and the ruin probability falls by a factor of about 2.8, not by a factor that grows exponentially in u.

theory.title: The Pollaczek–Khinchine formula and subexponential ruin
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \psi(u) = (1-\rho)\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \rho^k\, \overline{F_I^{*k}}(u), \qquad F_I(x) = \frac{1}{\mu}\int_0^x \bar F(y)\,dy \\ F_I \ \text{subexponential} \ \Longrightarrow \ \psi(u) \sim \frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\,\bar F_I(u) \quad (u \to \infty) \end{gathered}
assumptions: The Cramér–Lundberg model with ρ = λμ/c < 1 and a finite mean claim μ.

The integrated-tail law F_I is the law of a ladder height. A ladder height is the amount by which the maximum of the claim surplus grows at a new record. For Pareto II claims with index α, F_I is Pareto II with index α − 1.
The asymptotic needs F_I subexponential (Embrechts and Veraverbeke, 1982). It is a limit as u → ∞, not a bound at a given u.
theory.proof: The maximum M of the claim surplus is the sum of its ladder heights. A new record occurs with probability ρ. Each record adds an independent ladder height with law F_I (Wiener–Hopf factorisation). Thus M is a geometric sum, and ψ(u) = P(M > u). For a subexponential F_I, P(Y_1 + … + Y_k > u) ~ k F̄_I(u). Dominated convergence (Kesten's bound) then gives Σ (1 − ρ) ρ^k k F̄_I(u) = ρ/(1 − ρ) F̄_I(u).
theory.reference: P. Embrechts and N. Veraverbeke, Insurance Math. Econom. 1 (1982) 55–72. P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events, Springer, 1997, section 1.4. S. Asmussen and D. P. Kroese, Adv. Appl. Probab. 38 (2006) 545–558.
theory.counterexample: For exponential claims, F_I is exponential, which is not subexponential. Then ψ(u) = ρ e^(−(1−ρ)u/μ), while ρ/(1 − ρ) F̄_I(u) = ρ/(1 − ρ) e^(−u/μ): the two differ by a factor that grows exponentially in u.

theory.title: Dependence in extremes
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \lambda_U = \lim_{q \to 1} \mathbb P\!\left(U_2 > q \mid U_1 > q\right) \\ \text{Gaussian copula, } |r| < 1: \ \lambda_U = 0; \qquad \text{Gumbel copula, } \theta \ge 1: \ \lambda_U = 2 - 2^{1/\theta}, \quad \tau = 1 - 1/\theta \end{gathered}
assumptions: (U_1, U_2) has uniform margins and the copula C, so P(U_1 > q, U_2 > q) = 1 − 2q + C(q, q).
The limit exists. λ_U depends on the copula only, not on the margins.

Kendall's τ and the linear correlation summarise the dependence over the whole law. τ depends only on the copula, but the correlation also depends on the margins. λ_U measures only the joint extremes.
theory.proof: For the Gumbel copula, C(q, q) = exp(−(2(−log q)^θ)^(1/θ)) = q^(2^(1/θ)). Then (1 − 2q + q^(2^(1/θ)))/(1 − q) → 2 − 2^(1/θ) as q → 1, by l'Hôpital's rule. For the Gaussian copula, P(Z_2 > z | Z_1 > z) → 0 as z → ∞ when |r| < 1 (Sibuya, 1960). The reason is that Z_2 given Z_1 = z is normal with mean rz, and rz grows more slowly than z.
theory.reference: A. J. McNeil, R. Frey and P. Embrechts, Quantitative Risk Management, revised ed., Princeton University Press, 2015, section 7.2.4. M. Sibuya, Ann. Inst. Statist. Math. 11 (1960) 195–210.
theory.counterexample: The Gaussian and the Gumbel copulas with τ = 0.5 have the same Kendall's τ. But λ_U = 0 for the Gaussian copula and 2 − √2 = 0.59 for the Gumbel copula. In the catastrophe test, the common event loss also makes the insurers lose together. Thus the copula of the shares changes the probability of a systemic ruin less than λ_U suggests. A tail coefficient of one part of a model is not a property of the whole model.

theory.title: Tail sensitivity and ruin, in an explicit model
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} X \sim \text{Pareto II}(\sigma, \alpha): \quad \operatorname{VaR}_q = \sigma\left((1-q)^{-1/\alpha} - 1\right), \quad \operatorname{ES}_q = \frac{\alpha \operatorname{VaR}_q + \sigma}{\alpha - 1} \ (\alpha > 1), \quad \operatorname{ES}_q = \infty \ (\alpha \le 1) \\ \frac{\partial \log \operatorname{ES}_q}{\partial \alpha} \to -\infty \ \text{as } \alpha \downarrow 1; \qquad \mathbb P(\text{ruin within } k \text{ periods}) = 1 - (1-p)^k \to 1 \end{gathered}
assumptions: The loss has a Pareto II law with a known tail index α, and the periods are independent with the same ruin probability p > 0.
The value at risk and the expected shortfall are at the level q. ES_q = E[X | X > VaR_q] is finite only when E X is finite.
Taleb's arguments about fat tails and ruin are interpretations. The page states only the facts of this model, and it does not present an interpretation as a theorem.
theory.proof: For the Pareto II law, P(X > x) = (1 + x/σ)^(−α), which inverts to VaR_q. Given X > v, X − v is Pareto II with scale σ + v and the same α, so E[X − v | X > v] = (σ + v)/(α − 1), which gives ES_q. Thus log ES_q = log(α VaR_q + σ) − log(α − 1). The first term has a bounded derivative near α = 1, and the derivative of −log(α − 1) is −1/(α − 1), which tends to −∞ as α ↓ 1. The probability of no ruin in k independent periods is (1 − p)^k, which tends to 0 for any p > 0.
theory.reference: P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events, Springer, 1997, chapter 6. N. N. Taleb, Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails, STEM Academic Press, 2020 (the interpretation). A. J. McNeil, R. Frey and P. Embrechts, Quantitative Risk Management, 2015, section 2.3.
theory.counterexample: A sample mean of Pareto II losses with α = 0.9 is always finite, but E X = ∞. Thus a finite sample gives a finite ES estimate for a law whose ES is infinite. In the opposite direction, a truncation at a largest possible loss makes every moment finite, but no finite sample can show where the truncation is.

theory.title: Ergodic averages and the Markov chain CLT
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} P \text{ Harris ergodic with } \pi P = \pi, \ \pi|g| < \infty \ \Longrightarrow \ \bar g_n = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^{n} g(X_i) \to \pi(g) \ \text{a.s., from any start} \\ \text{geometric ergodicity}, \ \pi|g|^{2+\delta} < \infty \ \Longrightarrow \ \sqrt n\,(\bar g_n - \pi g) \Rightarrow N(0, \sigma_g^2), \quad \sigma_g^2 = \operatorname{Var}_\pi g \Bigl(1 + 2\sum_{k \ge 1} \rho_k\Bigr) = \operatorname{Var}_\pi g \cdot \tau, \quad \mathrm{ESS} = n / \tau \end{gathered}
assumptions: The kernel P keeps π stationary. Metropolis–Hastings and each coordinate update of the Gibbs sweep satisfy detailed balance, so the sweep keeps π stationary. In Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, the leapfrog map with a momentum flip keeps volume and is its own inverse. With the Metropolis step, the chain keeps π stationary.
The chain is φ-irreducible, aperiodic and Harris recurrent, so it is Harris ergodic.
For the central limit theorem: geometric ergodicity and π|g|^(2+δ) < ∞ for some δ > 0, or a reversible chain with π g² < ∞ and a finite asymptotic variance.
theory.proof: For the ergodic theorem, Nummelin's splitting gives regeneration times. The sums of g between regenerations are i.i.d., and the strong law of large numbers applies to them. For the central limit theorem, solve the Poisson equation ĝ − Pĝ = g − π g. Then the sum of g(X_i) − π g is a martingale plus the remainder ĝ(X₀) − ĝ(X_n), which is small compared with √n. The martingale central limit theorem applies. The variance of the martingale increments is Var_π g (1 + 2 Σ ρ_k).
theory.reference: G. O. Roberts and J. S. Rosenthal, General state space Markov chains and MCMC algorithms, Probability Surveys 1 (2004) 20–71. G. L. Jones, On the Markov chain central limit theorem, Probability Surveys 1 (2004) 299–320. C. J. Geyer, Practical Markov chain Monte Carlo, Statistical Science 7 (1992) 473–483. A. Vehtari, A. Gelman, D. Simpson, B. Carpenter and P.-C. Bürkner, Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: an improved R-hat, Bayesian Analysis 16 (2021) 667–718.
theory.counterexample: A random walk on two modes 11 units apart is ergodic, so the theorem holds. But the expected time to cross between the modes is far longer than any run. Chains that start in one mode agree with each other: split R-hat is near 1 and the ESS is large. But the estimate of P(x₁ + x₂ > 0) is near 0, and the exact value is 0.7. A theorem about n → ∞ says nothing about the n of one run, and the ESS is a diagnostic, not a proof of convergence.

theory.title: Importance weights, resampling and the unbiased likelihood
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \hat Z_T = \prod_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{i=1}^{N} W_{t-1}^i\, g_t(x_t^i), \qquad \mathbb E\,\hat Z_T = p(y_{1:T}) \ \text{for every } N \ge 1 \\ \mathrm{ESS}_t = \Bigl(\sum_i W_t^i\Bigr)^2 \Big/ \sum_i (W_t^i)^2 \in [1, N] \end{gathered}
assumptions: The particles move with the transition law f of the model, and g_t(x) = p(y_t | x_t = x) is the observation density.
The resampling scheme has no bias: given the weights, the expected number of copies of particle i is N W_i. Multinomial, stratified, systematic and residual resampling have this property.

E Ẑ_T = p(y_{1:T}) needs only these conditions. Error bounds for the filter law that do not grow with T need more: bounded potentials g_t and a mixing transition. Then the relative variance of Ẑ_T grows linearly in T.
theory.proof: Let F_t be the history of the particle system up to time t. The resampling has no bias. Thus, given F_(t−1), each new particle comes from the mixture Σ_i W_(t−1)^i f(· | x_(t−1)^i). Thus E[Σ_i W_(t−1)^i g_t(x_t^i) | F_(t−1)] = Σ_i W_(t−1)^i ∫ f(x | x_(t−1)^i) g_t(x) dx. By induction on t, E[Ẑ_t Σ_i W_t^i φ(x_t^i)] = ∫ φ(x) p(x_t = x, y_(1:t)) dx for every bounded φ. Take φ = 1 at t = T. The result is p(y_(1:T)).
theory.reference: P. Del Moral, Feynman–Kac Formulae: Genealogical and Interacting Particle Systems with Applications, Springer, 2004. C. Andrieu, A. Doucet and R. Holenstein, Particle Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 72 (2010) 269–342. A. Kong, J. S. Liu and W. H. Wong, Sequential imputations and Bayesian missing data problems, Journal of the American Statistical Association 89 (1994) 278–288. N. Chopin and O. Papaspiliopoulos, An Introduction to Sequential Monte Carlo, Springer, 2020.
theory.counterexample: Without resampling the estimator is still unbiased, but the variance of the weights grows about exponentially in T. After a few steps, one particle has almost all the weight, and the ESS is near 1. In most runs Ẑ is far below p(y_(1:T)). The mean is right only because rare runs give very large values. Also log Ẑ has a negative bias for every scheme, because log is concave.

theory.title: Randomised quasi-Monte Carlo: no bias and a smaller variance
theory.statement: \begin{gathered} \Bigl|\frac1n \sum_{i} f(u_i) - \int_{[0,1)^d} f\Bigr| \le V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)\, D_n^*(u_1, \dots, u_n) \quad \text{(Koksma–Hlawka)} \\ \text{scrambled } (t, m, d)\text{-net in base 2}, \ n = 2^m: \ \mathbb E \hat I = I, \quad \operatorname{Var} \hat I \le 2^t 3^d \, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}, \quad \operatorname{Var} \hat I = o(1/n) \ \text{for } f \in L^2 \end{gathered}
assumptions: The points are the first 2^m points of a Sobol sequence, a (t, m, d)-net in base 2, with Owen's nested uniform scramble. Owen (2003) shows that Matoušek's random linear scramble with a digital shift, which this page uses, has the same variance.
f is square-integrable on the unit cube. σ² is its variance: the variance of independent sampling with one point.
For smooth f, with the condition that Owen (1997) states, Var Î = O(n^(−3) (log n)^(d−1)). A jump that is not parallel to the axes removes this rate.
theory.proof: Expand f in base-2 Haar wavelets, grouped by the resolution k = (k_1, …, k_d) in each coordinate. The scramble makes each point uniform, so Î has no bias, and it makes the contributions of different groups uncorrelated. Thus Var Î = Σ_k Γ_k σ_k² / n, where σ_k² is the variance of f in group k. The net property gives Γ_k = 0 for groups with |k| ≤ m − t, and Γ_k ≤ 2^t 3^d for all k. The groups with Γ_k ≠ 0 carry a variance that tends to 0, so n Var Î → 0.
theory.reference: A. B. Owen, Monte Carlo variance of scrambled net quadrature, SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 34 (1997) 1884–1910. A. B. Owen, Scrambled net variance for integrals of smooth functions, Annals of Statistics 25 (1997) 1541–1562. J. Matoušek, On the L2-discrepancy for anchored boxes, Journal of Complexity 14 (1998) 527–556. A. B. Owen, Variance with alternative scramblings of digital nets, ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation 13 (2003) 363–378. S. Joe and F. Y. Kuo, Constructing Sobol sequences with better two-dimensional projections, SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 30 (2008) 2635–2654.
theory.counterexample: The indicator that a sum of 8 uniforms is above 5 jumps along a slanted plane, so V_HK = ∞ and the Koksma–Hlawka bound is empty. The scrambled points still have no bias and a smaller variance. But the variance ratio against independent points is about 5, against more than 10,000 for the smooth peak. Without randomisation the points give one deterministic value, and repeated runs cannot estimate its error.

glossary.definition: The probability law of a random variable X: it gives P(X ∈ A) for each set A.
The set of values with positive probability, for a discrete law.
Probability mass function: p(k) = P(X = k).
Cumulative distribution function: F(x) = P(X ≤ x).
F⁻¹(u) = min{x : F(x) ≥ u} for 0 < u < 1.
E[X^r] for an order r. The moment exists when E|X|^r < ∞.
Probability generating function: G(z) = E[z^X].
Moment generating function: M(t) = E[e^(tX)], where it is finite. It need not exist for any t ≠ 0.
Characteristic function: φ(t) = E[e^(itX)]. It exists for every law.
Probability density function: the density f of a continuous law, with P(X ∈ A) = ∫_A f(x) dx.
Independent and identically distributed: the variables are independent and have the same law.
The quantity that a run estimates, such as θ = E[g(X)] or θ = P(A).
A function of the draws that approximates the estimand, such as the sample mean.
One joint sample of all variables of a model, with the quantities computed from it.
The difference θ̂_n − θ that comes from the finite number of replicates.
An interval computed from the replicates. Its nominal coverage is the probability, as the method claims it, that the interval holds the estimand.
The probability that an interval method holds the estimand. A nominal coverage is the value the method claims.
The interval θ̂ ± 1.96 s/√n. Its coverage tends to 0.95 as n → ∞ when the variance is finite.
The score interval for a binomial proportion. It keeps its coverage better than the CLT interval near 0 and 1.
The exact binomial interval from the beta quantiles. Its coverage is at least the nominal value.
After 0 hits in n independent trials, the exact upper bound 1 − α^(1/n) for the probability. For α = 0.05 it is about 3/n.
An approximation of the variance of a smooth function of means by its linear part. The page uses it for a ratio of means.
The estimator of E[A]/E[B] by the ratio of the 2 sample means.
The difference of a quantity between 2 alternatives in the same replicate, with the same streams.
The same streams for each alternative. The differences between alternatives then usually have a smaller variance than with independent streams.
The integer that selects the key of the generator. The same seed and settings give the same run.
A named sequence of random numbers. The page derives each stream from the seed, the stream name, the replicate and the variable.
A generator whose output is a function of a key and a counter, so the page can compute any draw directly. Philox4x32-10 is one.
1,024 consecutive replicates: the unit of work that one worker computes.
A background thread of the browser. Workers compute blocks, so the page stays responsive.
A sampler that returns the quantile function at a uniform value.
A sampler that draws from a proposal law and accepts each proposal with probability p/(Mq).
The law q from which the rejection method takes its candidates, or from which importance sampling draws its paths.
The number M with p ≤ Mq. The acceptance probability is 1/M.
A sampler for a finite law that uses one table lookup and one uniform for each draw (Walker, Vose).
The value of a quantity from enumeration or a closed form, not from the simulation.
A sum over every point of the joint support, weighted by its probability.
The probability of the support points that an enumeration leaves out.
A claim tag: the statement follows from a theorem under the stated assumptions.
A claim tag: a computed value with a stated error source, such as round-off or neglected mass.
A claim tag: a value that one finite run showed. It is not a guarantee about the law.
A tail that decays as a power of k, so that some moments are infinite.
A tail P(X > x) = x^(−α) L(x) with a slowly varying function L.
A count variance larger than the count mean.
P(X ≥ s + t | X ≥ s) = P(X ≥ t) for all s and t. The geometric law has this property.
The factor (N − n)/(N − 1) by which draws without replacement reduce the variance.
A graph with an arrow from each name to each name that reads it.
One choice of the parameter values that a decision can make.
The quantity that a decision makes as small or as large as possible.
A limit that a quantity must meet, such as P(stockout) ≤ 0.05.
Maximum likelihood estimate: the parameter value that makes the observed data most probable.
A test that compares observed counts with expected counts through Σ (O − E)²/E.
Law of large numbers: for i.i.d. variables with E|X| < ∞, the sample mean converges to E[X] almost surely.
Central limit theorem: for i.i.d. variables with 0 < σ² < ∞, the normalised sample mean converges in law to the standard normal law.
The fraction of blocks whose own interval holds the reference value. It checks the interval method on this run.
A choice that breaks one assumption of a method on purpose, to show the effect on the result.
ζ(s, a) = Σ_{k ≥ 0} (a + k)^(−s) for s > 1. The zeta law has P(X > k) = ζ(s, k + 1)/ζ(s).
