Simplified Technical English, a controlled language for technical text.
One random value of one variable.
One Bernoulli or categorical experiment, such as one throw of a die.
The variable whose law the distribution plot shows.
The method that draws each value with the reference sampler of its law. All 3 methods of this group give independent replicates.
The exact sampler that a law uses for independent sampling, such as the alias method for the categorical law.
A draw of n items one at a time without replacement, as from an urn.
A verdict of the decision report. The interval of a quantity or of a paired difference still includes the limit or 0, so the run cannot decide yet.
A test or an interval from replicates of a fitted model, with the estimate in place of the unknown parameter.
A law that keeps its form under sums of i.i.d. copies, up to location and scale. The normal law is the stable law with index 2.
For i.i.d. cycles, the long-run reward for each unit of time is E[reward of a cycle]/E[length of a cycle].
A reliability model in which a fraction of the faults are common causes that stop all redundant units at once.
The ratio of the variance of an estimate under a complex survey design to its variance under a simple random sample.
A function L with L(tx)/L(x) → 1 as x → ∞ for every t > 0, such as a constant or log x.
Division of the sample space into strata with known probabilities, with a fixed number of replicates in each stratum.
One part of a stratification. Here: an interval of length 1/K of the first uniform of the stratified variable.
Pairs of replicates that use U and 1 − U for every uniform. Thus a large value and a small value fall in the same pair.
An expression C of the model with a known mean μ_C. The estimator subtracts β̂(C̄ − μ_C) from the sample mean of the quantity.
The variance of independent sampling over the variance of a variance-reduction design, for the same number of model evaluations. A ratio above 1 is a gain.
Each alternative draws from its own streams, so the alternatives are independent of each other.
A numerical integral that divides the interval where its error estimate is largest. The page uses the Gauss–Kronrod rules with 7 and 15 points.
The value x with P(X > x) = v. For a small v it keeps more precision than the quantile function at 1 − v.
The lower triangular matrix L with LLᵀ = Σ. Then μ + LZ has the covariance Σ for a vector Z of independent N(0, 1) values.
The set of vectors of k proportions that are 0 or more and have the sum 1.
The parameter ν of the chi-square law, Student's t law and the F law. For the variance of a sample of n values, ν = n − 1.
A prior law whose posterior after the data is in the same family. The beta law is the conjugate prior of a binomial success probability.
X = μ + sY: the location μ moves the law, and the scale s stretches it.

A tail that decreases at least as fast as an exponential function: P(X > x) ≤ C e^(−tx) for some t > 0. Then the MGF is finite near 0 and every moment is finite. Examples: the normal, exponential and gamma laws.
Two uniforms U₁ and U₂ give the standard normal value √(−2 log U₁) cos(2πU₂).
log(p/(1 − p)): the inverse of the CDF of the standard logistic law.
Program Evaluation and Review Technique: a method to plan projects. It gives a task duration a beta law from a minimum, a most likely and a maximum duration.
Generalised extreme value law: the law of a normalised maximum, with a shape ξ, a location μ and a scale σ. It includes the Fréchet (ξ > 0), Gumbel (ξ = 0) and reverse Weibull (ξ < 0) types.
Generalised Pareto law: the law of the excess X − u over a high threshold u, with a shape ξ and a scale σ.
A law on [0, ∞) with P(X₁ + X₂ > x) ~ 2 P(X > x) as x → ∞: a large sum comes from one large value. Regularly varying, lognormal and Weibull laws with k < 1 are subexponential.
The set of laws F whose normalised maxima (M_n − b_n)/a_n converge to one GEV law.
A property of a law G: the maximum of n independent G values has the law G again, after a change of location and scale. The GEV laws are the max-stable laws.
The largest value in a block of observations, such as the largest daily rainfall of a year.
The value z_T that the annual maximum passes with probability 1/T in each year.
T in years, for the return level z_T: the mean number of years between two exceedances of z_T, if the annual maxima are independent and have the same law.
An observation above a fixed high threshold u. Its excess is X − u.
E[X − u | X > u], the mean of the excess over the threshold u. For a GPD with ξ < 1 it is linear in u.
α in P(X > x) = x^(−α) ℓ(x) for a regularly varying tail. Moments of order r exist only for r < α.
The shape ξ of the GEV and GPD laws. For a regularly varying tail with the tail index α, ξ = 1/α.
An estimate of the extreme-value index from the k largest values. It is the mean of log(X_(n−i+1)/X_(n−k)) for i = 1 … k.
h(t) = f(t)/P(T > t): the rate of failure at the time t among the units that last to t.
The least or the greatest value of a support, such as the upper end point μ − σ/ξ of a GEV law with ξ < 0.
An observation mechanism that hides the exact value: right censoring shows only that T > C, and left censoring only that T < C.
An estimate of P(T > t) from censored times. It is the product of 1 − d_i/n_i over the event times t_i ≤ t, with d_i events among n_i units at risk.
LOD, the least concentration that a laboratory method can tell apart from 0. A value below it has left censoring.
Limit of detection: see detection limit.
Nolan's parameters (α, β, γ, δ) of a stable law: X = γZ + δ with Z standard. The density is a continuous function of all four parameters, also at α = 1.
An exact sampler of the stable laws from one uniform angle and one exponential value (1976).
The survival function P(X > x) against x on log–log axes. For large x, a regularly varying tail is close to a straight line of slope −α.
Each ordered observation against the quantile of a fitted law at its plotting position. Points near the diagonal agree with the fit.
Twice the difference of the maximised log-likelihoods of two nested models. For one extra parameter it has approximately the χ²(1) law in large samples when the smaller model is true.
The standard deviation of an estimator. Here it comes from the inverse of the observed information of the log-likelihood.
The behaviour of a subexponential law: a sum passes a high level because one value passes it, not because many values are large.
A law that draws a component j with probability w_j, then a value from the law of that component. The data do not show the component.
One of the laws of a finite mixture, with its weight and its parameters.
A mixture of a point mass at 0 and a count law, for data with more zeros than the count law gives.
The law of S = Y_1 + … + Y_N, with a Poisson number N of i.i.d. terms Y_i that are independent of N.
A recursion that computes P(S = s) of a compound Poisson sum with integer terms from the smaller values, with no enumeration of N.
The discrete law that gives each observed value its fraction of the data, or of the weights.
The law with the density that a kernel density estimate gives: the data values, each spread by a kernel. Here the kernel is normal with standard deviation h.
The scale h of the kernel of a kernel density model. A small h follows the data closely, and a large h smooths it.
The law of X conditioned on lower ≤ X ≤ upper. The values outside the interval do not occur and leave no record.
A law that one line of the model text defines by an expression. The input is a PDF, a log-PDF, an unnormalised density, a PMF, a finite table, a CDF, a quantile function, an MGF or a CF.
A function g ≥ 0 with a finite positive integral Z. The density is g/Z, and the page computes Z by quadrature.
The logarithm of a density. It avoids the overflow or underflow of the density itself far from the mode.
The condition that a law has total mass 1: ∫f = 1, Σp = 1, F(∞) = 1, M(0) = 1 or φ(0) = 1.
A check status: the page tested the condition by the method it states, on a grid or by a sum, and the condition held there. It is evidence, not a proof.
A check status: the page found a value where the condition does not hold. The page does not use a law with a failed check in a run.
A check status: the page has no test that decides the condition here, or its test did not settle.

A sampler that draws from a numerical approximation of the law, such as a tabulated CDF. The page states its approximation controls and error sources. The interval of an estimate does not include this error.
A sampler that draws from the law itself, up to floating-point round-off.
The inversion F(x) = 1/2 − (1/π) ∫_0^∞ Im[e^(−itx) φ(t)]/t dt of a CF at a point of continuity of F.
A quadrature rule that integrates a quadratic through 3 points of each cell. Its error falls as the fourth power of the cell width for a smooth integrand.
The largest difference between the empirical CDF of observations and the CDF of a law. Its p-value is asymptotic and assumes a continuous law.
Resampling from the empirical law of the data to estimate the variability of a statistic. Group 10 states its conditions.
A sequence of random states in which the law of the next state depends only on the present state, not on the earlier states.
The matrix P of a finite Markov chain: P_ij is the probability of a step from state i to state j. Each row adds to 1.
A law π of the states with π P = π: if the chain starts with the law π, it has the law π at each later time.
A set of states that communicate with each other and that a path cannot leave after it enters.
A state i with P_ii = 1: a path that enters it stays there for all later times.
An irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain on a finite state space: its law converges to the unique stationary law from each start, and its time averages converge to the stationary averages.
A Markov chain with states that do not all communicate. With two or more closed classes, its long-run behaviour depends on the start.
The average of a function of the state along one path, such as the fraction of time in state j.
The average over many independent paths at one fixed time, such as P(X_n = j).
The first number of steps n after which the TV distance between the law of X_n and the stationary law is at most 1/4, for the worst start.
Total variation distance: the largest difference of the probabilities that two laws give to one event; for discrete laws, half the sum of |p_j − q_j|.
A branching process in discrete generations: each individual has an independent random number of offspring with one fixed law.
The law of the number of offspring of one individual in a branching process.
The probability that a branching process reaches 0. For one ancestor it is the smallest root of f(s) = s in [0, 1], with f the PGF of the offspring law.
The mean number of new cases that one case causes, the mean m of the offspring law in a branching model of an epidemic.
Large differences between cases in the number of new cases: most cases cause few or none, and a few cause many. A small dispersion k of a negative binomial law models it.
The parameter k of a negative binomial law with mean m: the variance is m + m²/k, and k → ∞ gives the Poisson law.
Variance gamma: a Lévy process that is a Brownian motion with drift run on a gamma-process clock.
A process that starts at 0 with stationary and independent increments and paths that are continuous from the right.
A Lévy process with gamma-distributed increments; it only increases, and it has infinitely many small jumps.
E[(X − μ)⁴]/σ⁴. It is 3 for a normal law; a larger value shows heavier tails. The excess kurtosis is the kurtosis minus 3.
The fraction of the exposure that a lender loses when the borrower defaults.
An agreement to buy or sell an amount at a fixed rate on a future date.
A rule that closes a position when its value falls below a fixed level.
A joint law on [0, 1]^d whose margins are all uniform. It describes the dependence of a random vector without its margins.

Every joint CDF F with margins F_i can be written F(x) = C(F_1(x_1), …, F_d(x_d)) with a copula C. C is unique when the margins are continuous. Conversely, X_i = F_i⁻¹(U_i) with U from C has the margins F_i.
The limit λ_U = lim P(U_2 > q | U_1 > q) as q → 1, and λ_L = lim P(U_2 ≤ q | U_1 ≤ q) as q → 0. A positive value means that extremes come together.
The probability P(U_1 > q, U_2 > q) that both components exceed the level q. Divided by 1 − q, it gives P(U_2 > q | U_1 > q).
The probability that each component of a random vector falls in a given interval. For a copula it follows from the CDF at the corners of the box by inclusion and exclusion.
The probability of concordance minus the probability of discordance of two independent copies of a pair. It depends only on the copula.
The correlation of the ranks F_1(X_1) and F_2(X_2), equal to 12 E[U_1 U_2] − 3 for the copula pair.
The copula of an elliptical law, such as the multivariate normal or t law. The Gaussian and t copulas are elliptical.
A copula C(u) = ψ(ψ⁻¹(u_1) + … + ψ⁻¹(u_d)) with a generator ψ. Clayton, Gumbel and Frank copulas are Archimedean.
The decreasing function ψ with ψ(0) = 1 and ψ(∞) = 0 that defines an Archimedean copula. It must be d-monotone for dimension d.
A function ψ with (−1)^k ψ^(k) ≥ 0 for k ≤ d − 2, and with (−1)^(d−2) ψ^(d−2) non-increasing and convex. An Archimedean generator gives a copula in dimension d if and only if it is d-monotone.
A positive random variable V shared by all components. In the Marshall–Olkin algorithm the generator ψ is the Laplace transform of V.
The sampler U_i = ψ(E_i/V) of an Archimedean copula, with a frailty V whose Laplace transform is ψ and independent standard exponentials E_i. It is exact.
A sampler that draws U_1 and then each next component from its conditional law given the earlier ones, by the inverse transform.
The copula of U_1 = U_2 = … = U_d, the upper Fréchet–Hoeffding bound min(u_1, …, u_d).
The copula of U_2 = 1 − U_1 in two dimensions, the lower Fréchet–Hoeffding bound max(u_1 + u_2 − 1, 0).
D_1(x) = (1/x) ∫_0^x t/(e^t − 1) dt. It gives Kendall's tau of the Frank copula.
A copula with C(u_1^t, …, u_d^t) = C(u_1, …, u_d)^t for all t > 0. It is the copula of the limit law of componentwise maxima.
The limit λ_U = lim P(U_2 > q | U_1 > q) as q → 1 (upper), or λ_L as q → 0 (lower). λ > 0 means that joint extremes stay likely.
The values of one draw of a process at the grid times: a function of time, not one number.
A process whose time averages converge to the averages under its stationary law, for almost every path.
The first time at which a path reaches a given level. On a grid, the page sees only the grid times.
The difference between a quantity of the path at the grid times and the same quantity of the path in continuous time, such as its maximum.
The difference between the mean of a quantity of a time-discretised path and the mean for the exact process. More samples do not reduce it; a finer grid does.
The time discretisation X_{k+1} = X_k + a(X_k)h + b(X_k)ΔW_k of a stochastic differential equation, with the coefficients frozen on each step.
The rate r with E|X̂_T − X_T| ≤ c h^r: the error of each path. The Euler–Maruyama scheme has strong order 1/2.
The rate r with |E f(X̂_T) − E f(X_T)| ≤ c h^r: the error of a mean. The Euler–Maruyama scheme has weak order 1 for a smooth f.
Multilevel Monte Carlo: a sum of corrections between grids of increasing fineness, each estimated with its own sample size.
Stochastic differential equation: dX_t = a(X_t) dt + b(X_t) dW_t, with W a Brownian motion.
A model that draws a parent variable first and then a child variable whose law has parameters that read the parent value.
A conditional model with several levels, such as an uncertain rate, then a count given the rate.
Var Y = E[Var(Y | X)] + Var(E[Y | X]), when E Y² is finite. The second term is the variance that the parent adds.
Sampling of a conditional model in its order: each variable is drawn after the variables that its parameters read.
The fraction of a population that has a condition at a given time.
The probability that a test is positive for a person with the condition.
The probability that a test is negative for a person without the condition.
The probability that a person with a positive test has the condition.
A process with continuous paths and independent, stationary, normal increments: W_t − W_s ~ N(0, t − s).
Geometric Brownian motion: S_t = S_0 exp((μ − σ²/2)t + σW_t), a positive process with lognormal values.
Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process: dX_t = κ(θ − X_t) dt + σ dW_t, a Gaussian process that reverts to θ.
The first time at which a path reaches a given level.
For a Brownian motion without drift from 0, P(max over [0, t] of W ≥ b) = 2 P(W_t ≥ b) for b ≥ 0.
The property that time averages of one path converge to the ensemble averages of the stationary law.
The tendency of a process to move back to a long-run level, with a speed that grows with the distance to it.
The closed form of E[max(S_T − K, 0)] for a GBM: S_0 e^{μT} Φ(d_1) − K Φ(d_2).
A price model in which the price is a Brownian motion with drift, so it can become negative.
An interest-rate model in which the short rate is an OU process.
For one day, max(18 °C − the daily mean temperature, 0); the sum over a period measures the demand for heating.
The price of power minus the cost of the gas to make it, for each MWh.
A demand by a lender for more collateral when the value of a pledged position falls to a set level.
The loan divided by the value of the collateral.
A counting process with independent increments, in which the count in an interval has a Poisson law with mean equal to the integral of the rate over the interval.
The rate λ(t) of a point process: the probability of an event in [t, t + h] is λ(t)h + o(h), given the past.
Λ(t), the integral of the rate from 0 to t. For a Poisson process it is the mean count E N(t).
A rejection method for point processes. It draws candidate events at a rate λ̄ that is not below the intensity, and keeps each candidate with probability λ(t)/λ̄.
A process that adds i.i.d. jumps at the event times of a Poisson process. It is a Lévy process with finitely many jumps in a finite time.
The surplus model of an insurer: R_t = u + c t − S_t, with initial capital u, premium rate c and compound Poisson claims S_t.
θ = c/(λ E Y) − 1, the relative amount by which the premium rate c is above the mean claim rate. Ruin in infinite time is certain if θ ≤ 0.
The probability that the surplus of an insurer falls below 0. In finite time it is ψ(u, T); in infinite time it is ψ(u).
A reinsurance treaty in which the insurer keeps a fixed fraction q of each claim and of the premium, and cedes the rest.
A self-exciting point process: each event raises the intensity, here by α, and the rise decays at the rate β.
A point process in which each event raises the probability of further events for some time, so the events come in clusters.
n = α/β for a Hawkes process with an exponential kernel: the mean number of direct children of an event. A stationary version exists only if n < 1.
A Hawkes process seen as immigrants at the rate μ, in which each event has a Poisson(n) number of children after random delays.
The variance of a count divided by its mean. It is 1 for a Poisson count and above 1 for a clustered count.
A simulation of a process on a time grid, with the rates or coefficients frozen at the start of each step. Its error goes to 0 as the step goes to 0.
Epidemic-type aftershock sequence: a self-exciting model of earthquakes, in which each event triggers aftershocks with a power-law (Omori) decay and a magnitude-dependent productivity.
A Poisson process with a random rate. Its counts have a variance above the mean.
Susceptible–infected–removed: an epidemic model with a finite population, in which the spread slows as the susceptible part falls.
The data of the guided interview: questions, candidate models and rules. A rule goes from answers to candidates, to an unresolved assumption, or to “insufficient evidence”.
The rules that fired for the current answers, with the answers that fired each rule and the effect of each rule on the candidates.
A law or a model part that the interview proposes. It has a reason, other explanations, rejection tests and sampling methods. It is a hypothesis, not a result.
The result of the interview when the answers do not separate the candidate laws, or when a fact that the decision needs is not known.
A fact that the interview does not know, such as the dependence of the values. The model record assumes a value for it, and the reader must check it.
A test or a plot of data that can show that a candidate law does not fit. When a test does not reject a law, this does not prove the law.
The rate of an event at time t, given no event before t: h(t) = f(t)/S(t).
A value with a positive probability, such as an exact 0 in a law that is otherwise continuous.
An event whose probability is so small that direct simulation needs very many paths to see it often enough for an estimate.
An event in which an average of many variables is far from its mean. Its probability decays exponentially in n at the rate I(a) when the exponential moment exists.
I(a) = sup over θ of (θa − log E e^(θX)): the exponential rate of decay of P(S_n ≥ na) in Cramér's theorem.
For a ≥ E X, the bound P(S_n ≥ na) ≤ exp(−n I(a)). It comes from Markov's inequality applied to e^(θS_n) with θ ≥ 0.
E e^(θX) for some θ > 0. It is finite only when the tail of X decays at least exponentially.
The method draws the paths from a proposal law g, not from the nominal law f. It weights each path by the likelihood ratio f/g, so that the weighted mean has no bias.
The ratio f/g of the nominal density to the proposal density at a path: the weight of the path in importance sampling.
A Monte Carlo method that draws from a proposal law and weights each draw by the likelihood ratio.
The change of measure dF_θ = e^(θx) dF / E e^(θX). It exists only when the exponential moment is finite.
The proposal law with the survival function F̄^r for 0 < r: its hazard rate is r times the nominal hazard rate. With r < 1 the tail is heavier. For an exponential law it is an exponential tilt.
A proposal β f + (1 − β) g that keeps the nominal law f with the weight β, so that every likelihood ratio is at most 1/β.

For a Markov chain, n / τ: the number of independent draws that give the same variance of the mean. For weights w, (Σ w)² / Σ w². In both cases it is a diagnostic, not a proof that an estimate is accurate or that a chain has converged.
Effective sample size: n / τ for a Markov chain, or (Σ w)² / Σ w² for the weights w. A diagnostic, not a proof of convergence.
The standard error of an estimate divided by the estimate.
The square of the relative error times the work. A smaller value shows a more efficient method.
An estimator of p is logarithmically efficient when its second moment decays at least as fast as p^(2 − ε) for every ε > 0, as p → 0.
An estimator has a bounded relative error when its relative error stays bounded as p → 0.
A rare-event method that copies the paths that reach an intermediate level and restarts the copies from there, level by level.
The function h of the state that defines the levels of splitting. A good h orders the states by their probability to reach the event.
Splitting with the same number N of paths in each stage, drawn with replacement from the states that reached the previous level.
A rare-event method that writes the event as a sequence of nested events with conditional probabilities near p0. It samples each one with a Markov chain.

A Markov chain step of subset simulation. It makes one random-walk proposal for each component and accepts it against its own density. Then it accepts the whole move only if the move stays inside the current level set.
A method that fits a proposal law to the paths above levels that rise, by weighted maximum likelihood, until the level reaches the threshold of the rare event.
The paths whose score (the sum, or the importance of the catastrophe test) is at or above the current level γ_t of the cross-entropy method.
Importance sampling that adapts its proposal from the weighted samples of the earlier steps.
Importance sampling of a ruin probability under the measure tilted by the adjustment coefficient, under which ruin is certain.
The positive root R of λ(E e^(RX) − 1) = cR in the Cramér–Lundberg model. It exists only when the claims have an exponential moment.
ψ(u) ≤ e^(−Ru) for the Cramér–Lundberg model with the adjustment coefficient R.
ρ = λ E X / c < 1: the premium income is larger than the mean claim payment for each unit of time.
ψ(u) = (1 − ρ) Σ ρ^k P(Y_1 + … + Y_k > u), with Y_i i.i.d. ladder heights with the integrated-tail law F_I.
The amount by which the maximum of the claim surplus grows at a new record.
F_I(x) = (1/μ) ∫_0^x F̄(y) dy, the law of a ladder height of the Cramér–Lundberg model.
The total claims less the premium income up to time t: ruin occurs when it is above the initial capital.
VaR_q: the smallest x with P(L > x) ≤ 1 − q.
Value at risk: the smallest x with P(L > x) ≤ 1 − q.
ES_q = E[L | L > VaR_q] for a continuous loss. It is infinite when E L is infinite.
Expected shortfall: E[L | L > VaR_q] for a continuous loss.
Reinsurance that pays min((S − d)⁺, ℓ) of each event loss S: the layer ℓ in excess of the retention d.
The part d of each event loss that the insurers keep below a layer.
A sequence of defaults in which each default causes a loss to the other insurers that can cause a further default.
The default of m or more of the K insurers by the horizon T.
A law conditioned to lie below a bound M. A truncated loss has every moment and an exponential moment.
For a subexponential law, a large sum most likely comes from one large term, not by many moderate terms.
π(x) P(x, y) = π(y) P(y, x) for all x and y. A kernel with detailed balance keeps π stationary.
A Markov chain that is φ-irreducible, aperiodic and Harris recurrent: its averages converge almost surely to the expectations under π from every start.
The distance between the law of X_n and π decreases at least as fast as C(x) r^n for some r < 1.
Markov chain Monte Carlo: estimates from the draws of a Markov chain whose stationary law is the target law.
A Markov chain that proposes a move and accepts it with the probability min(1, π(y) q(y, x) / (π(x) q(x, y))). It needs π only up to a constant.
A proposal y = x + h s ⊙ Z with Z standard normal. The step h is in units of the scale s of each coordinate.
The fraction of the proposals that a Metropolis–Hastings or Hamiltonian chain accepts.
A Markov chain that draws each coordinate in turn from its full conditional law.
The law of one coordinate given all the other coordinates.
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo: a Markov chain that follows the Hamiltonian dynamics of −log π with a random momentum, then accepts or rejects the end point.
A numerical integrator of the Hamiltonian dynamics: a half step of the momentum, a full step of the position, a half step of the momentum. It keeps volume and is reversible.
A Hamiltonian proposal whose energy error is above 1,000 or not finite: the leapfrog path became unstable. It is a signal of bias.
The change of the Hamiltonian H along the leapfrog path. The exact dynamics keep H constant.
The first iterations of each chain, which the page discards so that the start point has less effect.
The correlation ρ_k between g(X_i) and g(X_(i+k)) in a stationary chain.
τ = 1 + 2 Σ ρ_k: the factor by which the variance of a chain average exceeds that of an average of independent draws.
The square root of the ratio of the pooled variance to the mean variance within the halves of the chains. A value above 1.01 shows that the chains disagree.
Monte Carlo standard error: the standard deviation of an estimate that comes from the finite run.
An estimate of τ from sums of pairs of autocorrelations, stopped when a pair is negative and made non-increasing.
Sequential Monte Carlo: a population of weighted particles that the method reweights, resamples and moves through a sequence of laws.
A path of laws π_β ∝ q^(1 − β) π^β from a simple law q at β = 0 to the target π at β = 1.
The normalising constant Z = ∫ p(y | θ) p(θ) dθ of a posterior law: the probability of the data under a model.
The ratio Z₁ / Z₀ of the evidence of two models. With prior odds, it gives the posterior odds.
The ratio of the target density to the density that made a particle. A weighted mean of the particles estimates an expectation under the target.
A state in which a few particles have almost all the weight, so the weight ESS is near 1.
A step that replaces the weighted particles by N particles drawn with probabilities equal to their normalised weights. Each new particle has the weight 1/N.
Resampling with one uniform U and the N points (i + U)/N: each particle gets ⌊N W_i⌋ or ⌈N W_i⌉ copies.
Sequential Monte Carlo for a state-space model: the particles follow the dynamics, and the observations weight them.
A hidden Markov process x_t with observations y_t that depend only on x_t.
The exact filter of a linear state-space model with normal noise. The filter law is normal, and the filter updates its mean and its variance at each time.
A filter that computes the filter law on a fixed grid of states. It is a numerical approximation for a model with a state of low dimension.
The ancestral lines of the particles back through the resampling steps.
The ancestral lines of the particles merge into few lines at early times, so the paths share their early states.
The probability of a future event under the model, averaged over the posterior law of the parameters.
A model in which the log odds of a probability are a linear function of the inputs.
Quasi-Monte Carlo: an integral estimate with points that fill the unit cube more evenly than independent points.
Randomised quasi-Monte Carlo: quasi-Monte Carlo points with a randomisation that makes each point uniform. Each estimate then has no bias, and independent randomisations give an interval.
A digital sequence in base 2. Its first 2^m points are a (t, m, d)-net. This page uses the direction numbers of Joe and Kuo.
A set of 2^m points such that each elementary box of volume 2^(t−m) holds exactly 2^t points.
A random permutation of the digits of the points that keeps the net property and makes each point uniform.
The bitwise exclusive or of each point with one random vector of bits.
|error| ≤ V_HK(f) D*_n: the error of an equal-weight rule is at most the variation of f times the star discrepancy of the points.
A construction of a Brownian path that sets the end point first, then the mid-points of each interval. The first coordinates then carry most of the variance.
The number of coordinates that carry most of the variance of an integrand.
An option whose payoff depends on the geometric average of the asset price at fixed dates.

groups.title: Core and discrete laws
groups.content: The 3 panels, the generator and the workers, the expression language and the model record. The expert editor and the examples. The 10 discrete laws, 3 methods to draw samples, the core diagnostics and the exports.

groups.title: Continuous laws and variance reduction
groups.content: Uniform, normal, multivariate normal, exponential, gamma, Erlang, beta, Dirichlet, chi-square, Student's t, F, logistic and Laplace. Stratification, antithetic variables, control variates and common random numbers.

groups.title: Positive, heavy-tailed and extreme-value laws
groups.content: Lognormal, Weibull, inverse Gaussian, Gompertz, log-logistic, Pareto I and II, Burr XII, Fréchet, Cauchy, Lévy and stable laws. The generalised extreme value (GEV), generalised Pareto (GPD), Gumbel and reverse Weibull laws. Censored observations, tail plots and the theory of extremes.

groups.title: Constructed laws and custom inputs
groups.content: Finite mixtures, compound Poisson, empirical and kernel density models, truncated laws, and custom PDF, PMF, CDF, quantile, MGF and characteristic function inputs with their checks.

groups.title: Dependence and processes
groups.content: Conditional models, and the Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel and Frank copulas. Finite-state Markov chains, Brownian motion, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU), Poisson, Hawkes, branching and Lévy processes. Multilevel Monte Carlo.

groups.title: The guided interview
groups.content: A rule graph that asks about the problem and proposes candidate models, each with a reason, other explanations, rejection tests and sampling methods. The reader can switch a rule off or choose another candidate, and the interview can return “insufficient evidence”. It makes the same model record as the editor.

groups.title: Rare events and ruin
groups.content: Valid exponential tilting, splitting, subset simulation, adaptive importance sampling, the cross-entropy method, and the catastrophe and ruin test.

groups.title: Markov chains, sequential and quasi-Monte Carlo
groups.content: Metropolis–Hastings, Gibbs, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, sequential Monte Carlo, particle filters and randomised quasi-Monte Carlo.

groups.title: Critical behaviour
groups.content: An energy landscape, annealing and tempering, a sandpile, finite-size scaling and coarse-graining.

groups.title: Local data and the acceptance gate
groups.content: CSV and JSON import, estimation, bootstrap methods, tail-threshold selection and the final acceptance gate.

measured.how: The page's Measure speed button gave these rates on 5 October 2026 in headless Chromium: about 1.9 million replicates a second with 4 workers for the Poisson experiment, and about 62,000 for the survey workflow with 1,000 draws in each replicate. With the main thread 4 times slower, as on an ordinary laptop, the main thread alone gives 211,000 and 4,300. Thus a run of 2^22 replicates of a light model takes about 10 s on an ordinary laptop, and the time limit pauses a longer run. On 6 October 2026 the same button measured the group 3 models: about 1.1 million replicates a second with the workers for a Pareto experiment, and about 105,000 for the slowest workflow, a censored trial with 100 patients and Kaplan–Meier estimates in each replicate (7,600 on the slowed main thread). Its default size of 2^13 thus takes about 1 s on an ordinary laptop, so the published limits hold. On 6 October 2026 the same button measured the group 5 models in headless Chromium. A Brownian path of 16 steps runs about 1.1 million replicates a second with 4 workers, a Clayton copula 1.4 million, and a t copula 860,000. Paths of 250 steps (a compound Poisson surplus, a Markov chain) run about 105,000 to 124,000 a second with the workers and 10,000 on the slowed main thread. A Brownian path at the limit of 4,096 steps with coarsen = 4 (16,384 draws) runs about 2,000 a second with the workers. So its 2^16 replicates take about 33 s, and a larger run reaches the time limit and pauses. Thus a path has at most 4,096 steps, a replicate at most about 20,000 path and copula draws, and a copula at most 16 dimensions.

rare.how: Measured on 6 October 2026 in headless Chromium with 4 workers: tilting of a sum of 20 claims, 64 replications of 65,536 paths, 0.68 s; direct simulation of the catastrophe test, 16 replications of 16,384 paths, 1.3 s; the cross-entropy method on the catastrophe test, 16 replications of 4,096 paths, 3.9 s; subset simulation of a Pareto II sum, 16 replications of 4,096 paths, 0.21 s. The time of a run grows in proportion to N R, so the largest catastrophe run with the cross-entropy method would take about 4 minutes, and the time limit of 180 s pauses it.

chains.how: Measured on 7 October 2026 in headless Chromium with 4 workers, 32 independent runs each: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on the O-ring model with 2^17 iterations in each chain, 2.7 s with 10 leapfrog steps and 36 s with 200; the sequential sampler with 65,536 particles and 20 moves, 15 s; the particle filter with 16,384 particles over 100 days, 2.4 s; scrambled Sobol points, 2^18 points in 16 dimensions, 1.7 s. An ordinary laptop is about 4 times slower, so the heaviest setting takes about 2.5 minutes, and the time limit of 180 s pauses a longer run.

alerts: Support and moments do not usually identify a unique distribution.
A marginal distribution does not define dependence.

topics.title: Bounds, thresholds, atoms, mixtures and tails

questions.text: What does one value of the quantity measure?
questions.help: The answer sets the support: the set of values that the law can give.

options.label: A count: 0, 1, 2, …
One result with two values: yes or no
One category from a fixed list
Counts in several categories, with a fixed total
A rank, such as the rank of a word by frequency
A waiting time or a lifetime
A proportion or a probability, from 0 to 1
Shares of a whole: proportions with the sum 1
A positive size or amount, such as a loss or a file size
The largest or the smallest value of each period or block
A measurement that can be negative, such as an error or a change
Several measurements together, which can have a correlation

questions.text: Which mechanism makes the count?
questions.help: A mechanism that you know gives the strongest reason for a law.

options.label: Successes in a fixed number n of independent trials, each with the same probability
Successes in n draws without replacement from a finite population
Independent events at a constant rate, in a fixed time, length or area
Failures before a success: the first success or success number r
Events at a rate that changes between units or periods
The total of a random number of groups, each with a random size
A value from a to b, each value with the same probability

questions.text: Which success ends the count?
questions.help: The count is the number of failures before this success.

options.label: The first success
Success number r, with r larger than 1

questions.text: Which mechanism makes the time?
questions.help: The hazard rate is the rate of the event at time t, given no event before t.

options.label: The chance of the event in the next short time does not depend on the time already waited
The time is the sum of k stages, each with the same constant hazard rate
The hazard rate changes with age: wear or early failures
The time is the product of many independent positive factors
The first time that a random process gets to a level

questions.text: How does the hazard rate change with age?
questions.help: Use failure records or knowledge of the wear mechanism.

options.label: It increases as a power of the age
It increases exponentially with the age, as human mortality does
It decreases: early failures
It increases, then decreases

questions.text: Does the process move toward the level on average?
questions.help: This is the drift of the process.

options.label: Yes: the process has a positive drift toward the level
No: the process has no drift

questions.text: Which mechanism makes the size?
questions.help: A size is a positive amount, such as a loss, a claim or a file size.

options.label: The product of many independent positive factors
The sum of many independent positive parts
The total of a random number of individual amounts
A power law: the number of values above x decreases as x^(−α)
The excess of a value over a high threshold
The total of many independent amounts with an infinite variance

questions.text: Where does the power law start?
questions.help: The power law describes the right tail. The body of the law can have a different shape.

options.label: At a minimum value x_m larger than 0: no value is below x_m
At 0: small values are possible, and the density decreases from 0
After a mode: small values are rare, and large values follow the power law

questions.text: What is the proportion?
questions.help: A proportion takes values in [0, 1].

options.label: A probability or a fraction that changes between units or is not known exactly
A value between known limits, with no other information

questions.text: Which extreme value is it?
questions.help: A block is a period or a batch, such as one year of daily values.

options.label: The maximum of many values in each block
The minimum of many positive values: the weakest part
Each value above a high threshold

questions.text: Which mechanism makes the measurement?
questions.help: Each mechanism here has a theorem or a definition that gives a law.

options.label: The sum of many small independent effects with a finite variance
Usually small, but sometimes very large deviations
The difference of two independent exponential times
The difference of two independent Gumbel values, such as a latent value in a logistic model
The ratio of two independent normal values with mean 0
The sum of many independent values with an infinite variance
A sum of squares of independent standard normal values
A ratio of two independent variance estimates
A mean divided by its estimated standard error
A value between known limits, each value equally likely

questions.text: Does the count have a known upper limit?
questions.help: An example is the number of machines that fail in a group of n machines.

options.label: Yes: the count cannot be more than a known number n
No: there is no fixed upper limit

questions.text: How does the variance of the count compare with its mean?
questions.help: Use data or knowledge of the mechanism. This is the dispersion of the count.

options.label: About equal
The variance is larger: overdispersion
The variance is smaller: underdispersion

questions.text: Are there more zeros than a Poisson or a negative binomial law gives?
questions.help: An example is a count of claims, with many policies that can never have a claim.

options.label: Yes: there are too many zeros
No

questions.text: How fast does the probability of a very large value decrease?
questions.help: This is the right tail of the law. A finite sample cannot identify the tail.

options.label: There is a finite upper limit
At least as fast as an exponential function: a light tail
Slower than all exponential functions, but all moments exist
As a power x^(−α): a heavy tail, and some moments do not exist

questions.text: Do some exact values occur with a positive probability?
questions.help: An example is a loss that is exactly 0 for most policies. Such a value is an atom of the law.

options.label: Yes: many values are exactly 0
Yes: other exact values
No

questions.text: Is the population a mix of groups that behave differently?
questions.help: An example is a histogram with two peaks.

options.label: Yes
No

questions.text: How are the values recorded?
questions.help: The observation mechanism decides the law of the recorded values.

options.label: Each value is recorded exactly
A value beyond a limit is recorded only as “beyond the limit”
A value beyond a limit is not recorded
The chance to record a value depends on the value

questions.text: Are the values independent of each other?
questions.help: A law of one value does not say how the values depend on each other.

options.label: Yes: they are independent
No: values close in time are related
No: each event makes more events likely soon after
No: each value makes the next values, as parents make offspring
No: several variables depend on each other or on a common cause

questions.text: How does the process change over time?
questions.help: A stationary process keeps the same law at all times.

options.label: It keeps the same behaviour: it is stationary
It moves between a finite number of states
It drifts or grows
It has sudden jumps at random times, a few in each period
It moves by jumps of all sizes, also many small jumps

questions.text: Do extreme values of the variables occur together?
questions.help: Tail dependence is the limit of the probability that one variable is extreme, given that another variable is extreme, as the level becomes more extreme.

options.label: Large values occur together
Small values occur together
Large values and small values occur together
No: extreme values do not occur together more than the correlation gives

questions.text: How many variables depend on each other?
questions.help: Some copulas give the same dependence to every pair of variables.

options.label: Two
More than two, with different dependence for each pair

questions.text: Which data do you have?
questions.help: The rejection tests need data. Without data, each candidate is a hypothesis.

options.label: No data: only knowledge of the mechanism
Fewer than about 30 values
About 30 values or more
Several thousand values, enough to use them directly

questions.text: On what does the decision depend?
questions.help: A decision on a tail needs more evidence about the tail than a decision on a mean.

options.label: A mean value, such as an expected cost
A tail probability or a high quantile, such as a capacity or a reserve
The largest value in a period
The whole distribution

evidence.label: Mean value
evidence.help: From data or from knowledge. For a yes-or-no result, the probability of yes.

evidence.label: Standard deviation
evidence.help: Larger than 0. A negative binomial law needs a variance larger than the mean.

evidence.label: Upper limit or number of trials n
Threshold of the decision
evidence.help: The record estimates P(X > c), or P(X ≤ c) for a rank.

examples.label: Pump seal faults at a constant rate
Ticket holders who come to the flight
Claims for each policy, with a rate that changes between policies
Failed attempts before the first good connection
A positive loss with an unknown tail, for a reserve

candidates.name: Bernoulli

competing.text: The probability depends on other variables. Then a conditional model gives each unit its own probability.
Several results of the same kind are counted together. Their sum is binomial when the results are independent.

tests: Independence: a runs test on the sequence of results.
Same probability for all units: compare the fractions of yes in groups with a chi-square test.

candidates.name: Binomial

competing.text: When n is large and p is small, Poisson(np) is close. The total variation distance is at most np².
The draws are without replacement from a small population. Then the trials are not independent.
The probability p changes between groups. Then the variance is larger than np(1 − p).

tests: Dispersion: the sample variance must be near np̂(1 − p̂). A much larger variance rejects a constant p.
Upper limit: no count is larger than n.
Goodness of fit: a chi-square test of the counts against Binomial(n, p̂), with cells pooled to an expected count of at least 5.

requires.text: The mean m must be at most n.

candidates.name: Categorical

competing.text: With many observations, the frequencies of the labels give the probabilities directly.
The probabilities depend on other variables, such as the time of day.

tests: Goodness of fit: a chi-square test of the label counts against the stated probabilities.
Stability: compare the frequencies of the labels in two halves of the data.

extra: probabilities of the labels 1, 2 and 3: illustrative values

candidates.name: Multinomial

competing.text: The probabilities change between groups. Then the counts vary more than the multinomial law permits.
Only the shares matter, not the counts. Then a Dirichlet law can model the shares.

tests: Goodness of fit: a chi-square test of the category counts, with k − 1 degrees of freedom.
Overdispersion: compare the variance of each count between groups with n p_i (1 − p_i).

extra: probabilities of the categories 1, 2 and 3: illustrative values
quantities: prob exceed = X[1] > c "category 1 above the threshold"
mean first = X[1] "mean count of category 1"

candidates.name: Discrete uniform

competing.text: Some values are more likely than others. A categorical law states each probability.
The value is a count of independent successes, so the middle values are more likely.

tests: Goodness of fit: a chi-square test of the counts against equal probabilities.
Limits: no value is below a or above b.

requires.expr: round(2*m) == 2*m and 2*m - lim >= 0 and 2*m - lim <= lim
requires.text: A discrete uniform law from a ≥ 0 to n has the mean (a + n)/2, so the mean m must be a whole or half number from n/2 to n.

candidates.name: Geometric

competing.text: The count ends at success number r, with r larger than 1.
The success probability changes between units. Then the tail is heavier than geometric.

tests: No memory: P(X ≥ k + j | X ≥ k) must equal P(X ≥ j). Compare the ratios in the data.
Dispersion: the variance must be near m(1 + m), with m the mean.
Goodness of fit: a chi-square test against Geometric(1/(1 + m̂)).

requires.text: The mean m must be at least 0.

candidates.name: Negative binomial

competing.text: The rate is the same for all units. Then the variance equals the mean.
Events occur in clusters of random size. A compound Poisson count also has a variance larger than its mean.
The rate takes a few distinct values, such as two types of units.

tests: Dispersion: the variance must be larger than the mean. A variance near the mean supports the Poisson law.
Goodness of fit: a chi-square test against NB(r̂, p̂), with the maximum likelihood estimates.
Clusters: when events occur in groups, test a compound Poisson law.

requires.text: The variance sd² must be larger than the mean m.

candidates.name: Poisson

competing.text: The rate changes between units or periods. Then the variance is larger than the mean.
Each count has a known upper limit n.
Events occur in clusters. Then the count of single items is compound Poisson.

tests: Dispersion: under the Poisson law, (n − 1)s²/x̄ has approximately the χ²(n − 1) law. A value far in either tail rejects the Poisson law.
Goodness of fit: a chi-square test of the counts against Poisson(x̄), with cells pooled to an expected count of at least 5.
Constant rate: compare the mean counts of early and late periods.

candidates.name: Hypergeometric

competing.text: The sample is a small part of the population, or the draws are with replacement.

tests: Limits: the count is at most min(n, K) and at least max(0, n − N + K).
Dispersion: the variance must be near n(K/N)(1 − K/N)(N − n)/(N − 1), smaller than the binomial variance.

extra: population size N: an illustrative value
success items in the population, from the mean

requires.text: The mean m must be at most n.

candidates.name: Zipf

competing.text: With enough data, the rank frequencies of the data need no law.
A lognormal law of the frequencies can also give a rank–frequency plot close to a straight line.

tests: Rank–frequency plot: log frequency against log rank must be close to a straight line with the slope −s.

quantities: prob top = X <= c "a rank of c or better"

candidates.name: Continuous uniform

competing.text: Values near the middle or near one limit are more likely.
The quantity has a law of its own, and the limits only cut it.

tests: Goodness of fit: a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test against the uniform law on [a, b].
Limits: no value is outside [a, b].

requires.text: The standard deviation must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Normal

competing.text: Large deviations are more frequent than a normal law permits.
The quantity is positive and has a long right tail.

tests: Normal Q–Q plot: the points must be close to a straight line.
Shapiro–Wilk test of normality.
Tails: count the values more than 3 standard deviations from the mean. Expect about 0.27 %.

candidates.name: Multivariate normal

competing.text: Extreme values of the variables occur together. A Student-t copula has tail dependence.
One variable depends on the others in a way that is not linear.

tests: Each marginal law: a normal Q–Q plot.
Mardia's tests of multivariate skewness and kurtosis.

extra: correlation of the two measurements: an illustrative value

candidates.name: Exponential

competing.text: The hazard rate changes with age.
The time is a sum of several stages.
A mix of units with different constant rates. Then the hazard rate decreases.

tests: No memory: the excesses over a threshold must have the same mean as the whole sample.
A plot of log survival against time must be close to a straight line.
Coefficient of variation: it must be near 1.

candidates.name: Gamma

competing.text: The right tail is heavier, and log X looks normal.
The hazard rate is a power of the age.

tests: Gamma Q–Q plot with the fitted shape.
Compare a gamma fit with a lognormal fit and a Weibull fit by the likelihood.

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Erlang

competing.text: The number of stages is not an integer, or the stages have different rates.
There is only one stage.

tests: Coefficient of variation: it must be near 1/√k.

extra: number of stages, from the mean and the standard deviation

candidates.name: Beta

competing.text: Only the limits are known.
The values form two or more groups, such as many values near 0 and near 1.

tests: Beta Q–Q plot with the fitted parameters.

extra: a + b, from the mean and the variance

requires.text: The mean m must be between 0 and 1.

candidates.name: Dirichlet

competing.text: The data are counts, not shares.
The shares form distinct groups.

tests: Each share: a beta Q–Q plot, because each marginal law of a Dirichlet law is beta.

extra: concentration of the shares: an illustrative value

candidates.name: Chi-square

competing.text: The statistic is a ratio of two variance estimates.
The degrees of freedom are not known. A gamma law has a free shape.

tests: The mean must be near k and the variance near 2k.

candidates.name: Student's t

competing.text: The degrees of freedom are large. Then the t law is close to normal.
Large deviations are frequent, but the tails are exponential.

tests: Q–Q plot against the fitted t law. Points far from the line in the tails reject it.

candidates.name: F

competing.text: The denominator has many degrees of freedom. Then d₁F is close to χ²(d₁).
The ratio is of two positive amounts that are not sums of squares.

tests: Conditions of the theorem: independent normal samples in the numerator and the denominator.

extra: numerator degrees of freedom: an illustrative value
denominator degrees of freedom: an illustrative value

candidates.name: Logistic

The density has a sharp peak at the centre.

tests: Q–Q plot against the fitted logistic law.

candidates.name: Laplace

competing.text: The density is smooth at the centre.
The tails are heavier than exponential.

tests: Q–Q plot against the fitted Laplace law.

candidates.name: Lognormal

competing.text: The right tail is lighter: exponential, not lognormal.

candidates.name: Gompertz

competing.text: The hazard rate is a power of the age, not an exponential function.

candidates.name: Gaussian copula

competing.text: Extreme values occur together.
There are only two variables.

tests: Joint exceedances of high quantiles: they must be rare, because a Gaussian copula with correlation below 1 has no tail dependence.

candidates.name: Student-t copula

candidates.name: Clayton copula

candidates.name: Gumbel copula

competing.text: Small values occur together, not large values.

tests: Joint exceedances above high quantiles must be frequent, and below low quantiles rare.

candidates.name: Frank copula

competing.text: There are more than two variables, with different dependence for each pair.

tests: Joint exceedances of high and low quantiles must be rare: the Frank copula has no tail dependence.

candidates.name: Finite Markov chain

competing.text: The state is a continuous value, not one of a few states.

tests: Markov property: the next state must not depend on earlier states, given the current state. Compare chains of order 1 and 2.

candidates.name: Brownian motion with drift

competing.text: The quantity is positive and grows by percentages.
The path has jumps.

tests: Increments: they must be independent and normal, with a variance proportional to the time step.

candidates.methods: Exact simulation at the grid times: add independent normal increments.

candidates.name: Geometric Brownian motion

competing.text: The quantity can be negative, and changes add instead of multiply.

tests: Log increments: they must be independent and normal.

candidates.methods: Exact simulation at the grid times: the exponential of a Brownian motion with drift.

candidates.name: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process

competing.text: The process does not go back to a mean level.

tests: Autocorrelation: it must decrease exponentially with the time lag.

candidates.methods: Exact simulation at the grid times: an AR(1) recursion with the exact transition law.

candidates.name: Poisson process

competing.text: Events make more events likely.

tests: Gaps between events: they must be independent and exponential.
Counts in disjoint windows must be independent.
candidates.methods: Add independent exponential gaps until the end of the window.

candidates.name: Compound Poisson process

competing.text: The process has infinitely many small jumps.

tests: Jump times: the gaps must be independent and exponential.
Jump sizes: they must be independent of the jump times.
candidates.methods: Draw the jump times as a Poisson process, then add independent jump sizes.

candidates.name: Branching process

competing.text: Events in continuous time trigger later events.

tests: Offspring law: check the counts of offspring of each parent.
Mean offspring: a mean above 1 gives growth with a positive probability. At most 1, the process ends with probability 1, unless each parent has exactly one offspring.
candidates.methods: Draw the offspring count of each member of each generation.

candidates.name: Hawkes process

competing.text: Events do not trigger other events.
