tests: Time change: after the compensator transform, the gaps must be independent and exponential.
Branching ratio: the estimate must be below 1 for a stationary process.
candidates.methods: Ogata thinning, or the cluster method: immigrants as a Poisson process, then offspring of each event.

candidates.name: Lévy process

competing.text: There are only a few jumps in each period.
The path is continuous.

tests: Increments: they must be independent, with the same law for windows of the same length.
Small jumps: count the jumps above smaller and smaller thresholds.
candidates.methods: Exact increments when the page knows the law of an increment, or a compound Poisson approximation of the small jumps.

rules.reason: A yes-or-no result is a Bernoulli variable. Its law has one parameter: p = P(yes).
Each law on a finite list of labels is categorical. The parameters are the probabilities of the labels.
The counts of n independent draws, each with the same category probabilities, have the multinomial law.
Rank–frequency data often follow a power law. Zipf's law is a regularity of data, not a theorem.

rules.source: The standard law on the simplex
rules.reason: The Dirichlet law is the standard law for proportions with the sum 1. It is conjugate to the multinomial law. This is a common choice, not a theorem.
A vector of sums of many independent effects with finite variances, and no effect that dominates, is approximately multivariate normal.
The number of successes in n independent trials, each with probability p, has the Binomial(n, p) law.
The number of success items in n draws without replacement, from N items with K success items, has the Hypergeometric(N, K, n) law.

rules.source: Binomial limit of the hypergeometric law
rules.reason: When n is a small part of N, Binomial(n, K/N) is close to the hypergeometric law.

rules.source: Poisson process: independent increments and a constant rate
rules.reason: Independent events at a constant rate λ, in a window of size t, give a Poisson(λt) count. The counts in all windows form a Poisson process.
The number of failures before the first success, in independent trials with probability p, has the Geometric(p) law.

rules.source: Definition of the negative binomial law
rules.reason: The number of failures before success number r has the negative binomial law NB(r, p).

rules.source: Definitions of the geometric and negative binomial laws
rules.reason: The failures before the first success give a geometric law. The failures before success number r give a negative binomial law.
A Poisson count with a rate that has a gamma law between units is negative binomial.
A rate with a finite number of values gives a finite mixture of Poisson laws.
A rate that changes between units makes the variance larger than the mean. A Poisson law has a variance equal to its mean.

rules.source: Definition of the compound Poisson law
rules.reason: A total of N groups, with N ~ Poisson and independent group sizes with the same law, has a compound Poisson law.
A compound Poisson sum of group sizes with the logarithmic law is negative binomial.

rules.source: Definition of the discrete uniform law
rules.reason: Equal probabilities on the integers from a to b define the discrete uniform law.
These laws are common for counts. Without a mechanism, the rule graph cannot rank them.
A count with a fixed upper limit n needs a law on {0, …, n}. The binomial law is the simplest one with independent trials.
These laws give a positive probability to each count, also to counts above n.
These laws have a finite upper limit.
A Poisson law has a variance equal to its mean. This agreement supports the Poisson law, but it does not prove it.

rules.source: Moments of the negative binomial law
rules.reason: A negative binomial law has the variance μ + μ²/r, larger than its mean μ.
A compound Poisson count with group sizes above 1, a mixture of Poisson counts, and a geometric count all have a variance larger than the mean.

rules.source: Moments of the binomial and hypergeometric laws
rules.reason: A binomial variance np(1 − p) is smaller than the mean np. A hypergeometric variance is smaller still.
A Poisson law has a variance equal to its mean.

rules.source: Moments of the binomial and hypergeometric laws
rules.reason: These laws have a variance smaller than their mean.

rules.source: Moments of the negative binomial and geometric laws
rules.reason: These laws have a variance larger than their mean.
A Poisson law has a variance equal to its mean.
A count with extra zeros is a mixture of a point mass at 0 and another count law.
A Poisson law sets P(0) = e^(−λ) from its mean, so extra zeros do not fit it.
The exponential law is the only continuous law with no memory: P(T > s + t | T > s) = P(T > t).
The sum of k independent exponential stages with the same rate has the Erlang(k, λ) law.
A gamma law with a fitted shape is a common approximation when the stages have different rates.
The Weibull law has a hazard rate that is a power of the age. It is the most common law for wear and early failures.

rules.source: Other laws with a hazard rate that changes
rules.reason: These laws also have a hazard rate that changes with age.

rules.source: Constant hazard of the exponential law
rules.reason: Only the exponential law has a constant hazard rate. A hazard rate that changes with age excludes it.
A Weibull law with the shape k > 1 has the hazard rate (k/λ)(t/λ)^(k−1), which increases.
A gamma law with a shape above 1 has a hazard rate that increases to a constant.
The Gompertz law has the hazard rate b·e^(ct) with c > 0, which increases exponentially.
A Weibull hazard rate is a power of the age, not an exponential function.
A Weibull law with the shape k < 1 has a hazard rate that decreases.
A mix of strong and weak units, each with a constant hazard rate, has a hazard rate that decreases, because the weak units fail first. The hazard rate α/(σ + t) of the Pareto II law also decreases.

rules.source: Hazard rates that increase, then decrease
rules.reason: The log-logistic law with a shape above 1 and the lognormal law have a hazard rate that increases, then decreases.
The Weibull and Gompertz hazard rates are monotone.

rules.source: Central limit theorem for log T
rules.reason: When T is a product of many independent positive factors, log T is a sum. When the logarithms have a finite variance, T is approximately lognormal.

rules.source: First passage of Brownian motion with drift
rules.reason: The first time that a Brownian motion with a positive drift gets to a level above its start has the inverse Gaussian law.
Without drift, the first passage time of a Brownian motion to a level has the Lévy law. Its mean is infinite.
A first passage time of a Brownian motion is inverse Gaussian with a positive drift, and Lévy without drift.
These laws are common for times. Without a mechanism, the rule graph cannot rank them.

rules.source: Central limit theorem for log X
rules.reason: A product of many independent positive factors has a logarithm that is a sum. When the logarithms have a finite variance, the size is approximately lognormal.

rules.source: A common law for positive sums
rules.reason: The gamma law is a common law for a sum of positive parts. Independent gamma parts with the same scale have a gamma sum.

A sum of many independent parts with a finite variance, and no part that dominates, is approximately normal. A normal law also gives negative values, so use it only when the mean is many standard deviations above 0.

rules.source: Definition of the compound Poisson law
rules.reason: A total of a Poisson number of independent amounts with the same law has a compound Poisson law.
A power law above a minimum value is the Pareto I law. A power law that starts at 0 is the Pareto II law.

rules.source: Definition of the Pareto I law
rules.reason: The Pareto I law has the survival function (x_m/x)^α for x ≥ x_m.

rules.source: Definition of the Pareto II law
rules.reason: The Pareto II law has the survival function (1 + x/σ)^(−α) for x ≥ 0, with a density that decreases from its maximum at x = 0.

rules.source: Special cases of the Burr XII law
rules.reason: The Pareto II law is the case c = 1 of the Burr XII law.

rules.source: Body and tail shapes of the Burr XII law
rules.reason: When c > 1, the Burr XII law has a mode above 0 and a power-law tail, with separate shape parameters for the body and the tail.

rules.source: Special cases of the Burr XII law
rules.reason: The log-logistic law is the case k = 1 of the Burr XII law.
The excesses over a high threshold have approximately a generalised Pareto law, when the law is in the domain of attraction of an extreme-value law.
A normalised sum of many independent values with the same law, and a balanced regularly varying tail of index α < 2, converges to a stable law.
These laws are common for positive sizes. Without a mechanism, the rule graph cannot rank them.

rules.source: The standard law for a probability
rules.reason: The beta law is the standard law for an unknown probability. It is conjugate to the binomial law, so data change it in closed form.
With only the limits known, the uniform law is a common default. It has the largest entropy of all laws on the interval, but that is a choice, not knowledge.
These laws are common for proportions.
When the normalised maximum of a block has a limit law that is not a point mass, that limit is a generalised extreme value law.

rules.source: Limit laws of maxima and minima
rules.reason: The Weibull law is a limit law of minima. For maxima, its reflection, the reverse Weibull law, is the limit.
Values with a regularly varying tail of index α give maxima in the Fréchet domain, with the GEV shape ξ = 1/α > 0.
Values with an exponential, normal or lognormal type of tail give maxima in the Gumbel domain, with the GEV shape ξ = 0.
Values with a finite upper limit and a power law near that limit give maxima in the reverse Weibull domain, with ξ < 0.

rules.source: Limit law of minima: the weakest-link theorem
rules.reason: The minimum of many independent positive values, with a lower tail that behaves as a power near 0, is approximately Weibull.
The excesses over a high threshold have approximately a generalised Pareto law, when the law is in the domain of attraction of an extreme-value law.

rules.source: The two limit laws of extremes
rules.reason: Block maxima approximately follow a GEV law, and excesses over a threshold a generalised Pareto law.
A sum of many small independent effects, with finite variances and no effect that dominates, is approximately normal.

rules.source: Heavy tails of the t law
rules.reason: Student's t law has power-law tails, so large deviations are more frequent than for a normal law.
The Laplace and logistic laws have exponential tails, heavier than normal tails. The Cauchy law and the other stable laws with α < 2 have power-law tails with an infinite variance.
A normal law gives P(|X − μ| > 5σ) < 6·10^(−7). Frequent very large deviations do not fit it.
The difference of two independent exponential values with the same rate has the Laplace law.
The difference of two independent Gumbel values with the same scale has the logistic law.
The ratio of two independent normal values with mean 0 has the Cauchy law. Its mean does not exist.
A normalised sum of many independent values with the same law, and a balanced regularly varying tail of index α < 2, converges to a stable law.
A sum of squares of k independent standard normal values has the χ²(k) law.
A ratio of two independent chi-square values, each divided by its degrees of freedom, has the F law.
For normal data, the mean minus μ, divided by its estimated standard error, has Student's t law with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
Equal probability for all values between the limits defines the continuous uniform law. Make sure that all values between the limits have equal probability.
These laws are common for measurements. Without a mechanism, the rule graph cannot rank them.
These laws have a finite upper limit.
These laws have no upper limit: they give a positive probability above each level.
These laws have a tail that decreases at least exponentially.
These laws do not have an unbounded light tail.
These laws have a tail that decreases slower than each exponential function, with all moments finite.
These laws have a different tail: a finite limit, an exponential tail or a power-law tail.
These laws have a power-law tail: P(X > x) = x^(−α)L(x), with L slowly varying.
These laws have all moments finite, or a finite upper limit. A power-law tail excludes them.
With a power-law tail of index α, the moments above order α do not exist. The moment of order α can also be infinite. Check the moment status of each quantity before you use an interval.
A compound Poisson total of positive amounts is exactly 0 with the probability e^(−λ). A point mass at 0, mixed with a continuous law, also gives exact zeros.
A continuous law gives the probability 0 to each exact value.
A law with atoms and a continuous part is a mixture of point masses and a continuous law.
With many data, the empirical law keeps the atoms of the data.
A population of groups with different laws has the mixture law Σ w_i f_i.
For counts, a continuous mix of Poisson rates with a gamma law gives the negative binomial law.
A value recorded only as “beyond the limit” is a censored observation. Its likelihood term is the survival function at the limit.
Fit and test the law with methods for censored data. A histogram of the recorded values has a bias.
When the record leaves out each value beyond the limit, the recorded values have the truncated law f(x)/F(limit).
The chance to record a value depends on the value. Then the recorded values do not have the law of the quantity. Without a model of the selection, the data cannot identify the law.
The interview does not know the observation mechanism. The model record assumes an exact record of each value.
The interview does not know if the values are independent. A marginal law does not define dependence. The model record assumes independent values.
Values close in time depend on each other. A law of one value does not define this dependence, so the model needs a process.
In continuous time, a stationary Gaussian Markov process that is continuous in probability and not constant is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.
A finite Markov chain that starts from its stationary law is a stationary process.
A process on a finite set of states, with a next state that depends only on the current state, is a finite Markov chain.
Brownian motion with drift has independent normal increments. Geometric Brownian motion has independent normal log increments, so it stays positive.
A positive quantity needs a process that stays positive. Geometric Brownian motion stays positive.
A quantity that can be negative, with changes that add, fits Brownian motion with drift.
An Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process goes back to its mean level, and it is stationary when it starts from its stationary law. A drift excludes it.

rules.source: Definition of the compound Poisson process
rules.reason: A process with jumps at the times of a Poisson process, and independent jump sizes, is a compound Poisson process.
Brownian motion has continuous paths, so jumps exclude it.
A process with stationary independent increments and infinitely many small jumps in each time interval is a Lévy process with an infinite jump intensity.
A point process in which each event raises the rate of later events is a Hawkes process.
A Hawkes process is a branching process of immigrants and their offspring. Its counts in windows have overdispersion, so a negative binomial count can approximate them.
Self-excitation makes the counts in windows overdispersed, so a Poisson count does not fit.
A population in which each member has an independent random number of offspring is a branching process.
The law of a generation size follows from the offspring law. In general it has no closed form, so simulate the process.
A conditional model states the law of one variable given the others. It suits a variable that depends on a cause.
A Gaussian copula keeps the marginal laws and adds a correlation matrix.
A joint law is its marginal laws and a copula. A marginal law does not define dependence, so choose the copula apart from the marginal laws.

rules.source: Tail dependence of the Gumbel copula
rules.reason: The Gumbel copula has the upper tail dependence 2 − 2^(1/θ), larger than 0 for θ > 1, and no lower tail dependence.
The Gaussian copula with correlation below 1 and the Frank copula have no tail dependence. The Clayton copula has no upper tail dependence.

rules.source: Tail dependence of the Clayton copula
rules.reason: The Clayton copula has the lower tail dependence 2^(−1/θ), larger than 0 for θ > 0, and no upper tail dependence.
The Gaussian copula with correlation below 1 and the Frank copula have no tail dependence. The Gumbel copula has no lower tail dependence.

rules.source: Tail dependence of the t copula
rules.reason: When the correlation is above −1, the Student-t copula has the same tail dependence, larger than 0, in both tails.
These copulas have no tail dependence, or tail dependence in one tail only.
The Gaussian copula with correlation below 1 and the Frank copula have no tail dependence.
These copulas have tail dependence.
With two variables, the Frank copula gives negative or positive dependence with no tail dependence. Its parameter has a closed-form relation to Kendall's τ.
Gaussian and t copulas have a correlation matrix, so each pair can have a different dependence.
These copulas, with one parameter, give the same dependence to every pair of variables.
There are no data. Each candidate is a hypothesis, and the rejection tests must wait for data.
With fewer than about 30 values, the rejection tests have little power. A test that does not reject a candidate does not confirm it.
The empirical CDF of independent data with the same law converges uniformly to the true CDF. With several thousand values, the data can be the law, but only inside the range of the data.
A kernel density model smooths the data. Its tail follows the kernel, not the data, so it is not valid far beyond the data.
The decision depends on the tail, but the interview does not know the tail. Candidates with light and heavy tails give very different tail probabilities. A finite sample cannot settle the tail.
A tail probability from few data depends mostly on the chosen law. Compare the decision under two candidates with different tails.
The decision uses the largest value in a period. Simulate the whole period, or model the block maximum with an extreme-value law.
The mean can be infinite with a power-law tail. Check the moment status before you use a mean.
The empirical law gives the probability 0 above the largest observation, so it cannot estimate a rare tail event.
The interview does not know what one value measures. The support is the first fact that limits the candidate laws.
The interview knows neither the mechanism nor the tail of the time. Support and moments alone do not identify a law.
The interview knows neither the mechanism nor the tail of the size. Support and moments alone do not identify a law.
The interview knows neither the mechanism nor the tail of the measurement. Support and moments alone do not identify a law.
The interview knows neither the mechanism nor the tail of the extreme value. Support and moments alone do not identify a law.
No candidate has strong support: no candidate has a score of 2 or more. The answers do not separate the candidate laws.

problems.title: The tail of a sum of claims
problems.statement: An insurer pays claims in one period. There are n claims, and they are independent. Find the probability that the total S_n is above the reserve b.
problems.decision: Decision: keep the reserve b, or raise it. Estimated quantity: P(S_n > b), against the largest acceptable probability.
problems.reason: A sum of i.i.d. jumps is the simplest model of an aggregate loss. Its tail has an exact value for exponential jumps and a known asymptotic for heavy-tailed jumps. These values let you check each method.
problems.inputs: The inputs are n claims, the threshold b in loss units and the jump law. The jump law is one of three laws: exponential (light tail), Weibull with k < 1, or Pareto II. All moments of the Weibull law are finite, but it has no exponential moment. The Pareto II law has only the moments of order r < α. The parameters are illustrative.
problems.dependence: The claims are independent and have the same law. Positive dependence between claims, such as a common shock, makes the tail heavier. This model does not show it.
problems.diagnostics: Compare the estimate with the exact Erlang tail, or with the Asmussen–Kroese reference for a heavy tail. Read the relative error, the work and the effective sample size of the weights. Other candidate models: a compound Poisson sum with a random number of claims, or a sum with dependent claims.
problems.interpretation: For a light tail, a large sum comes from many moderately large claims. Then P(S_n > na) for a fixed a > E X decays exponentially in n. For a heavy tail, it comes from one very large claim, and P(S_n > b) ≈ n P(X > b) for large b. Reject the model when the claims are clearly dependent. Reject it also when a plot of the data shows a tail that the chosen law does not have.
problems.data: Synthetic: the jump law and its parameters define the data. They are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

problems.title: The probability of ruin of an insurer
problems.statement: Claims arrive as a Poisson process with rate λ, and the premium income is c per year. Find the probability ψ(u) that the capital, which starts at u, ever goes below 0.
problems.decision: Decision: the initial capital u that the insurer holds. Estimated quantity: the probability of ruin ψ(u) over an infinite horizon, against the largest acceptable probability.
problems.reason: The Cramér–Lundberg model is the classical model of ruin theory. The Pollaczek–Khinchine formula writes ψ(u) as the probability that a sum of K ladder heights is above u. The number K is geometric, with P(K = k) = (1 − ρ) ρ^k and ρ = λ E[X]/c. Thus the methods for a sum also apply to it. Exponential tilting applies only to exponential claims.
problems.inputs: The inputs are the claim rate λ and the premium rate c, each per year, and the capital u in money units. The claims are exponential or Pareto II, with a finite mean. The parameters are illustrative.
problems.dependence: The claim sizes are i.i.d. and independent of the Poisson arrivals. The catastrophe test removes these assumptions: it has clustered arrivals, losses that several insurers share, and a finite horizon.
problems.diagnostics: For exponential claims, compare the estimate with the exact value ρ exp(−(1 − ρ)u/μ). For Pareto II claims, compare it with the Asmussen–Kroese reference. Other candidate models: a model with a finite horizon, or with a premium that depends on the capital.
problems.interpretation: With exponential claims, ψ(u) decays exponentially in u at the adjustment coefficient R. With Pareto II claims, no R exists, and ψ(u) decays as a power of u. Double the capital, and the ruin probability falls only by a factor of about 2^(α−1). When ρ ≥ 1, ruin is certain (ψ(u) = 1), and no capital is enough. Reject the model when the claims arrive in clusters, or when their sizes depend on each other.
problems.data: Synthetic: the claim law, the claim rate and the premium define the data. They are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

problems.title: The catastrophe and systemic ruin test
problems.statement: Each of K insurers takes a random part of each catastrophe loss in one region for T years. On average, the parts add up to the loss. A systemic ruin is m or more defaults. Choose the cheapest policy that keeps the probability of a systemic ruin at or below the target.
problems.decision: Decision: no action, a catastrophe layer ℓ xs d that the insurers buy together, or extra capital for each insurer. Estimated quantity: P(at least m defaults by T) for each policy. The page also estimates the probability of one default and the expected number of defaults. It also estimates the value at risk and the expected shortfall of the total loss, and the probability of an extreme single event.
problems.reason: The test joins five parts. Each part can change the probability of ruin. The losses have a heavy tail. The events cluster in time (Hawkes arrivals). The shares depend on each other through a copula. A cascade of defaults can occur. The capital grows only with the premium.
problems.inputs: The inputs are the horizon T and K insurers, each with the capital u and the premium c. The arrivals are a Hawkes process with the baseline rate ν, the branching ratio η and the decay δ. The event loss S is exponential, Weibull or Pareto II, with an optional truncation M. The shares are W_j = 2 U_j, with U from a copula with Kendall's τ. The other inputs are the contagion κ, the layer, its loading and the cost of capital. Each insurer loses S W_j / K in an event. The parameters are illustrative.
problems.dependence: Each insurer takes a part of the same event loss S, so they lose together. The copula of the shares adds more dependence. A default costs each other insurer κ u, and a further default can follow in the same event (a cascade). The Hawkes arrivals make a cluster of events after each event.
problems.diagnostics: No exact reference exists. Direct simulation, importance sampling and splitting must agree within their intervals. The mean number of events must agree with the exact E N(T). Read the effective sample size and the largest weight of each change of measure. Other candidate models: Poisson arrivals (η = 0), independent shares, no cascade, or a truncated loss law.
problems.interpretation: The decision follows the tail of the event loss. With light-tailed losses of the same mean, ruin needs many large events, and no action is enough. With heavy-tailed losses, one event can ruin several insurers at once. With these parameters, the layer, which pays for the large events, is then the cheapest policy that meets the target. Reject a result when the methods disagree. Reject it also when a few weights of a change of measure carry most of the estimate. Reject it also when the target is inside the interval of the chosen policy.
problems.data: Synthetic: the arrival, loss and share laws define the data. The parameters are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence of any region or insurer.

methods.name: Direct simulation
methods.estimatorText: The fraction of N independent paths of the nominal model that are in the event A. Its relative error is about 1/√(Np), so a probability of 10^−6 needs about 10^8 paths for a relative error of 10 %.
assumptions: The paths are independent and come from the nominal model.
N p is large enough for the Wilson interval. With no path in the event, the page shows the exact one-sided bound 1 − 0.05^(1/N) ≈ 3/N.
settings: N = 2^size paths for each replication, and R replications.
The interval pools all R N paths, because they are i.i.d.

suitable.text: In the heavy-tailed regime of the catastrophe test, a systemic ruin has a probability of about 0.04. Direct simulation then gives a relative error of about 2 % with 65,536 paths, and it needs no assumption about a change of measure. Here it is also more efficient than the changes of measure, whose weights vary over the many events of a path.

failure.text: P(S_20 > 50) = 4.8 · 10^−7 for exponential claims. With 524,288 paths, direct simulation sees no path in the event. It then shows only the zero-hit bound 3/N ≈ 6 · 10^−6, which is 12 times the true value.

comparison.text: Exponential tilting draws every path near the event and weights it. With the same work it gives a relative error below 1 %, where direct simulation sees nothing.

methods.name: Exponential tilting
methods.estimator: \hat p = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} e^{\,n\kappa(\theta) - \theta S^{(i)}}\,\mathbf 1\{S^{(i)} > b\}, \quad S^{(i)} \sim F_\theta^{*n}, \quad dF_\theta = \frac{e^{\theta x}}{\mathbb E e^{\theta X}}\,dF, \quad \kappa'(\theta^*) = \frac{b}{n}
methods.estimatorText: Draw each jump from the tilted law F_θ and weight the path by the likelihood ratio exp(n κ(θ) − θ S), with κ(θ) = log E exp(θX). The tilt θ* makes the mean of the tilted jumps b/n, so the event is typical. For the ruin problem, θ = R solves ρ E exp(θY) = 1, every tilted path reaches u, and the weight is exp(−R S_τ) (Siegmund's algorithm). In the catastrophe test, the page tilts the exponential event losses to a larger mean. It also tilts the baseline rate of the arrivals to a larger rate.
assumptions: E exp(θX) < ∞ for the tilt θ. For a Pareto II law, and for a Weibull law with k < 1, E exp(θX) = ∞ for every θ > 0, so the page refuses the method.
The jumps are independent. In the catastrophe test the copula acts on the shares, not on the tilted losses, so the likelihood ratio has no copula density.
The weights have a finite variance: E_θ[w²] < ∞ holds for these tilts.
settings: The sum: θ* = 1/μ − 1/a with a = b/n, from the large-deviation equation κ'(θ*) = a.
The ruin problem: θ = R = (1 − ρ)/μ, the adjustment coefficient.
The catastrophe test: the tilted mean loss is tilt × the nominal mean, and the tilted baseline rate is arrivals × ν (settings tilt and arrivals).

suitable.text: For a sum of exponential claims, tilting with θ* is logarithmically efficient (Sadowsky and Bucklew, 1990). The relative variance grows only as √n, and the relative error as n^(1/4), while p decays as exp(−n I(a)). 524,288 tilted paths give P(S_20 > 50) with a relative error below 1 %.

failure.text: For Pareto II claims, E exp(θX) is infinite for every θ > 0. No tilted law exists, and the page refuses the method with this reason. A tilt that ignores this condition is not a valid change of measure.

comparison.text: Splitting needs no exponential moment, but on this light-tailed sum it uses about twice the work for a relative error about 10 times larger. Tilting uses the exact structure of the law. Splitting uses only the path.

methods.name: Multilevel splitting
methods.estimatorText: Fixed-effort splitting: stage j starts N paths from states that reached level ℓ_(j−1). It draws these states with replacement and counts the paths that reach ℓ_j before they end. The product of the fractions is an unbiased estimate of the probability to reach the last level. See Del Moral (2004) and Cérou, Del Moral, Furon and Guyader (2012). The interval comes from R independent replications.
assumptions: The state is Markov: the future of a path depends only on its present state. Thus a path can restart from a copy of a state.
The levels form a nested sequence: a path that reaches ℓ_j also reached every lower level.
The importance function h puts the states in order by their probability to reach the event. A poor h does not make a bias, but it makes a large variance.
settings: N paths in each stage, and L stages. The page takes L from the reference value so that each stage has a probability of about 0.1, unless the setting levels says otherwise.

The sum: h(k, s) = s + (n − k) μ, with μ the mean jump (the median when the mean is infinite). The ruin problem: h = s. The catastrophe test: h = number of defaults + the largest used fraction of capital of an insurer that is not in default, with 3m stages.

suitable.text: With exponential claims a path reaches the threshold by many moderate steps. Each level is a step of about the same probability. Splitting then gives a relative error of a few per cent, where direct simulation sees no path.

failure.text: With Pareto II claims the event comes from one very large claim. With one jump, a path goes past several levels at once. Thus the stages do not divide the probability. For the same work, splitting gives little gain over direct simulation. The panel shows the fraction of paths that enter a stage already past its level.

comparison.text: Adaptive importance sampling makes the one large claim common with the one-big-jump mixture and weights it. It reaches a relative error about 5 times smaller than splitting with about the same work.

methods.name: Subset simulation
methods.estimator: \hat p = p_0^{\,L-1}\,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf 1\{g(Z_i^{(L)}) > b\}, \qquad \gamma_j = \text{the } (1 - p_0)\text{-quantile of } g \text{ at level } j
methods.estimatorText: Au and Beck (2001): write the sum as a function g(Z) of the inputs Z. The inputs Z are independent and standard normal. Each level sets the threshold γ_j at the (1 − p0) quantile of g. It keeps the N p0 samples above γ_j as seeds. It grows each seed into a Markov chain by the modified Metropolis algorithm, which stays above γ_j. When γ_j reaches b, the last factor of the product is the fraction of samples above b.
assumptions: The inputs are a fixed number of independent random variables. Thus the page refuses the method for the catastrophe test, because its number of events is random.
The chains mix within each level. The estimator then has a bias of order 1/N and a variance larger than that of independent levels. The interval comes from R independent replications.
The geometric count of the ruin problem is cut at k_max, where the mass beyond is below 10^−12.
settings: N samples for each level and p0 = 0.1 (setting p0).

The proposal of each component is a normal step with the standard deviation spread = 1. The page accepts or rejects it against the standard normal density. The page keeps the move only if g stays above γ_j.

suitable.text: For Weibull claims with k = 0.5 no exponential tilt exists, and the event comes from one or two large claims. Subset simulation needs no change of measure. Its levels find the large claims through the chains, and it gives a relative error of a few per cent.

failure.text: With the step spread = 0.05, the page accepts almost every component proposal, but each chain hardly moves. The samples of a level stay near their seeds, the levels are strongly dependent, and the replications vary much more than with spread = 1.

comparison.text: The cross-entropy method fits a hazard-rate twist of the Weibull law. It uses the structure of the law and reaches a smaller relative error with less work. But it depends on the choice of the family, and subset simulation does not.

methods.name: Adaptive importance sampling
methods.estimatorText: A defensive mixture (Hesterberg 1995) of the nominal law f and the one-big-jump proposal (Dupuis, Leder and Wang 2007). With probability 1 − β, one jump chosen at random comes from the hazard-rate twist g_r, and the other jumps come from f. The survival function of g_r is F̄^r. In each step of the adaptation, the page updates r by weighted maximum likelihood. It uses the largest jump of each path in the event. This follows population Monte Carlo (Cappé, Guillin, Marin and Robert 2004). A fresh sample from the last mixture gives the estimate. The weights are at most 1/β, so their variance is finite for any target. The catastrophe test changes one event loss, chosen at random, in the same way.
assumptions: The event comes mostly from one large jump, as for a subexponential law. For a light tail, a large sum needs many moderate jumps, and one twisted jump helps little.

The first twist gives some paths in the event. The page starts at r = 1/H(x0), with H = −log F̄ the cumulative hazard and x0 the threshold. Thus the twisted jump has the size of the threshold. A start at the nominal law gives no path in a rare event, and then no step can adapt.
The adaptation uses earlier samples only to choose r. The final sample is independent of them, so the estimate has no bias.
settings: β = 0.1 (setting beta), 4 adaptation steps (setting iters) of N/4 paths, then N paths.
The interval comes from R independent replications, each with its own adaptation.

suitable.text: For Pareto II claims, ruin comes from one large ladder height. The one-big-jump mixture makes that jump common and keeps every weight below 1/β = 10. Its work-normalised relative variance is about 50 times smaller than that of splitting.

failure.text: Started at the nominal law, the adaptation sees no path with S_20 > 60 (p ≈ 6 · 10^−10). It cannot update r, the final mixture is the nominal law, and the estimate is 0 with no interval.

comparison.text: The cross-entropy method starts at the nominal law too. But it raises its level step by step through the quantiles of the sum, so it reaches the rare event. Use it when you know no good first proposal.

methods.name: Cross-entropy method
methods.estimatorText: Rubinstein (1997), Rubinstein and Kroese (2004): an optimisation of the proposal. Each iteration sets the level γ_t at the (1 − ρ_CE) quantile of the sum under the current proposal. Then it fits the proposal to the elite paths above γ_t by weighted maximum likelihood. This fit minimises the cross-entropy to the zero-variance law. The levels rise until γ_t = b. A fresh sample from the last proposal gives the estimate. The final proposal also shows, within the family, the most likely way that the event happens.
assumptions: The family g_v holds a good proposal. The page uses the hazard-rate twist F̄^r of the jump law. For an exponential law, this twist is the exponential tilt. For a Pareto II law, it gives a heavier tail.
The weights of the final proposal have a finite variance. A family with a lighter tail than the target breaks this: then f/g has no upper bound and the variance is infinite.

The interval comes from R independent replications, each with its own adaptation. If the levels do not reach the event within the iteration limit, the page uses the last proposal. The estimate then still has no bias, but it can have a large variance.
settings: ρ_CE = 0.1 (setting rho), N/4 paths for each iteration, smoothing 0.7, at most 20 iterations (8 for the catastrophe test), then N paths. A level that does not rise doubles the sample size, up to 4N.
The ruin problem also fits the parameter of the geometric count. The catastrophe test also fits the baseline rate of the arrivals.

suitable.text: For Weibull claims with k = 0.5 no exponential tilt exists, but the hazard-rate twist F̄^r does. The cross-entropy method finds r from the nominal law, level by level. It gives a relative error of about 2 % with less work than subset simulation.

failure.text: With an exponential family for Pareto II claims, the weights f/g grow without bound in the tail and their variance is infinite. Most replications give an estimate below the reference, and a few give a very large one. The effective sample size of the weights is small. A diagnostic does not prove convergence.

comparison.text: Adaptive importance sampling keeps the nominal law in a defensive mixture, so its weights stay below 1/β whatever the family. Its interval is valid where the light family of the cross-entropy method fails.

presets.title: 20 exponential claims above 50: exponential tilting
presets.observe: Direct simulation sees no path in the event, so it shows only the zero-hit bound. Tilting draws paths near the threshold and weights them, and its interval holds the exact Erlang value 4.8 · 10^−7.

presets.title: 20 exponential claims above 50: splitting against tilting
presets.observe: Both intervals hold the exact value. The stages of splitting have fractions near 0.1, and the work of each method shows its cost.

presets.title: 10 Pareto II claims above 400: the page refuses tilting
presets.observe: The page refuses exponential tilting and states why: E exp(θX) = ∞ for every θ > 0. Subset simulation is still available, and its interval holds the reference.

presets.title: One big claim: splitting against adaptive importance sampling
presets.observe: Many paths enter a stage already past its level: one claim carries them past several levels. Splitting has a relative error about 5 times larger than adaptive importance sampling for about the same work.

presets.title: Finite moments, no exponential moment: a Weibull sum
presets.observe: Every moment of the Weibull law with k = 0.5 is finite, but E exp(θX) is not. Tilting is not available. Subset simulation and the cross-entropy method agree with the reference.

presets.title: A Weibull sum: the cross-entropy method
presets.observe: The cross-entropy method climbs from the nominal law to the event in a few levels. The final twist r < 1 gives the claims a heavier tail. The panel shows the level and the twist of each iteration.

presets.title: Cross-entropy with a light-tailed family on a heavy tail
presets.observe: The exponential proposals have a lighter tail than the Pareto II claims, so the weights have an infinite variance. Most replications fall below the reference, and the replication interval is not valid. Adaptive importance sampling, with bounded weights, holds the reference.

presets.title: Adaptive importance sampling from the nominal law
presets.observe: No path of the nominal law reaches 60, so no step can adapt, and the estimate is 0. The cross-entropy method climbs to the event through its levels.

presets.title: Subset simulation with a very small step
presets.observe: With the step 0.05, the page accepts almost every component proposal, but the chains stay near their seeds. The replications spread more than with the step 1.

presets.title: Cramér–Lundberg ruin with exponential claims: Siegmund's algorithm
presets.observe: The exact value ψ(40) = 0.8 exp(−8) = 2.7 · 10^−4. Siegmund's estimator is at most exp(−Ru), so its relative error stays bounded as u grows. Direct simulation sees few paths in the event.

presets.title: Pollaczek–Khinchine ruin with Pareto II claims
presets.params: lam=1; c=1.25; u=400; sigma=1.5; alpha=2.5; target=0.001
presets.observe: No adjustment coefficient exists, so the page refuses tilting. ψ(u) is near the Embrechts–Veraverbeke asymptotic ρ/(1 − ρ) F̄_I(u), which decays as a power of u.

presets.title: Catastrophe and systemic ruin: light-tailed losses
presets.observe: A systemic ruin has a probability of about 10^−3. All three policies meet the target, so no action is the cheapest choice. Splitting and direct simulation agree. Splitting gives a narrower interval for more work.

presets.title: Catastrophe and systemic ruin: heavy-tailed losses
presets.observe: The mean event loss is the same as in the light-tailed regime, but a systemic ruin is more than 30 times more likely. Only the layer meets the target: the decision changes with the tail.

presets.title: Systemic ruin: a Gaussian copula with the same Kendall's τ
presets.observe: The Gaussian copula has no tail dependence. The Gumbel copula with τ = 0.7 has λ_U = 2 − 2^0.3 = 0.77. In 65,536 paths with seed 1, the probability of a systemic ruin was 0.039 with this copula. It was 0.038 with the Gumbel copula and 0.043 with independent shares. Most of the dependence comes from the common event loss. With independent shares, one insurer often gets a large share and defaults. Then the cascade can cause a second default. Thus stronger dependence of the shares lowers the risk a little here. The difference between the two copulas is smaller than the Monte Carlo error.

presets.title: Systemic ruin when the events do not cluster: Poisson arrivals
presets.observe: The Poisson arrivals with ν = 3.333 have about the same mean number of events as the Hawkes arrivals, but no clusters. The probability of a systemic ruin is about 0.037, against about 0.040 with clusters.

presets.title: An infinite mean loss: no expected shortfall
presets.observe: With α = 0.9 the mean event loss is infinite. The value at risk exists, but the expected shortfall is infinite. So the page shows no number for it, and the premium has no safety loading.

presets.title: Truncation at the largest possible loss
presets.observe: A truncation at M = 60 removes the largest events. The probability of a systemic ruin falls from about 0.04 to 0.03, and the layer meets the target with a wide margin. No finite sample of the past shows whether such a bound exists.

examples.title: A normal law with correlation 0.95: random walk, Gibbs sweep and Hamiltonian paths
examples.problem: The target is a bivariate normal law with unit variances and correlation ρ. The page knows its density up to a constant, and every result has an exact value. Thus you can check each sampler and each diagnostic.

params.name: rho
params.note: the correlation of x₁ and x₂, strictly between −1 and 1

quantities.name: E[x₁]
quantities.note: the mean of the first coordinate

quantities.name: P(x₁ + x₂ > 2)
quantities.note: the probability that the sum is above 2

quantities.name: E[x₁x₂]
quantities.note: the mean of the product, which is ρ

examples.observe: The random walk takes small steps along the narrow ridge of the law, so its autocorrelation decays slowly and its effective sample size is small. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo follows the ridge with the gradient and gives a much larger effective sample size from the same number of draws. Set rho = 0.995 and choose the Gibbs sweep. Each coordinate then moves by about √(1 − ρ²) in each sweep, so the chain mixes slowly.

data.text: Synthetic: ρ fully states the target law. No data.

examples.title: Two modes far apart: a large effective sample size and a wrong estimate
examples.problem: The target is a mixture of two normal laws with identity covariance and means (−b, −b) and (b, b). The mode at (b, b) has the weight w. Between the modes, the density is about e^(−b²) times its value at a mode.

params.name: b
params.note: the distance of each mode from 0 along each coordinate

params.name: w
params.note: the weight of the mode at (b, b)

quantities.name: P(x₁ + x₂ > 0)
quantities.note: the probability of the upper mode's half plane

quantities.name: E[x₁]
quantities.note: the mean of the first coordinate, b(2w − 1)

examples.observe: Every chain starts at (−b, −b) and stays in that mode. The chains agree, so split R-hat is near 1 and the effective sample size is large. But the estimate of P(x₁ + x₂ > 0) is near 0, and the exact value is 0.7. No diagnostic of the chains can show a mode that no chain visited. Sequential Monte Carlo starts from a wide law and finds both modes with their weights. Set the start to dispersed: then the chains start in different modes, and split R-hat becomes large.

data.text: Synthetic: b and w fully state the target law. No data.

examples.title: Neal's funnel: divergent transitions in the neck
examples.problem: The target is Neal's funnel: v is N(0, s²), and x given v is N(0, e^v). For small v the law of x is very narrow, and for large v it is very wide. One step size cannot suit both regions.

params.name: s
params.note: the standard deviation of v

quantities.name: P(v < −3)
quantities.note: the probability of the narrow neck

quantities.name: E[v]
quantities.note: the mean of v, which is 0

examples.observe: With the leapfrog step 0.5, the leapfrog paths become unstable in the neck. The energy error becomes very large there, and the page counts these divergent transitions: more than 1,000 here. The chains seldom enter the neck. Thus the estimate of P(v < −3) is below the exact Φ(−1) = 0.159, and the estimate of E[v] has a bias. A divergent transition is a signal of bias. Its absence does not prove that there is no bias.

data.text: Synthetic: s fully states the target law. No data.

examples.title: Recalibrate a laboratory balance from 12 weighings of a reference mass
examples.problem: A laboratory weighs a 500 g reference mass 12 times on one balance. The bias μ − 500 g and the scatter σ of the balance are unknown. The posterior law of (μ, σ) has no closed form, but the full conditional laws are a normal law and an inverse gamma law.

params.name: mu0
params.note: the prior mean of μ: the nominal mass

params.name: tau0
params.note: the prior standard deviation of μ

params.name: a0
params.note: the shape of the inverse gamma prior of σ²

params.name: b0
params.note: the scale of the inverse gamma prior of σ²

params.name: c
params.note: the bias that requires a recalibration

quantities.name: P(μ − 500 g > c | y)
quantities.note: the posterior probability of a bias above c

quantities.name: E[μ − 500 g | y]
quantities.note: the posterior mean of the bias

quantities.name: E[σ | y]
quantities.note: the posterior mean of the scatter

examples.decision: Decision: recalibrate the balance, or keep it in service. Recalibrate when P(μ − 500 g > 0.5 g | y) ≥ 0.9. Estimated quantity: that posterior probability, with the posterior means of the bias and of σ.
examples.reason: The weighings are sums of many small independent errors, so a normal model is reasonable. The semi-conjugate priors make each full conditional law a standard law. Thus the Gibbs sweep draws each full conditional law exactly, and it has no step size to tune.
examples.inputs: y: 12 weighings in g. Prior: μ ~ N(500 g, (1 g)²) and σ² ~ inverse gamma(2, 1 g²), independent. The chain moves on (μ, log σ). The prior values are illustrative.
examples.dependence: Given μ and σ, the weighings are independent. A drift during the series, or a temperature effect, would make them dependent. This model does not include it.
examples.method: The Gibbs sweep draws μ from its normal full conditional law and σ² from its inverse gamma full conditional law. Each chain discards its warm-up and averages the indicator of μ − 500 g > 0.5 g. The comparison is a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings chain on the same target.
examples.diagnostics: Read split R-hat, the effective sample size and the autocorrelation of each series. Compare the estimate with the numerical reference by quadrature. Other candidate models: a Student t error law for weighings far from the others, or a model with a linear drift in time.
examples.interpretation: With these data the posterior probability is about 0.95, so the rule says recalibrate. The prior of μ has its centre at zero bias. Thus the data, not the prior, make the probability larger than 0.9. Reject the model when the residuals show a trend in time, or when one result is far from the others.

data.text: Synthetic: 12 weighings drawn from N(500.6 g, (0.7 g)²) with the page's generator (Philox4x32-10, seed 8) and rounded to 0.01 g. They are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

examples.title: Does the balance have a bias at all? The evidence of two models
examples.problem: Model 0 says that the balance has no bias: μ = 500 g. Model 1 gives μ a normal prior. With prior odds 1 to 1, the posterior probability of model 1 is Z₁ / (Z₀ + Z₁), where Z is the evidence of a model. Z₀ has a closed form. Sequential Monte Carlo estimates Z₁.

params.name: mu0
params.note: the nominal mass; model 0 fixes μ at this value

params.name: tau0
params.note: the prior standard deviation of μ in model 1

params.name: a0
params.note: the shape of the inverse gamma prior of σ²

params.name: b0
params.note: the scale of the inverse gamma prior of σ²

params.name: c
params.note: the bias that requires a recalibration

quantities.name: P(model 1 | y)
quantities.note: the posterior probability of a bias, with prior odds 1 to 1

quantities.name: log Z₁
quantities.note: the log evidence of model 1

quantities.name: P(μ − 500 g > c | y, model 1)
quantities.note: the posterior probability of a bias above c in model 1

rule.no: Do not send the balance for service yet.

examples.decision: Decision: send the balance for service when P(model 1 | y) ≥ 0.95, with prior odds 1 to 1. Estimated quantity: the posterior probability of model 1, from the evidence Z₁.
examples.reason: Markov chain Monte Carlo gives draws from a posterior law, but no direct estimate of its normalising constant. The sequential sampler moves its particles from a wide reference law to the posterior law, and the product of its mean incremental weights estimates Z₁.
examples.inputs: The 12 weighings of the balance workflow, in g, and the same priors. The reference law of the sampler is N(500 g, (2 g)²) for μ and N(0, 1) for log σ. The prior values are illustrative.
examples.dependence: Given μ and σ, the weighings are independent. The evidence depends strongly on the prior of μ: when the prior is already wide, a wider prior lowers Z₁. Always give the prior with a Bayes factor.
examples.method: Geometric tempering from the reference law to the posterior law. The adaptive schedule chooses each step so that the weight ESS falls to half of its value. Then the sampler resamples and moves each particle with 5 random-walk Metropolis steps. The estimate of Z₁ is the product of the mean incremental weights.
examples.diagnostics: Read the weight ESS at each step and the number of steps. Then read the distinct ancestors and the spread of log Z₁ over the runs. Compare with the numerical reference by quadrature. Other candidate models: model 1 with a wider or narrower prior of μ, or a Student t error law.
examples.interpretation: The evidence of model 1 is about 177 times that of model 0. Thus P(model 1 | y) is about 0.994, and the rule says send the balance for service. The estimate of Z₁ has no bias for a fixed schedule. The adaptive schedule adds a small bias that decreases with the number of particles. Reject the comparison when the result changes much for a reasonable change of the prior of μ.

data.text: Synthetic: the 12 weighings of the balance workflow, drawn from N(500.6 g, (0.7 g)²) with seed 8. They are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

examples.title: O-ring distress at a launch temperature of 31 °F
examples.problem: Before 28 January 1986, 23 Space Shuttle flights recorded the number of field-joint O-rings, of 6, with thermal distress, and the launch temperature. A logistic regression gives the probability of distress for each O-ring as a function of the temperature. The forecast for the launch was 31 °F, far below every earlier launch.

params.name: sa
params.note: the prior standard deviation of α, the log odds at 70 °F

params.name: sb
params.note: the prior standard deviation of β, the change of the log odds for each 10 °F

params.name: t0
params.note: the launch temperature of the forecast

quantities.name: P(at least 1 of 6 O-rings with distress at t₀ | data)
quantities.note: the posterior predictive probability

quantities.name: E[p(t₀) | data]
quantities.note: the posterior mean of the probability of distress for one O-ring

quantities.name: P(β < 0 | data)
quantities.note: the posterior probability that a colder launch gives more distress

rule.no: The model alone does not require a delay.

examples.decision: Decision: delay the launch, or not. Delay it when the posterior predictive probability of distress in at least 1 of the 6 field-joint O-rings at 31 °F is at least 0.5. Estimated quantity: that probability.
examples.reason: Each flight gives a count of the 6 O-rings with distress. The standard model is a binomial law with a probability that depends on the temperature. The posterior law of (α, β) is smooth on the whole plane, so Hamiltonian Monte Carlo applies. Its full conditional laws are not standard laws, so the page has no Gibbs sweep for it.
examples.inputs: Temperatures in °F and counts of distressed O-rings from 23 flights. Model: k_i ~ binomial(6, p_i) with logit p_i = α + β (t_i − 70 °F)/10 °F. Priors: α ~ N(0, 5²) and β ~ N(0, 2.5²). They are weakly informative after Gelman and others (2008), with normal laws in place of Cauchy laws and the scale 5 for α in place of 10.
examples.dependence: The model treats the 6 O-rings of one flight as independent given the temperature. The O-rings of one flight share the same conditions, so the counts can have overdispersion. A beta-binomial law would allow it.
examples.method: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with 10 leapfrog steps of size 0.3 in units of the scale of each coordinate. The estimate averages the predictive probability 1 − (1 − p(t₀))⁶ over the draws after the warm-up. The comparison is a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings chain.
examples.diagnostics: Read split R-hat, the effective sample size, the acceptance rate and the divergent transitions. Compare with the numerical reference by quadrature on a grid. Other candidate models: a probit link, a complementary log-log link, a beta-binomial law for overdispersion, or a model with the leak-check pressure.
examples.interpretation: The estimate is about 0.96. But 31 °F is 22 °F below the coldest earlier launch (53 °F). Thus the value comes from the logistic form of the model, not from data at that temperature. A different link function gives a different value. Distress is not failure. Reject the model for a decision when its forecast depends on the link function. This analysis uses information after the event. The engineers in 1986 did not do it.

data.text: Real data: thermal distress of the field-joint O-rings on 23 flights before 28 January 1986.

examples.title: Start a transfer pump before a tank overflows
examples.problem: An ultrasonic sensor reads the water level of a tank every 10 minutes, with noise. The level rises by about 0.4 cm in each interval, with random changes. Find the law of the present level, given the 60 readings, and the probability that it is above 80 cm.

params.name: d
params.note: the mean rise of the level in one interval

params.name: sx
params.note: the standard deviation of the random change in one interval

params.name: sy
params.note: the standard deviation of the sensor noise

params.name: m0
params.note: the mean of the initial level

params.name: s0
params.note: the standard deviation of the initial level

params.name: h
params.note: the level at which the pump must run

quantities.name: E[x_T | y₁, …, y_T]
quantities.note: the filter mean of the present level

quantities.name: P(x_T > h | y₁, …, y_T)
quantities.note: the probability that the present level is above h

quantities.name: log p(y₁, …, y_T)
quantities.note: the log likelihood of the readings

examples.decision: Decision: start the transfer pump now when P(x_T > 80 cm | readings) ≥ 0.2, or wait for the next reading. Estimated quantity: that filter probability.
examples.reason: The level changes by many small inflows and outflows, so a random walk with drift and normal noise is a simple model. For this linear model with normal noise, the Kalman filter gives the exact answer. Thus you can check the particle filter before you use it on a model with no exact filter.
examples.inputs: y: 60 readings in cm. Model: x_t = x_(t−1) + d + sx ε_t and y_t = x_t + sy η_t with independent standard normal ε and η, and x₀ ~ N(m0, s0²). The parameters are illustrative.
examples.dependence: The level is a Markov process, and each reading depends only on the present level. Foam or a tilted float makes the sensor errors dependent in time. This model does not include it.
examples.method: A bootstrap particle filter with 512 particles: each particle moves with the dynamics and takes the density of the reading as its weight. The filter resamples with the systematic scheme when the weight ESS falls below N/2. Each of 16 independent runs gives one estimate.
examples.diagnostics: Read the weight ESS at each time, the number of resampling steps and the number of distinct ancestors. Compare with the exact Kalman filter. Other candidate models: a model with a pump schedule, or a sensor law with a heavy tail for false echoes.
examples.interpretation: The exact probability is about 0.22, so the rule says start the pump, but the margin is small. With 512 particles, the filter estimate has a bias of order 1/N, about +0.015 here. The spread of independent runs cannot show a bias. Only the comparison with the Kalman filter shows it. 4,096 particles remove most of it. Reject the model when the innovations y_t − E[y_t | earlier readings] show a trend or outliers.

data.text: Synthetic: 60 readings made by the level model with the stated parameters and the page's generator (Philox4x32-10, seed 11), rounded to 0.1 cm. They are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

examples.title: Reduce a position when the daily volatility is high
examples.problem: A desk holds a position in one asset. The daily return in % is σ_t η_t, and log σ_t² follows a stationary autoregression: a stochastic volatility model. Find the law of the present volatility σ_T, given 100 daily returns.

params.name: mu
params.note: the stationary mean of x_t = log σ_t²

params.name: phi
params.note: the persistence of x_t, strictly between −1 and 1

params.name: s
params.note: the standard deviation of the change of x_t in one day

params.name: c
params.note: the daily volatility that requires a smaller position

quantities.name: E[σ_T | returns]
quantities.note: the filter mean of the present daily volatility

quantities.name: P(σ_T > c | returns)
quantities.note: the probability that the present volatility is above c

quantities.name: log p(returns)
quantities.note: the log likelihood of the returns

examples.decision: Decision: halve the position when P(σ_T > 1 % | returns) ≥ 0.1, or keep it. Estimated quantity: that filter probability.
examples.reason: Daily returns show volatility clusters: large changes follow large changes. In the stochastic volatility model the observation depends on the state through a non-linear function, so the Kalman filter is not exact. A particle filter applies to any model whose dynamics it can simulate and whose observation density it can compute.
examples.inputs: y: 100 daily returns in %. Model: x_t = mu + phi (x_(t−1) − mu) + s ε_t, y_t = exp(x_t / 2) η_t, with x₀ from the stationary law. The parameters are illustrative, not estimates from market data.
examples.dependence: The volatility is a Markov process. Given the volatility, the returns are independent with a normal law. Real returns also have a heavier tail and a leverage effect: a negative return raises the next volatility. This model has neither.
examples.method: A bootstrap particle filter with 1,024 particles and systematic resampling when the weight ESS falls below N/2. The reference is a point-mass filter on 601 grid points, a numerical approximation.
examples.diagnostics: Read the weight ESS over time and the genealogy of the particles. After many resampling steps, the particles of the last day have few distinct ancestors on the first days. Compare with the grid filter. Other candidate models: a GARCH(1, 1) model, or a model with a Student t law for η.
examples.interpretation: The probability is about 0.05, so the rule says keep the position. The filter estimates the present volatility well, but the genealogy shows that the particle paths of the early days come from few ancestors. Thus a smoothing estimate of an early volatility needs another method. Reject the model when the standardised returns y_t / E[σ_t | y_(1:t−1)] have a heavier tail than the normal law.

data.text: Synthetic: 100 daily returns made by the volatility model with the stated parameters and the page's generator (Philox4x32-10, seed 12), rounded to 0.001 %. They are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence.

examples.title: A smooth integrand in 4 dimensions: scrambled Sobol points against independent points
examples.problem: The integrand is Genz's product peak, f(u) = ∏ 1 / (a⁻² + (u_j − 1/2)²) on [0, 1)^d. It is smooth, and its integral has a closed form.

params.name: d
params.note: the dimension, an integer from 1 to 21

params.name: a
params.note: the inverse width of the peak

quantities.name: ∫ f(u) du
quantities.note: the integral over the unit cube

examples.observe: The error of independent sampling decreases as n^(−1/2). The error of the scrambled Sobol points decreases much faster for this smooth integrand. At n = 16,384 its variance is more than 10,000 times smaller. Set the randomisation to none. Then every run gives the same value, and the spread of the runs says nothing about the error.

data.text: Synthetic: d and a fully state the integrand. No data.

examples.title: A discontinuous integrand in 8 dimensions: the gain becomes small
examples.problem: The integrand is the indicator that a sum of d uniforms is above c. Its integral is the tail of the Irwin–Hall law. The indicator jumps along a plane that is not parallel to any axis.

params.name: d
params.note: the dimension, an integer from 1 to 21

params.name: c
params.note: the threshold of the sum, in [0, d]

quantities.name: P(U₁ + … + U_d > c)
quantities.note: the tail probability of the sum

examples.observe: The scrambled points still have no bias, and their variance is still smaller than that of independent points. But the ratio of the variances is about 5, not more than 10,000: the jump of the integrand removes most of the gain. The Koksma–Hlawka bound gives nothing here, because the variation of the indicator is infinite.

data.text: Synthetic: d and c fully state the integrand. No data.

examples.problem: A dealer quotes 6.50 for a call option on the geometric average of a share price at 16 equally spaced dates in one year. Under the Black–Scholes model the price is an integral over 16 dimensions. For the geometric average it also has a closed form, so you can check each method.

params.name: K
params.note: the strike price

params.name: r
params.note: the risk-free rate, continuously compounded, for each year

params.name: sigma
params.note: the volatility for each year

params.name: T
params.note: the maturity

params.name: m
params.note: the number of dates: 2, 4, 8 or 16

quantities.name: e^(−rT) E[max(G − K, 0)]
quantities.note: the price of the option, with G the geometric average

quantities.name: P(G > K)
quantities.note: the risk-neutral probability that the option pays

rule.yes: Accept the quote of 6.50: it is not above the model price.
rule.no: Refuse the quote of 6.50: it is above the model price.

examples.decision: Decision: accept the quote of 6.50 when it is at most the model price. Otherwise, refuse it. Estimated quantity: the price e^(−rT) E[max(G − K, 0)].
examples.reason: A price is an expectation of a function of normal increments, so it is an integral over the unit cube after the inverse normal transform. The payoff is continuous, and the Brownian bridge puts most of the variance in the first coordinates, where the Sobol points are best.
examples.inputs: S0 = 100, K = 100, r = 3 % a year, σ = 25 % a year, T = 1 year and 16 equally spaced dates. The parameters are illustrative, not market data.
examples.dependence: The log price is a Brownian motion with drift, so the increments are independent and normal. A model with stochastic volatility or jumps would change the price, and the closed form would no longer hold.
examples.method: Randomised quasi-Monte Carlo: 16 independent randomisations of 16,384 scrambled Sobol points. The Brownian bridge sets the end point from the first coordinate, then the mid-points. The interval comes from the spread of the 16 randomisations.
examples.diagnostics: Read the variance ratio against independent sampling and the error at each n on the rate plot. Set the path to standard, so that each coordinate is one time step: the gain becomes smaller. Other candidate models: a Heston model or a jump-diffusion model, which need their own reference.
examples.interpretation: The exact price is about 6.41, so the quote of 6.50 is about 0.09 above it, and the rule says refuse it. The interval of the randomised points is dozens of times narrower than that of independent points with the same n. Reject the model when the market prices of plain options show a volatility smile.

data.text: Synthetic: the parameters are illustrative values, not calibrated evidence. No data.

methods.name: Metropolis–Hastings
methods.estimator: \hat\theta_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} g(X_i), \quad X_{i+1} = \begin{cases} Y & \text{with probability } \min\!\left(1, \frac{\pi(Y)}{\pi(X_i)}\right) \\ X_i & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad Y = X_i + h\, s \odot Z
methods.estimatorText: The chain proposes a random-walk step Y and accepts it with the probability min(1, π(Y)/π(X)). Only the ratio of densities enters, so the method needs π only up to a constant. The estimate is the mean of g over the draws after the warm-up.
assumptions: The target π has a density, known up to a constant, that is positive where the chain must go.
The proposal is symmetric, so the acceptance probability has no proposal ratio. The chain then satisfies detailed balance with respect to π.
The chain is irreducible and aperiodic, so the ergodic theorem applies. A central limit theorem needs more, such as geometric ergodicity and a finite moment of g of order 2 + δ.
settings: The step h in units of the scale s of each coordinate. The page does not tune it.
2^size warm-up iterations, which the page discards, then 2^size draws in each chain.
R independent chains from dispersed points or from one point.

suitable.text: The posterior law of the balance has one mode and no strong correlation. A random walk with the step 1.5 mixes well: split R-hat is near 1, and the interval of the 4 chains holds the reference.

failure.text: With two modes far apart and every chain started in one mode, no chain crosses to the other mode. The diagnostics look good, but the estimate of P(x₁ + x₂ > 0) is near 0, not 0.7.

comparison.text: On the correlated normal law, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo gives an effective sample size many times larger for the same number of draws. Each of its draws costs 10 gradients, so compare the effective sample size for each second, not for each draw.

methods.name: Gibbs sampler
methods.estimatorText: Each sweep draws each coordinate from its full conditional law given the other coordinates. The sweep accepts every draw. The estimate is the mean of g over the sweeps after the warm-up.
assumptions: Each full conditional law is a standard law that the page can sample exactly.
The chain is irreducible: the full conditional laws connect every region of positive density.
Strong dependence between the coordinates makes each move small, so the chain mixes slowly.
settings: A systematic sweep: x₁, then x₂.
2^size warm-up sweeps, then 2^size draws in each chain, and R independent chains.
The page offers the Gibbs sweep only where it has the full conditional laws: the correlated normal law, the two modes and the balance.

suitable.text: In the balance model, μ given σ is normal and σ² given μ is inverse gamma. The Gibbs sweep needs no step size, and its effective sample size is close to the number of draws.

failure.text: With ρ = 0.995 each full conditional law has the standard deviation √(1 − ρ²) ≈ 0.1. The chain moves along the ridge in tiny steps, so the effective sample size is a small fraction of the draws.

comparison.text: On the balance model, the Gibbs sweep gives an effective sample size about 10 times that of the random walk. It also has no step to tune.

methods.name: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
methods.estimator: H(x, p) = -\log \pi(x) + \tfrac12 p^{\top} M^{-1} p, \quad (x', p') = \Phi^{\varepsilon}_{L}(x, p), \quad \text{accept with } \min\!\left(1, e^{H(x, p) - H(x', p')}\right)
methods.estimatorText: Each iteration draws a momentum p and follows L leapfrog steps of the Hamiltonian dynamics with the gradient of log π. It accepts the end point with the Metropolis probability. The leapfrog map with a momentum flip keeps volume and is its own inverse. With the Metropolis step, the chain keeps π invariant. The estimate is the mean of g over the draws after the warm-up.
assumptions: log π is differentiable on the whole space. A target with a boundary needs a change of variables first, as log σ in the balance model.
The step ε suits every region of the target. Where the curvature is much larger than 1/ε², the leapfrog path is unstable.
The page counts a divergent transition when the energy error is above 1,000 or not finite, and rejects that proposal. A divergent transition is a signal of bias.
settings: The step ε in units of the scale of each coordinate (mass M = diag(1/s²)), with a random change of ±10 % in each iteration.
L leapfrog steps, from 1 to 200.
2^size warm-up iterations, then 2^size draws in each chain, and R independent chains.

suitable.text: The posterior law of the O-ring regression is smooth and has correlated coordinates. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo accepts about 98 % of its proposals, and its effective sample size is close to the number of draws.

failure.text: In Neal's funnel the leapfrog step 0.5 is too large for the neck. More than 1,000 transitions diverge, the chains avoid the neck, and the estimate of P(v < −3) is too small.

comparison.text: On the O-ring regression the random walk has an effective sample size about 10 times smaller. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo needs a gradient. The random walk needs only the density.

methods.name: Sequential Monte Carlo sampler
methods.estimator: \pi_\beta \propto q^{1-\beta}\, \pi^{\beta}, \quad w_k^i \propto W_{k-1}^i \left(\frac{\pi(x^i)}{q(x^i)}\right)^{\beta_k - \beta_{k-1}}, \quad \hat Z = \prod_k \sum_i W_{k-1}^i \left(\frac{\pi(x^i)}{q(x^i)}\right)^{\beta_k - \beta_{k-1}}, \quad \hat\theta = \sum_i W^i g(x^i)
methods.estimatorText: N particles start from a wide normal law q. The sampler raises β from 0 to 1 in steps. At each step it reweights the particles and resamples them when the weights become uneven. Then it moves them with Metropolis steps that keep π_β invariant. The weighted mean at β = 1 estimates E_π g, and the product of the mean incremental weights estimates the normalising constant Z.
assumptions: q covers the target: π/q is finite where π has mass. A narrow q misses a mode, and no later step can find it.
Each step is small enough that the weights stay usable. The weight ESS shows the spread of the weights; it does not show whether a mode is missing.
With a fixed schedule, Ẑ has no bias. With the adaptive schedule, the steps depend on the particles, and the bias tends to 0 as N grows.
settings: N = 2^size particles and R independent runs.
The adaptive schedule: each step multiplies the weight ESS by the threshold. The fixed schedule: K equal steps of β.
The resampling scheme, the ESS threshold and the number of Metropolis moves after each step.

suitable.text: The wide law q puts particles near both modes, and tempering keeps them with their correct weights. The estimate of P(x₁ + x₂ > 0) is near 0.7, and the interval of log Ẑ contains the exact value log 2π.

failure.text: With one fixed step and no moves, the sampler is plain importance sampling from the wide law q to the narrow posterior law. The weight ESS falls to about 2 % of N. The spread of log Ẑ over the runs is about 3 times that of the adaptive schedule.

comparison.text: On the two modes, the random walk from one point stays in one mode, and the sampler finds both. The sampler also estimates Z directly, and a Markov chain does not.

methods.name: Particle filter
methods.estimator: x_t^i \sim f(\cdot \mid x_{t-1}^{a^i}), \quad W_t^i \propto W_{t-1}^i\, g(y_t \mid x_t^i), \quad \hat p(y_{1:T}) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{i=1}^{N} W_{t-1}^i\, g(y_t \mid x_t^i), \quad \widehat{E}[h(x_t) \mid y_{1:t}] = \sum_i W_t^i h(x_t^i)
methods.estimatorText: The bootstrap filter moves each particle with the state dynamics f and weights it with the density g of the observation. When the weights become uneven, it resamples: each particle gets an expected number of copies in proportion to its weight. The weighted particles estimate the filter law at each time, and the product of the weighted mean densities estimates the likelihood.
assumptions: The page can simulate the dynamics and compute the observation density.
The resampling scheme has no bias: particle i gets N W_i copies in expectation. Then the estimate of the likelihood has no bias for each N, but its log has a negative bias.
Each step adds uncertainty. Without resampling, the weights degenerate, and after resampling, the paths share their early ancestors.
settings: N = 2^size particles and R independent runs.
The resampling scheme: multinomial, stratified, systematic, residual or none.
The ESS threshold τ: the filter resamples when the weight ESS is below τN.

suitable.text: In the tank model the filter resamples when the weight ESS falls below N/2, so the weights never degenerate for long. The estimates agree with the exact Kalman filter, up to a bias of order 1/N that 4,096 particles make small.

failure.text: Without resampling, the filter is sequential importance sampling of whole paths. After a few readings, one particle has almost all the weight. The weight ESS is near 1, and in most runs the likelihood estimate is far below the exact value.

comparison.text: Without resampling, the filter draws independent paths from the dynamics and weights each one by its likelihood: independent sampling with importance weights. Resampling stops the weight degeneracy, at the cost of shared ancestors.

methods.name: Randomised quasi-Monte Carlo
methods.estimator: \hat I = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(\tilde u_i), \quad \tilde u_i = L \, u_i \oplus e, \quad \bar I = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R} \hat I_r
methods.estimatorText: The first n = 2^m Sobol points fill the unit cube more evenly than independent points. A random linear scramble L and a random digital shift e make each point uniform. They keep the even spread, and each estimate has no bias. R independent randomisations give an interval from their spread.
assumptions: The quantity is an integral of f over [0, 1)^d, with f square-integrable. Then the variance is o(1/n).
The gain is largest for a smooth f with a low effective dimension. A jump that is not parallel to the axes removes most of it.
Without randomisation, the points give one deterministic value with no error estimate.
settings: n = 2^size points, a power of 2, so each prefix of length 2^k is a digital net.
The randomisation: a linear scramble with a digital shift, a digital shift only, or none.
R independent randomisations, and for the option the path construction: standard or Brownian bridge.

suitable.text: With the Brownian bridge, most of the variance of the option payoff is in the first coordinates. The variance of the scrambled estimate is more than 1,000 times smaller than that of independent points.

failure.text: The indicator of a sum above a threshold jumps along a slanted plane. The variance ratio against independent points falls to about 5.

comparison.text: Each run also computes the estimate with independent uniforms and the same n. The rate plot shows both errors: independent points give n^(−1/2), and the scrambled points are much faster for the smooth peak.
